passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abanoub El-Nehissy, p. 33
passages.text:
Saint: ABANOUB EL-NEHISSY (The martyr)

St. Abanoub was born in Nehissah, in the city of Talkha in the 4th Century. His parents were pious loving parents who raised him with Christian values and planted in him the love for God and the Holy Bible. He was only 12 years of age when both his parents departed to Paradise. Missing his parents was so devastating to the young Abanoub, that he was called the lamented boy for he was sorrowful for so long. Some might ask wonder how could he manage to withstand all the sufferings that he encountered later on and yet could not resist the loss of his parents.

It is true that despite our faith in heavenly life, it will not strip us from our human feelings; instead, it would sanctify them. We can see an illustration of that in the presence of St. Paul, who wrote about the door being opened for evangelism in Troas, and yet he could not find peace in his soul, for he could not find his friend Titus, so he left the city. "Furthermore, when I came to Troas to [preach] Christ's gospel, and a door was opened to me by the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, because I did not find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave of them, I departed for Macedonia” (2 Cor. 2:12-13). This situation shows the vulnerability of human nature, and God may allow those weaknesses to prevent us from boasting. Another example of weakness was with our great father Abraham, who said that his wife Sarah was his sister for fear that the king might kill him to take her for a wife (Gen. 20:2). Also, our beloved St. Mark, who left Paul and Barnabas and caused them to have an argument and ended up separating from each other (Acts 13:3), and St. Peter, who was leaving Rome for fear of persecution and Jesus appeared to him too and kindly corrected him. Therefore, we should not be troubled when we show weakness despite the grace given to us, for it is beneficial in keeping us humble and urging us to ask God to work in us and with us.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abanoub El-Nehissy, pp. 33–34
passages.text:
Saint: ABANOUB EL-NEHISSY (The martyr) — In the village's church

In the village's church:

One day, Abanoub went to the church and heard the priest during the sermon encouraging the congregation to endure with joy the suffering and persecution they were getting for their faith. After the Holy Communion, the young Abanoub went home, while the priest’s words still ringing in his ears.

At home, he knelt to pray, asking for God’s guidance. Then, he stood up and started walking towards the city of Semenood (about 12 miles away), while rejoicing in the spirit and desiring to have the heavenly crown.

In Semenood:

The young Abanoub went around the city and saw how the churches were destroyed, and the pagan cursed their neighbors the Christians for their faith. He was distressed for what he saw and asked God to help him. God sent him Archangel Michael to assure him of the heavenly support and rewards that await him. He guided Abanoub to see the governor in the morning and declare his Christian faith and assured him that he will be strengthened during his suffering and will be healed until he receives the crown of Martyrdom.

What is the secret of his strength?

1. While the names of his parents were not mentioned, the beauty of his parent’s faith was reflected on their only son Abanoub and provided him with hope in eternal life with our Lord.

2. No doubt that his parents were sustaining him with their prayers before the throne of God.

3. The pious priest who touched Abanoub's life and who encouraged his congregation not only to withstand the suffering and persecutions but also to accept it with a joyful heart, knowing that they will win the eternal kingdom.

4. Heaven rejoiced for young Abanoub, and God has sent him Archangels Michael and Gabriel to support him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abanoub El-Nehissy, pp. 34–35
passages.text:
Saint: ABANOUB EL-NEHISSY (The martyr) — Before the governor

Before the governor:

Early in the morning, Abanoub got up to see the governor and tell him openly about his faith. This action surprised the governor, who initially treated him nicely and promised him to be rewarded if he renounces his faith. Nevertheless, Abanoub was steadfast in his conviction of the true faith. The governor got furious that he could not sway a little boy like Abanoub, and he ordered him to be whipped so hard on his belly; that his intestines did come out. Archangel Michael appeared and healed him. Then, they throw him in prison, and all the Christian captives there were so happy to see him and were encouraged because of his strong faith and lack of fear.

The next day the governor killed about 1000 of the prisoners, and they all received the crown of Martyrdom.

On the following day, the governor called for Abanoub and ordered that he would be tied by his feet and hanged from the top of the mast of the boat that was sailing to Atrib [Banha] (about 40 miles away). He was mocking him, saying, "Let us see if his Jesus will come to save him." Moreover, they kept sailing from morning until evening. Finally, they brought the mast down, and the governor sat down to eat, and suddenly his hands were paralyzed, and his soldiers were hit with blindness. Suddenly, the governor did see the Archangel Michael coming closer to Abanoub, and he wiped the blood from his mouth and nose and released him from the ropes around his feet and brought him to the front of the boat, then the angel disappeared.

At this point, the governor asked Abanoub to pray for him so that he and his soldiers could be healed. Abanoub told him that God would heal them in Atrib. When they got there, Abanoub prayed for the governor and treated him in the Lord’s name in the presence of Atrib’s governor. This miracle caused many pagans to believe in the Lord, and some were martyred.

In Atrib (Banha)

Regardless, the governor of Atrib tortured Abanoub with all kinds of torture methods and put him in boiling oil and cut up his feet and hands and blinded his eyes with hot rods. During all these trials, God did not leave Abanoub, but He always sent Archangel Michael to heal him. Many witnesses became Christians and gladly became martyrs, from watching the young Abanoub enduring all that suffering and still praising his God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abanoub, the Confessor, pp. 35–36
passages.text:
Saint: ABANOUB, THE CONFESSOR, ST.

The word ‘Abanoub’ is derived from the Coptic word ‘Pi-Noub’ meaning (gold). This saint was a virtuous monk in one of the monasteries of Upper Egypt in the days of Diocletian, who tortured and shed the blood of 80 martyrs in a single day.

It so happened when the name of St. Abanoub was mentioned before Arianius, the governor of Ansena, that the governor called him and asked him to worship the idols. The saint answered, saying: “How can I forsake my Lord Jesus Christ, and worship the idols made of stone?!” Therefore, he tortured him severely, and then he sent him to the five western cities (the Pentapolis), where he was imprisoned for as long as seven years until Diocletian perished. When the righteous Emperor Constantine reigned, he gave his command to set free all those Christians who were in prisons and to bring them forth to him to have their blessing. He specified that in case it is difficult to bring them all, to bring only the prominent ones among them, such as ‘Zacharias Al-Ahnasy,’ Maximianus of Fayum, Agabius of ‘Dakhnin,’ and Abanoub of ‘Balaos.' The saints came out of their imprisonments, singing praises to God.

At that time, St. Abanoub, the confessor, returned from ‘Pentapolis’ and dwelt on a mountain close to his homeland. When the Emperor’s envoy came, they took him on a boat to Ansena, where he encountered the believers, and the bishops ordained him as a priest. And, it so happened that, while he was uttering: “The Holies are for the holy,” that he saw the Lord Christ transfiguring in the church with His exalted glory.

The Emperor’s envoy traveled together with 72 saints and put every two of them in a carriage, and while passing through one of the cities, where there was a nunnery of virgins, 700 of them came out singing hymns before them.

When they reached the capital, the king sought from them to change their worn-out clothes to expensive new ones, but they declined his offer. He then kissed their wounds, honored them, and offered them precious gifts, which they also refused, except for some curtains and vessels for their churches, to which they returned, and St. Abanoub returned to his monastery.

Finally, after fulfilling his strife, he reposed in peace.

[Synaxarion, 23 Paona]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abanoub El-Nehissy, p. 35
passages.text:
Saint: ABANOUB EL-NEHISSY (The martyr) — Before the governor

During all these trials, God did not leave Abanoub, but He always sent Archangel Michael to heal him. Many witnesses became Christians and gladly became martyrs, from watching the young Abanoub enduring all that suffering and still praising his God.

In Alexandria

After the governor of Atrib saw the multitude of people accepting Abanoub's faith, he tied him up with reliable chains and sent him to Alexandria. There, he met a woman who had an evil spirit, and he forced the spirit out of her, and she became Christian. Consequently, the soldiers killed her because she said that she believed in Christ.

Abanoub continued to confess his faith in our Lord Jesus before the governor Arminius of Alexandria who also tortured him and put him in a room filled with snakes and serpents and the Archangel Michael got him out of it, and the snakes followed him, and one of them coiled itself around the governor's neck. He cried out to Abanoub, and he saved him, which caused many to believe and become martyrs.

Abanoub suffered more tortures and was finally beheaded outside the city on a high rock where he stood to pray, asking God to forgive him and to accept his soul.

St. Julius El-Akfahsy took his body and buried him in his town Nehissah, and wrote his story. His body was moved from Nehissah to Semenood, and the church celebrates his martyrdom on the 24th of Abib.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yusab El-Abaĥ, the Bishop, pp. 371–372
passages.text:
Saint: YUSAB EL-ABAĤ, THE BISHOP, ST. — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

St. Yusab el-Abaĥ set forth to the monastery of Abba Anthony, where Fr. Ibrahim St. Anthony, the Abbot of the monastery welcomed him and gave him his blessings. Then, the Abbot sought from the elder Fathers to test him for a while. After that, they joyfully admitted him. Yousef lived among them with the gladness of heart. Earning their love and trust, they prayed over him, clothed him with the monastic attire by the name of Yousef St. Anthony.

He started to study the old manuscripts which were kept in the monastery library, and he searched through the wealth of Church literature and theology until he acquired a good deal of the religious culture and the general knowledge. And, in addition to his spiritual strife in prayers, fasting, and asceticism, he used to serve the elderly fathers with love; until they recommended him for the grace of the priesthood. He was ordained as a priest, then as a hegumenus. He ministered the holy altar and the Holy Sacraments with humility and a contrite heart; that he was filled with the Divine Grace and became well-known.

His Relationship with the Popes of Alexandria:

Abba Yusab was a contemporary of 5 of the popes of Alexandria: 1- He was born during the reign of the 105th Pope Yoannes XVII (1727-1745). 2- He became a monk during the reign of the 106th Pope Marcos VII (1745- 1769). 3- He was ordained as a bishop by the 107th Pope Yoannes XVIII (1769-1796). 4- He participated in the election and the ordination of the 108th Pope Marcos VIII (1796-1809). He also was the head of the bishops who prayed over his body after he departed, and gave a eulogy in which he enumerated that pope’s virtues. 5- He took part in the election and the ordination of the 109th Pope Butros VII (El-Gawli: 1809-1852).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ebn Al-Abaĥ, p. 6
passages.text:
Saint: EBN AL-ABAĤ

He was the secretary of the Fatimid caliph Al-Mustansir (1036-1094 AD) during the 11th century. He managed to reconstruct the churches of Abu Serga, and SS. Abakir and John in Old Cairo.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yusab El-Abaĥ, the Bishop, pp. 373–374
passages.text:
Saint: YUSAB EL-ABAĤ, THE BISHOP, ST. — His Departure

His Departure:

When Abba Yusab became advanced in age, carrying on his shoulders the troubles of 91 years in serving the Church he loved, he took refuge in the hospitality of pope Butros VII (El-Gawli). However, he was longing to set forth to heaven in the monastery of Abba Anthony, so he moved there and delivered his soul in the hands of the Lord on the 24th of January 1826; within a few days of his arrival to the monastery. He was cared for and buried by the monks of the monastery. After several years of his burial, his body was found intact. So, they took it out and put it in a special burial place in the church of the monastery. The Coptic Church honored that revered bishop and righteous theologian by including him in the Synaxarion in the day he reposed.

Of his Words:

• If we break our fast while the Church is fasting; we would be removing ourselves, and would become a stumbling block to others and a reason behind the fall of the weak. • Do not fast on bread and salt, while you are devouring the flesh of the others by condemnation and abomination. And, do not proclaim that you fast clean fasting while getting dirty through all those iniquities.

[Amir Nasr: St. Abba Josab (El-Abah), Bishop of Girga and Akhmim, Cairo 1985]

[The Coptic Encyclopedia: Yusab, by Khalil Samir, S.J.; pp. 2360-62]

Notes: [1] Such as the custom of celebrating martyrs by large banquets, for which musicians, singers and poets were hired, out of vainglory; and to which the poor were not invited… [2] Book title in Arabic is: "سالح المؤمنين”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Fr. Abdel-Mesih El-Masoudy, the Great, p. 51
passages.text:
Saint: ABDEL-MESIH EL-MASOUDY, THE GREAT, FR. — In The ‘Muharraq’ Monastery

In The ‘Muharraq’ Monastery:

This saint was born in the year 1819 in the village of ‘Sheikh Masoud,’ at the west of the city of ‘Tahta’ in Upper Egypt. Therefore, he was known by the title ‘El-Masoudy.' On reaching the age of 17 years old, he longed for the angelic life and set forth to the ‘Muharraq’ monastery where he became a monk. In the monastery, he became a disciple of Fr. ‘Boulus El-Delgawy’ (who later on became the bishop of ‘El-Fayum,’ St. ‘Abba Abraam’). He absorbed from him the meekness, peaceful soul, and spirituality.

In The Baramus Monastery:

After spending 22 years in the ‘Muharraq’ monastery, Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih’ decided to move on with some of his brethren monks to the ‘Baramus’ monastery. They arrived at that monastery while Fr. ‘Yohanna El-Nasekh’ (the Scribe) was still there; before he was selected to become the 112th Pope of the See of St. Mark by the name ‘Cyril V’ (1874-1927).

When Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih’ left the ‘Muharraq’ monastery, the fathers there said about him: “A jewel has left our monastery.” He did deserve that appreciation because they realized that he had been an ascetic scholar, a striving spiritual man, distinguished with pure faithfulness away from pride; and above everything else, possessed a practical love-giving heart, which forced everybody who got close enough to know him, to love him dearly.

When Pope ‘Cyril V’ (Kyrillus) appointed him as the head of the monastery after the repose of ‘Fr. Awad,’ he cared for his brethren monks, both physically and spiritually. Through his love, they follow his instructions with great pleasure. By his wisdom, peace dwelt on the ‘Baramus’ monastery during all his time; that Abba ‘Yoannes,’ the metropolitan of ‘Beheira’ (also from the ‘Baramus’ monastery) gave him the title, “Father of the ‘Baramus’ monastery’s monks."

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul of Tamouh, pp. 380–381
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL OF TAMOUH, ST. ABBA

The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of this saint on the 7th of Baba, and seeks his prayers in the commemoration of the saints in the Liturgy, along with St. Ezekiel his disciple.

After the devastation of the wilderness of the Scetis around the year, 408 AD; St. Abba Bishoi fled the area and went to mount Anesna in Upper Egypt. There, he met with Abba Paul the Hermit and they both had an amazing spiritual friendship, that an angel appeared to St. Paul, saying: “Your body will be with that of Abba Bishoi.” (The two bodies are still together in one tube in the Monastery of Abba Bishoi up to this very day). It was said that later on when the bishop of Anesna decided to move the body of Abba Bishoi; his boat did not move until a hermit named Jeremiah told them about the promise of the Lord to Abba Paul, so they brought the body of Abba Paul to the boat and they moved them together to the Monastery of Abba Shenouda in Akhmim. Later on, the bodies of these two saints were moved again together in the days of the 52nd Pope Yusab I in the 9th century (831- 849 AD) to the Monastery of Abba Bishoi in the Scetis. The bodies of the two saints were kept in one tube; and this is a testimony of the spiritual friendship full of love that bound the two saints together; that even death could not separate them. This is not on the level of this mortal world but the level of the Eternal glory of both the body and the soul.

Abba Paul was known for his great love of worship, particularly for the perpetual prayers, as well as his serious asceticism, that his disciple Ezekiel told about him that he faced death six times because of his harsh asceticism.

He lived in solitude as a hermit, in perpetual strife, that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him saying: “Enough labor, My beloved Paul”. St. Abba Paul answered Him: “O my Master, let me exhaust my body for the sake of Your Name; as You have done for the sake of mankind. Even though You are God, You delivered Yourself for our sake, we who are unworthy.”

[O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt; p. 223-4]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abahor, the Monk, p. 29
passages.text:
Saint: ABAHOR, THE MONK, ST.

This father from ‘Abraht’ in the area of the ‘Ashmonein,’ was an elect monk who surpassed many saints in his worship. Loving solitude and living alone in the wilderness, he was envied by the devil who appeared to him and said: “In the wilderness, you can overcome me because you are there alone, but I challenge you if you are brave, go to Alexandria." He instantly set forth to Alexandria, where he stayed sometimes serving the prisoners.

It so happened that some horses were galloping in midtown, and one of them knocked down a little kid who instantly died. As St. Abahor was standing at the place where that incident took place, the devil provoked some people around to shout aloud, claiming that it was the old monk who killed him. When many started to revile and to scoff him, St. Abahor calmly took the kid to his bosom, prayed in his heart to the Lord Christ, and then made the sign of the cross on him. The kid came back to life, and he gave him to his parents. Those around him glorified God and started to make it up to the old monk, who, fearing from the vainglory, he fled to the wilderness, where he dwelt for days in a monastery.

When it was time for him to depart from this world, he saw a group of saints calling him to join them, for which he greatly rejoiced, became joyful, called his spiritual disciples to inform them that he will soon depart to the Lord Christ, and provided them with his last commandment. Hearing that, they much grieved that they will be orphans after his departure. He felt sick for a little while, and then he delivered his soul in the Lord’s hand.

[The Synaxarion: 2 Kiahk]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 357–358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

Through the friendship of this saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came out in the wilderness in his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise ‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12).

Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near the church. It so happened that while they were setting forth to visit Abba ‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.”

St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described his ascetic life.

[Manuscript# 438/250: Asceticisms and Teachings of Abba Bishai (Peter), Library of the Patriarchate] [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abu Fana, p. 80
passages.text:
Saint: ABU FANA, ST. — Examples of His Miracles

2- A man came to him with his son to get his blessing. But, it happened that the son fell from the mountain and died. The father carried him to the cave of the saint, placed him in front of the entrance, and without telling the saint about what happened, he asked him to bless him. The saint made the sign of the cross on the boy, and said to him, “Get up, go to your father, and hold his hand.” So the boy did. In great joy, the father cast himself on the ground before the saint, thanking him and glorifying God who performs miracles through His saints. 3- Getting to know the day of his repose, he asked the priest to come over to perform the Holy Eucharist. He had communion standing on his swollen feet, bid farewell from the brethren, blessed them, sought their blessing, prayed, and delivered his soul in the hands of the Lord on 25 Amshir.

His Monastery in Delga:

A monastery was built in his name close to ‘Beni Khaled, a village of ‘Delga’ about 20 kilometers south of the province of El-Ashmonein.

[Nabil Selim: Monasteries of the Fathers (9): St. Epiphanius (Abu Fana) on Mount Delga; an annex of his book on ‘The Monasteries of the Fathers (8) on SS Bishai and Basentaos of the Tod]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abdel-Mesih El-Manahry, the Priest, p. 50
passages.text:
Saint: ABDEL-MESIH EL-MANAHRY, THE PRIEST — His Worship

His Worship:

Nobody knows about his prayers, but he used to live in seclusion praying in his cell for periods extending to several weeks. He used to tie a rope to the ceiling of his cell and tie its other end around his waist to pull him up in case he would fall asleep while praying. He memorized all the praises and the church hymns by heart. He ate only once every day at sunset.

He always gave alms generously to the needy, yet in his own crazy and halfwit ways. He never had two mantles at the same time, and he lived in a cell built with mud bricks and not painted from the inside. In that manner, he gave a great example of monastic life.

God honored him by the gift of performing miracles. And spiritually, he reached the rank of the hermits, as testified by the 116th Pope St. ‘Kyrillos VI’ (1959-1971). Besides, this saint has prophesied in advance about the ordination of Fr. ‘Mina El-Motawahid’ (St. ‘Kyrillos VI’) as a pope over the See of St. Mark.

He finally reposed in peace on the morning of the Great feast of the Resurrection (the Easter) on the 6th of Baramouda 1679 AM (14 April 1963). Moreover, since the Palm Sunday, before he reposed, the saint kept saying, “I shall be crowned and rejoice the day of the Feast.” However, at the time, nobody paid attention to that statement, because it was also taken lightly as one of his usual crazy way of talking.

[Abba Mena, bishop of Girga: The Biography of a Contemporary Saint: Fr. Abdel-Mesih St. Macar]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Badaba, p. 287
passages.text:
Saint: BADABA, ABBA (The martyr) — Their Monastic Life

This saint was born in the city of ‘Armant’ in the governorate of ‘Qena,’ to a pious family; his father was called ‘Mina.’ The name ‘Badaba’ is derived from the Hieroglyphic word ‘Batby’: meaning (the principal/the essential) and from the Coptic word ‘Bataby’: meaning (related to the head).

A strong friendship developed between this saint and his cousin ‘Andrew,’ who was two years older. Since their childhood, both carried the same love for the heavenly Kingdom; they encountered one another on the level of the spirit, despised the pleasures of the world, concentrated on the study of the Holy Scriptures and religious books, used to fast two consecutive days with no food or drink, in addition to praying day and night.

Their Monastic Life:

They set forth together to the Eastern mountain at ‘Qasr el-Sayyad’ in the district of 'Nagh Hamadi.' There, they became disciples of St. abba ‘Isaac’ and dwelt in a cell where they performed their spiritual practices. They took upon themselves to copy down the religious manuscripts for their spiritual benefit and to sell them for little money to cover their living expenses and to give what was left to the poor.

As the sweet fragrance of Christ spread from them, their cell became a center of spiritual radiation. Abba ‘Tadros,’ the bishop of the area, came to them and ordained St. ‘Badaba’ as a priest and Andrew as a deacon. They used to perform the holy Liturgy once every forty days in a neighboring church.

It so happened that abba ‘Tadros’ once entered into that church, and he saw the face of St. ‘Badaba’ shining with an amazing splendor and a crown as though of gold on his head. So, he longed to have him and deacon ‘Andrew’ to stay with him in the diocese. However, St. ‘Badaba’ excused himself and returned to his cell, whereas ‘Andrew’ consented to do so. And, when St. ‘Badaba’ perceived that everyone was chasing him, he fled away from his cell, which the bishop dedicated as a church, later on.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abu Fana, pp. 78–79
passages.text:
Saint: ABU FANA, ST. — His Life as a Monk

St. ‘Abu- Fana’ or ‘Epiphanius’ lived in the days of the Emperor Theodosius the Great. He practiced the life of solitude in the Western Desert, in the province of ‘El-Ashmonein.' He lived in a cave in which he shot himself in to contemplate. Despite his strict asceticism, he did not cease to practice the handwork to give to the poor. He also cared to counsel the brethren, and God granted him the gift of performing miracles. In other words, his solitude was founded on an open heart full of love for God and men. His disciple ‘Ephraim’ gave us a concise account of his life.

His Life as a Monk:

The saint was born to Christian parents; they raised him on the fear of the Lord. He grew loving the life of seclusion and contemplation, together with his love for the needy.

While still a young man, he spent a lot of time among the monks and was trained on the ascetic life and the handwork to be able to give alms to the poor. When he became a monk, his love for solitude grew stronger that he lived in a very dark cave, where God granted him a fountain of water to drink from. He trained himself on fasting, by eating once a day in summer and once every two days in winter. He practiced the perpetual prayers and was making 300 metanoias by day and 300 by night until his skin stuck to his bones and came to be as a burnt stick.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abu Al-Karam, p. 76
passages.text:
Saint: ABU AL-KARAM

He was among the 13th century Copts. His full name was ‘Botros Abu Shaker Ebn Al-Raheb.' In the year 1260 AD, he was an active deacon in the church of the Virgin St. Mary, known as (the Hanged church).

When the 76th Pope ‘Athanasius III’ (1250-1261 AD) reposed in the Lord, unfortunately, ‘Abu El-Karam’ nominated himself to take his place on the papal throne. Also, he let his followers use illegal means, such as paying a certain sum of money to the treasury to help him in the process. However, God did not allow it, and he failed.

After that, he concentrated his efforts on writing some books, among which: 1- A book entitled: “Healing by revealing what is hidden in Christ’s Divinity." 2- An Introduction to “The Trinity and the Unification.” 3- On the ‘Epacts Reckoning,’ with a Coptic and Arabic introduction. 4- History books: “The Histories,” “History of Ebn El-Raheb” and “The Seven Local Councils."

[Kamel Saleh Nakhla: Series of History of the Patriarchs: V. 1; 1951; p. 122]

records.question: How did St. Moses the Black come to faith?
records.answer: St. Moses the Black came to faith after hearing a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread at that time. He went there carrying his sword and met St. Isidore, who asked him what he wanted. Moses confessed that he had heard of St. Isidore's goodness and had come seeking salvation from God despite his countless sins and great evils. St. Isidore questioned him about his past, and Moses confessed all his sins. After hearing Moses' confession, St. Isidore preached to him about the word of God and the judgment to come, then left him to contemplate. Moses was deeply remorseful, shedding many tears and disturbed in his sleep. He returned to St. Isidore, prostrated himself, and confessed all his crimes with contrition, which drew compassion. St. Isidore took him to Abba Macarius the Great, who baptized him and put him under St. Isidore's supervision [1][3].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 249–250
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

Not much is known about the past of St. Moses the Black before his repentance. He was most probably one of the Barbarian tribes. His life was so evil that it was said that there was no sin he did not commit. He was born between the years of 330 and 340 AD. It seems that he was a slave of a head of a tribe that worshipped the sun, but because of his extreme evil nature, his master got rid of him. He turned into a gangster who lived on robbing and killing people. He had a large, muscular stature, which helped him to become the head of an evil gang.

Having Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ:

Even though an extreme evil-doer, yet he kept raising up his eyes towards the sun, believing that it was the true God, seeking from it to proclaim itself to him. Then, he heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread all over the area at that time. He went there, carrying his sword, where he happened to meet with St. Isidore (The Priest of the Cells) coming out of his cell and heading to the church. Terrified by his appearance, the saint asked him: “What do you want from here, O brother?” Moses answered: “I heard that you are a good servant of God. Therefore, I escaped and came to you to let God save me the way he saved you.” He continued in persistence and with submission, saying: “I want to remain with you, despite my countless sins and my great evils.”

St. Isidore kept asking him about his past life and where he has been. Moses confessed to him all the sins he committed. On seeing how he opened his heart to him, St. Isidore started to teach him and preached him at length the word of God, he told him about the judgment to come and then left him to contemplate.

For hating evil and deciding to rid himself of it, Moses shed so many tears, and deep remorse swept his soul and disturbed his sleep, like a dreadful ghost. Then, he went to St. Isidore, prostrated himself before him, and in a loud voice, he confessed all his evil crimes again, with such contrition of heart that drew his compassion. He took him to Abba Macarius the Great, who put him under his care, taught him and guided him, gave him the grace of baptism, then put him back under the supervision of St. Isidore.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 252–253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Ordained as a Priest

Ordained as a Priest:

Because of his strife and virtues, they decided to ordain him as a priest. They arranged that the ordination would be performed at the patriarchate in Alexandria. However, the patriarch wanted to test Moses before ordaining him, so he ordered his priests that once they see him about to enter into the sanctuary, to drive him out saying: “Get out of here, O you with the blackface.” When they did that to him, the patriarch sent a deacon after him, and he heard him saying: “They did what you deserved Moses, for you are not a human, but dared to mix with men. Why then would you venture to sit among them?” St. Moses was ordained as a priest by the hand of the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), who heard at the time a voice saying: “Worthy, Worthy, Worthy,” and after putting the white robe on him, they said to him: “There you became all-white Moses.” He responded by saying with humility: “I wish this to be true on the inside as it is on the outside.”

His Virtues:

He lived denying himself that a governor, hearing about his virtues, longed to see him. When Moses knew about that, he ran away, but it happened that the saint passed by the governor in his way to the monastery, and he inquired from him about the location of father Moses' cell. St. Moses told him: “What do you want from such an old man, who is far from being upright.” The governor was disturbed and went to the monastery and told the monks about what happened. On understanding the monks how that monk looked like, they knew that it was no one but Fr. Moses, who denied himself.

Because of his love, humility, strife, and intense asceticism, he was granted by God to perform miracles and signs.

A monk fell into a specific iniquity, and a meeting was held to discuss an appropriate penance. Moses was invited to attend, but he refrained from going. When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

After a while, Moses sought from Abba Isidore to make him a monk. However, Abba Isidore started to explain to him how tough the monastic life is with the constant fight against the demons and the other physical needs. He told him as a way of testing him: “It is better for you son, to go and live in the populated areas,” but after seeing his real intention and solid stand, St. Isidore sent him back to Abba Macarius the Great, the father of the wilderness.

Moses stood in the church and confessed publicly about all his sins and evil deeds. Abba Macarius said afterward that he saw during Moses confession a whiteboard with black writings, and with every sin Moses proclaimed, an angel wiped it out off that board until the board became allwhite. After Abba Macarius instructed him, he sent him back to the priest Isidore who clothed him in the monastic attire. He advised him: “Remain, my son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would leave it, all evil will come back to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure God will do mercy and grace on you and will crush the devil under your feet.”

His Strife:

St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macarius to find for him a secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept counseling him to stand fast until the devil would get tired of him. He gave him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it.” Father. Abba Isidore took him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 251–252
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Strife

There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly angels, about whom the saint said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and returned to his cell.

Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks at night, take their water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to move, until some brethren happened to come to the well, and they carried him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he regained his ability to move.

Once four thieves tried to rob his cell, but he tied them together and carried them to the church. When the thieves realized that he was Moses, who used to be the head of a gang of thieves, they repented and wanted to become monks. St. Moses preached them with words that moved their hearts.

Because of his great strife, the devils were stirred more against him, that his mentor Abba Isidore counseled him to moderate in his ascetic practices to keep them from causing him more troubles. He sought from him to deliver himself to God, and He alone would be able to alleviate that fight on him. Abba Isidore told him that, to keep him from thinking that by his ascetic efforts, he could overcome the demons, but by humility and spiritual repentance, God would fight on our behalf.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Virtues

When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

For some reason, it was proclaimed an obligation in the Scetis to fast for a week. During that week, some guests came to visit Fr. Moses. He prepared food for them to eat. On seeing smoke rising from his cell, the brethren said to one another: “Look, Moses has broken his fast and is preparing food for himself. We shall talk to him about it.” When they got to know the facts, they said to him: “Father Moses! You have disregarded the commandment of men, but kept that of God (i.e., giving hospitality to strangers).”

His Martyrdom:

Then, it happened that the Barbarians came to attack the monastery, an incident St. Moses knew by Spirit beforehand, and he sought from the brethren to escape. However, seven brethren stayed behind, and they asked him: “Are you not going to escape, father?” He answered: “For a long time, I waited for this day, for the words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be fulfilled: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). They said to him: “We shall stay with you and will not escape.” He told them: “There, they are already at the gate.” The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed them all. However, when one of the seven escaped to the stronghold out of fear, he saw seven crowns coming down from heaven on the seven martyred monks. Then, he hastened to come down and ran forward to receive his crown of martyrdom.

So, Abba Moses completed his strife on the 24th of Paona in the year 408 AD, when he was seventy-five years old (or eighty-five). He earned three crowns: the 1st for love and intense asceticism, the 2nd for monasticism and priesthood, and the 3rd for martyrdom. He was counted the first martyr in the Scetis, and he had so many great teachings. His body was kept along with that of his spiritual guide Abba Isidore in one tube at the Paramus monastery in Natrun Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 254–255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?" (Psalm 118:6)” • Then, the brother asked: “If a man beat his servant for something wrong he did, what should the servant say?” The saint answered: “If he was a good servant, he would possibly say: ‘Have mercy on me, for I made a mistake.’ Thus, he would blame himself and draw the mercy of his master.” • In general, a man should never condemn his neighbor. When in the Old, the hand of God came heavy on the firstborn of the Egyptians, there was no house without a dead son in it. For us, it meant that we should concentrate on our sins and not worry about those of our neighbors, for it would be unreasonable for a man to leave his dead son, and go to mourn that of his neighbor.

To die about your neighbor means to worry about your sins and not to care for the sins of any man, good or bad. You should not do wrong to anyone, or think bad about anyone else in your heart or despise anyone for doing wrong. You should not obey anyone who harmed his neighbor or rejoice for him. You should never slander anyone, but always say that God knows everybody's heart. Do not go along with the man who talks bad about his neighbor, because it would make you fall in condemnation. Do not have hatred against anyone. Do not have a grudge in your heart against anyone, and do not hate the man who is hostile toward his neighbor. This would bring you peace.

[Sayings of the Strong Saint Abba Moses, Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria- Diocese of Los Angeles] [Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of OrthodoxWiki]

[Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of Wikipedia]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, p. 258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands

If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take the monk to the nearest location of the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.

Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not having a steady residence, teaching, preaching, and converting multitudes to Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in the year 372 AD.

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347]

[Baring-Gould: February 7]

Notes: [2] These tribes were known by the name ‘Saracens’… It is worth mentioning that the name ‘Saracens’ was given by the Greeks and the Romans to the nomadic tribes in the ‘Sino-Arabian’ desert…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, pp. 255–256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.

Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him in the form of a girl. She managed to convince him to spend the night at her place. Then, she claimed to him that she was the daughter of one of the kings and that she wanted him to marry her, quoting the honor of the marriage of the fathers: Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He accepted her request. Then, she claimed that she was a Jew, and he had to convert to her religion to be able to marry her. So, Moses was blinded, and he denied his Christ. Then, she (the deceptive devil) took him back to the wilderness, where a whole gang of devils ridiculed him and made so much fun of him. Finally, the hermit woke up and cast himself on the dust and kept crying and supplicating to the Compassionate God to forgive him. God sent him Abba Samuel, who told him that he would be departing after three days. Then, he took him to the church, where he gave him Communion in the Holy Sacraments after confessing all that the devil has done to him. St. Moses, the hermit, reposed in peace and was buried by Abba Samuel, who wrote his biography, and handed it to someone traveling to Alexandria for the benefit of the believers.

[The Hermit Fathers, Part 2, p. 25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, pp. 257–258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — The Tribes of Saracens

The Tribes of Saracens:

The Arabian tribes populating the area of Rhinoclura in-between the eastern Egyptian border and the Asian shores, used to worship the stars. Then in the year 226 AD, these tribes embraced Christianity through the efforts of Origen (184-253 AD). Then, those tribes joined forces together and formed one State under the reign of a queen called Mavia. By their unity, they created a power block that brought fear to the Arian Emperor Valens (364- 378 AD) and forced him to seek a peace treaty with them.

Choosing Moses as a Bishop:

Those Christian tribes having united together, they felt the need for a bishop to shepherd them. It happened that in those days, there was a recluse monk named Moses in the eastern desert, he was so beloved by those tribesmen that they decided to choose him to be their bishop. Then, when Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those united tribes.

Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands:

On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then, St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Confessor, p. 257
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE CONFESSOR

This St. Moses (Moyses) was a Roman priest of Jewish roots. He was one of the main members of a congregation of confessors in the time of Cyprian, at the start of the heresy of Novatian. The rest of the confessors were: Fr. Maximus, the priest, the two deacons Nicostratus and Rufinus, the laymen Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, and Celerinus. According to Cyprian, they were the first group of confessors in the days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Decius (249-251 AD). At the time of the persecution, they wrote down a message to exhort the confessors in Carthage to be committed to the system and wrote another message to Cyprian.

After spending about a year in prison (eleven months and few days), St. Moses reposed in January 251 AD, and was counted as a confessor, and even as a martyr. It was said that a little while before his departure, Moses refused to have any contact with Novatian or the five priests who were supporting him and followed his views. St. Moses was considering their faith and views as unorthodox.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. III, p. 948]

[Baring-Gould: November 25]

Notes: [1] ‘Novatian’ was a Roman bishop and theologian of the 3rd century who took a strict position on readmission of apostates during the persecutions at the time…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, p. 255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went deep in the wilderness and lived for thirty-five years in a spot having olive and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended the wild beasts.

His Multiple Falls and Repentances:

Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the devil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, pp. 240–241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — The Bitterness of Anguish

St. Moises (Moses) was one of the prominent fathers and saints of the church in the 8th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.

St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Scetis, where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox faith. He used to spend most of his time in worship, that it was said that he did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

The Bitterness of Anguish:

During his bishopric, the Umayyad rulers of Egypt subjected the Copts to extremely severe persecutions, and great anguish dwelt upon the church. The bishops returned to their monasteries to concentrate on prayers and fasts, imploring God to lift that anguish. However, St. Moises remained among his people to encourage them and to keep them holding fast to their faith against the snatching wolves. St. Moises also got the grace to perform miracles and signs, healing sicknesses, as well as the grace of prophecy.

Due to these intolerable persecutions at the time, the number of Copts who converted to Islam reached 24,000 persons. When some archons came to seek from St. Moises to pray to the Lord to lift the anguish from His people, he told them: “My children, be assured that the governor who is persecuting you will perish within this month,” and this was what did happen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 253–254
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

Of his Sayings:

• To a brother in the Scetis who sought from him a word of encouragement, he said: “Go and sit in your cell, it will teach you everything.” • The man who flees from the world is like ripe grapes, but he who dwells among the distractions of men is like sour grapes. • If we keep the commandments of our fathers, I promise you that the Barbarians would never come here, but if we do not, this place will soon become desolate. • According to Fr. Poemen, Fr. Moses was once asked: “How can a man become like dead to his neighbor?” The older saint said to him: “Unless a man keeps in his heart that he has been three days in the grave, he will not be strong enough to do that.” • It is better for a man to put himself to death rather than his neighbor, and he should not condemn him in anything. • It is good for a man to die to every work which is evil before he departs from the body, so as not to offend anyone. • Unless a man feels in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not listen to him. A brother asked him about the meaning of that, and the saint said: “Whoever focuses on his sins, would never see those of his neighbor.” • Unless your prayers conform to your behavior, your struggle would not be of any benefit. When the saint was asked to explain, he said: “We should apply what we pray about, for when man forsakes his own will, he reconciles with God and God will listen to his prayers.” • A brother asked him: “What would help the man in his every endeavor?” He answered him: “God is the One who helps, for it is so written: "God is our refuge and strength. A very present help in trouble" (Psalm 46:1).” • When the brother added: “What then is the benefit of fasting or spending sleepless nights, father?” The saint answered: “These practices make the soul meek and humble, for it is written: "Look on my affliction and my pain, and forgive all my sins" (Psalm 25:18). So, once the soul reaps the fruits of these practices, God would have compassion on her.” • Then, the brother asked: “What will man do with every temptation he encounters or every evil thought coming to him?” The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?"

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Libyan, p. 256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE LIBYAN, ST.

This saint was from Libya. He was so humble and compassionate all the time that God granted him the grace to perform the miracles of healing the sick. He once said: “When I was young, I lived in a monastery. There, it happened that eight monks dug a well, and seventy others built a wall around it, in the hope that they would get water from it. They dug it down to the depth of about twenty yards, but no water was found. They were very much grieved and intended to fill it up with dirt. However, by noontime, when Abba Pieour came over suddenly to the location of the well and was informed about what they were doing, he rebuked them saying: ‘Why did you despair, O you of little faith?’ Then, he went down to the bottom of the well, and he prayed there. Afterward, he pushed an iron rod in the well bottom three times, saying: ‘O God of the saints, I pray, do not waste the effort of these men, but send them plenty of water.’ In a short while, the water erupted from the well and wetted everyone around.

After praying a thanksgiving prayer, Abba Pieour intended to go in his way. They tried to make him have a meal with them, but he said: ‘I have accomplished what I came here to do, I did not come here to eat.’”

This was a good lesson for the brethren about faith and the trust in God.

[The Paradise of the Saints, p. 69]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Guirgis El-Mozaĥem, pp. 213–214
passages.text:
Saint: GUIRGIS EL-MOZAĤEM (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

The setting of the Fatimid State in Egypt (909-1171 AD), had unique importance, as the Fatimid turned Egypt from a colony into an independent state, and the Caliph El-Muåzz Li-Din Allah (953-975 AD) was a role model in dealing with all Egyptians with justice, without discrimination between a Christian and a Muslim. Still, under the Caliph El-Aziz Bi-Allah (975-996 AD), a wave of anger prevailed on the Muslim mobs, when they saw how some of the Copts reached the position of a minister and gained the favor and trust of the Caliph.

The most serious of those incidents was what happened in the region of Talkha in the governorate of Daqahlyia, near the end of the 10th century AD, because of a person named El-Mozaĥem. El-Mozaĥem was the son of a Christian widow called Mariam and a Muslim father by the name of Gomoåa el-Ăatawy, who married his wife by force against the will of her parents who were from a village called Daroteen in the province of Talkha. El-Mozaĥem was the third son among six brothers and one sister. He spent his first twelve years on his father's religion, but noticing how his mother used to go to church every Sunday, he felt a great urge to follow her to see what was going on in the church. On her return from the church, he used to ask her to give him a piece of the Corban she usually would bring back with her, which he greatly savored. He continued to follow his mother every Sunday, and eventually, he decided to become a Christian. On the occasion of the feast of the Virgin St. Mary, he headed to Abba Zacharias, the bishop of Damietta, and asked him to baptize him. However, the church priests were afraid of the consequences. So, he asked them a favor, not to drain the Holy Water from the font of baptism, and after the departure of the entire congregation from the church, he took off his clothes and plunged in the water three times in the name of the Holy Trinity. Afterward, he felt as being a Christian, and he was just eighteen years of age at the time. Later on, he got married to a girl named Siola. She was the daughter of hegomen Abanob of the church of Busat el-Nasara in the province of Talkha.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — Imprisoned along with the Pope

Imprisoned along with the Pope:

The last of the Umayyad caliphs Marwan ibn Muĥammad (Marwan II: 744-750 AD), arrested the 46th Pope of Alexandria, St. Khael I (743-767 AD). Bishop Moises stayed in the company of the pope, and he longed to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When the soldiers brought them to the tent of Marwan, they forced St. Moises on his knees, raised his feet, and beat him with bronze clubs on his sides and neck. His tormentors were seeking from him a bribe to set him free. The saint did not utter a single word, for he did not understand their Arabic language. When Marwan gave the order to cut the head of Pope Khael I, and the swordsman led him to the place of execution, St. Moises ran after him, despite the attempts of the swordsman to keep him away. An angry soldier intended to kill him if it was not for some officials who did not let him do it. Then, he was cast in prison along with Pope Khael I, and their feet were placed in chains, among many others. However, St. Moises prophesied that they would eventually come out safe from that prison, which was realized when Marwan was defeated by the Abbasids dynasty.

His Prophesy concerning the Umayyad Caliphate:

During the revolt of the Coptic Bashmurians (Coptic rebels) due to the intolerable Umayyad persecution, St. Moises disciple asked him a question concerning when that calamity would come to an end, the saint prophesied: “God will not forsake His church to the end, but He will save her, and this caliphate (of Umayyad) will vanish and be replaced by some other.” This prophecy was realized in 750 AD when the Umayyad dynasty was replaced by the Abbasids.

records.question: Who was St. Bishoy?
records.answer:
St. Bishoy was a Coptic Orthodox saint born around the year 320 AD in the village of Shansa in the governorate of El-Menufyia. He was one of six brothers, raised by their mother after their father passed away. An angel appeared to his mother, indicating that St. Bishoy was chosen by the Lord to serve Him all his life, despite being weak and frail in body, with the angel saying, "My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12:9) [1].

At the age of twenty, in 340 AD, St. Bishoy went to the wilderness of Scetis (Shiheet) and became a disciple of Abba Bemwah, who was a disciple of St. Macarius. He lived in seclusion for three years, worshipping and growing in virtue and love for God [1].

After Abba Bemwah's death, St. Bishoy and Abba John the Short prayed for guidance. An angel told them that Abba John should remain, and St. Bishoy moved to a cave two miles away. He practiced intense asceticism, including tying a rope to his hair to keep himself awake during prayer, fasting the whole week and eating only on Saturdays, and memorizing much of the Bible, especially the Book of Jeremiah, which he loved deeply and was called "Bishoy the Jeremian" [2].

He valued manual labor as part of spiritual life and rejected wealth, telling a rich man who offered gold to distribute it to the poor instead. He had spiritual encounters with the Lord Jesus Christ, who appeared to him multiple times, encouraging him and promising to sustain monks who love one another and keep His commandments. St. Bishoy also washed the Lord's feet and drank water from the basin, which he shared with his disciple [3][12].

In 407 AD, due to Berber attacks on Scetis, St. Bishoy fled to Mount Ansena in Upper Egypt, where he formed a close friendship with St. Paul of Tamouh. They wished to remain together after death, and their bodies were eventually buried together in the Monastery of Abba Bishoy in Scetis [6][7].

St. Bishoy reposed on the 8th of Abib in 417 AD at the age of 97. His body is said to have never decayed, and he is remembered for his simple life, intense love for God, ascetic struggles, and close fellowship with Jesus Christ [1][7][12].
