passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, pp. 154–155
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — Unusual and Amazing Personality

Unusual and Amazing Personality:

As much as the personality of St. Simeon (Semåan) was unique and unusual in its lifestyle and behavior, as much as God has confirmed its authenticity. Deacon Yousef Ĥabib (1909-1981) and his brother Melika stated in the introduction of their book about St. Simeon, the Stylite:

This saint, in his life and behavior, was admired, not only by the believers among the inhabitants of the Roman empire but by the non-believers and the Barbarians as well. He was greatly honored by the Persians, the Midianites, and the Ethiopians. The Roman Emperors sought his prayers and used to seek his counsel for critical issues. His biography was written by his disciple Theodoret who remained beside him until the end of his life. He wrote what he saw by his own eyes, and his testimony was confirmed by many other people from all categories. He stated: “Those who are under the rule of the Roman Empire know about the well- known Simeon, whom they indeed called The Wonder of the World. Yet, despite the many witnesses, I am reluctant to write about the strife of that saint; lest it might be difficult for the coming generations to believe what is written. For man usually measures everything according to the natural ways of things; while counting anything out of the usual as wrong or unbelievable. But those who know the greatness of the Grace of God would never refuse to believe what I am saying.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, p. 155
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

That saint was born in the year 390 AD in Sisan, a village close to the city Aleppo on the northern border of Syria, to a father called John, and a mother called Martha. Because of him, many strange things happened, among them in a dream, St. John the Baptist came to his mother, gave her the good news about his birth and told her about what he would become as a grownup.

The young St. Simeon worked as a shepherd of his father's sheep. He had many siblings, all of whom died, except for one older brother called Samson.

One Sunday because of the heavy snow, St. Simeon was not able to go out to the pastures to shepherd the sheep, so he went instead to attend the Divine Liturgy in one of the Churches; something he didn't do very often. That Sunday, he heard the words spoken by Jesus during the Sermon of the Mount: “Blessed are the pure in heart... Blessed are the peacemakers, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” (Matthew 5:4-9) Simeon asked the preacher to explain more about the Christian faith, and Simeon listened hard. He explained to him the happiness brought by asceticism for the sake of the enjoyment of the joy of Christ. He talked to him about the fellowship in the passion of the Crucified for the sake of the eternal enjoyment of Heaven.

From that time on, he used to go early to Church to stay a long time there, and sometimes he spent all night long kneeling to pray, and he used to exhaust himself in prayers. He often denied himself eating his ration of food to give it to the poor and the needy.

When both his father and his aunt died, he and his brother inherited all their possessions. St. Simeon gave the land to his brother and distributed the rest of his inheritance on the poor and the monasteries; besides some flocks of sheep, he donated to the monastery he later joined.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, pp. 155–156
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

Then, St. Simeon forsook everything and set forth to the wilderness. He fasted a whole week while praying with tears. He approached Fr. Heliodore, the Abbot of a nearby monastery called Euzebona, hoping that he would admit him. The grace of God was so evident in his life that the Abbot of the monastery introduced him to the bishop just after three days. And, the bishop admired him and ordained him as a monk. It was said that, during praying over him, the bishop saw an angel standing next to St. Simeon, who told the bishop that he would be a chosen vessel, in whom God would pour His precious gifts.

St. Simeon became a disciple of Fr. Heliodore for ten years. And, because his cousin was a monk in the same monastery and he did not go out of it for 35 years, St. Simeon planned to follow suit. He also used to give his portion of food to the poor and remained to fast for six days every week.

Having his Eyesight Back after Losing it:

It happened that, one day while praying, the devil appeared to him in a terrifying dark cloud, struck him on his eyes, causing him to lose his eyesight. The Abbot of the monastery felt very sad for his dilemma and intended to bring a physician to treat him, but St. Simeon took his permission and went to the tombs, where he kept praying for 40 days; and Lo! A light shone around him, and the saint had his eyesight restored, and he returned to the monastery to resume his worship.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, p. 160
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — His Repose

His Repose:

St. “Simeon the Stylite lived for 70 years, and God allowed him to suffer much through the deterioration of his physical health. And he knew that his departure from this world was near. The saint departed to heaven in the year 459 AD Before his departure, he increased his prayers, knelt, and delivered his soul. So, he remained that way for some time, and his disciple did not know that he has already departed. On hearing about his departure, the patriarch of Antioch came, together with six bishops, some leaders of the army, and 6,000 soldiers in a grand procession to bid him farewell. During his funeral, many miracles were performed in the name of the Lord.

Remark:

There are three persons who carried the name of Simeon el-Ăamoudi (the Stylite). The first is the one mentioned here, called Simeon el-Ăamoudi the Great. The second: Simeon el-Ăamoudi Minor, at the end of the 5th century, mentioned by Fr. John of Damascus in his 3rd sermon on the icons. And the third, who lived in the land of Cilicia who died by a strike of lightning falling on him; and mentioned by Saphronius in chapter 57 of his book: “The Spiritual Gardens.”

Of His Words:

“Whoever talks, let him utter the words of the Lord with the humility of heart; doing so by his works before his words.”

[Jesuit Fr. Botros Farmag: Pastures of the Pious in the Biographies of the Righteous; 1877: January 5] [Synaxarion: 29 Bashons and 3 Mesra]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, p. 156
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — Expelling Him from the Monastery

Expelling Him from the Monastery:

St. Simeon kept progressing in his ascetic practices. He used to bind a rough rope around his waist so hard that it did cut wounds through his flesh, and he refused to be treated. The other monks sought from the Abbot of the monastery to send the saint away for fear that his behavior might probably cause the weak to doubt themselves. The monastery Abbot went along with their request. St. Simeon left the monastery, entered a wilderness nearby, and dwelt in a dry well, where he spent his days praying and singing praise to God.

Five days later, the Abbot of the monastery, in a night vision, saw men clothed in shining attire, seeking from him to bring St. Simeon back. The next day, he sent some monks to bring him back, which he barely consented to do.

Living a Solitary Life:

St. Simeon remained for another three years in the monastery, practicing strict ascetic routines. When his fellow monks kept honoring him, he was very uncomfortable and sought the permission of the Abbot to leave the monastery. He set forth to a deserted area, where he dwelt alone for another three years.

He decided to fast every year for 40 days without any food or drinks. At the time his disciple Theodoret wrote his biography, St. Simeon was going through his 28th fasting period.

St. Simeon considered everything as nothing, whenever he thought about the Crucified Lord Christ. He used to climb to the top of a high mountain and would sit on the rocks with his eyes continually focused on heaven, and his heart is sighing with love for the Lord Christ.

He put iron chains on his feet to keep him from much movement. And when Meletius, the bishop of Antioch (360-361 AD) visited him, he said to the saint: “These chains are for the beasts and not for humans. What bind us men are not iron chains, but those of love for the Lord Christ.” The saint obeyed and sought from a blacksmith to remove them.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Daniel, the Stylite, p. 559
passages.text:
Saint: DANIEL, THE STYLITE, ST. — His Monastic Life

In the biography of St. ‘Daniel the Stylite’ (409-493 AD) and of others like St. ‘Simon the Stylite,’ many emphasized the challenge faced by these saints from even nature itself. Our saint lived a strange life on a pillar for so many years.

Writing the biography of that great among the saints reveals the depth of the exalted Divine love, which swallowed his heart, preoccupied his mind, and made him dedicate all his energies to the account of the kingdom of God.

It was not strange that, while adoring seclusion, he loved people, sought their salvation, and cared to talk to them for the sake of their improvement. Refraining from having gifts from the elites, he loved giving; and urged those who listened to him to have the same spirit.

His Monastic Life:

St. ‘Daniel the Stylite,’ is considered the most famous among the ‘Stylite’ saints after St. ‘Simon the Stylite.’ He was born in the town of ‘Maratha,’ near ‘Samosata’ in upper Mesopotamia (in Iraq), to parents who vowed him to God before his birth. On reaching 12 years of age, he went to a monastery close to his hometown, where he became a monk after several years.

On his way to visit Antioch, the abbot of the monastery took ‘Daniel’ along with him. On passing through ‘Telanissae,’ they went to visit St. ‘Simon the Stylite,’ who allowed ‘Daniel’ to ascend to him on his pillar, blessed him, and prophesied that he would endure much for the sake of the Lord Christ.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Armenian Bishop, p. 151
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE ARMENIAN BISHOP (The martyr)

He was a bishop on Persia, and he was martyred along with 150 other martyrs. He lived in the days of King Shapur II (309-379), the son of Hormizd II, the king of Persia. This king treated the Christians oppressively, cruelly and unjustly. Simeon wrote to the king a message in which he said: “Those whom the Lord Christ purchased by His precious blood to save them from the servitude of evil should never serve those who break the law.” On reading this message, the angry king called the saint, put him in chains, and cast him in prison. There, finding some prisoners who worshipped the fire, he taught them and preached them. They proclaimed faith in the Lord Christ before the governor, who ordered to cut their heads by the sword; and did the same to the saint. In this way, all of them received the crowns of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 19 Baramouda]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, pp. 157–158
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — A Man of Prayer

A Man of Prayer:

Once his disciple was watching the saint praying and started to count the number of times of his kneeling (metanoias). The disciple scored 1,240 metanias that the saint did, then he stopped counting.

It was said that when an elite came to visit the saint, the man implored him, saying: “In the name of Him who incarnated for our sake, I beg from you to tell me; Are you a human or of another creation, which appears as human?” Here, the saint sought from his disciple to bring a ladder and to let the man climb up on it. Once he did reach up to him, he showed him his wounded legs, to assure him about his human nature.

An Exalted Fatherhood:

Along with his firmness and cruelty on himself, the saint was so compassionate, meek, and cheerful toward all others. The two sermons he gave every day raised the hearts of his listeners to heaven. He gave them a chance to ask questions. And, he used to reconcile the adversaries. Together with his love, he never complimented anyone at the expense of his salvation. He counseled the kings and the elites and cared for the Church leaderships.

A Heavenly Message:

In a night vision, he felt that someone was calling his name. He instantly woke up, to see a person of heavenly beauty, clothed with splendid light and holding a golden rod in his hand. Then for his fear, he fell on the ground, but the angel gave him peace and said to him: “Do not be afraid; follow me and listen carefully to what I am about to say: The Lord is planning to use you for the glory of His Name, for the improvement of His Church and to bring back so many people from their sinful ways. But, you have to know that you are committed to suffer much. And you have to condition your heart into complete perseverance and love for all men regardless of their characters. And above everything else, you have to take away from your mind every thought of pride or vainglory; and to put yourself in a level lower than any other man in the world.” The angel then brought him forth to the top of the mountain, instructed him to build an altar using four rocks. Then, he took him over to a Church, where he saw a crowd of people from all races in heavenly attire, with the portrait of humility and piety on their faces. And, the angel told him that these were the people who returned to God, because of his sermons and by following his role model.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, pp. 158–159
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — A Heavenly Message

Then, he took him over to a Church, where he saw a crowd of people from all races in heavenly attire, with the portrait of humility and piety on their faces. And, the angel told him that these were the people who returned to God, because of his sermons and by following his role model.

Entering into the Church and approaching the altar to pray, he saw the Lord Christ, more splendid than the sun. The Lord Jesus greeted him and said: “Have courage and never fear.”

A Heavenly Support:

In another night's vision, he saw Elijah the prophet on a fiery chariot. Elijah counseled him to have no fear before the elites of the world, for as long as God would be his support, no one could ever harm him.

His Humility:

As some recluses developed some doubts concerning the saint's strange way of worship, dwelling on a pillar, his long prayers and continuous sermons to the people; two of them approached him and said that they were sent by the elders, to tell him that, by so doing, he deviates from the way of virtue and follow a way different from that of the saints. And, they said to him that the elders were ordering him to come down from his pillar.

On seeing how Simeon instantly sent his disciple to bring a ladder and intended with humility to come down his pillar, the two messengers said to him: “We are now sure of your obedience. May God is with you, and may His Spirit guide you in this unique way. Keep it on, do not come down, for so have those who sent us commanded us to do.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Daniel, the Stylite, pp. 559–560
passages.text:
Saint: DANIEL, THE STYLITE, ST. — His Seclusion

His Seclusion:

When the abbot of the monastery reposed, the monks intended to choose ‘Daniel’ to replace him; but he declined. He went again to visit St. ‘Simon the Stylite,’ and stayed for 14 days in a monastery close to his place. Intending to visit the Holy Land, but the war did not allow him to do so, he went to ‘Constantinople’ instead, where he stayed seven days in a church outside the city walls. He then prepared for himself a place to live as a hermit, in which he lived for nine years under the care of patriarch ‘Anatolios.’

Dwelling on a Pillar:

St. ‘Daniel’ intended to follow the lead of St. ‘Simon the Stylite,’ whose garment he got from St. ‘Simon’s disciple after he reposed in the year 459 AD. He chose a location on the ‘Bosphorus Sea’ few miles from ‘Constantinople,’ established a pillar with a full top, then ascended on it and lived there. On learning that one night, he almost froze from the severe cold; the emperor ordered him a shelter to be built over two pillars. There, he dwelt until he reached the age of 84 years. During that time, he never forsook his support, even during the cold waves that came upon the land from time to time. When St. ‘Gennadius’ the patriarch of Constantinople (458-471 AD), ordained him as a priest despite his protest, the patriarch had to stand below the pillar reading his prayers; then he ascended to put his hand on the head of the saint and to give him the Holy Communion.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Stylite, p. 157
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE STYLITE, ST. — A Wonder-Maker

A Wonder-Maker:

As many miracles and signs were performed on his hands, in the name of God, multitudes came to him from Persia, Ethiopia, France, Spain, England, and Italy, to seek counsel and healing from St. Simeon. Kings and bishops came from Europe to ask him about specific issues, which he answered according to the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and many people put his portrait in their houses for a blessing. As testified by his disciple Theodoret, who saw it by his eyes, being burdened by having his hands kissed and his robe touched for blessing by many, he made for himself a six cubits (1 cubit=1.73 feet) high pillar; increased it by six cubits, then by 8 cubits more, to reach 30 cubits high [= 52 feet]; with a top circle of 6 spans (1 span=9 inches) wide [= 4.5 feet], surrounded by a low fence to keep him from falling off.

St. Simeon drew many believers to repent. He had a fantastic influence on pagans who proclaimed their faith in the Savior of the world. And, he was the cause of comfort to so many who came to listen to his sermons.

The Repentance of a Thief:

Antiochus Agonatus, the head of a gang of thieves, had such a very strong body, that he was feared even by soldiers. When he went too far with his crimes, a large regiment of soldiers was sent to chase him. Finding him in a night club, once he raised his sword, they were so terrified that he could flee away. By the grace of God, he went to St. Simeon to present repentance with tears. When the soldiers came to arrest him and asked the saint how he would protect such a criminal, He answered them that the thief came to him seeking the mercy of God and offering repentance.

When the soldiers withdrew, the saint sought from the thief not to resume his crimes. The thief cried out, exploring the mercies of our Lord Jesus Christ, raised his hands toward heaven, and said: “O my Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, receive my spirit.” Crying for two hours, the saint and all who were present, were so impressed that they all cried when they saw the thief lean his head on the pillar, and then deliver his soul.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon Clopas, the Apostle, p. 151
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON CLOPAS, THE APOSTLE

This saint was the son of Clopas (Cleophas), the brother of the righteous Joseph, the fiancé of the Virgin St. Mary. He received the grace of the Comforter in the upper chamber of Zion, then eventually was ordained a bishop of Jerusalem, after the martyrdom of St. James the Apostle. He drew so many Jews to faith in the Lord Christ. And through him, God performed so many signs. On hearing how he used to urge the people on chastity and purity, emperor Trajan (98-117 AD) called him, tortured him, and ordered his beheading. He received the crown of martyrdom when he was 120 years old.

[The Synaxarion: 9 Abib]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon of Menouf, p. 151
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON OF MENOUF (The martyr)

This saint Simeon (Samåan) was from the city of Menouf. He is celebrated by the Church on the 14th of Kiahk. He was martyred in the days of the Arabs.

[The Synaxarion: 14 Kiahk]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon, the Elder, pp. 153–154
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON, THE ELDER (The Priest & the Prophet) — Simeon and the Septuagint Bible Translation

The king generously rewarded them.

This translation was used in the Jewish synagogues in Egypt to be able to read the Holy Bible in the Greek Koine dialect, which was widely spoken all over the East after Alexander the Great (356-323 BC).

Of course, this translation was through a Divine ordinance, since it became possible for the whole world to become familiar with all the Prophesies concerning the Lord Jesus Christ. So, when the apostles came to preach the Christian faith, people were more opened to accepting it, particularly that the translation was done by Jewish scholars before the Christian preaching has started.

“Behold, the virgin shall conceive”:

While Simeon, the Elder was translating the book of Isaiah at the verse (7:14): “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel,” he was unwilling to translate the Hebrew word meaning Virgin into its equivalent Greek word Ti Parthenos (η παρθένα), for fear that the king would ridicule him So, he was leaning towards replacing it with the name “the Girl,” since he was full of doubt about How could a virgin conceive and give birth? Through his inner struggle between his trust in the Holy Bible, his honesty in the translation and the apparent unfeasibility of the Text in hand; it happened that in a night vision, it was revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had witnessed Emanuel being born by a Virgin. So, Simeon was allowed to live for about 300 years, and his vision got weaker and weaker. Then, he came by the Spirit into the temple and took up the Child Jesus in his arms, blessed God, and his eyes were opened. • The elder sat on the road of the world and patiently anticipated the coming of the Lord of the world, as He promised to do. Generations passed him by, death passed here and there but kept away from him; the older man remained steadfastly alert so that he would be a witness for the Lord of the Time because the Word kept him safe in the road until He comes.

[Mar. Jacob of Serugh]

• Why do you linger? Come and take the Child from Simeon, the Elder, and hold him in your arms; in order, that out of your mortal body, fragrant smell of life would spread from His Holy Body.

[St. John Saba]

The eyes of Simeon, the Elder, were opened to see the Divine Child; so did his inner insight to perceive the salvation, and his tongue was loosened to praise and prophesy.

[Hegomen Bishoi Abdel Messih: Simeon the Elder, the Priest, and Prophet]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Simeon Barsabae, the Bishop and his Companions, p. 150
passages.text:
Saint: SIMEON BARSABAE, THE BISHOP AND HIS COMPANIONS (The martyrs) — His Arrest

His Arrest:

This saint was the bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon in Persia. He was also called Barsabae. When king Shapur II (309-379) gave the order to arrest him, the soldiers chained him and brought him up to be tried before malicious governors. He refused to worship the sun and firmly testified with a loud voice to the Lord Christ. He was imprisoned for a long time, along with hundreds of believers among them were bishops, priests, and deacons of different ranks.

His Support for the King’s Counselor:

Among those arrested was Usthazanes (Chusdazat), the king's counselor, who had weakened earlier and denied his Christian faith. However, later on, he repented on the hands of bishop Simeon and were arrested and condemned to death. He was steadfast until he was martyred. On the next day, it was the memorial of the passion of the Lord Christ, and all the others were condemned to death and their heads were cut off by the sword in front of St. Simeon. The saint zealously encouraged every one of them to receive his crown of martyrdom. Finally, he was martyred in the same way, in the year 341 AD.

Among those tortured and martyred at that time, were the two priests: Abdechalas (Abdella/Abdhaihla) and Ananias (Hannanja), together with Pusicius (Pusai), the overseer of the king's workers. Because he kept encouraging the priest Ananias to stand firm before the persecution, Pusicius was killed in a wrong way. His tongue was cut off, then his head, and after him, his virgin daughter Askitrea was slained too.

[Butler, April 21]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sisinnius, pp. 167–168
passages.text:
Saint: SISINNIUS, ST.

He was initially a Cappadocian slave, but he gained his freedom. Then, he proclaimed his faith in the Lord Christ and became a disciple of St. Albidius. He dwelt with him on the mountain, confined himself in a cave for seven years, then settled in a tomb for three more years. He was granted the gift of driving the demons out. Then, when he was ordained as a priest, he led the people to holiness. He cared for the strangers, dedicated himself to voluntary poverty, and used to rebuke the mean rich people. God has granted him also with the victory over the carnal desires.

[The Paradise of Saints; p. 53]

records.question: Who was St. Barbara the martyr?
records.answer:
St. Barbara was a Christian martyr born in the village of Gamis near the city of Leopolis in Nicomedia at the beginning of the 3rd century AD, during the reign of Emperor Maximinus I (235-238 AD). Her father, Dioscorus, was a pagan who strongly hated Christians. To protect her from the corrupt world, he built a high tower for her, filled with idols and entertainments, and provided her with advanced teachers. However, Barbara loved meditation and praised the Creator God. She was influenced by Christian servants and met Origen, who taught her about the Holy Scriptures. She secretly got baptized and vowed to live as a virgin dedicated to God.

Barbara refused marriage proposals, including one from a rich young man, and during her father's absence, she had a third window added to a bathhouse to symbolize the Holy Trinity. She destroyed the idols in her tower and set crosses on the bathhouse basin and the tower. When her father returned, he was angry at her faith and virginity vow, beat her, and imprisoned her.

Her father reported her to Governor Martinianus, who tried to force her to worship idols. Barbara endured severe tortures, including whipping, being hit with nails, having her breasts cut off, and being led naked through the streets, during which God covered her with divine light. A girl named Juliana was moved by Barbara's faith and was also martyred alongside her. Eventually, Barbara and Juliana were beheaded, with Barbara's father executing her himself. Their bodies were placed in a church outside the city of Galatia. Barbara's father and the governor died shortly after. The water from the bathhouse basin with the cross was said to have healing powers. St. Barbara's body is now kept in a church named after her in Old Cairo, and some historians believe she was martyred in Heliopolis, Egypt. The Coptic Church celebrates her feast on the 8th of Kiahk [1][2][3][4].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barbara, pp. 298–299
passages.text:
Saint: BARBARA, ST. (The martyr) — Her Upbringing

Saint ‘Barbara’ has gotten great fame in the East and the West; she endured so much to hold dearly to her faith. The Coptic Church celebrates her feast on the 8th of Kiahk and the Western Church as well as the Greek Church on the 4th of December.

Her Upbringing:

She was born in the village of ‘Gamis’ near the city ‘Leopolis’ in ‘Nicomedia,’ at the beginning of the 3rd century AD, during the days of Emperor ‘Maximinus I’ (235-238 AD). Her father ‘Dioscorus’ was a firm believer in his pagan worship and strongly hated Christians.

On seeing how beautiful she was and worrying about the corruption of that time, her father built for her a high tower and surrounded it by guards, and filled it with idols and all kinds of entertainments. He also provided her with great teachers who cared for her advanced learnings.

‘Barbara’ having been a lover of meditation, she used to lift her eyes to look at the sun, the moon, and the stars, praising the God who created the earth with everything on it for the sake of humans.

One day, some of her Christian servants told her so many good things about ‘Origen,’ and she longed to meet him. And, when he eventually traveled to that area, somehow, she got the chance to see him. Talking to her about the Holy Scriptures, she came to love the Lord Christ with her whole heart. Then, without the knowledge of her father, she managed to get baptized. Having her heart inflamed with the love of God, she vowed her life for Him and longed to live as a virgin dedicating her life to worship.

Many proposed to marry her; among them was a rich young man, the son of a prince. Her father came to tell her about the good news, thinking that she would be exultant by it. However, she wisely declined the offer saying that she was not ready to get married. As her father was leaving the next day for business out of town, he postponed the whole issue until he would return, hoping that she would change her mind by then.

During this time, a luxurious bathhouse was being built at her father’s house. By his orders, the workers prepared to put two windows on the south side. But ‘Barbara,’ taking advantage of her father’s absence, asked them to make a third window, thereby forming a Trinity of light. She turned the bathhouse into a place to worship God with prayers, fasting, and unceasing watching the nights. She destroyed all the idols in her tower; set a cross on the basin of the bathhouse, as well as on the top of the tower.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barbara, pp. 299–300
passages.text:
Saint: BARBARA, ST. (The martyr) — Her Upbringing

She turned the bathhouse into a place to worship God with prayers, fasting, and unceasing watching the nights. She destroyed all the idols in her tower; set a cross on the basin of the bathhouse, as well as on the top of the tower.

And, as the doxology dedicated to her says: “The light of the Holy Trinity shone on that virgin St. ‘Barbara,’ the bride of Christ.”

Facing the Cruelty of her Father:

Returning from his trip, her father noticed all those changes in her and the place. Enquiring from her about the reason, she started preaching him the faith in the Holy Trinity, and how he should believe in the One God of the three Hypostasis. He rebuked her in great anger; however, she did not care for his reaction. And, she openly and declared her faith and told him about her intention of keeping her virginity. The father in a fury jumped on her, pulled her by the hair, and was about to strike her with his sword, but she escaped from him and ran through the gate of the palace. While chasing her, it was said that rock on her way split open to let her pass through it, then returned to its original form to block her chasing father. When he finally found her hidden in a cave, he jumped on her like a wolf on a lamb, violently beating her and put her in a dark dungeon in his palace.

Before Martinianus the Governor:

Her father ‘Dioscorus’ relayed the problem with his daughter to the governor ‘Martinianus,’ and sought from him to torture her. However, when the governor saw her great beauty, he fell in love with her. He rebuked her father for his cruelty, and he promised to bestow on her so many honors if she obeyed the creed of the emperor and worshipped the idols. But, she, with great courage, talked to him about her faith in Christ.

St. ‘Barbara’ was then whipped until her blood started pouring. They also tore her flesh by hitting her with sticks full of sharp nails. During that time, she kept silent and continued praying to her God. Then, they clothed her in rough sackcloth over her torn body full of wounds, and she was cast in a dark dungeon.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barbara, p. 300
passages.text:
Saint: BARBARA, ST. (The martyr) — Before Martinianus the Governor

During that time, she kept silent and continued praying to her God. Then, they clothed her in rough sackcloth over her torn body full of wounds, and she was cast in a dark dungeon.

While she was suffering from her wounds, the Lord Christ appeared to her in the dungeon, comforted her, and healed her completely.

When the governor called for her on the next day, he was astonished to find her exultant with no traces of any wounds on her body. He grew much more violent and sought from the executioners to comb her body with sharp iron combs, to put flames on her sides, and to cut off her breasts. Then, he ordered them viciously to lead her naked along the streets of the town. At this point, she cried out to the Lord to cover her nakedness, and God responded by engulfing her in Divine light.

On seeing her amid her incredible sufferings, a girl by the name of ‘Juliana’ bitterly cried; and the governor ordered to torture her along with St. ‘Barbara,’ and to cast them together in the same dungeon. There, they kept praying all night long.

Their Martyrdom:

Governor ‘Martinianus’ gave the command to cut the heads of the two saints by the sword. While being lead to the arena outside the city, they kept on praying. And once they arrived there, ‘Dioscorus’ sought from the governor to let him kill his daughter by himself, and he was allowed. So, both St. ‘Barbara’ and St. ‘Juliana’ finally received the crowns of martyrdom. Their bodies were placed in a church outside the city of ‘Galatia.' St. ‘Barbara's father perished shortly after their martyrdom, and so did the governor who tortured her. The water of the basin that had the cross over it in the bathhouse had the power to heal everyone who washed with it.

The body of St. ‘Barbara’ is kept now in a church under her name in Old Cairo. And, according to some historians, she might have been martyred in Heliopolis, Egypt.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Juliana, p. 468
passages.text:
Saint: JULIANA (The martyr)

St. Juliana (Yuliana) was present at the time when governor Marcianus was torturing St. Barbara in the days of Emperor Maximianus in the 3rd century AD. Juliana was so impressed, and believed in Christianity when she saw how the Lord Christ comforted and strengthened St. Barbara. Getting to know that Juliana converted to Christianity, governor Marcianus ordered cutting off her head on the 8th of the Coptic month of Kiahk. A church was built on the location where she was buried and was dedicated on the 26th of Kiahk. Her biography could be found together with that of St. Barbara under the letter ‘B’: St. Barbara.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barlaam, pp. 303–304
passages.text:
Saint: BARLAAM (The martyr)

He was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD). ‘Barlaam’ was a simple farmer from ‘Cappadocia Caesarea,’ who, by his faith, managed to testify to the Lord Jesus Christ before the rulers.

When the fire of persecution was inflamed, he was arrested along with a significant number of Christians. They were chained and brought forth to the court of justice. The judge asked him about his name, work, and faith, and he mocked the saint as an illiterate man who did not know much in his life except the bull that pulled his plow and the land he planted. On seeing how he held so fast to his faith, he threatened him by severe punishments, for which the poor man did not care.

‘Barlaam’ endured so many insults and whips, but remained silent. They tore his body with iron claws while he was very steady. They skinned him and cut off some of his members, without him losing his faith. Those present felt embarrassed before him, and they finally brought him over to the temple of idols, put incense on his hand, and placed his hand on the fire so that when the incense, drop from his hand and burn in the fire, he would look as though he offered incense to the idols, but they were amazed to see that he did not move his hand at all to keep the incense from dropping into the fire. All were terrified before such exalted bravery. He eventually fell unconscious, and his spirit departed from his battered body to fly in complete freedom to the heavenly Paradise.

The Greek Church celebrates his memorial on the19th of November.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barsaba, pp. 305–306
passages.text:
Saint: BARSABA, ST. (The martyr)

This saint was one of the men of God in the 4th century AD, the abbot of a group of 10 monks in the land of Persia.

At the beginning of the persecution, which was stirred up in the year 340 AD by the king of Persia ‘Shapur II’ (309-379 AD), that Father was put under arrest along with his monks. They were led in chains to the city of ‘Istakhr,’ near the remains of the city of ‘Persepolis.’

The governor of the province tried hard to make those men deny their Christ. He used every fierce mean against them, but he failed utterly. He found them consistently testifying to their Christ with joy. So, he issued his order to cut their heads off. The pagan mob became exulted while watching them being led to the arena of martyrdom.

It happened that a rich man was on his way out of the city with his family, and they passed by the execution arena. There, the rich man noticed how St. ‘Barsaba’ was getting hold of each of his men, to deliver them by himself one after the other to the swordsman, as though he was offering a sacrifice to God.

Suddenly, the rich man saw a splendid Cross shining over the bodies of the martyrs and his soul got enflamed to partake of their glories. He whispered in the saint's ear, and the later got hold of him and delivered him to the swordsman. Then, he went back to consummate his work with the rest of his men; then, with joy, he approached the swordsman.

On seeing that, the wife and children of the rich man hastened to have their portions with that holy congregation.

[Butler’s Lives of Saints, Dec. 20]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Soteris, the Virgin, pp. 186–187
passages.text:
Saint: SOTERIS, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This saint was the pride of her noble family of rulers and counsels, according to St. Ambrosius (Ambrose: 340-397 AD). She preferred to forsake her position, riches, beauty, and all her possessions in the world, for the sake of the Lord Christ. She granted her youth to God whom she loved; forsook all the pleasures of the world and got away from any potential risks she might face because of her beauty. After the decrees and laws issued by Emperors Diocletian and Maximilian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, she confessed her faith and was brought forth before the judges and rulers. During her trial, when the judge ordered to strike her on her face, she was delighted to be treated like her Savior. And, despite the many and diverse tortures she endured, she did not utter a word or shed any tears. And with time, before her steadfastness and perseverance, she was condemned to have her head cut off by the sword. This happened in the year 304 AD. It was not clear whether all the events of her torture occurred at the same time, or the saint was arrested and tortured while being a small girl during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD); then was martyred 50 years later during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

[Butler: February 19]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Merob, pp. 198–199
passages.text:
Saint: MEROB (The martyr)

The lady St. Merob was the wife of a pious man in Alexandria during the days of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD), who intended to bring an utter end to Christianity and the memory of martyred Christians by destroying their bodies. She bravely used to go to prison in the darkness of the night, pay generous bribes to the guards, to let her take the relics and bodies of the martyrs. Then, she used to keep them as precious jewels.

On hearing about what she was doing, the tyrant emperor ordered to put her under arrest and to bring her to trial. The judge charged her with three crimes, all of which were punishable by death: 3- Believing in Christianity as a forbidden religion. 4- Giving bribes to the guards over the bodies of the martyrs. 5- Opposing the civil authorities. The saint did not show any fear and did not deny her actions, but bravely proclaimed her faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and her care for the bodies of the holy martyrs. The judge condemned St. Merob to be scourged until death. Her hands and feet were tied with ropes to a post erected for this purpose. Then, she was scourged so violently that her flesh and blood scattered all over the place. All that was happening while she was praying to God, her Savior, in whose Hands she soon delivered her soul.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martha, p. 110
passages.text:
Saint: MARTHA (The martyr)

On the 9th of Baramhat, the Church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Martha and her husband, St. Anderianus. St. Eusebius, St. Erma, and 40 other martyrs were exposed first to severe torture in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ before their martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 9 Baramhat]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bertanuba, the Virgin, p. 347
passages.text:
Saint: BERTANUBA, THE VIRGIN, ST. (The martyr) — With the King of Persia

She asked Him to receive her life as a sacrifice of love before the pagan king would break her vow by defiling her and corrupting her chastity. Then, she joyfully entered into the fire to have her clothes stick to her body and to deliver her spirit without a hair burnt on her head.

When the saint did not come out of her room, the king's eunuchs went in looking for her, to find her as though fallen asleep amid the fire. They bitterly mourned her and did not dare to tell the king for some time. When the king came to realize what happened, he intensively lamented her, and because of his vow to her, he sent her body to her convent after clothing her in royal attire. When those who carried her body told the nuns about what happened, they glorified God on His work with her.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barsenophius, p. 307
passages.text:
Saint: BARSENOPHIUS, ST. (The martyr)

The Church celebrates the feast of the martyrdom of St. ‘Barsenophius’ (Warshenofius/Aurshenofa) on the 29th of Abib.

This saint was characterized by knowledge and piety. He went to live in seclusion in the wilderness to practice a life of peaceful asceticism. When his fame spread, he was sought to be ordained as a bishop, which he declined for fear of the temporal honor. He escaped to the town of ‘Tahmun’ (Galgamun/Dalgamun), where he took refuge in the house of a woman by the name of ‘Sofia’ with her two sons ‘Edmon’ and ‘Epistemon’ who were all living in fear and love of God. In a night vision, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and sought from him to go to the governor and confess the Lord Jesus Christ. Joyfully, he relayed that vision to the two brothers and their mother. When he was about to set forth to the governor, the two brothers insisted on going with him to partake of his crown. They set forth to the governor in ‘Balbil,’ where the three of them proclaimed their faith and suffered cruel torture. From there, they were sent to ‘Sanhur,’ where the mother ‘Sofia’ insisted on joining them in their strife. They were tortured and cast in prison, where the angel of the Lord came to encourage them. Then they were moved to the town of ‘Sa,’ where all the catechumen were gathered to listen to the decree of emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD), committing the believers to deny their Christ. Here, St. ‘Barsenophius’ zealously rushed toward the governor, snatched the decree from his hands, and tore it to pieces. In great anger, the governor ordered to put him in a big fiery furnace and kept torturing him until he received the crown of martyrdom on the 29th of Abib. Whereas, the two brothers and their mother preceded him in martyrdom on the 10th of Abib.

[O’Leary: The Saints of Egypt; pp. 210-211]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Edessa, pp. 124–125
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF EDESSA

In the days of Caesar Trajan (98-117 AD), there was a violent persecution against Christians in Edessa (El-Roĥa) in the Syrian section of Upper Mesopotamia. The bishop Barsimaeus (Barsamya) was arrested, violently tortured, and martyred in the year 114 AD. However, according to another version, he was only arrested but not killed; then, he was released after the persecution and later on reposed in peace.

Among those who were martyred was Sarbelius and his sister Barbea, who were baptized by the bishop Barsimaeus; and they were martyred during the persecution. Sarbelius in particular was viciously tortured because he was initially a pagan priest before he converted to Christianity.

The Church in the West celebrates those martyrs on the 30th of January.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. II, p. 41]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Barbasymas, the Bishop, pp. 300–301
passages.text:
Saint: BARBASYMAS, THE BISHOP, ST. (The martyr)

St. ‘Barbasymas’ (Barba'shmin) succeeded his brother St. ‘Shahdost’ as a bishop on the diocese of ‘Seleucia-Ctesiphon’ in the year 342 AD.

This saint was inflamed with zeal on faith and the care of God’s people, and this stirred up the devil to consider him of being an enemy of the Persian religion. By the command of the king ‘Shapur II’ (309-379 AD), he was called to deny his faith, along with 16 of his priests. Then, they were cast in a dark prison. Now and then, they were whipped and insulted, in addition to suffering hunger, thirst, and disgusting smell.

St. ‘Barbasymas’ and his companions endured the sufferings for 11 months, as though saying together with the apostle ‘Paul’: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35).

When they were called before the crowds, their appearance was so distorted and altered that no one could recognize any of them. The king presented the saint with a golden vessel containing 1,000 pieces of gold and promised to make him a governor if he worshipped the sun. The saint answered him that if he preferred gold or even the whole empire over His Holy Commandment, he would not be able to stand before the Lord Christ in the last day, nor would he endure His rebukes. The saint proclaimed his readiness to suffer death with joy for the sake of his Savior. All of them were then condemned to death by having their heads cut off on the 14th of January 346 AD in ‘Karka d’Ledan’ in ‘Beth Huzaye.'

[Asseman: Acts Martyrum Orientalium; I; pp. 111–116]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Burrier of Martyrs, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE BURRIER OF MARTYRS

This saint Theodora was a woman who dedicated her life and energy to serve the martyrs during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), And when the available cemeteries were all filled by the tombs of the martyrs; she had them buried in her land on Flaminian Way, about 26 miles from Rome. In that land, she hid the martyrs Abundius, the priest, Abundantius, the deacon, Marcianus, and Joannes.

The West celebrates this saint’s feast on the 17th of September.

[Henry Wace: A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Literature, Sects & Doctrines; 4 Vol.; London 1877-1887]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Encratis, p. 22
passages.text:
Saint: ENCRATIS (The martyr)

She was martyred in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) around the year 304 AD on the 16th of April, by Dacian the Governor. The Spanish Christian poet Prudentius used to boast that his city Saragossa delivered to paradise a significant number of martyrs, more than any other city in Spain. In a poem, he narrated the events of the martyrdom of St. Obthatius along with seventy others who testified to the Lord Jesus Christ in one day. When he mentioned those martyrs by name, he included a girl by the name of Encratia whom he called ‘The Girl on Fire’ and ‘The Girl with the Exalted Spirit,’ because she endured extraordinary wounds in her body. They broke her bones, pulled out her nails, cut off her breasts, opened up her belly, and dragged her intestine and liver out. Finally, her head was cut off to receive the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anastasia, pp. 175–176
passages.text:
Saint: ANASTASIA, ST. (The martyr)

This Saint was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD) around the year 250 AD, and celebrated by the Coptic Church on the 1st of Baba...

She was the daughter of Christian parents in Rome; they raised her in fear of God. Her heart was full of the Love of God, longing for the angelic life of virginity since her childhood. She joined a convent in Rome to practice the monastic life with firmness, eating food once every two days, and in the Great Lent only on Saturdays and Sundays.

When the mother-superior went to attend a feast in the city, she took with her the virgin Anastasia. In the town, they happened to see soldiers torturing some Christians. So, the virgin Anastasia stopped to rebuke them on their oppression and the hardness of their hearts. However, the soldiers arrested her and brought her forth to the governor. Before the governor, she confessed the Lord Christ. He tortured her severely, crucified her and ignited fire underneath her. And as she persisted in her faith, he ordered to cut her head off by the sword, for which she became exultant, prayed, and delivered her head to the swordsman to receive the crown of martyrdom.

records.question: Who was St. Paul the First Hermit?
records.answer:
St. Paul the First Hermit, also known as St. Paul of Thebes, was born in Alexandria around the year 228 AD. He inherited a great wealth from his father along with his older brother Peter, who tried to take the larger share by force. On his way to court to settle the dispute, Paul saw a wealthy man's funeral procession and realized that no one takes worldly possessions after death. This led him to despise temporal life and seek the eternal inheritance. He left the city and spent three days praying in a deserted tomb, after which an angel guided him to the wilderness in the East Desert, where he lived in solitude on Mount Nimra near the Red Sea for eighty years. During this time, he wore a tunic made of palm tree leaves and was sustained by half a loaf of bread daily, brought by a raven, along with dates, herbs, and water from a nearby spring [1].

St. Paul was known for his angelic life and great love of worship, particularly perpetual prayers and serious asceticism. His disciple Ezekiel reported that Paul faced death six times due to his harsh asceticism. Jesus Christ appeared to him, telling him to rest, but Paul replied that he wished to exhaust his body for the sake of God's name, as Christ did for mankind [3].

St. Anthony the Great, the father of monasticism, met St. Paul when he was 113 years old. Paul recognized Anthony by name and they spoke about God's works. At sunset, a raven brought a full loaf of bread instead of the usual half, confirming Anthony's divine mission. Before his death, Paul asked Anthony to bring him the priestly garment of St. Athanasius the Apostolic, which he used for burial. After Paul died in prayer on 2 Amshir, 343 AD, two lions helped dig his grave under Anthony's direction. Anthony then buried him and took the palm fiber garment to Pope Athanasius, who wore it annually on major feasts [1][2][5].

A monastery was later built at the site where St. Paul lived, dedicated to joyful praise of the Lord [2].

In summary, St. Paul the First Hermit was the first Christian hermit, living a life of solitude and prayer in the desert for eighty years, sustained miraculously by God, and recognized by St. Anthony the Great as a man of God [1][2][3][5].
