passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 382–383
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — His Upbringing

Through Divine care, St. Abba Anthony the Great the Father of the Monastic family and its founder in the whole world, encountered this St. Paul who preceded him by long years in monastic life in the wilderness, where no one but God knew anything about him. God kept sustaining him by half a loaf of bread, carried to him by a raven every day all along many decades; in which God smelled the sweet fragrance of his prayers and praise, to call him: “My beloved Paul.”

His Upbringing:

St. Paul the 1st hermit was born in Alexandria around the year 228 AD. His father passed away leaving a great wealth for him and for his older brother Peter. However, Peter conspired to acquire the greater portion of the inheritance for himself, and when the disagreement escalated between the two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court. However, on his way to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened to be passing by. St. Paul asked himself: “Has that rich man taken anything from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he totally despised the temporal life. His heart was so inflamed with the Eternal inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking the Divine guidance.

Then, an angel appeared to St. Paul and guided him to the wilderness in the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea. There he lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven. The saint lived all that time on that bread with some dates from the palm trees or herbs from the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul of Tamouh, pp. 380–381
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL OF TAMOUH, ST. ABBA

The Coptic Church celebrates the feast of this saint on the 7th of Baba, and seeks his prayers in the commemoration of the saints in the Liturgy, along with St. Ezekiel his disciple.

After the devastation of the wilderness of the Scetis around the year, 408 AD; St. Abba Bishoi fled the area and went to mount Anesna in Upper Egypt. There, he met with Abba Paul the Hermit and they both had an amazing spiritual friendship, that an angel appeared to St. Paul, saying: “Your body will be with that of Abba Bishoi.” (The two bodies are still together in one tube in the Monastery of Abba Bishoi up to this very day). It was said that later on when the bishop of Anesna decided to move the body of Abba Bishoi; his boat did not move until a hermit named Jeremiah told them about the promise of the Lord to Abba Paul, so they brought the body of Abba Paul to the boat and they moved them together to the Monastery of Abba Shenouda in Akhmim. Later on, the bodies of these two saints were moved again together in the days of the 52nd Pope Yusab I in the 9th century (831- 849 AD) to the Monastery of Abba Bishoi in the Scetis. The bodies of the two saints were kept in one tube; and this is a testimony of the spiritual friendship full of love that bound the two saints together; that even death could not separate them. This is not on the level of this mortal world but the level of the Eternal glory of both the body and the soul.

Abba Paul was known for his great love of worship, particularly for the perpetual prayers, as well as his serious asceticism, that his disciple Ezekiel told about him that he faced death six times because of his harsh asceticism.

He lived in solitude as a hermit, in perpetual strife, that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him saying: “Enough labor, My beloved Paul”. St. Abba Paul answered Him: “O my Master, let me exhaust my body for the sake of Your Name; as You have done for the sake of mankind. Even though You are God, You delivered Yourself for our sake, we who are unworthy.”

[O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt; p. 223-4]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paul, the Monk, p. 384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE MONK

About Abba Ur (Hur), we know that he had a disciple by the name of Paul (Boulus) who cared much for the life of prayers, even though he misunderstood its meaning. He considered his prayers as a race to recite the greatest number of church praises. He was eventually corrected by St. Macarius.

About him it was said: He did not approach the hard handworks or the assignments of selling and buying; except for the little things he eats every day. However, he was very advanced in one thing, which was praying without ceasing. He set for himself a rule; to pray 300 prayers every day. He used to put some little pebbles in his pocket, and then he used to hold in his hand one of them for every prayer he prayed. One day, he came to St. Macarius, saying: “Father, I am very sad.” When the elder monk asked him the reason for his anguish, he answered: “I heard about a virgin who spent thirty years of her monastic life, reciting 500 prayers every day. On hearing that, I despised myself, for I am not able to pray more than 300 prayers every day.”

Here, St. Abba Macarius told him: “I lived for sixty years in the monastic life, reciting only fifty prayers every day; worked for what was enough to earn my need of food; and received the brethren who come to seek my counsel. Now, here you are who pray 300 prayers every day, condemned by your thoughts. You probably, either do not pray them with purity; or you can do more of other things and you do not want to.”

[The Diocese of Beni-Suef: The Garden of Monks; pp. 24-25]

[Budge: The Paradise, vol. 2, art. 356]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Nofer, the Hermit Anchorite, pp. 312–313
passages.text:
Saint: NOFER, THE HERMIT ANCHORITE, ST. — Among his Words to Abba Paphnutius

Among his Words to Abba Paphnutius:

• Longing daily, to live a life of seclusion with God, I felt that I want to separate from all, to unify with the Great Holy One without limit. Therefore, I decided to forsake the monastery and set forth deep into the inner wilderness, to the depth with Jesus. • God made the wild beasts come to be friendly and company with me day and night. Whenever and wherever I went, they used to follow me, as though guarding me. In that way, I lived all along those years, glorifying God for His planning and His goodness for the sake of the salvation of my soul.

[The Faithful Synaxarion: 16 Paona] [Amir Nasr: The Two Hermits: Abba Nofer and Abba Timothy, 1989] [Melika Habib Yousef and Yousef Habib: St. Abba Nofer the Anchorite; 1970] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Onophrius-Saint, by René-Georges Coquin; pp. 1841-2]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paul, the Simple, p. 385
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST.

This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer who got married to a very beautiful girl. After living together for so many years, he started to take notice of so many rumors about his wife's evil behavior. However, whenever he inquired from her about the matter, she would pretend to be a pure woman. Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the evil act. On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples.

Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age. Before his persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in the valley to practice with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not leaving that mountain.

Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance, and obedience. Among those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching him lest he would collapse. He sought from him to remain a whole week outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, to loosen it and weave it anew. In all that he was obedient, worked with joy and extreme simplicity.

On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Karas, the Hermit Saint, p. 489
passages.text:
Saint: KARAS, THE HERMIT SAINT — Abba Karas Enters into the Wilderness

The biography of St. Abba Karas (Cyrus) presents a living portrait of a great example of the Hermit Fathers. Reaching the rank of a "monastic Pilgrimage" is achieved only by the prominent support of God’s grace to the striving ascetic to enjoy an exceedingly exalting level of union with God.

Abba Karas lived 57 years, during which he did not see any human face. Finally, St. Bambu (Bemwa/Bamu/Bambunius) found him and got to know him. And, St. Bambu was the one who shrouded St. Karas and buried him. Then, he documented a few lines about his biography, which nobody could know its mysteries other than those who have experienced it themselves.

The Spiritual Elder (St. John of Dalyatha/Saba) (690-780 AD) in the 8th century was contemplating to God about those great hermits saying, “Those on whom You have shone Your Love Spark; were not able to endure the dwelling among humans.”

Abba Karas Enters into the Wilderness:

Getting to know the corruption and the impending mortality of the world, St. Karas, the brother of Emperor Theodosius II (402-450 AD), forsook everything and set forth to an unknown location, to be guided by God to the inner western wilderness, where he spent many years in seclusion, seeing neither men nor beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paphnutius, the Hermit, p. 362
passages.text:
Saint: PAPHNUTIUS, THE HERMIT, ST.

He was the head of a little congregation of monks at Heracleoplis (Ahnasia, in Upper Egypt).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, the Hermit, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA

The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ The three of them were considered among the first monks who became disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite).

He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his prayers day and night. He was also known for his love of the book of the prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books of the prophets).

Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders appeared.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Patra, p. 377
passages.text:
Saint: PATRA, ABBA

Abba Patra was one of the early Fathers of the wilderness of the Scetis. He was a close friend of Abba Ambicus. Probably, he was the same Abba Patra mentioned by the fathers Selwanus and Lot. These two saints put him on the same spiritual level as the great Fathers Bamu (Bambu), Aghathon, and John.

[Budge: The Paradise, Vol. 2, p. 115, 207]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Badaba, p. 287
passages.text:
Saint: BADABA, ABBA (The martyr) — Their Monastic Life

This saint was born in the city of ‘Armant’ in the governorate of ‘Qena,’ to a pious family; his father was called ‘Mina.’ The name ‘Badaba’ is derived from the Hieroglyphic word ‘Batby’: meaning (the principal/the essential) and from the Coptic word ‘Bataby’: meaning (related to the head).

A strong friendship developed between this saint and his cousin ‘Andrew,’ who was two years older. Since their childhood, both carried the same love for the heavenly Kingdom; they encountered one another on the level of the spirit, despised the pleasures of the world, concentrated on the study of the Holy Scriptures and religious books, used to fast two consecutive days with no food or drink, in addition to praying day and night.

Their Monastic Life:

They set forth together to the Eastern mountain at ‘Qasr el-Sayyad’ in the district of 'Nagh Hamadi.' There, they became disciples of St. abba ‘Isaac’ and dwelt in a cell where they performed their spiritual practices. They took upon themselves to copy down the religious manuscripts for their spiritual benefit and to sell them for little money to cover their living expenses and to give what was left to the poor.

As the sweet fragrance of Christ spread from them, their cell became a center of spiritual radiation. Abba ‘Tadros,’ the bishop of the area, came to them and ordained St. ‘Badaba’ as a priest and Andrew as a deacon. They used to perform the holy Liturgy once every forty days in a neighboring church.

It so happened that abba ‘Tadros’ once entered into that church, and he saw the face of St. ‘Badaba’ shining with an amazing splendor and a crown as though of gold on his head. So, he longed to have him and deacon ‘Andrew’ to stay with him in the diocese. However, St. ‘Badaba’ excused himself and returned to his cell, whereas ‘Andrew’ consented to do so. And, when St. ‘Badaba’ perceived that everyone was chasing him, he fled away from his cell, which the bishop dedicated as a church, later on.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon of Thebes, p. 159
passages.text:
Saint: AMON OF THEBES, ABBA

St. Jerome wrote about Abba Amon, whom he saw in the region of Thebes (nowadays: Luxor) in Egypt. He was ahead of 3000 monks who lived together in life more like a life of seclusion, rather than a life of Cenobite. His group was called ‘the Men of Tabenna,' and most probably, they were living in a Pachomian monastery in ‘Tabennisi.' St. Jerome mentioned that while they were having their meals, they used to cover their faces (by their head cover). Also, they perpetually looked down to the ground, so that no one of them would see his brother. They lived in utter silence, as though in the wilderness. Each of them was hiding his refined ascetic life from his fellows.

St. Jerome mentioned that they were sitting at the meal table just as a matter of appearance, while each of them trying to appear as though he was eating. Some lower his hand down to the plate and bring it back empty; while they ate no more than a morsel of bread, one olive or a little bit of the food in front of them, even though the food before them was enough for them all. Their souls indeed have despised everything worldly. St. Jerome says, “We were amazed by, and had benefited from their glorified work and their style of monasticism."

[Budge: The Paradise; Vol. 1; p. 336]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, p. 160
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

He was the founder of the monastic movement in ‘Nitria’ (Bernoug). Here, we need to distinguish between three monastic zones within the Natron Valley (Wadi El-Natrun) which often get mixed up:

1- The ’Nitria’ (Bernoug) zone, which received the first spark of the monastic movement through Abba Amon. 2- The ‘Celia’ (the Cells) zone, which is about 10 miles south of the ‘Nitria’ zone. 3- The ‘Scetis’ (Askeet) zone, which is located to the south of the former two zones.

His Monastic Life:

Saint Amon the great was born around the year 275 AD near the region of Marriott. He was raised as an orphan, and when he reached 22 years of age, his uncle forced him to get married despite his refusal. When he got married, he and his bride agreed on living virgins. Eighteen years later, the saint set forth to the desert of ‘Nitria’ (the city of Nitria or Bernoug is 14 kilometers Southwestern of the city of Damanhur). He was the first monk to reach that area, and he built for himself a cell there, in which he lived for 22 years. During that time, he used twice a year to visit his wife, who was living with many pious virgins. The location of the ‘Nitria’ zone was convenient to be the cradle of the commencement of that monastic movement. That area was close to the countryside and to the desert at the same time. In the beginning, the monks, who followed St. Amon, worked to earn their living by cropping the wheat, and it was easy for them also to acquire the linen to weave, instead of the palm leaves. The area also provided them with the ‘Natron’, which they could extract from the lake and sell to the villages around them. However, the region was always infested by mosquitos because of its swamps.

A congregation of hermits started to gather around the saint. They all lived in a life midway between the system of seclusion and that of the cenobite. Abba Amon was the first head of such a monastic congregation in Nitria, and many of his disciples became great fathers. Abba Amon used to visit Abba Anthony to seek his blessing and guidance. And when Abba Anthony came to visit him, he asked his advice concerning some pious monks, who tried to live a solitary life and build for themselves cells far away from the congregation. After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abu Fana, pp. 78–79
passages.text:
Saint: ABU FANA, ST. — His Life as a Monk

St. ‘Abu- Fana’ or ‘Epiphanius’ lived in the days of the Emperor Theodosius the Great. He practiced the life of solitude in the Western Desert, in the province of ‘El-Ashmonein.' He lived in a cave in which he shot himself in to contemplate. Despite his strict asceticism, he did not cease to practice the handwork to give to the poor. He also cared to counsel the brethren, and God granted him the gift of performing miracles. In other words, his solitude was founded on an open heart full of love for God and men. His disciple ‘Ephraim’ gave us a concise account of his life.

His Life as a Monk:

The saint was born to Christian parents; they raised him on the fear of the Lord. He grew loving the life of seclusion and contemplation, together with his love for the needy.

While still a young man, he spent a lot of time among the monks and was trained on the ascetic life and the handwork to be able to give alms to the poor. When he became a monk, his love for solitude grew stronger that he lived in a very dark cave, where God granted him a fountain of water to drink from. He trained himself on fasting, by eating once a day in summer and once every two days in winter. He practiced the perpetual prayers and was making 300 metanoias by day and 300 by night until his skin stuck to his bones and came to be as a burnt stick.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abahor, the Monk, p. 29
passages.text:
Saint: ABAHOR, THE MONK, ST.

This father from ‘Abraht’ in the area of the ‘Ashmonein,’ was an elect monk who surpassed many saints in his worship. Loving solitude and living alone in the wilderness, he was envied by the devil who appeared to him and said: “In the wilderness, you can overcome me because you are there alone, but I challenge you if you are brave, go to Alexandria." He instantly set forth to Alexandria, where he stayed sometimes serving the prisoners.

It so happened that some horses were galloping in midtown, and one of them knocked down a little kid who instantly died. As St. Abahor was standing at the place where that incident took place, the devil provoked some people around to shout aloud, claiming that it was the old monk who killed him. When many started to revile and to scoff him, St. Abahor calmly took the kid to his bosom, prayed in his heart to the Lord Christ, and then made the sign of the cross on him. The kid came back to life, and he gave him to his parents. Those around him glorified God and started to make it up to the old monk, who, fearing from the vainglory, he fled to the wilderness, where he dwelt for days in a monastery.

When it was time for him to depart from this world, he saw a group of saints calling him to join them, for which he greatly rejoiced, became joyful, called his spiritual disciples to inform them that he will soon depart to the Lord Christ, and provided them with his last commandment. Hearing that, they much grieved that they will be orphans after his departure. He felt sick for a little while, and then he delivered his soul in the Lord’s hand.

[The Synaxarion: 2 Kiahk]

records.question: What is prayer, and why does God sometimes delay answering it?
records.answer:
Prayer is the conversation or converse with God, a way to speak boldly and inwardly with Him even in silence, as God continually hears the inward converse of the heart [10][16]. It is a means to keep the relationship between God and the person alive and effective, offered from a pure and unsoiled heart, with trust in God's love, wisdom, and will, and beginning with thanksgiving [2]. Prayer is also described as a remedy against grief and depression, a privilege to converse with God as sons with a father, and a powerful weapon when offered from a pure heart and accompanied by good deeds [5][10][16].

God sometimes delays answering prayers so that the person’s zeal and desire to approach Him may increase, and so that the gift received may be more appreciated and carefully guarded [1]. The delay also shows the value of God's good things, as things long desired are obtained with greater pleasure, while those given quickly are held cheap [1]. Sometimes God refuses requests because they are opposed to the person’s salvation, as He sees what is truly good for us better than we do [1]. Also, the delay or lack of answer can be because the prayer is not connected with abiding in Christ or His words, or because the request is inappropriate, lacking faith, or offered negligently [1][4]. Sometimes the lack of an answer is preferable to the prayer being answered [2]. God’s grace is sufficient, and strength is made perfect in weakness, as shown in the example of St. Paul who prayed thrice but was told, "My grace is sufficient for you" [1][7].

In summary, prayer is a heartfelt conversation with God that sustains our relationship with Him, and delays in answering are part of God's loving providence to increase our faith, protect us from harm, and bring about what is truly good for our salvation [1][2][4][7][10][16].

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q900 “Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He sometimes not answer them at all?”, pp. 23–24
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 900. Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He sometimes not answer them at all?

St. Basil the Great says, “It may be that He delays answering a prayer so that your zeal and your desire to approach Him may be multiplied, and that you may appreciate the gift of God and guard it carefully when you have received it. That which a person receives with great effort, he strives to protect, lest in losing it his labor will have been in vain.”

St. Augustine says, “He, who was not willing to give [the unjust judge in Luke 18:2], gave what was asked, because the other did not faint in asking. How much more then shall that Good One give who exhorts us to ask, who is displeased if we ask not? But when at times He gives somewhat slowly, it is that He is showing us the value of His good things; not that He refuses them. Things which have been long desired, are obtained with the greater pleasure, whereas those which are given quickly, are held cheap.”

“Some things, indeed, we wish because we are in Christ, and other things we desire because still in this world … Abiding, therefore, ourselves in Him, when His words abide in us we shall ask what we will, and it shall be done unto us. For if we ask, and the doing follows not, what we ask is not connected with our abiding in Him, nor with His words which abide in us, but with that craving and infirmity of the flesh which are not in Him, and have not His words abiding in them. For to His words, at all events, belongs that prayer which He taught, and in which we say, Our Father, who art in heaven (Matt. 6:9). Let us only not fall away from the words and meaning of this prayer in our petitions, and whatever we ask, it shall be done unto us … But when His words abide only in the memory, and have no place in the life, the branch is not to be accounted as in the vine, because it draws not its life from the root.”

Abba Isaac, the disciple of St. Anthony, says, “We sometimes ask for things opposed to our salvation and that we are most providentially refused our requests by Him who sees what is good for us with greater right and truth than we can. And it is clear that this also happened to the teacher of the Gentiles when he prayed that the messenger of Satan who had been for his good allowed by the Lord’s will to buffet him, might be removed, saying: ‘For which I besought the Lord thrice that he might depart from me. And He said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness’ (2 Cor. 12:8– 9).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q898 “How can we offer prayer that is acceptable before God?”, p. 22
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 898. How can we offer prayer that is acceptable before God?

The purpose of prayer is to keep the relationship between God and the person alive and effective. Therefore, we should consider the following when we pray:

a. Trust in God who has complete love for humanity, ability, wisdom, and knowledge (cf. Col. 2:2; Eccl. 8:17).

b. Pray for the will of God in every matter, for He is the Pantocrator: “Thy will be done” (Matt. 6:10).

c. Offer prayer from a heart that is unsoiled and pure.

d. Begin every prayer with thanksgiving for the things that God has granted us, for there is no gift that is not increased except that which is received without thanksgiving, according to St. Isaac the Syrian.

e. Believe in the verse that says, “Unless the lord builds the house, they labor in vain who built it” (Ps. 127:1).

f. Acknowledge that divine grace works in synergy with human striving. The Lord saved the child Moses and at the same time He rewarded the two midwives for ignoring pharaoh’s evil decree (Ex. 1:20).

St. Basil the Great says, “There are conditions for a prayer to be answered: it must be according to the will of God (Matt. 26:39); we must be steadfast and persistent (Luke 11:8); we must realize that God’s wants us to reform our conduct, which is much more important than answering our prayers (Isa. 1:15); we must be aware of our unworthiness of that for which we ask (1 Chron. 17:4) or the unworthiness of those for whom we pray (Jer. 14:11); and that sometimes the lack of an answer to prayer is preferable to it being answered (2 Cor. 12:7) … If all these conditions are met, then there is no doubt that God will answer our prayers.”

Abba Zeno says, “If a man wants God to hear his prayer quickly, then before he prays for anything else, even his own soul, when he stands and stretches out his hands towards God, he must pray with all his heart for his enemies. Through this action God will hear everything that he asks.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q902 “What practical steps lead us to practice prayer?”, p. 29
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 902. What practical steps lead us to practice prayer?

Without doubt, He knows, and He gives us abundantly all temporal things even before we ask. However, we should first ask for the things that are good and for the kingdom of heaven, and thereafter we receive what we desire; but let us ask patiently and faithfully, ask for what is good for us, and let us not hinder our prayers by disobeying our consciences.”

St. Cyril the Great says, “It is our duty therefore to ‘pray without ceasing’ (1 Thess. 5:7), according to the words of the blessed Paul, as well knowing, and being thoroughly assured, that He Whom we supplicate is able to accomplish all things. ‘For let a man’ it says, ‘ask in faith, in nothing divided: for he who is divided is like a wave of the sea, troubled and blown about by the wind. For let not,’ it says, ‘that man think that he will receive anything of the Lord’ (James 1:6–9) … for if you do not believe that He will incline unto you, and gladden you, and fulfill your request, do not draw near to Him at all … But that God will incline His ear to those who offer Him their prayers, not carelessly nor negligently, but with earnestness and constancy, the present parable assures us. For if the constant coining of the oppressed widow prevailed upon the unjust judge, who feared not God, neither had any shame at men, so that even against his will he granted her redress (Luke 18:1–8), how shall not He Who loves mercy, and hates iniquity, and Who ever gives His helping hand to them that love Him, accept those who draw near to Him day and night, and avenge them as being His elect?”

Fifth: Leave matters in God’s hands. St. Augustine believes that the secret behind God answering David’s prayers and giving ear to the words of his mouth (Ps. 54:2) is that David surrendered matters into God’s hands; leaving decisions in His hands: “For sick you are; do not dictate to the physician the medicines he may choose to set beside you. If the teacher of the Gentiles, Paul the Apostle, says, ‘For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought’ (Rom. 8:26) how much more we?” He again says, “Let not a sick man draw back from the hands of the physician, let him not give advice to the physician. So it is with all these things temporal.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q902 “What practical steps lead us to practice prayer?”, pp. 28–29
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 902. What practical steps lead us to practice prayer?

Not at all is God in need of glory, but He wishes you to be worthy of winning glory. Therefore, ‘What a man sows, he will also reap’ (Gal. 6:7). Sow glorification, that you may reap crowns and honors and praises in the kingdom of heaven. This statement, ‘In his temple all shall seek his glory,’ was made not unfittingly in a digression, because some in the temple of God talk endlessly until their tongue aches; and these enter without profit. Would that it might be only without profit and not with harm!”

Fourth: Be earnest in prayer with faith and flee the distractions of the thoughts. St. Basil says, “We ought to pray for divine help, not with laziness or a scattered mind here and there. Such a person not only fails to receive what he asks, but even angers God. If a person stands before a ruler, his eyes are steady, inside and out, for fear of punishment; how much more should we stand before the Lord with alertness and awe? But if you are beset by a certain sin, you will not be able to pray steadily and with all your strength. Examine yourself, so that whenever you stand before God, your thoughts are fixed on Him, and God will forgive you; for it is not out of negligence, but out of weakness that you are unable to be present before Him as you ought. If you commit yourself to this, you will not leave Him until you receive. If you do not receive what you ask, this is because your request was inappropriate or lacking in faith, or because you offered your prayer negligently, or because you ask for things that are not good for you, or because you ceased from praying. Oftentimes, people ask: Why do we pray? Is God ignorant of our needs? Without doubt, He knows, and He gives us abundantly all temporal things even before we ask. However, we should first ask for the things that are good and for the kingdom of heaven, and thereafter we receive what we desire; but let us ask patiently and faithfully, ask for what is good for us, and let us not hinder our prayers by disobeying our consciences.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q901 “What are the effects of prayer?”, pp. 25–26
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 901. What are the effects of prayer?

Should my prayers ascend on high, my enemies would perish, and the righteous person would stand firm (Wisd. of Sol. 5:1); the net would be broken, and the bird would be liberated and fly freely (Ps. 124:7); the oppressors would bow their heads, and the oppressed would rejoice (Matt. 5:10–12).”

Second: Prayer propagates the spirit of inner joy. St. Cyril the Great says, “For it is, I affirm, the duty of those who set apart their lives for His service, not to be sluggish in their prayers, nor again to consider it as a hard and laborious duty: but rather to rejoice, because of the freedom of access granted them by God; for He would have us converse with Him as sons with a father. Is not this then a privilege worthy of being valued by us most highly? For suppose that some one of those possessed of great earthly power were easy of access to us, and were to permit us to converse with him with full license, should we not consider it as a reason for extraordinary rejoicing? What possible doubt can there be of this? When therefore God permits us each one to offer our addresses unto Him for whatever we wish, and has set before those who fear Him an honor so truly great and worthy of their gaining, let all slothfulness cease that would lead men to an injurious silence therein; and rather let us draw near with praises, and rejoicing that we have been commanded to converse with the Lord and God of all, having Christ as our Mediator, who with God the Father grants us the accomplishment of our supplications. For the blessed Paul somewhere writes, ‘Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ’ (2 Cor. 1:2). And He somewhere Himself said to the holy apostles, ‘Hitherto you have asked nothing in My Name: ask, and it shall be given unto you’ (John 16:24). For He is our Mediator, our Propitiation, our Comforter, and the Bestower of every request.”

St. Nilus of Sinai says, “Prayer is a remedy against grief and depression.” “Do not grieve if you do not at once receive from God that which you ask. He wishes to benefit you still more by making you persist longer in your patient prayer before Him. For what can be higher than to address one’s converse to God and be in communion with Him?”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q918 “What is the connection between prayer and purity of heart?”, pp. 38–39
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 918. What is the connection between prayer and purity of heart?

Pope Gregory the Great was known for his love of the writings of the Eastern Fathers such as St. Athanasius and St. Cyril the Great, and thus he organized a group to translate their writings from Greek to Latin. He says:

“Now if we thoroughly wipe away these two [hands’ iniquity and wickedness in the tabernacle], we then directly ‘lift our face without spot’ to God. For the soul is the inner face of man, by which same we are known, that we may be regarded with love by our Maker. Now we are to lift up this same face, to raise the soul in God by appliance to the exercises of prayer. But there is a spot that pollutes the uplifted face, when consciousness of its own guilt accuses the mind intent; for it [the soul] is forthwith dashed from all confidence of hope, if when busied in prayer it be stung with recollection of sin not yet subdued. For it distrusts its being able to obtain what it longs for, in that it bears in mind its still refusing to do what it has heard from God. Hence it is said by John, Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God; and whatsoever we ask we shall receive of Him (1 John 3:21–22). Hence Solomon says, He that turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination (Prov. 28:9). For our heart blames us in offering up our prayers, when it calls to mind that it is set in opposition to the precepts of Him, Whom it implores.”

“For they make their prayer to God, but never obtain to be listened to, who set at nought the precepts of the Lord, when He enjoins them. Whence it is written: He that turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination (Prov. 28:9). So long then as Eliphaz believed that blessed Job was not heard, he determined that that person had surely done wrong in his practice.”

“God in his justice rejects iniquity, and does not accept sin (Job 14:17), but since He ministers our salvation, He longs for man, the work of His hands. In the midst of distress, Job cries out to God but it is as though God cannot hear him. However, when it is time for the resurrection, God will call him to rise and Job will answer; thus he encounters God who longs for the work of His hands, for Job will bear the reflection of the glory of God upon him.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q900 “Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He sometimes not answer them at all?”, p. 24
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 900. Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He sometimes not answer them at all?

And He said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness’ (2 Cor. 12:8– 9).”

Pope Gregory the Great says, “why is it that Paul three times besought the Lord and did not merit to be heard, but was told: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9). Did the great preacher not ask in the name of the Son? Then why didn’t he receive what he asked? … The Son’s name is Jesus. Jesus means ‘saviour’ or ‘saving.’ One who asks in the Saviour’s name asks what pertains to actual salvation. If what he asks for is not for his good he is not asking the Father in Jesus’ name. Hence the Lord says to his apostles while they were still weak, Up to now you have asked nothing in my name (John 16:24) … That is the reason too why Paul was not heard. If he had been freed from temptation it would not have been of help to his salvation … consider your requests, I beseech you, and see if you are asking in the name of Jesus, if you are asking for the joys of eternal salvation … Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be given you as well (Matt. 6:33).”

Notes: [49] See St. Basil of Caesarea, Const. Mon. 1 (PG 31:1325–1338). [50] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament 11.6 (NPNF I/6:296) amended. [51] St. Augustine of Hippo, Lectures or Tractates on the Gospel According to St. John 81.4 (NPNF I/7:346) amended. [52] St. John Cassian, The Conferences 9.34 (NPNF II/11:399). [53] Gregory the Great, Forty Gospel Homilies, trans., Dom David Hurst (Kalamazoo, Michigan: Cistercian Publications, 1990) 27: pp. 216–217.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q918 “What is the connection between prayer and purity of heart?”, p. 39
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 918. What is the connection between prayer and purity of heart?

In the midst of distress, Job cries out to God but it is as though God cannot hear him. However, when it is time for the resurrection, God will call him to rise and Job will answer; thus he encounters God who longs for the work of His hands, for Job will bear the reflection of the glory of God upon him.”

“You shall call me, and I will answer You (Job 14:15) … For now so long as we are subject to corruption, we do not in any wise ‘answer’ our Creator, seeing that whereas corruption is far from incorruption, there is no similarity suitable to our answering. But of that change it is written When He shall appear, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is (1 John 3:2). Then therefore we shall truly ‘answer God,’ Who ‘calls,’ when at the bidding of the Supreme Incorruption we shall arise incorruptible; and because the creature is not able to earn this by itself, but it is brought to pass by the gift of Almighty God alone, that it should be changed to that exceeding glory of incorruption, it is rightly subjoined: You will stretch forth Your right hand to the work of Your hands.

“As if he said in plain words; ‘For this reason Your corruptible creature is able to hold fast unto incorruption, because he is lifted up by the hands of Your power, and is kept by the grace of Your regard, that he should hold fast.’ For the human creature by this alone, that it is a creature, has it inherent in itself to sink down below itself, but man has obtained it from his Creator, that he should both be caught above himself by contemplation, and held fast in himself by incorruption [cf. 1 Cor. 15:53]. And so that the creature may not fall away beneath himself, but hold on in incorruption, he is lifted to the steadfastness of immutability by the right hand of His Maker … who can estimate the bountifulness of Divine Mercy, that He should bring man after sin to such a height of glory? God takes account of the bad things we do, yet by the grace of His lovingkindness He remits them to us in mercy. And hence it is added; For now You number my steps, but You spare my sins (Job 14:16).”

Notes: [107] Gregory the Great, Morals on the Book of Job 1.10.27 (LFHCC 18:599) amended. [108] Gregory the Great, Morals on the Book of Job 1.16.26 (LFHCC 21:241). [109] Gregory the Great, Morals on the Book of Job 1.12.18–19 (LFHCC 21:56–58).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q898 “How can we offer prayer that is acceptable before God?”, pp. 22–23
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 898. How can we offer prayer that is acceptable before God?

Abba Zeno says, “If a man wants God to hear his prayer quickly, then before he prays for anything else, even his own soul, when he stands and stretches out his hands towards God, he must pray with all his heart for his enemies. Through this action God will hear everything that he asks.”

“Abba Macarius was asked, ‘How should one pray?’ The old man said, ‘There is no need at all to make long discourses; it is enough to stretch out one’s hands and say, “Lord, as you will, and as you know, have mercy.” And if the conflict grows fiercer say, “Lord, help!” He knows very well what we need and he shews us his mercy.’”

Abba Isaac says, “For so far will one be heard and obtain an answer, as he believes that he is regarded by God, and that God can grant it. For this saying of our Lord cannot be retracted: ‘Whatsoever you ask when you pray, believe that you shall receive, and they shall come to you’ (Mark 11:24).”

St. John Cassian says, “He is quite certain that his prayers will not be answered. Who is this wretch? It is he who prays and does not believe that he will receive an answer.”

Notes: [44] St. Basil of Caesarea, Regulae Brevis Tractatae (The Short Rules) 261 (PG 31:1257–1258). [45] Ward, Benedicta. The Sayings of the Desert Fathers: The Alphabetical Collection, trans., Benedicta Ward (Liturgical Press, 1984) Zeno 7: p. 65. [46] Ward, Benedicta. The Sayings of the Desert Fathers: The Alphabetical Collection, trans., Benedicta Ward (Liturgical Press, 1984) Macarius the Great 19: p. 131. [47] St. John Cassian, The Conferences 9.32 (NPNF II/11:398) amended.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q947 “What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?”, p. 79
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Prayer of the Mind and Contemplation — 947. What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?

St. Clement of Alexandria says, “Prayer is, then, to speak more boldly, converse with God. Though whispering, consequently, and not opening the lips, we speak in silence, yet we cry inwardly. For God hears continually all the inward converse.”

St. Aphrahat says, “Again our Savior taught the prayer and said, ‘You should pray secretly to the Hidden One; He sees everything’ (Matt. 6:6). For he said, ‘Enter the inner chamber and pray secretly to your Father, and the Father who sees in secret will reward you’ (Matt. 6:6). But why, my beloved, did our Savior teach and say, ‘Pray to your Father in secret with the door closed?’ I will explain this to you as much as I have understood. For he said, ‘Pray to your Father in secret with the door closed.’ What is the door that he said to close? If not your mouth, which is (the door to) the temple in which Christ dwells as the Apostle said, ‘You are the temple of the Lord’ (1 Cor. 3:16), for him to enter into your inner man, to this house, cleanse it from everything that is unclean, while the door, that is your mouth, is to be closed. If that was not so, how would you understand this matter? For if it happens to you that you were in a land, and there is no house and door, would you not pray in secret? Or if it happens to you again that you were on the top of a mountain, would you not pray?

“And our Savior showed this that God knows the will of the heart and of the thought, just as our Lord said, ‘Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him’ (Matt. 6:8). It is written in the prophet Isaiah, ‘Before they who were chosen by me call, I will hear them, and before they make the cry I will answer them’ (Isa. 65:24). Isaiah said again about the wicked, ‘Even though you multiply prayer I will not listen’ (Isa. 1:15). He said again, ‘They may cry in my ears with a loud voice, but I shall not hear them’ (Ezek. 8:18). But he said this about deceitful prayer, which is not accepted. For you must hear with excellence all the words, then you will understand their power.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q904 “Why do we pray? Does God not know what we need?”, p. 32
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 904. Why do we pray? Does God not know what we need?

St. Basil the Great says, “He undoubtedly knows [what we need] and He gives us abundantly all temporal things even before we ask. However, we should first ask for the things that are profitable and for the kingdom of heaven, and thereafter we receive what we desire; but let us ask patiently and faithfully, ask for what is good for us, and let us not hinder our prayers by disobeying our consciences.”

Notes: [84] See St. Basil of Caesarea, Const. Mon. 1 (PG 31:1325–1338).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q902 “What practical steps lead us to practice prayer?”, pp. 30–31
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 902. What practical steps lead us to practice prayer?

And what follows, ‘Hitherto you have asked nothing in My name,’ may be understood in two ways: either, that you have not asked in my name, because a name that you have not known as it is yet to be known; or, you have not asked anything, since in comparison with that which you ought to have asked, what you have asked is to be accounted as nothing.”

“God does not forbid you to love these things, [but He wants you] not to set your affections upon them for blessedness, but to approve and praise them to this end, that you may love your Creator … For this the bridegroom gives earnest, that in his earnest he may himself be loved. Well then, God gave you all these things: love Him that made them.”

“Do not look for anything else from God, except God.”

“Does he say, ‘I will confess to Your name, O Lord,’ because You give me fruitful manors, because You give me gold and silver, because You give me extended riches, abundant money, most exalted dignity? No. But what? ‘For it is a good thing.’ Nothing I find is better than Your name.”

“Let us not, therefore, be prompt in arguments and indolent in prayers [for them]. Let us pray, dearly beloved, let us pray that the God of grace may give even to our enemies, and especially to our brethren and beloved.”

“‘The Eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous’ (Ps. 34:15) … I cry unto Him, and yet have tribulation. Only hold fast to His ways, and when you are in tribulation, He hears you. But He is a Physician, and still have you something of putrefaction; you cry out, but still He cuts, and takes not away His Hand, until He has cut as much as pleases Him. For that Physician is cruel who hears a man and spares his wound and putrefaction. How do mothers rub their children in the baths for their health; do not the little ones cry out in their hands? Are they then cruel because they spare not, nor hearken unto their tears? Are they not full of affection? …. So our God also is full of charity, but therefore He seems not to hear, that He may spare and heal us for everlasting.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q901 “What are the effects of prayer?”, pp. 24–25
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 901. What are the effects of prayer?

First: The soul is inflamed with the love of God. St. Basil the Great says, “Prayers, too, following reading, take hold upon a fresher and more vigorous soul already stirred to a longing for God. And prayer which imprints in the soul a clear conception of God is an excellent thing. This abiding of God in our memory is the indwelling of God. Thus we become in a special manner the temples of God when earthly thoughts cease to interrupt our continual remembrance of Him.”

Tertullian says, “Prayer is alone that which vanquishes God [cf. Gen. 32:22–30; Matt. 11:12]. But Christ has willed that it be operative for no evil: He had conferred on it all its virtue in the cause of good. And so it knows nothing save how to recall the souls of the departed from the very path of death, to transform the weak, to restore the sick, to purge the possessed, to open prison-bars, to loose the bonds of the innocent. Likewise it washes away faults, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, consoles the faint-spirited, cheers the high-spirited, escorts travelers, appeases waves, makes robbers stand aghast, nourishes the poor, governs the rich, upraises the fallen, arrests the falling, confirms the standing. Prayer is the wall of faith: her arms and missiles against the foe who keeps watch over us on all sides. And, so never walk we unarmed. By day, be we mindful of Station; by night, of vigil. Under the arms of prayer guard we the standard of our General; await we in prayer the angel’s trump … What more then, touching the office of prayer? Even the Lord Himself prayed; to whom be honour and virtue unto the ages of the ages!”

St. Hesychius of Jerusalem says, “‘Oh, that I my request may be fulfilled before the Lord.’ Should my prayers ascend on high, my enemies would perish, and the righteous person would stand firm (Wisd. of Sol. 5:1); the net would be broken, and the bird would be liberated and fly freely (Ps. 124:7); the oppressors would bow their heads, and the oppressed would rejoice (Matt. 5:10–12).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q949 “What are the signs of purity of heart?”, pp. 80–81
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Prayer of the Mind and Contemplation — 949. What are the signs of purity of heart?

You forgive the hundred denarii according to your poor condition and the Lord, your Creditor, will forgive you the ten thousand talents according to his greatness (Matt. 18:23–35). He will not reckon with you for any payment or interest.’

“If you are willing and forgiving then, he (Gabriel) takes your offering, the prayer, raises and brings it up with him. If you do not forgive, in such a case he will say to you, ‘I will not bring an unclean offering before the holy throne. But, see, you go there to give an account to your Creditor, taking your offering with you’; and he leaves your offering and goes off. Now listen to what the prophet had said, ‘Cursed is he who has a good ram in his flock, but he vows and sacrifices a sick one to the Lord’ (Mal. 1:14). For he said, ‘Offer it to your governor, and (see) whether he is pleased with you or will he give you favor?’ (Mal. 1:8). Therefore you ought to forgive your debtor before your prayer and then pray. And when you pray, your prayer will ascend before God on high, and it is not left on the earth.”

Second: Comforting the weary, for the comfort of God resides in comforting the weary. St. Aphrahat says, “For God said through the prophet, ‘This is my rest, give rest to the weary’ (Isa. 28:12). Therefore give the rest of God, o man. There is no need to you to say ‘forgive me.’ Give rest to the weary, visit the sick, provide for the poor (Matt. 25:35–36); this is prayer. I shall convince you, my beloved, about this, that (if) all the time a man does the rest of God, this is prayer. For it is written thus, ‘When Zimri committed fornication with a Midianite woman, Phineas, the son of Eleazar saw him and he entered into the cell and killed both of them’ (Num. 25:6–8; Sir. 45:23–26). Their killing was considered as prayer to him; David says about him thus, ‘Phineas has stood up and prayed, and it was considered a victory to him for generations, forever’ (Ps. 106:30–31). He killed them (lit. their killing which he killed) for the sake of his God and it was considered as prayer for him.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q901 “What are the effects of prayer?”, p. 26
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Life of Prayer — 901. What are the effects of prayer?

He wishes to benefit you still more by making you persist longer in your patient prayer before Him. For what can be higher than to address one’s converse to God and be in communion with Him?”

St. Hesychius of Jerusalem says, “If you offer your prayers with a pure and blameless heart on behalf of any inappropriate act, and if you offer groanings for yourself before Him, you will encounter God. Instead of sorrow, you will have joy; instead of misfortunes, you will receive blessings; and the expressions on your face will be bright, like pure water … You will no longer fear other defects, for God will cast them away from you. You will find rest from your troubles and thanksgiving for the calmness which will overshadow you. You shall not fear temptations, for you will be like one who found rest in a safe harbor; you will fear no billows, for the sea is not able to harm you.”

Third: By prayer, the divine commandments are fulfilled. St. John of Dalyatha says, “Our Lord said to Simon, chief of the Apostles: I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of heaven, that you may close and open to all whom you wish (Matt. 16:19) … [prayer] wears itself out giving rest to the weary and when they have been refreshed sees that they not become weary again.”

“Sanctify your bed by the descent of the Spirit over you and the fragrance of your members will be wafted like perfume.”

“Through prayer, the mind is mingled with God. Through prayer, one can open the treasures of God and divide His spoils. Through prayer, one is made worthy of the vision of of God, of entering within the clouds of the light of His greatness in the country of the spiritual beings. Through prayer, a person becomes the dwelling of God. Through prayer, the soul is united with Christ, and beholds the radiance of His great glory. Through prayer, the fire of Christ’s love is kindled in the soul and the heart burns with desire for God; this desire that burns away every lustful desire of one’s members. Through prayer, the soul exults in love and goes beyond her rank, and the world is cast out from her heart.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q947 “What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?”, pp. 79–80
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Prayer of the Mind and Contemplation — 947. What is the hidden (or secret) prayer to which the Lord Christ invites us?

But he said this about deceitful prayer, which is not accepted. For you must hear with excellence all the words, then you will understand their power.”

Also, Anthimus of Jerusalem says, “Prayer is the hidden conversation of the heart with God, or a form of connection with Him. Even if it were silent, many times God hears the cries of our hearts which we cannot express in words. There is no weapon that is more powerful than prayer. If it is offered from a pure heart, the Lord will hear it. And if it is accompanied with good deeds, He will respond and listen to it.”

Notes: [262] St. Clement of Alexandria, The Stromata, or Miscellanies 7.7 (ANF 2:534). [263] St. Aphraphat, Aphrahat: Demonstrations I, trans., Kuriakose Valavanolickal (Kottayam, India: St Ephrem Ecumenical Research Institute, 2005) 4.10: pp. 85–86.

details.fact: Part 1: Prayer is converse and union with God (St. Clement of Alexandria, St. John Climacus).
details.quote: Prayer is the conversation or converse with God, a way to speak boldly and inwardly with Him even in silence, as God continually hears the inward converse of the heart

details.fact: Part 2: God sometimes delays answering prayer so that our zeal and desire for Him grow and we treasure the gift when it comes (St. Basil).
details.quote: God sometimes delays answering prayers so that the person’s zeal and desire to approach Him may increase, and so that the gift received may be more appreciated and carefully guarded

details.fact: Part 2: God sometimes delays answering prayer to show us the value of His good things rather than refusing them (St. Augustine).
details.quote: The delay also shows the value of God's good things, as things long desired are obtained with greater pleasure, while those given quickly are held cheap

records.question: Who was St. Demiana, and on which day is her martyrdom commemorated?
records.answer:
St. Demiana was born to two pious Christian parents near the end of the 3rd century AD. Her father, Marcus, was a governor in the Nile delta region. She was baptized at the age of one in El-Mayma monastery. Known for her piety, beauty, and virtues, she chose to live as a virgin dedicated to God rather than marry. Her father supported her decision by building a separate palace where she lived with 40 other virgins who also vowed virginity. They lived an ascetic life of fasting, prayer, and praise to God [1][2].

During the persecution by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), her father initially renounced his faith but was restored by St. Demiana’s prayers and rebuke. He was later martyred for his faith. St. Demiana and the 40 virgins were arrested and tortured for refusing to worship idols. Despite severe tortures, including being placed in the Hinbazeen chamber and other brutal punishments, she was miraculously healed by the Archangel Michael. Ultimately, she was beheaded along with the 40 virgins, receiving the crown of martyrdom [2][3][5].

Her martyrdom is commemorated on the 13th of Toba in the Coptic calendar. Her body rests in a church built by Queen Helena near the town of Bilqas in the Nile Delta, and several churches in Egypt bear her name [4].
