passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Her Upbringing

Her Upbringing:

St. ‘Demiana’ was born to two pious Christian parents near the end of the 3rd century AD. Her father ‘Marcus’ was a governor on ‘El-Burullus,’ ‘Zaåfaran,’ and the ‘Saysaban valley’ (northeast of Gharbiah governorate) in the Nile delta. When St. ‘Demiana’ reached the first year of age, she was baptized in ‘El-Mayma’ monastery, south of the city of ‘Zaåfaran;’ and her father for three days held a massive banquet for the poor and the needy. After a little while, her mother reposed.

A Prince Propose to Marry the Saint:

Growing up, the saint was known for her piety, beauty, richness, and virtues. Then, when her father told her that a prince proposed to marry her, she answered him: “Why do you want me to get married, while I want to live with you? Why do you want me to leave you?”

Amazed at her response, her father postponed talking about the issue of marriage for a while. Then, her father noticed how his daughter adored reading the Holy Bible, and how she used to resort to her private room to pour a flow of tears of love before God her Savior. She had a secure attachment to the church, and the frequency of her prayers and fasting was so high. She had so many of her girl-friends spending time with her practicing an ascetic way of life in prayers and continuous praise to God.

On reaching the age of 18 years, she proclaimed to her father her decision to live as a virgin, which was welcomed by him. He also, to fulfill her wish, built for her a separate palace of her own in the region of ‘Zaåfaran,’ to worship God along with 40 other girls who vowed virginity as well.

St. ‘Demiana’ rejoiced and appreciated her father’s actions, which surpassed the mere emotional love, to offer his only daughter as a lovesacrifice to God. The saint, together with her friends, lived a marvelous ascetic life of fasting combined with prayers and praise, turning the palace into heaven, in which the sound of exaltation was perpetually heard.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, pp. 556–557
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — A Prince Propose to Marry the Saint

St. ‘Demiana’ rejoiced and appreciated her father’s actions, which surpassed the mere emotional love, to offer his only daughter as a lovesacrifice to God. The saint, together with her friends, lived a marvelous ascetic life of fasting combined with prayers and praise, turning the palace into heaven, in which the sound of exaltation was perpetually heard.

The Fall of Her Father;

During the wave of persecution, stirred up by emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284- 305 AD), Demiana’s father ‘Marcus’ was scared and became feeble and burned incense before the idols. On hearing about it, ‘Demiana’ came out of her seclusion, after seeking from her friends to keep praying for the sake of her father to return from his vanity.

When she met with her father, she bravely and firmly said to him: “I wish I heard the news of your death, rather than to hear that you have forsaken the true God. If you persist on your vanity, I shall denounce you as my father here and before the throne of the Divine Judge, and you would have no portion in the eternal inheritance, kept by God for those who love Him and keep His covenant.” She bitterly rebuked him on his denial of His Christ under whatever circumstances. She sought from him not to fear death, but to fear the destruction of the soul and body together. She begged him not to appease the emperor at the expense of his faith and eternity. Along with her firmness and complete frankness, her tears of love unceasingly flowed while she was telling him: “If you persist in denying the True God; You would not be any longer my father and I would not be your daughter.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, p. 557
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Her Father Returned to His Faith

Her Father Returned to His Faith:

His daughter’s words and tears inflamed ‘Marcus’ heart that he cried out with bitterness and remorse for his shameful deed. In true repentance and with the spirit of humility and renewed hope, he said to her: “Blessed is the moment I saw you, my daughter, for you brought me up from the deep pit in which I have fallen. My life is renewed in preparation for encountering my Great Lord, who, I am sure, will receive my soul.”

Then, with the spirit of thanksgiving to God who woke his heart up, he proclaimed: “O my God, I give You thanks for You have taken away the darkness of infidelity from my heart; ‘The snare is broken, and we have escaped’ (Ps. 124:7)”. He then instantly set forth to Antioch, to proclaim his Christian faith before Emperor Diocletian and show his regret for having burnt incense before the idols.

The emperor was amazed by the new attitude of that governor, who was always known for his obedience, and on seeing how he proclaimed his faith with such strength, the emperor gently rebuked ‘Marcus’ and did not hasten to punish him. He was hoping to convince him to re-deny his living faith. But, as ‘Marcus’ persisted on his stand, the angry emperor ordered his head to be cut off. This happened on the 6th of Abib, on the feast of the saintly apostles.

The news spread in the whole land, and the heart of his daughter St. ‘Demiana’ became jubilant; for the sake of her father who was saved from the eternal destruction, to partake of the glories of his Christ.

The emperor felt sorrow to lose ‘Marcus,’ whom he appreciated and cherished. Then, he heard that his daughter was behind the restoration of her father to his Christian faith. So, he sent a regiment of his soldiers with their tools of torture to take revenge from her and the virgins who lived with her. On seeing the soldiers surrounding her palace, and how they set the instruments of torture to terrify them; St. ‘Demiana’ assembled the virgins, and she proclaimed with the spirit of conquest that the emperor has the intention to scare them; and it was the time to receive the crowns of martyrdom for whoever wanted to take advantage of the occasion. Then, she asked them, whoever among them intended to enjoy it, let her stay, but whoever has fears, let her flee through the back door. However, none of the 40 virgins had a fear of death, but with great joy, all proclaimed that they hold fast to their Christ, and would never flee.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, p. 558
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Fellowship of Passion with Christ

Whenever that leader tortured her, the Lord was glorified in her. Finally, the leader ordered cutting her head off, together with all the heads of the other virgins with her, and all of them received the crowns of martyrdom.

Before the sword struck the saint’s neck, the saint cried out: “I confess the Lord Jesus Christ; on His name I die, and by it, I shall forever live.”

She was martyred on the 13th of Toba. Her body is still there in the church built by Queen ‘Helena,’ the mother of Emperor ‘Constantine the Great’ (306- 337 AD), located close to the town of ‘Bilqas’ in the north of the Nile Delta. That church was consecrated by pope ‘Alexander I’ (312-328 AD) on the 12th of Bashons. Annexed to that church is the convent of St. ‘Demiana.’

Several churches were built all over Egypt in the name of this great martyr.

[El-Mahaba Bookstore: The Biography of St. Demiana]

Notes: [1] The ‘Henbazin’ is a machine made of two wheels with sharp blades, a person is pressed between the wheels, then on turning them in opposite directions, the person’s flesh is torn out into shreds.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Demiana and the Fourty Virgins, pp. 557–558
passages.text:
Saint: DEMIANA AND THE FOURTY VIRGINS, SS. (The martyrs) — Fellowship of Passion with Christ

Fellowship of Passion with Christ:

The leader of the regiment met with the saint, told her that the emperor promised to give her great wealth and to make her a noble princess if she worshiped his gods. She answered him: “Are you not ashamed to call those idols gods when there is no god except the Lord of heaven and earth? I am prepared to die for His name’s sake, along with all those who are with me.”

Provoked to anger, the leader ordered four soldiers to place the saint into the ‘Hinbazeen’ chamber and to start her torture. The other virgins bitterly cried out when they saw their matron being pressed and her body being slashed. Then barely alive, the saint was thrown into prison. There, the Archangel ‘Michael’ came down at midnight and healed all her wounds.

In the morning, the soldiers came to check up on her, expecting to declare her death to their leader, but to their amazement, they saw her free of any wounds. Provoked to anger, the leader assumed that ‘Demiana’ was a sorcerer, and he declared that all effort would be made to disable her sorcery.

On seeing the saint was restored to full health, the multitudes cried out: “We believe in the God of ‘Demiana.’” So, the soldiers’ chief ordered killing them all, and considering that the saint was responsible for leading so many ‘astray,’ he put in his heart to double her tortures. He ordered combing her body with sharp iron combs, then rubbed into her wounds gypsum soaked with vinegar, but she kept being exultant, counting herself unworthy to partake of the passions of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Then, she was cast again in jail. On the next day, the leader himself went to check on her expecting to see a corpse, but he almost collapsed when he saw her entirely healed by the Archangel ‘Michael’ who revisited her. He furiously tortured her in so many different ways: breaking her skull and skinning her body. A white dove came down from heaven, hovered above her, and healed her from all her wounds.

Whenever that leader tortured her, the Lord was glorified in her. Finally, the leader ordered cutting her head off, together with all the heads of the other virgins with her, and all of them received the crowns of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dominica, the Virgin, p. 637
passages.text:
Saint: DOMINICA, THE VIRGIN, ST. (The martyr)

This saint was living at the time of emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), and she was accused of breaking the idols down. The emperor ordered to cast her to the wild hungry beasts. However, the beasts did not harm her. So, they cut her head off around the year 303, and she received the crown of martyrdom.

[Butler: July 6]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Medius, p. 184
passages.text:
Saint: MEDIUS (The martyr)

His martyrdom is celebrated with the deaconess Dionisa(Denisa) by the Church on the 13th of Baramouda.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Soteris, the Virgin, pp. 186–187
passages.text:
Saint: SOTERIS, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This saint was the pride of her noble family of rulers and counsels, according to St. Ambrosius (Ambrose: 340-397 AD). She preferred to forsake her position, riches, beauty, and all her possessions in the world, for the sake of the Lord Christ. She granted her youth to God whom she loved; forsook all the pleasures of the world and got away from any potential risks she might face because of her beauty. After the decrees and laws issued by Emperors Diocletian and Maximilian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, she confessed her faith and was brought forth before the judges and rulers. During her trial, when the judge ordered to strike her on her face, she was delighted to be treated like her Savior. And, despite the many and diverse tortures she endured, she did not utter a word or shed any tears. And with time, before her steadfastness and perseverance, she was condemned to have her head cut off by the sword. This happened in the year 304 AD. It was not clear whether all the events of her torture occurred at the same time, or the saint was arrested and tortured while being a small girl during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD); then was martyred 50 years later during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

[Butler: February 19]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anastasia, pp. 175–176
passages.text:
Saint: ANASTASIA, ST. (The martyr)

This Saint was martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD) around the year 250 AD, and celebrated by the Coptic Church on the 1st of Baba...

She was the daughter of Christian parents in Rome; they raised her in fear of God. Her heart was full of the Love of God, longing for the angelic life of virginity since her childhood. She joined a convent in Rome to practice the monastic life with firmness, eating food once every two days, and in the Great Lent only on Saturdays and Sundays.

When the mother-superior went to attend a feast in the city, she took with her the virgin Anastasia. In the town, they happened to see soldiers torturing some Christians. So, the virgin Anastasia stopped to rebuke them on their oppression and the hardness of their hearts. However, the soldiers arrested her and brought her forth to the governor. Before the governor, she confessed the Lord Christ. He tortured her severely, crucified her and ignited fire underneath her. And as she persisted in her faith, he ordered to cut her head off by the sword, for which she became exultant, prayed, and delivered her head to the swordsman to receive the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Menodora, Metrodora & Nymphodora, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: MENODORA, METRODORA & NYMPHODORA (The martyrs)

They were three orphan sisters who lived a life of seclusion, with works of mercy and love, in Bithynia. In the days of the persecution against the Christians stirred up by Emperors Diocletian and Maximian (284-305 AD), they were arrested and brought before Fronto, the governor of the province. Fronto was attracted to their beauty and simplicity and suggested to defend them and release them if they agree to worship his gods. The virgin saints rejected his request, preferring death instead. Failing to make them change their minds, the governor ordered to beat their eldest sister Menodora so violently to death to bring fear to her other two sisters. Yet, even the scene of her torn off corpse, which they left to rot in the intense heat of the sun, did not terrify them. Then Metrodora said to the governor: “Being three branches of the same blessed tree, we shall never bring shame to our good roots by fulfilling your request.” So, she was tortured by fire after being violently beaten; then, she was beheaded. Nymphodora, the youngest, was also martyred as a result of her severe beating by her tormentors. They all were martyred in the year 304 AD.

[Butler: September 10]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Demetrius, pp. 577–578
passages.text:
Saint: DEMETRIUS (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

The emperor was amazed and embarrassed; how a man like ‘Nestor’ could prevail over his vast wrestler, and he inquired about the situation and was informed by his men that ‘Demetrius’ prayed for him and made the sign of the Cross over his face.

In anger, the emperor ordered to strike ‘Nestor’ until he would consent to burn incense before his gods and to worship them. When he refused, the emperor ordered to stab him by spears to tear his body off until his death. So, they did that in front of ‘Demetrius’ to terrify him and lead him to deny his faith in the Lord Christ. However, he told them: “Do whatever you like, for I shall never worship or burn incense, except before my Lord Jesus Christ the True God.” So, the soldiers stabbed him with spears until he delivered his pure spirit in the hands of the Lord.

Some believers took his holy body, and they kept it hidden in a marble coffin until the end of persecution. Then, a great church was built in his name in ‘Thessalonica,’ where his relics were hidden. In the saint’s name, many miracles were performed, and fragrant myrrh oil flowed from his tomb, which healed whoever has used it with faith. Since the 7th century, a large quantity of the miraculous myrrh oil flowed on the walls and columns of that Church; and it was plenty enough for all people present to wipe it off and transfer it into their vessels.

[The Synaxarion: 29 Baba] [Orthodox Church in America Web Site: Lives of the Saints: Demetrius the Myrrh-Gusher of Thessalonica]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sophia and the Fifty Virgins, p. 180
passages.text:
Saint: SOPHIA AND THE FIFTY VIRGINS (The martyrs)

In one of the convents close to the city of Edessa (El-Roha) in Iraq, fifty virgins were living with their pious mother-superior Sophia. All of them earnestly worshipped God with continuous prayers and fasting. The pagan Emperor Julian (360-363 AD), on his way to fight with his army the Persian king Shapur II (309-379 AD), they passed by this convent. The evil emperor ordered his men to kill all the nuns and their mother-superior and cut them into pieces, and then to rob all that in their convent. So, they all received the crowns of martyrdom. This took place on the 10th of Hator.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, the Burrier of Martyrs, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, THE BURRIER OF MARTYRS

This saint Theodora was a woman who dedicated her life and energy to serve the martyrs during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), And when the available cemeteries were all filled by the tombs of the martyrs; she had them buried in her land on Flaminian Way, about 26 miles from Rome. In that land, she hid the martyrs Abundius, the priest, Abundantius, the deacon, Marcianus, and Joannes.

The West celebrates this saint’s feast on the 17th of September.

[Henry Wace: A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Literature, Sects & Doctrines; 4 Vol.; London 1877-1887]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Damian, p. 551
passages.text:
Saint: DAMIAN, ST. (The martyr)

This saint was martyred in Antioch. He endured vicious tortures until he delivered his soul into the Lord’s hand.

[The Synaxarion: 23 Mesra]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Reparata, the Virgin, p. 13
passages.text:
Saint: REPARATA, THE VIRGIN (The martyr)

This lady, St. Reparata was from Caesarea of Palestine. When she was 12 years old, she was arrested during the persecution of Emperor Decius (249- 251), because of her being Christian. Once the governor saw her, admiring her beauty, he tried to seduce her by tender words. But, when he failed in making her worship his idols, he ordered to torture her by casting her into a furnace of fire. In there, like the Three Young Men, she was not harmed, but kept singing praise to God, and proclaimed to the governor from inside the furnace that she holds fast to her Christ. Finally, when the governor ordered his men to cut her head off, she walked with them singing praise. Finally, when she was beheaded, her soul was seen coming out of her body in the form of a dove, flying up toward Heaven. Her relics were eventually moved to Italy, where she was honored by several dioceses.

[Butler: October 8]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mania, p. 47
passages.text:
Saint: MANIA, ST.

So many saintly virgins used to live in Ancyra in Turkey. They lived in convents following a strict blessed ascetic life. Their numbers reached about 2,000 virgins. One of them, her name was Mania, was quite well known. She was forced by her mother to get married. However, she kept on excusing herself from any physical relationship with her husband, by claiming illness. After a little while, her husband died, and she dedicated her whole life to Christ.

She lived such a holy life in the fear of God that the other virgins used to seek her blessing. They felt ashamed of their sins whenever they see her around. She was always compassionate toward the poor and the strangers, and she worshipped the Lord from her whole heart until she reposed in peace.

[The Paradise of Saints, p. 44]

records.question: What does St. Anthony say about practicing it?
records.answer:
St. Anthony says about practicing the Jesus Prayer:  
“If you sit in your cell, work with your hands, while repeating the name of Jesus. Hold it fast in your heart and mind and sing it with your tongue: ‘My Lord Jesus, help me,’ ‘I praise You my Lord Jesus Christ.’” [1]

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 971. What does St. Anthony say about the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

“If you sit in your cell, work with your hands, while repeating the name of Jesus. Hold it fast in your heart and mind and sing it with your tongue: ‘My Lord Jesus, help me,’ ‘I praise You my Lord Jesus Christ.’”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q965 “How can someone with family commitments implement the practice of this pilgrim?”, pp. 100–101
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 965. How can someone with family commitments implement the practice of this pilgrim?

The prayer practices described by this pilgrim have been practiced both by monastics and married people for many generations. Each person practices this prayer according to his own circumstances and abilities. From this pilgrim, we learn a number of things:

a. Faith in the power of the name of Jesus and of calling upon Him.

b. Awareness that prayer is the mother of virtues and good deeds.

c. Concern for nurturing conversation with the Lord Christ, whether in communal or personal worship, as part of any work, or while eating, drinking, sleeping, etc.

d. To ask for the grace of God to work in our lives, bestowing patience in our striving with a spirit of humility.

e. In our spiritual exercises, we should be chiefly concerned with focusing our attention on interior prayer if we wish our lives to be fruitful.

f. The confession of our weaknesses and sins, and our need for the mercy of God.

g. That we need times of silence in order to hear to the voice of God.

h. The focusing of our attention on attaining salvation and forgiveness of sins.

i. Even though the Jesus Prayer is extremely simple with few words, St. John Chrysostom reminds us of the awe with which the seraphim utter this name, as they glorify Him and worship Him; so, let us not practice this prayer carelessly.

j. The need to appreciate the power of the name of our Lord Jesus.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q960 “What is the “Jesus Prayer”?”, p. 93
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 960. What is the “Jesus Prayer”?

The goal of sacred worship — and of prayer in particular — is closeness to God through constant dialogue with Him. Hence, both scripture and holy tradition provide a varied approach to prayer through which the believer is able to attain to constant prayer without ceasing. The believer begins with prayer in every work he undertakes; even before he sleeps. He participates in liturgies, prays the psalms, and his own personal prayers. To preserve his thought from distraction, he offers up prayers that cannot be counted with words or sentences, remembering always the presence of God in his life, so that he lives in a state of constant communication with Him; prayers that he can recite or repeat at any time, even when he is performing any kind of work. Being confident in the power of the name of Jesus, the believer repeats it often. This is what we call the Jesus Prayer.

The Desert Fathers often recited this prayer or other short prayers, which represent a cry to the Lord. St. Augustine used to repeat this prayer: “Make haste, O God, to deliver me. Make haste to help me, O Lord” (Ps. 70:1); and he encouraged the faithful to repeat it on every occasion: at home; at work; while eating or drinking; while awake or asleep; in grief or joy; when spiritually zealous or lukewarm in worship — for this prayer is particularly helpful. St. Augustine used to call this short prayer, “the arrow prayer,” for it shoots an arrow into the heart of the devil and prevents him from distracting our thoughts so long as we pray it. St. John of the Ladder (Climacus) urges us to employ this short prayer saying, “Let your prayer be completely simple. For both the publican and the prodigal son were reconciled to God by a single phrase.”

Notes: [293] St. John Climacus, The Ladder of Divine Ascent, trans., Colm Luibheid and Norman Russell (Paulist Press, 1982) 28.5: p. 251.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q976 “What practical steps can one take to practice the Jesus Prayer?”, pp. 105–106
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 976. What practical steps can one take to practice the Jesus Prayer?

First: Concentrate all your thoughts on our Lord Jesus Himself. Remember the name of Jesus slowly, gently, and calmly.

Second: Let the recitation of the name be from the soul’s inner depths, without loudness or violence, even internally. When Elijah was commanded to stand before the Lord and prepare to encounter Him, he was told, “‘Stand on the mountain’ … and behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind tore into the mountains and broke the rocks in pieces, but the Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire, And after the fire a small voice. When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out and stood in the entrance of the cave. Suddenly a voice came to him and said, ‘What are you doing here Elijah?’” (1 Kings 19:1–13).

Third: Recite your prayer in serenity and simplicity, or more specifically, with gentleness. As a bird that flies up to the height it intends and then gently glides, flapping its wings only from time to time to maintain its altitude, so the soul, if it flies up to glide upon the thought of Christ Jesus and is sated by remembering Him, can cease to repeat the holy name and instead rest in other thoughts; namely, thinking about Jesus. It is natural for moments of lukewarmness to intrude upon this practice. But if at any time you begin your recitation once more, you find the name of Jesus upon your lips spontaneously, and returning to your thoughts continually, silently, and internally. Thus, you will experience the verse: “I sleep but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). However, this prayer cannot be prayed inattentively: “Because of the fragrance of your ointment, the virgins love you. Draw me away; the daughters of Jerusalem will run after you” (Song 1:3–4).

Fourth: We should be drawn toward the name of Jesus by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that calling on the name of Jesus becomes in our lives one of the fruits of the Holy Spirit Himself.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q966 “What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?”, pp. 102–103
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 966. What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?

Thirst after Jesus; then he will satisfy you with his love. Shut your eyes to the precious things of the world; then you will be deemed worthy of a peace given by God to reign in your heart.”

St. Gregory the Theologian says that all Christians should repeat the name of the Lord in their prayer, more times than the number of their breaths: “Not only should we pray the name of Jesus Christ without ceasing, but we must also practice it and teach it others, to every person on the face of the earth, for it is fitting and beneficial for all.”

St John Cassian says, “It is not some kind of imagination, conversation, or mere words — it is like a spark that flies off that burning coal which is the movement of the heart, and from the activity of the inextinguishable Spirit who raises the mind above every materialistic thing which can be seen or touched; and thus he pours out his prayers with groanings and sorrows which cannot be uttered.”

St. John Chrysostom says, “I implore you, brethren, never to neglect the rule of this prayer. Whenever you eat, drink, travel, or do anything, cry without ceasing: ‘Lord, Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy upon me!’” He also says, “Do not estrange your heart from God, but abide in Him and guard your heart always by remembering the Lord Jesus Christ, until the name of the Lord becomes rooted in the heart and it ceases to think of anything else. May Christ be glorified in you.”

Abba Agathon says, “There is no labor greater than praying to God. For every time a man wants to pray, his enemies the demons try to prevent him; for they know that nothing obstructs them so much as prayer to God. In everything else that a man undertakes, if he perseveres he will attain rest. But in order to pray a man must struggle to his last breath.”

St. Athanasius says, “Christ did not command us to fill our prayers with ten thousand phrases and to come before Him merely to recite them … We do not come to teach Him, but to wrestle with Him; that we may cling to Him with the persistent cry: ‘Lord Jesus Christ Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner!’ He is living and active, working day after day for the salvation of all.”

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 976. What practical steps can one take to practice the Jesus Prayer?

Draw me away; the daughters of Jerusalem will run after you” (Song 1:3–4).

Fourth: We should be drawn toward the name of Jesus by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that calling on the name of Jesus becomes in our lives one of the fruits of the Holy Spirit Himself.

Fifth: We should be careful not to despise other forms of prayer.

Sixth: We must forget ourselves and put our egos to death while the name of the Holy God comes alive in our spirits: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Seventh: Repetition of the Jesus Prayer should not lessen our participation in the divine liturgy or in other Church rites such as the Midnight Praises.

Eighth: The best kind of prayer is that which is prayed when we are moved by the Holy Spirit.

Ninth: The goal of the Jesus Prayer is to praise Him, crying out with Thomas the apostle: “My Lord and God!” (John 20:28). We should be concerned most of all with the Lord of glory, Jesus, being present in our lives.

Tenth: Calling on the name of Jesus grants us salvation in every kind of need in our lives.

Eleventh: Through the name of Jesus, we receive more than we ask: “Whatever you ask the father in my name, He will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in My name. Ask and you will receive” (John 16:23–24). He is both the one who grants the gift and the gift itself, satisfying all our needs. “He became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30).

“Always remember the holy name, our Lord Jesus Christ. This is the pearl which the wise merchant purchased (Matt. 13:45–46) by selling all the desires of his heart, brought into the inner rooms of his house, and found it sweeter than honey in his mouth. He who keeps this jewel in his heart shall be granted a great reward in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q408 “What is “the Jesus Prayer”?”, p. 303
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › Titles and Names of the Savior that Witness to the Works of His Love — 408. What is “the Jesus Prayer”?

Let us conclude this survey of the names and titles of Christ by mentioning the effectiveness of the “Jesus Prayer” in our lives. When the believer experiences the power of the name of Jesus, he cries out with blind Bartimaeus, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47, Luke 18:38). This prayer is found in the biography of Abba Philemon (6th to 7th century). It is also found in the letters of Saints Barsanuphius and John of Gaza (beginning of the 6th century), Dorotheus of Gaza, and St. John Climacus. The Church employs it as a spiritual practice for her children, with the addition of part of the prayer of the tax collector who beat his chest saying, “God be merciful to me a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).

St. Anthony the Great says, “Do not cease from reciting the name of the Lord Jesus, but hold onto to His name with your mind, repeat it with your tongue, and say in your heart: ‘My Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me; My Lord Jesus Christ help me.’ Also say: ‘I praise You, my Lord Jesus Christ.’”

It was also known to St. Macarius the Great and St. Evagrius.

St. Macarius the Great says, “Be attentive to the name of our Lord Jesus Christ with a remorseful heart and let it pour forth from your lips. Let the name reflect back upon you. Do not bury it in your thoughts only for display, but be alert whenever you cry it out, saying, “O my Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me!” Then, in serenity you shall see His divinity resting in you; He will bring to naught the darkness of pain that is in you; and He shall purify your inner man to be like the purity of Adam dwelling in paradise. This is the blessed name that St. John the Evangelist called, “the light of the world” (John 8:12); the sweetness of which no one can ever have enough and the true “bread of life” (John 6:35).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q964 “What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, p. 99
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 964. What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

Now do you understand what prayer without ceasing is?’

‘Yes indeed, Father, and in God’s name teach me how to gain the habit of it,’ I cried, filled with joy.

‘Read this book,’ he said. ‘It is called The Philokalia, and it contains the full and detailed science of constant and interior prayer, set forth by twenty-five holy Fathers. The book is marked by a lofty wisdom and is so profitable to use that it is considered the foremost and best manual of the contemplative spiritual life’ …

He opened the book, found the instruction by St. Symeon the New Theologian, and read: ‘Sit down alone and in silence. Lower your head, shut your eyes, breathe out gently and imagine yourself looking into your own heart. Carry your mind, i.e., your thoughts, from your head to your heart. As you breathe out, say, “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.” Say it moving your lips gently, or simply say it in your mind. Try to put all other thoughts aside. Be calm, be patient, and repeat the process frequently.’”

The old man asked the pilgrim to return to him so he could monitor his progress, and for honest confession, for it is silly to attempt such spiritual works without a guide to mentor us. The pilgrim felt a powerful desire to experience interior and continual prayer. The pilgrim learned that there was a village near the monastery, so he went and sought accommodation there, in order to remain near the old man. He found work tending the garden of a peasant for the summer, and was provided with a small, isolated hut in which to live.

For a week he followed the instructions of the old man, but he was soon beset by feelings of laziness and boredom and sleepiness. Certain thoughts assailed him, so he began to read the words of the Fathers and force himself to recite the Jesus Prayer. He confessed all this to the old man, who then asked him to repeat the prayer three thousand times a day, while standing or sitting, lying down or walking. The pilgrim received this instruction with joy and returned to his hut. It was difficult for the first two days, but after that it became an easy matter, so that whenever he ceased, he felt an urge to continue again.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q966 “What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?”, pp. 101–102
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 966. What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our Lord Jesus?

The Lord Christ granted His name to His disciples, not only so they could perform wonders, heal the sick, and cast out demons — He assured them of the power of His name when He said, “Whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you” (John 16:23). Thus, by His name we approach the Father and enjoy His eternal glories. Indeed, the seventy apostles came to understand the power of the name of Jesus, as is evident from their words upon their return from their mission: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name!” (Luke 10:17). Isaiah the prophet, in his song of thanksgiving, expressed the power of the name of God, saying, “The desire of our soul is for Your name, and for the remembrance of You. With my soul I have desired You in the night. Yes, by my spirit within me I will seek you early” (Isa. 26:8–9).

St. John Climacus (of the ladder) says, “Flog your enemies with the name of Jesus, for there is no stronger weapon in heaven or earth.”

St. Cyril the Great says, “He among those who do not yet believe in God and who despises the name of God confesses the power of the Most Holy One when the rays of the truth shine upon him.”

St. Barsanuphius and St. John say, “The remembrance of God’s name utterly destroys all that is evil and wicked.”

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “If any disbelieve the power of the Crucified, let him ask the devils.”

St. Ephrem the Syrian says,

“Jesus, glorious name, Secret bridge which leads across from death to life, to you I have come and stopped, at yod your letter I am held. Be a bridge for my speech, that it may cross to the truth. Make your love a bridge for your servant: by you let me cross to your Father. Let me cross and say ‘Blessed be he who made his might gentle through his Child.’”

St. Isaac the Syrian speaks of the practice of the Jesus Prayer, saying, “It is not becoming that great things should fall into our hands easily: lest the gift of God should be thought to be cheap because of its being acquired without difficulty. All that is acquired with labour, is guarded with caution. Thirst after Jesus; then he will satisfy you with his love. Shut your eyes to the precious things of the world; then you will be deemed worthy of a peace given by God to reign in your heart.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q964 “What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, pp. 99–100
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 964. What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

The pilgrim received this instruction with joy and returned to his hut. It was difficult for the first two days, but after that it became an easy matter, so that whenever he ceased, he felt an urge to continue again.

He returned to the old man, who told him to stay calm and to increase the number of recitations with the grace of God. He returned to his hut and continued to recite the prayer for a whole week without much trouble. And he learned how to keep his mind from distraction. The old man then said to him: “Now I give you permission to say your Prayer as often as you wish and as often as you can. Try to devote every moment you are awake to the Prayer, call on the Name of Jesus Christ without counting the number of times, and submit yourself humbly to the will of God, looking to Him for help. I am sure He will not forsake you, and that He will lead you into the right path.”

The pilgrim goes on to say, “After no great lapse of time I had the feeling that the Prayer had, so to speak, by its own action passed from my lips to my heart. That is to say, it seemed as though my heart in its ordinary beating began to say the words of the Prayer within each beat. Thus for example, one, ‘Lord,’ two, ‘Jesus,’ three, ‘Christ,’ and so on. I gave up saying the Prayer with my lips, I simply listened carefully to what my heart was saying. It seemed as though my eyes looked right down into it; and I dwelt upon the words of my departed mentor when he was telling me about this joy. Then I felt something like a pain in my heart, and in my thoughts so great a love for Jesus Christ that I pictured myself, if only I could see Him, throwing myself at His feet and not letting them go from my embrace, kissing them tenderly, and thanking Him with tears for having of His love and grace allowed me to find so great a consolation in His Name, me, His unworthy and sinful creature! … ”

“Again I started off on my wanderings. But now I did not walk along as before, filled with care. The calling upon the Name of Jesus Christ gladdened my way. Everybody was kind to me, it was as though everyone loved me.”

passages.text:

This is the blessed name that St. John the Evangelist called, “the light of the world” (John 8:12); the sweetness of which no one can ever have enough and the true “bread of life” (John 6:35).”

Abba Evagrius says, “Tormented by the thoughts and passions of the body, I went to find the Abbot Macarius. I said to him: ‘My father, give me a word that I may live by it.’ Then Macarius said to me: ‘Attach the rope of the anchor to the rock and, by God’s grace, the ship will cross the diabolic waves of the deceptive sea and the tempest of the darkness of this vain world.’ I said to him: ‘What is the ship, what is the rope, what is the rock?’ The Abbot Macarius said to me: ‘The boat is your heart: guard it. The rope is your spirit: attach it to our Lord Jesus Christ who is the rock that has power over all the diabolic waves and surges that the saints are contending with; for is it not easy to say with each breath: Our Lord Jesus, the Christ, have mercy on me; I bless You, my Lord Jesus, help me? And as the fish struggling against the current can be caught unawares, we also, if we patiently persist in faithfully reciting the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, He will snare the devil by his nose (“one pierces his nose with a snare” Job 40:24) because of what he has done to us, and we who are weak shall know that help comes to us from the Lord Jesus Christ.”

And Abba Jacob says, “I once went to Abba Isidore and I found him writing, so I sat by him and noticed that from time to time he raised his eyes to heaven and his lips would move without me hearing any sound; so I said to him, ‘What are you doing, Abba?’ He said to me, ‘Do you not do the same?’ I said to him, ‘No, Abba.’ He then told me, ‘If you do not do that, Abba Jacob, then you have not yet become a monk, not even for a single day.’ And this is what he used to say: ‘My Lord Jesus Christ, help me. My Lord Jesus Christ have mercy on me. I praise You, My Lord Jesus Christ.’”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q964 “What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, pp. 98–99
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 964. What is the story of the Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

As they walked together to the monastery, he chatted with the old man about the topic of prayer without ceasing. The old man told him the following:

a. This question needs spiritual understanding and not academic teaching.

b. Some employ worldly wisdom inappropriately to explain divine matters. Some think that preparatory good works are necessary before prayer. On the contrary, prayer is the mother of virtues and good works.

c. The apostle testifies that prayer has the priority over good works when he says, “I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made” (1 Tim. 2:1). Without prayer, no good work can be performed; and without prayer, we cannot know how to encounter God and enter into dialogue with Him.

As they spoke, they came up to the monastery and the end of their conversation, so the pilgrim hastened to ask the wise old man:

“‘Be so kind, Reverend Father, as to show me what prayer without ceasing means and how it is learnt. I see you know all about these things.’

He took my request kindly and asked me into his cell. ‘Come in,’ said he; ‘I will give you a volume of the holy Fathers from which with God’s help you can learn about prayer clearly and in detail.’ We went into his cell and he began to speak as follows. ‘The continuous interior Prayer of Jesus is a constant uninterrupted calling upon the divine Name of Jesus with the lips, in the spirit, in the heart; while forming a mental picture of His constant presence, and imploring His grace, during every occupation, at all times, in all places, even during sleep. The appeal is couched in these terms, “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.” One who accustoms himself to this appeal experiences as a result so deep a consolation and so great a need to offer the prayer always, that he can no longer live without it, and it will continue to voice itself within him of its own accord. Now do you understand what prayer without ceasing is?’

‘Yes indeed, Father, and in God’s name teach me how to gain the habit of it,’ I cried, filled with joy.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q975 “How can we persevere in the practice of the Jesus Prayer?”, p. 105
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Jesus Prayer or the Arrow Prayer — 975. How can we persevere in the practice of the Jesus Prayer?

To persevere in the practice of the Jesus Prayer is to persevere in seeking to encounter the Lord Jesus and to surrender our hearts to Him, that His kingdom may abide within them. The scholar Origen says, “Let us search for Him with abundant labor that we may find that for which we search in abundance … He is within us.”

records.question: Why was he called 'Bishoy the Jeremian'?
records.answer: St. Bishoy was called "Bishoy the Jeremian" because he had a special love for the Book of Jeremiah. It was said that whenever he read the Book of Jeremiah, he used to see the prophet Jeremiah himself before him; he would kiss Jeremiah's head and then watch him ascending to heaven. This deep connection to the prophet Jeremiah gave him that title [6][9].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — In Scetis (Shiheet)

Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it and reign with power and dominion!

St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El- Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them up. One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: ‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life.’” She answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9).

In Scetis (Shiheet):

Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disciple of Abba ‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 360–361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian

An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian:

By a Divine arrangement, Mar ‘Ephraim the Syrian’ came once to meet with Abba ‘Bishoy.’ As St. ‘Ephraim’ talked in the Syrian tongue, while St. ‘Bishoy’ talked in the Coptic tongue; the later sought from God to give them both the ability to understand each other without the need for an interpreter, and God granted them that, and they managed to spend a tremendous spiritual time together. St. ‘Ephraim’ learned from St. ‘Bishoy’ about the monastic experiences of the Egyptian fathers, particularly of St. ‘Macarius the Great.’

After a week, St. ‘Ephraim’ left. Then, a brother came to seek St. ‘Ephraim's’ blessing, but when St ‘Bishoy’ told him that he just left, the brother started to run to catch him. St. ‘Bishoy’ called him and said he would never be able to because St. ‘Ephraim’ was carried away by a cloud. It was also said that St. ‘Ephraim’ has left behind his stick, in front of the cave of St. ‘Bishoy.’

Emperor Constantine visited Him:

St. ‘John the Short’ once went to visit his friend St. ‘Bishoy,’ and while he was still outside his cell, he heard him talking to someone inside. Knocking on the door and entering, he found no one with the saint. Asking him with whom he was talking, he answered: “Emperor Constantine came to visit me and told me: ‘I wish I have abandoned my kingdom and became a monk; for I did not imagine how the monks enjoy such an honor and great glory. I see how those who depart were carried by the wings of eagles; and how they were received with great honor in heaven.’”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 361–362
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Forsaking Scetis

Forsaking Scetis:

In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John the Short’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “Do you fear death, O man of God?” He answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell because of me!”

St. ‘John the Short’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba ‘Anthony’ where he reposed. Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain. There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose, and God granted them their wish.

St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. ‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints' bodies and buried them together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El- Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

They are now in the monastery of Abba ‘Bishoy’ in the Natron Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

As the monks knew that the saint would see the Lord now and then; they sought from him to intercede for them to enjoy seeing Him as well, so the Lord promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren greatly rejoiced, and all of them set forth toward the mountain. The saint, because of his old age, was at the rear. There, he encountered an older man overcome with weakness and frailty, not able to walk, and none of the passingby monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he did carry him and walked without feeling any labor. However, the older man started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one but the Lord Jesus Christ Himself. He then looked at Him and said: “The heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the earth; how can a sinner like me carry You?” To this, the Lord Jesus Christ smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your body will never see decay!” Then, He disappeared. St. ‘Bishoy's’ body is still kept in his monastery without deterioration up to this very day. Once the brethren knew about what happened, they grieved deeply for passing by that Old Man and not gaining the blessing of carrying Him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai of Antioch, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI OF ANTIOCH, ST. (The martyr)

‘Bishai’ (Abshai) was the brother of St. ‘Hur’ (Abahur) of Antioch. He was ordained as a priest because of his piety. His brother and his mother went to Alexandria, where they were martyred. Their brother, the priest, went there to take care of their bodies. Then, he felt the longing to partake in their crowns. So, he set forth to the governor to proclaim his faith, endured sufferings until he died. In vain, the governor attempted to burn their bodies.

The Church celebrates his feast on the 1st day of the short Coptic month: ‘Nasie’ (the forgotten days).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 358–359
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Life in Seclusion

Life in Seclusion:

When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the guidance of God. An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the Short’ should remain alone in that location. In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left the place forsaking his friend, and dug for himself a cave near the southern rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’

His Strife:

As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it. Then, he used to tie the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his heart; that it was said that he used to see the prophet Jeremiah during his reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’

He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. He believed in the saying: “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.” (2 Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus;

Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on a friendship level. He used to see Him, to talk with Him, and to enjoy His Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persistent in his great ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and behold, I shall always be with you!”

Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored at all!”

A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: “Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My commandments; I shall save him from all temptations!” He then blessed him and ascended.

Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted him and blessed him. The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with water in a basin, then the Lord ascended. St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water and left a portion for his disciple. The saint sought from him more than once to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Love for the Salvation of All Souls

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls:

Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted to Judaism and lived with her. When he happened to encounter some monks, he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something?” They answered in the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?! Nobody can overcome the tricks of Satan in women, except that one whom God is with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God saved him, and he came back and repented.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, the Hermit, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA

The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ The three of them were considered among the first monks who became disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite).

He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his prayers day and night. He was also known for his love of the book of the prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books of the prophets).

Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders appeared.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 357–358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

Through the friendship of this saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came out in the wilderness in his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise ‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12).

Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near the church. It so happened that while they were setting forth to visit Abba ‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.”

St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described his ascetic life.

[Manuscript# 438/250: Asceticisms and Teachings of Abba Bishai (Peter), Library of the Patriarchate] [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bishai Anoub, p. 355
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI ANOUB, ST. (The martyr)

He was a soldier in the days of ‘Cyprian,’ the governor of ‘Atrib’ (now Banha). When Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) stirred up persecution on the Christians, this soldier came forward and proclaimed his faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. He was arrested, and the governor tortured him, but when he did not forsake his faith, or deny his Christ, his head was cut off in ‘Matarieh’ in the region of ‘Ăin-Shams;’ a suburb of Cairo, on the 19th of Paona.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Jeremiah, the Monk of Menoufia, p. 357
passages.text:
Saint: JEREMIAH, THE MONK OF MENOUFIA

The Roman Emperor Anastasius I (491-518), was exiled to Egypt before he sat on the throne. There, he resided in the province of Menouf, where he had so many friends. One of the nobles counseled him to visit a saintly monk living in the neighborhood by the name of Jeremiah, to get his blessing. He went in the company of some friends. When they asked the monk to bless them, he gave every one of them a special blessing, except for Anastasius. Anastasius was very sad and told his friends that the man refrained from blessing me because he was aware of my sins. When they could not cheer him up, they went and told the monk about it. So, Jeremiah called Anastasius over to him and told him in the presence of three of his friends: “When I saw God's hand raised above your head, I felt no need of further blessing after that of God's.” Then, he advised him, saying: “God who will appoint you an emperor, seeks from you to keep away from bad behavior; and in particular not to approve of the decree of the council of Chalcedon.” The prophecy of the saintly has fulfilled in the year 491, and Emperor Anastasius had a significant relationship with the Egyptian Church, and his days were full of peace. Yet, some of the followers of the papal throne of Rome who were uncomfortable with the situation, provoked a man by the name of Webtalianus to proclaim the zeal over the Chalcedonian decree; and he gathered so many people around him and tried to take over the throne from Emperor Anastasius. However, he failed and was defeated.

[Fr. Manasseh Johanna: History of the Coptic Church; 1983; pp. 276-277]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Jerome, p. 359
passages.text:
Saint: JEROME (HIERONYMUS), ST. — In Antioch

In Antioch:

St. Jerome's relatives were all stirred up against him because he encouraged his sister to hold on to virginity and asceticism. So, he lefte Italy and went to the East through Greece. He settled down in Antioch in the year 374. There, he was welcomed and given hospitality by St. Evagrius, whom he loved so much and by whom he was strongly influenced and became attached to the Eastern world and its monastic life. He also was acquainted with Apollinaris, the bishop of Laodicea, whom he later opposed when he deviated from the Orthodox Faith.

Beside his ascetic life, St. Jerome dedicated his time to study the Holy Bible. He lived a solitary life in the wilderness of Chalcis, southeast of Antioch, for four years, where he learned the Hebrew language, at the same time, he suffered severe physical troubles, as was evident from what he wrote candidly to his spiritual daughter Eustochium. “Although the sun was so fiercely hot to terrify even the native monks here, I counted myself as though living amid the luxuries of the busy Rome. In this exile or prison, which I chose for myself to avoid hell, although I lived in the company of scorpions and beasts, yet I counted myself as though dwelling among the exotic Roman dancers. My face was so pale from the intense fasting, yet my soul became strong in its strife against evil desires. My cold body, which became entirely dried up and looking as if it was dead before its time, was still persistent in carrying evil desires. Therefore, I cast myself spiritually at the feet of the Lord Jesus, washing them with my tears and training my body on fasting the whole week. I was not ashamed to reveal the temptations which dwelt upon me, and I did not cease striking my chest day and night until I regain the peace.” When St. Jerome returned from the wilderness to Antioch in the year 377, his talents started to show up. So, bishop Paulinus applied some pressure on him to force him to accept the priesthood. However, he received the ordination under the condition that it would not be bound to a specific church. That was to dedicate himself to the word of God wherever God would call him to go.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef Ĥabib, the Deacon, pp. 364–365
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF ĤABIB, THE DEACON

After the Holy Liturgy and the rites of ordination, he went back to his work. He submitted his resignation on the same day in order to dedicate all his time and effort to a better activity.

When Fr. Bishoy came back from the Syrian Monastery in the Natrun Valley after the 40 days the new priest has to spend after his ordination; he found Yousef Ĥabib had dedicated himself to serve, day and night, in that new church of St. George in the district of Sporting in Alexandra. He took upon himself, without being asked by anyone, to support Fr. Bishoy at the beginning of his ministry in a new church that had no deacons, cantor, or ministers. Yousef Ĥabib was a first-class ecclesiastical man who elaborately knew by heart all the Church hymns and sang them with the spirit of prayer in a very touching voice. With that beginning, Yousef Ĥabib became the teacher of the Church’s young men and boys and let them absorb the spirit of the Fathers. He raised them on the love of the church and her hymns. Then, when the church came to have a cantor, her beautiful choir of deacons and her affairs started to settle down. Yousef Ĥabib withdrew himself in humility and self-denial and shifted his whole effort towards a new field to revive our ecclesiastical heritage.

Yousef Ĥabib, for a long time, has been fond of the biographies of the Saints, in particular of those whose fragrant life stories had not been published before. He started to travel to the desert monasteries to search in their libraries treasures about what was hidden, and he brought to light tens of biographies and rare stories. He also used to research in the libraries of the Coptic Museum and the library of the Patriarchate, etc. He even purchased a permanent train travel permit to go back and forth to Cairo twice a week for that purpose. He used to translate, research in the biographies of the Saints and their sayings, then returned home to publish them in small booklets, to the benefit of ministry, and for the improvement of the souls.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidhom Bishai, p. 144
passages.text:
Saint: SIDHOM BISHAI (The martyr)

On the 17th of Baramhat in the year 1561 AM (25 March 1844), the Coptic Church celebrates the martyrdom of St. Sidhom Bishai.

Sidhom Bishai was a trader of wood in the city of Alexandria. He used to go twice every year to Damietta to purchase lumber, which was imported through its harbor. Being an archdeacon who loved the old churches, Sidhom Bishai on hearing that the wooden roof of St. George el-Muzaĥem Church in the town of Basat in the district of Sherbin had collapsed; he took on himself the responsibility of repairing the damage done and provided a full ship load of wood for that purpose. At the same time, during his visits to Damietta, he used to attend the Holy Liturgies in St. George Church. One time, it happened that a non-Christian stroked shoulder against him on his way to the church aiming to block him from going to the Church. But, seeing how muåallem Sidhom Bishai paid little attention to that evil man, he was provoked to anger and paid some street boys to insult him. Then, it happened that the Mofti of the town was passing by; and these boys falsely accused Sidhom Bishai of insulting Islam, its “Prophet” and the “Quran.” Those false accusations, finding the expected fertile soil in the Moftis ears; he chose two of equally evil people around as witnesses. Through these people, they rigged the case against muåallem Sidhom Bishai. He was then 40 years of age, well known for meekness, kind-hearted and loving for all, not at all expected to utter what they falsely claimed that he has done.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius of Jerusalem, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS OF JERUSALEM — Monk, Priest, and Theologist

Monk, Priest, and Theologist:

Fr. Hesychius (Hezecius/Esytius/Isysius/Isacius) of Jerusalem is known to have been born in Jerusalem in the 2nd half of the 4th century AD and lived through the 1st half of the 5th century. He was thought to have been a disciple of St. Gregory, the Nazianzus (329-390 AD). He was a monk and probably a presbyter in the church of Jerusalem; and, he was considered by his contemporaries as a great theologian. Fr. Hesychius devoted himself to a solitary life, plunged into the wilderness, where he, with a bee-like enthusiasm, gathered the flowers of virtue from the Fathers there.

He was ordained as a priest by the patriarch of Jerusalem against his will. According to Theophanes, the Confessor (760-818 AD). in the year 412 AD, Fr. Hesychius got great fame as a priest and a preacher of the church of Jerusalem and was commended by St. Cyril of Sythopolis (525-559 AD) as being the teacher of the church, and a theologian of great fame. It was also said that he accompanied Juvenal, the patriarch of Jerusalem, to consecrate the church of the monastery of Euthymius around the year 428 AD. He reposed in the middle of the 5th century around 438 AD.

He was fond of meditating in the Holy Bible. From these interpretations, and got broad knowledge about the Divinities. Fr. Hesychius followed the approach of Origen, in using the symbolic interpretation for every verse in the Holy Bible, and he refused the literal interpretation. He also was an opponent of philosophy, since the heretics used it to corrupt the teachings of the Church. He gave so many sermons and recorded the Ecclesiastical History around the year 428 AD. All this work has been lost, including an attack on Nestor, in which he posed so many tough questions with their right answers. Fr. Hesychius defended the faith against the Arians, the Apollinarians, and the teachings of the Antiochians. In his debates concerning the Nature of the Lord Christ, he depended upon the statements made by St. Cyril of Alexandria (412- 444 AD) and adopted the theological views of Alexandria concerning the Nature of Christ though he did not utilize the exact theological expressions used by Alexandria.

records.question: Why did Christ tell us to pray it in the plural?
records.answer:
Christ told us to pray the Lord's Prayer in the plural because God bids us to love our neighbor, so we pray for fellow believers as well as non-believers. This way, our will aligns with God's will, who desires all people to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Even when praying privately, a believer should pray on behalf of the entire Church, as he is a member of it.

St. John Chrysostom explains that Christ teaches us to make our prayer common for our brethren, saying "our Father" instead of "my Father," always looking to the neighbor's good rather than only his own.

St. Augustine emphasizes that by calling God "our Father," we recognize that all Christians, regardless of social status, are brethren under one Father in heaven.

St. Cyprian adds that the prayer is public and common, not individual, because the whole people are one, and God willed that we pray for all, just as the three children in the fiery furnace prayed together with one heart and one spirit.

Furthermore, the apostles and disciples prayed together with one accord after the Lord's ascension, showing the communal nature of prayer [1][2].
