passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 196–197
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST.

He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family’ and ‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement’ in the whole world, even though there have been some monastic movements prior to his.

The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched his life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never get bored." That came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life.

One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they started to undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

His Order of Seclusion:

In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with some beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of kings." However, when he was pressured, he answered the emperor’s message, for the sake of the Church peace. 5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the Church. That is why he eventually came down to help Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians came back to the Church.

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who founded the system of congregations; as one of his disciples and greatly rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any particular order. 8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it.

Of His Words:

 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ.  Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack of discernment, they stayed away from God.  There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are not like us.  Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over the beasts of the wilderness. The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba.

[The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthonius, and Other Saints with That Name, pp. 195–196
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONIUS, and Other Saints with that Name (The martyrs) — ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr

Often confusion takes place between the martyrs who carried the name ‘Anthony,' among whom are:

ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr:

He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop assigned him to build a Church, the pagans were stirred up against him and killed him.

ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr:

St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to ‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his Christ, he ordered him chained and sent him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built. Abba Anthony’s idea was that if a monk wished to visit those living there, he could start walking after he finished eating at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone.

His Personality and the Role of Nitria;

Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away from the crowd and refrained from performing any miracles, claiming that he was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba Amon.

St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM

Besides his discipleship to Alexander, there were two other great influences in his life:

1- From his seventh year to the fifteenth he lived during a period of severe persecution (303 - 311 CE). He knew many among the Alexandrian martyrs and confessors from whom he learned the Orthodox faith and a loving intimacy with the Holy Scriptures. He did not accompany them to the arena of persecution but his heart was aflame with divine love, facing every struggle for the sake of Christ.

2- After he heard about St. Anthony the hermit, he hurried to the wilderness and lived with him for about three years, practicing the ascetic and righteous life and the deep fellowship with God. Providence arranged this close relationship with Anthony so that during his exiles and flight he never felt lonely. Instead he considered it a good opportunity for him to have a bit of solitude and seclusion, praying for his people and writing to them. He was obliged to become the historian of St. Anthony .

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of St. Anthony Mountain, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF ST. ANTHONY MOUNTAIN

On the 26th of Baba, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of seven martyrs who were martyred at the hands of the Barbarians, on the Mountain of St. Anthony, the Father of all monks.

[The Synaxarion: 26 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidrak St. Anthony and his Companions, p. 147
passages.text:
Saint: SIDRAK ST. ANTHONY AND HIS COMPANIONS (The martyrs)

A monk from the monastery of St. Anthony by the name of Sidrak, left his monastery with a colleague by the name of Fadl-Allah and accompanied them their close friend Daoud el-Banna. They all came down together from the mountain of St. Anthony to receive the crowns of martyrdom Those saints were martyred during the rule of the Circassian Mamluks (1382-1517) .

They were following the lead of St. Anthony, the Father of all Monks, who came down to Alexandria in the days of Emperor Maximian (286-305 AD) saying: “Let me go to where the fire of sufferings is. If the Divine care allowed for my martyrdom, I would be ready; and if not, I shall at the least stand by those persecuted among the children of St. Mark the Evangelist...”

[The Patriotism and History of the Coptic Church, p. 250]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sisoes, the Great, pp. 168–169
passages.text:
Saint: SISOES, THE GREAT, ST. — Abba Anthony his Role Model

After the repose of Abba Anthony the Great, St. Sisoes (Shishoi/Shishai) was one of the most shining pillars of faith among the Fathers of the wilderness. Therefore, this saint is referred to as St. “Sisoes the Great.” Shishoi means: The Son of the High One. He was an Egyptian by birth, and when he reached 20 years of age, he forsook the world and sought refuge in the wilderness of Scetis in the year 340 AD, and became a disciple to St. Macarius. In the year 356 AD, longing for a life of more tranquility, he crossed the Nile to the Mountain of St. Anthony right after his departure, to have the blessings of the life and virtues of St. Anthony as light and helper in his new life. He set forth to a life of seclusion until the year 426 AD when he reached the age of 106 years, and because of old age, he returned to the wilderness of Scetis, and reposed after a little while when he reached 110 years of age. About him, Abba Poemen (Bemen) said: “He exalted beyond every limit, and surpassed all the achievements of the other saintly Fathers.”

Abba Anthony his Role Model:

St. Sisoes was acting as if Abba Anthony the Great was watching him and listening to his instructions to his disciples. He strove to imitate that great teacher in all his life: in his asceticism, in his spiritual practices, in his commitment to silence and his longing for prayers. Therefore, his fame spread, and so many people came to him requesting to be his disciples. At this point, he had to forsake his love for silence and seclusion, to fulfill a higher goal, namely loving care of his disciples. Abba Sisoes’s brother came to visit him in the cave of Abba Anthony, where he was staying. The saint amiably said to his brother: “In this cave, a lion used to live; now it is inhabited by a fox.”

St. Sisoes always was complaining that he did not reach the statue of St. Anthony. Once, a monk asked him: “Father! Have you not reached the level of St. Anthony?” He answered: “If I had only one of the virtues of that monk, I would have become a torch of Divine Love.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 667–668
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia): He was born in upper Egypt around the year 290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the year 290 A. D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he established many monasteries in Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles.

St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church.

St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart. He led an ascetic life in a small hut in a village for about ten years under the guidance of an ascetic. He longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness to become his disciples.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pelosianus, p. 396
passages.text:
Saint: PELOSIANUS, ST.

This saint was a friend of Abba Anthony the Great (251-356 AD). He took part in burying Abba Anthony along with his fellow monk Isaac. It seems that St. Jerome (342-420 AD), who told us about him, has met him somewhere.

[Jerome: Vita Hilarionis, 30; 31]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Yousef, Father [a Contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great], p. 367
passages.text:
Saint: YOUSEF, FATHER [A Contemporary of Abba Anthony the Great]

This Father Yousef was one of the prominent elders of the wilderness in the 4th century. All we know about him is that he happened to go to visit St. Anthony the Great in the company of two fellow elder hermits. St. Anthony tried to put them to the test, so he asked them about specific topics in the Holy Bible. The first and second hermits gave some answers. To them, St. Anthony said that their responses were not satisfactory. However, when Fr. Yousef said humbly: “I truly say, O Father, I do not know. I am utterly helpless in that concern.” Over his response, St. Anthony said: “Fr. Yousef alone found the right answer, by saying: ‘I do not know.’”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 258–259
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony

Many researchers talked about St. Hilarion (Ilarion), as being the disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who founded the monastic movement. Whereas, St. Jerome, who recorded his biography, said about him: “Many people glorified his asceticism; others were amazed by the miracles God performed on his hands; while still others admired the wisdom and virtues with which he was adorned, I (Jerome), on the other hand, do not marvel about any of these, as much as I do about how he despised the temporal glory, with which everyone surrounded him, and honored him everywhere whenever he was, and how the bishops, the priests, the monks, the rulers, the judges, the elites, and the commons approached him seeking his guidance, blessing, and prayers. He did his best to disappear from the scene. He fled from the East to the West, hiding in the most isolated locations where no one could endure to dwell.”

With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony:

St. Hilarion (291-371 AD) was born in a village called Tabatha, five miles south of Gaza, to wealthy pagan parents who sent him to Alexandria to learn the philosophical and practical knowledge. In Alexandria, he encountered a lot of scholars, mostly Christians, and the Holy Spirit led him to faith in the Lord Christ; and he was baptized when he was about fifteen years of age. As a Christian, he loved to pray and to worship in an ascetic manner.

By the year 306 AD, the sweet fragrance of Abba Anthony the Great filled the whole of Egypt and reached outside its borders. Then, once Hilarion heard about him, he put in his heart to visit him to get his blessing and listen to his teaching. When he finally met him, he viewed him as an angel of God and became one of his disciples for one year. Yet, because of the large crowds that came to see and seek the blessing of Abba Anthony, Hilarion sought his permission to leave Egypt and go back to Palestine, to live there in an atmosphere of seclusion, away from people.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, p. 160
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

He was the founder of the monastic movement in ‘Nitria’ (Bernoug). Here, we need to distinguish between three monastic zones within the Natron Valley (Wadi El-Natrun) which often get mixed up:

1- The ’Nitria’ (Bernoug) zone, which received the first spark of the monastic movement through Abba Amon. 2- The ‘Celia’ (the Cells) zone, which is about 10 miles south of the ‘Nitria’ zone. 3- The ‘Scetis’ (Askeet) zone, which is located to the south of the former two zones.

His Monastic Life:

Saint Amon the great was born around the year 275 AD near the region of Marriott. He was raised as an orphan, and when he reached 22 years of age, his uncle forced him to get married despite his refusal. When he got married, he and his bride agreed on living virgins. Eighteen years later, the saint set forth to the desert of ‘Nitria’ (the city of Nitria or Bernoug is 14 kilometers Southwestern of the city of Damanhur). He was the first monk to reach that area, and he built for himself a cell there, in which he lived for 22 years. During that time, he used twice a year to visit his wife, who was living with many pious virgins. The location of the ‘Nitria’ zone was convenient to be the cradle of the commencement of that monastic movement. That area was close to the countryside and to the desert at the same time. In the beginning, the monks, who followed St. Amon, worked to earn their living by cropping the wheat, and it was easy for them also to acquire the linen to weave, instead of the palm leaves. The area also provided them with the ‘Natron’, which they could extract from the lake and sell to the villages around them. However, the region was always infested by mosquitos because of its swamps.

A congregation of hermits started to gather around the saint. They all lived in a life midway between the system of seclusion and that of the cenobite. Abba Amon was the first head of such a monastic congregation in Nitria, and many of his disciples became great fathers. Abba Amon used to visit Abba Anthony to seek his blessing and guidance. And when Abba Anthony came to visit him, he asked his advice concerning some pious monks, who tried to live a solitary life and build for themselves cells far away from the congregation. After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, pp. 297–298
passages.text:
Saint: IGNATIUS, THE THEOPHORUS, ST. — Setting the System of Praise

He was born around the year 30 A.D. and was raised in Syria. Some scholars believe that he was the child whom the Lord Jesus Christ carried when He presented him as an example of humility (Matt. 18:2-4).

Seeing his kindled zeal, the apostles ordained him as a bishop on Antioch. However, there was a disagreement concerning which apostle has ordained him. According to some, Peter, the apostle, ordained Evodius as a bishop for the Christians from Jewish origin; and John, the apostle, ordained Ignatius for the Christians from Gentile origin. When bishop Evodius reposed, bishop Ignatius was put in charge of the region's Christians from both origins. Being known for his eagerness for the salvation of souls, he gained so many new Gentiles for the Lord Christ. His intense love for his people was recorded in his conversation with those who came to welcome him in Smyrna, during his trip to Rome to be martyred. He kept mentioning his congregation to them and asked them to pray for his people.

Setting the System of Praise:

While in Rome, he saw in a night vision, the angels praising and glorifying the Holy Trinity. He transferred what he heard to be used by the Church of Antioch. And from there, it was spread to all other Churches.

His Encounter with Trajan:

Hearing about his zeal on spreading Christianity, Emperor Trajan (98-117) called him and entered with him into a debate concerning the Crucified Jesus, which St. Ignatius declared that he carried in his heart. Then, the argument ended by the emperor giving an order to chain him to be sent to Rome, where he would be offered as food to the wild beasts, to please the people there.

When the bishop heard the order, he greatly exulted, knowing that the hour he was longing for has come at last. He considered that the imperial command was the best gift he has ever received. He knelt and cried out with joy: “I thank You, O Lord, for granting me the honor of the perfect love towards you; and for allowing me to be chained by iron chains like your apostle Paul.” Then, he kissed the chains, supplicating to God to keep His Church safe, after the Lord entrusted him to serve it for over forty years.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, pp. 298–299
passages.text:
Saint: IGNATIUS, THE THEOPHORUS, ST. — To Rome

To Rome:

The saint was led guarded by ten soldiers, accompanied by two people from his Church: Philon and Agathopus. Observing how much his people loved him and how they gathered around him before his departure, the guards intentionally treated him with great despise and cruelty. In his documented account on what happened, he called them wild lions since they ignored his usual compassion toward them and what the people paid to them to treat their bishop with tenderness. They arrived at Smyrna, where he was received by St. Polycarp its bishop, besides many delegations from the Churches of Ephesus, Tralliah, and Magnesia. He used that chance to write letters to those Churches, as well as to the one in Rome; for he has heard that some believers there were trying hard to save him from martyrdom, in which he said: “I am afraid that your love for me will cause me harm. Pray that I would not be given a greater gift beyond being sacrificed to God, as long as the altar is ready. I ask you not to show me undue compassion. Allow me to be offered as food to the wild beasts; by that way, I would be granted the grace to reach God. I am the bread of God. Let me be crushed by the fangs of the beasts and let them become my grave. And let nothing be left of my body that no one has to worry about. Once the world does not see my body, I shall be truly a disciple of Christ.”

In Troas:

He was taken in a boat from Smyrna to Troas, where he wrote three more letters to Philadelphia, Smyrna, and St. Polycarp. From Troas, he sailed to Neopolis, to Philippi, then to Epirus and Tyrone. Finally, he arrived at the region of Portus, where he met with the brethren, whose joy to see him was mixed with the sadness of his close departure. He received them with love, asking them to have the courage and show him true love.

He knelt and prayed to God to put an end to the wave of persecution against His Church and to increase the love of the brethren toward each other.

Finally, the guards rushed him to the arena and released the wild beasts, which he received with a cheerful countenance. Two lions jumped on him and devoured him to leave off his body, only a few bones. The believers gathered his precious relics and sent them to Antioch. His martyrdom took place around the year 108 AD. The Church celebrates him on the 7th of Abib.

[Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty: The Two Martyrs: Ignatius and Polycarp; 1964]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theognostus, p. 278
passages.text:
Saint: THEOGNOSTUS

Theognostus (Theogust) was a priest and a theologian in Alexandria in the 3rd century AD. He was the Dean of the School of Alexandria, most probably before Fr. Peros. About him, we know very little through quotations that came in the writings of Fotius, Athanasius, and Gregory bishop of Nyssa.

His doctrinal work “Hypotyposes” came in seven books, these books were available in the time of Fotius, but they have been lost later on. In his first book, he followed the style of Origen. In the second and third books, there were some Arian tendencies. In the fifth book, he denoted bodies to the angels and demons.While in the sixth and seventh books, he dealt with the Divine Incarnation in a sound Orthodox manner. The 20th Pope Athanasius the Apostolic considered his work as one of the best testimonies against Arianism.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Fr. Theognostus, p. 278
passages.text:
Saint: THEOGNOSTUS, FR.

He was a priest from Alexandria, who was sent as a deputy of the 24th Pope Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to Constantinople, along with Fr. Sharmocinus the priest and Liontius the deacon [Cyril: Letters 37, 41]

[Smith & Wace; Vol 4, p. 990]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore Tiro, pp. 262–263
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE TIRO (The martyr)

The Byzantine Church celebrates three great saints who were officers in the army: Theodore (Tadros) (Tiro was the title of his family), Georguis and Demetrius. There is a mymar about this St. Theodore attributed to St. Gregory of Nazianzus.

This saint was a pious young officer in the Roman army. His regiment was sent to Pontus in the wintertime. And, he went to Amasea, where he refused to partake in pagan worship with his fellow officers. When he was called by the governor and the leader of his regiment to be asked about the reason for his action, he proclaimed his faith in Jesus Christ. When he was threatened of being killed, he bravely said: “Jesus Christ is my God. In case my words disturb you, cut my tongue off, and even cut every member of my body. And, may God receive them as acceptable sacrifices.” On seeing how he firmly held to his faith, he was left alone for some time, with the hope that he might reconsider and deny his Christ. When he was called again, they tried to seduce him with many promises, which he rejected. He was then violently whipped, and he endured it as a fellowship in the passion of His Christ. Then, he was cast in prison, and God sent his angels to comfort him. When he was called for the third time, he was burned alive and gained the crown of martyrdom. And, Ausiba buried his remains in Euchaita. He was martyred on the 9th of November in the year 306 AD. St. Gregory of Nyssa said about him describing his courage and the power of his intercession that he kept Pontus safe from the attacks of the Scythians who destroyed all the surrounding States. He also said about the saint: “As a soldier, he defended us; and as a martyr, he intercedes for us and seeks peace for all of us.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore, the Monk, p. 266
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE, THE MONK (The martyr)

This St. Theodore was born in Alexandria and was raised in a pure Christian family atmosphere. He loved the life of serenity that he abandoned the world and lived as a monk in one of the monasteries close to Alexandria, where he practiced his prayers, fasting, and studies in the Holy Bible and the books of the Fathers. When the 20th pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373) was exiled and an intruding Arian archbishop by the name of Georgius, was installed in his place; the whole congregation was in a turmoil. It did not stop at the believers boycotting the intruder, despite the high price they had to pay, but the fathers the monks did their decisive role in that critical situation. St. Theodore, the monk left his monastery and went to Alexandria to support the people and to hold them fast to their faith. Besides, he debated the Arian clergy. When the Arian intruder archbishop, the denier of the Godhead of the Lord Christ, saw the danger of St. Theodore’s work towards his plans, he arrested him. He threatened the saint and finally ordered his men to have him tied up to the tail of a wild horse, and was set free to peel St. Theodore’s flesh off and to cover the streets of Alexandria with his blood. He eventually delivered his soul and received the crown of martyrdom on the 6th of Paona.

Even though the soul of this martyr longed to a life of solitude and a fellowship with God; yet his heart was burning for the salvation of others. He could not find comfort in his monastery, while the other souls were getting into perdition because of the deception of the Arians in the absence of their pope and their bishops. Therefore, he set forth to do his role joyfully to testify for his Christ.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch, pp. 283–284
passages.text:
Saint: THEOPHILUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH, ST. — His Writings

According to Eusebius, this saint was the 6th bishop of Antioch in Syria, near the end of the 2nd century. St. ‘Theophilus’ was born to pagan parents in an area close to the Euphrates river. He was educated by the Hellenic (Greek) culture. On studying the Christian Holy Bible, he perceived that the Holy Spirit granted the prophets many prophesy about the things to come. So, he believed and obeyed God.

His Writings:

This St. Theophilus was one of the Christian apologists. However, only three books survived out of his many written works. Those books were dedicated to his pagan friend Autolycus, in which he introduced the Christian thoughts about God and His creation before the pagan world with its wrong diverse fantasies. Among his lost writings were essays against Marcion and the heresy of Hermogenes.

Of his Sayings:

+ No one can see God except those who are capable of seeing Him, when their souls’ eyes are open wide. When there is dirt on a mirror, man cannot see his face in it. Likewise, it is with the sinful. He cannot see God. + I indeed honor the emperor, yet not by worshipping him, but by praying for him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Isidore of Alexandria, p. 329
passages.text:
Saint: ISIDORE OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — His troubles

St. Theophilus attempted to recommend him as a patriarch on the throne of Constantinople, but St. Chrysostom opposed that attempt. Then, St. Theophilus sent him to Palestine with a message. There, St. Isidore sided with St. John, the bishop of Jerusalem. His position stirred up St. Jerome, who accused him of being a follower of Origen (184-254 AD). St. Jerome was totally against Origen's philosophy, while St. John of Jerusalem was supporting him.

Around the year 391 AD, there was a dispute between St. Isidore and Pope Theophilus, who accused him of giving communion to one of the followers of the Mani's heresy. The pope drove him away from Alexandria to go back to his old cell in Nitria. However, when the pope made it more difficult for him, he joined the Tall Brothers and went with them to St. John Chrysostom in Constantinople, where there were a lot of Origen's supporters. On returning from Constantinople, St. Isidore reposed in the year 403 AD, at the age of 85 years and was buried in Alexandria. The Western Church celebrates him on the 15th of January.

[Palladius: The Lausiac History, Ch. 1]

Notes: [1] This part has a lot of similarity to what happened to St. Isidore of Farma.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ephothes, pp. 24–25
passages.text:
Saint: EPHOTHES (The martyr)

The following saints: Ephothes (means "the Perfumed"), Calesti (the Splendid), and Hermoganes (the descendant of Atared), were martyred in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) and his partner Maximianus. We do not know much about them except their names and that they were from the city of Syracusa on the island of Sicily.

[Archimandrite Michael Ăssaf: The Book of Synaxarion, Aylol 1]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodotus, Bishop of Ancyra, p. 275
passages.text:
Saint: THEODOTUS, BISHOP OF ANCYRA

Bishop Theodotus was a supporter of the Nestorian theology of the heretic Nestor. However, in the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 AD, he reversed his position and became a prominent supporter of the 24th Pope St. Cyril of Alexandria (412-444) against Nestor. This bishop was defrocked by the Nestorians at their Synod of Tarsus in the year 432 AD. Bishop Theodotus wrote so many articles, among which were: Essays against Nestor (lost); an explanation of the Nicene Creed of Faith; several essays on the feast of Nativity; and on the Purification. Also, there is a mymar which has been attributed to him, dealing with the martyrdom of St. George and his miracles...

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodore, the Roman, pp. 266–267
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORE, THE ROMAN (The martyr)

This St. Theodore was an inhabitant of Astir, in the days of the two emperors Maximian and Diocletian (284-305). When they heard that the saint did not worship the idols, they called him and sought from him to worship their gods, which he declined. After promising to give him many honors if he denied his Christ, he rejected them and held fast to his faith. Then, they started torturing him. They whipped him, pressed him by the Henbazin, cut some of his limbs, and burned his sides with fire. In all this, he endured for his love of the Lord Christ. And, the Lord sent his angel to strengthen and comfort him. Finally, they cut his head off, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

The Church celebrated his feast on the 28th of Amshir.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q538 “Why does St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, call the Church “a congregation of love”?”, p. 424
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Eminence of the Church — 538. Why does St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, call the Church “a congregation of love”?

St. Ignatius the Theophorus says, “All these things are good together, if you believe in love.” He also says that Christ is eternal life for He grants us life through His divine love, “for the drink of God is His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.”

Notes: [1092] St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Philadelphians 9 (LCL 24:293). [1093] St. Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Romans 7 (LCL 24:279).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodosia, p. 270
passages.text:
Saint: THEODOSIA (The martyr)

The West celebrates the two martyrs Epiphanius and Theodosia together on the 2nd of April. The story of their martyrdom has been documented by Eusebius in his account about the Martyrs of Palestine. He was affected greatly, as an eye-witness, by their sufferings around the year 318 AD. He was astonished by their bravery at their young age; for Epiphanius was 20 years old, whereas Theodosia was 18 years old. He wrote: “In Caesarea, during the fifth year of the persecution, in the feast of the resurrection of our Savior, a virgin girl by the name of Theodosia of the city of Tyre, a serious believer of less than 18 years of age, set forth to the prisoners who were charged of testifying to the Kingdom of Christ before the court of justice, to greet them and to seek from them to remember her when they stand before the Lord. She was arrested and brought before the governor, who came over her like a vicious maniac, he tortured her by cutting her breasts off down to the bones; and seeing how she kept on standing with a cheerful countenance, he ordered to throw her into the sea; then turned to the other confessors, and gave the order to send them over to work in the copper mines in Pheno (Faynan), Palestine.”

[Eusebius of Caesarea: Martyrs of Palestine 7, translated by Fr. Marcus Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Iris, p. 306
passages.text:
Saint: IRIS (The martyr)

The first martyr among Origen's students was Plutarch about whom Eusebius said, “While being taken to death, he was approached by Origen who accompanied him until the end; whom the Divine care kept him safe this time as well; even though the martyr's relatives were furious about Origen for being the cause of his death by urging him to reject the pagan religion.”

The second martyr among Origen's students was Serenus, whose testimony was louder than the fire of the furnace into which he was cast. He was followed by the third martyr Heraclides, a simple catechumen in Origen's school, and who was beheaded. The fourth was Hero, who received baptism a short time before he delivered his neck to the sword for his faith. The fifth was another Serenus, who was also beheaded after a long ordeal of tortures. Eusebius called him “an athlete of piety.” The sixth one was a woman by the name Iris (Herais), who was martyred, while still a catechumen. According to Eusebius, “she received the baptism by fire, as Origen himself says.” The seventh martyr was Basilides, who led to martyrdom, the celebrated virgin martyr Potamiæna.

[Eusebius: The Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, Ch.1-5]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athenogenes, pp. 271–272
passages.text:
Saint: ATHENOGENES, ST. (The martyr)

The Roman Church celebrates the birthday of this theologian martyr on the 18th of January; and his martyrdom on the 16th of July. And, St. ‘Gregory, the Enlightened’ fixed a feast for him in Armenia.

This saint was born in ‘Pontes,’ even though some others believe he was born in ‘Sebastia’ in Armenia. He was ordained as a bishop and was martyred around the year 305 AD, together with 10 of his disciples in the days of Emperor ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD). When he was cast in the fire, he kept singing praise for the Holy Spirit: “Phos Hilaron” (Φῶς Ἱλαρόν) of his writing, as a sign of his gratitude to the Holy Spirit who granted him the gift of martyrdom. In an essay about the Holy Spirit, St. ‘Basil the Great’ (330-379 AD) referred to this praise, saying: “Whoever get to know the praise of St. ‘Athenogenes’ by which he hastened to achieve perfection by the fire, and which he left as a farewell gift to his friends, could understand the mind and thoughts of the martyrs concerning the Spirit.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — Fr. Isaac, the Confessor, pp. 313–314
passages.text:
Saint: ISAAC, THE CONFESSOR, FR.

The life of that anchorite reveals the heart of a Christian, whatever his position or role is, that is inflamed with love and zeal, and is working boldly within the Church. That father loved the life of solitude and intended to live his whole life, unceasingly worshipping God, away from the confusion and preoccupations of the world. However, hearing about how the Arian Emperor Valence (364-378 AD) persecuted the Church, he could not stand sitting tighthanded. So, after continuous profound prayers, he set out to Constantinople to face the emperor. Then, he warned the emperor more than once, that very tough tribulation would dwell upon him unless he would stop persecuting the upright in faith (the Orthodox) and give them back their churches. He meant by that those churches which he took away from them by force to deliver to the Arians; but, the emperor despised him and his warnings.

When he once met the emperor coming out of the city, he got hold of the bridle of his horse and started to rebuke him. The emperor ordered his men to cast him in the nearest swamp, but the Lord saved him from it in a miraculous way. As he repeated his prophecy against him, he threw him in prison. Shortly after, the saint's prophecy was realized, and Valence was killed in the battle of Adrianople. Emperor Theodosius I (379-396 AD), who replaced Valence, released the saint and honored him.

Intending to resume his life of solitude again, his disciples insisted that he would not forsake them. So, Fr. Isaac established a monastery for them called The Dalmatian, referring to Dalmatius, one of his disciples. That monastery is considered to be the oldest monastery in Constantinople.

The saint attended the second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople; then, he reposed in good old age.

[Butler's Lives of Saints; May 30]

records.question: What does the Coptic Orthodox Church teach about purgatory?
records.answer:
I could not find anything about purgatory in the loaded sources.

The sources do cover related topics such as the state of the soul after death and before the final judgment, describing that the soul enjoys the extension of life in Christ and may experience a partial judgment leading to paradise or bitterness and deprivation of the vision of the Lord until the final day of judgment, when eternal life or eternal punishment is fully realized [4]. They also discuss asceticism as a preparation for eternal life and the longing for the world to come [2][5][6]. However, purgatory as a specific doctrine or teaching is not mentioned.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q4 “What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?”, pp. 7–8
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?

It is worth laying out the circumstances through which the Coptic Church has endured, from her foundation till the present day, that we may grasp the truth of her teachings, and benefit from her long experience over twenty centuries.

Our Coptic Church has continuously faced persecution since the middle of the first century and until the present time. Thus, Mrs. Butcher, a Professor of History at Oxford University, expressed her amazement when she stated that the endurance of the Copts to this day is one of the wonders of the world.

In the eighth century B. C., Isaiah the prophet anticipated the Coptic Church and wrote with the spirit of prophecy of her marvelous beginnings.

The Church suffered many persecutions, even from fellow Christians. Such were the persecutions by the Emperors of Constantinople who persecuted her and appointed patriarchs with the power and authority to continually oppress even the monks in their monasteries and deserts, pressuring them to accept the Tome of Leo.

We are indeed thankful to God who allowed our Egypt, blessed by Isaiah the prophet, to endure these long-lasting periods of extremely bitter persecution. And yet, they have afforded us opportunities to praise the Crucified One, together with the Apostle Paul, saying, “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

A friend once showed me a letter that someone had sent to several influential companies and personalities in America. In it, he asked for their aid to further his missionary work in Egypt, thinking that he would present Christ to the Copts, who, although they produce martyrs, are a dead Church, ignorant of Christ (in his opinion)! We need not defend our Church. For the Day of the Lord is at hand and many simple martyrs, shepherds, and pure theologians will be revealed as a heavenly bride, sitting at the right hand of the King of Kings!

The trials that have befallen the Church through the ages have contributed to revealing her living faith, her Orthodox teachings, and the work of the Holy Trinity within her. The Church did not deviate to pursue worldly glories or transient politics, but rather fixed her eyes on the second coming of the Lord on the clouds.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q871 “What is the goal of ascetic life according to the Copts?”, p. 664
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 871. What is the goal of ascetic life according to the Copts?

While most ancient civilizations were attached to the temporal life and so they pursued worldly pleasures, the Egyptian mind was consumed with the world to come. Ancient Egyptians believed in the so-called “resurrection,” which is the belief in the resurrection of the dead to eternal life, if certain rituals were performed. This is why bodies were mummified in sealed tombs, such that no one would be able to visit the tomb or live in it except for the soul. The tombs were supplied with one’s daily needs (clothes, food, drink, vessels, knives, chairs, weapons, chariots, jewelry, toys for children … etc.).

When the Copts accepted Christianity, their longing for the world to come grew, and their hearts were inflamed with longing for it, but now on a biblical basis. Instead of being concerned with the souls’ return to their bodies in the tombs, they desired for their souls, thoughts, and hearts to be lifted up to enjoy the heavenly life even when their bodies were still treading on the earth. In other words, their longing for the world to come drove them to lead an ascetic life on a biblical basis.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q3 “How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?”, p. 7
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 3. How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?

I greatly desired to present a Coptic Orthodox Catechism to reveal our Christian understanding concisely and briefly; particularly because, due to ecclesiastical and political circumstances, our Church was isolated from Western churches in the fifth century A. D. and remained so to a large extent up until the twentieth century, when she was accused by many in the West of adhering to Eutychianism. The Coptic Church, therefore, did not have the opportunity to reveal her true teachings through the writings of her Fathers and her liturgies. Despite the Church’s participation in many international theological conferences in recent years, insisting upon her rejection of Eutychianism, some sources continue to attribute this heresy to our Church, of which the Church is completely innocent and strongly opposes through her liturgies and praises.

In a certain dialogue with the Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches, theologians were surprised to observe that the liturgies and praises that we enjoy to the present day lack even the slightest hint of Eutychianism, but rather, positively oppose it in a beautifully Christian manner; especially the daily Theotokias and those of the festal celebrations. Some of the theologians observed that they harmonize with the thought St. Cyril, or that perhaps he was their author.

A Greek theologian once asked me whether we use the word “Theotokos” to describe St. Mary and was astonished to learn that it is a term beloved in Coptic texts in every age.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1390 “What will be the state of the soul after it departs from the body and until the day of the Lord’s final coming?”, pp. 507–508
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › The Two Comings and the Rapture — 1390. What will be the state of the soul after it departs from the body and until the day of the Lord’s final coming?

Living faith, working through love, gives the believer a token of heaven. So, the believer lives in the spirit of hope, longing to meet the Lord Christ face to face. This does not exempt him from the death of the body when the soul departs from it and goes on to enjoy the extension of her life in Christ.

Some ask: Will the soul be judged immediately, or will she wait until the day of judgment? Some believe that the soul that enjoys God’s grace on earth will be subject to a partial judgment and then enjoy paradise with the saints and behold the Lord and His angels until the day of the coming of the Lord, at which time her glory will be perfected. Similarly, the wicked soul that denies the Lord will fall into bitterness be deprived of the vision of the Lord in His glory; and she shall not have a share in the praise of the heavenly beings, until the day of the Lord when she will be cast out into hell with the devil and his angels.

Some distinguish between paradise and eternal life, believing that paradise is the period between the death of the body and the day of the final judgment. It is only in the subsequent eternal life that we will experience the fullness of our eternal inheritance. Similarly, they distinguish between Hades and hell: Hades being the interim period, bitter because they are deprived of the Lord and His angels; which is followed by the fires of hell and eternal suffering. The Lord spoke of this in the Sermon on the Mount: of the eternal life prepared for the faithful; and of hell, prepared for the devil and his angels.

Notes: [1246] H. E. Panteleimon Lampadarios, The Catechism of the Orthodox Church: Questions and Answers (Greece, 2006): p. 319.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q872 “What is the motive of asceticism for the Copts?”, pp. 664–665
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 872. What is the motive of asceticism for the Copts?

Asceticism in the Coptic Church is not a goal in its own, but it is one’s practical response to the divine love. If our Lord offered His life for us, it is fitting for us to desire to offer our lives as a sacrifice of love to God. We despise worldly pleasures as a sign of our inner longing to enjoy the eternal joy of the new life in Christ Jesus. Believers, especially monks, have a single goal, that is to enjoy the inner Kingdom of God as a preliminary step to encountering God face to face in eternity.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q870 “Is asceticism, as it is practiced in the Coptic Church, biblical?”, p. 664
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 870. Is asceticism, as it is practiced in the Coptic Church, biblical?

The Coptic Church is known for its ascetic inclinations, not only due to the monastic movement that started in it, but asceticism is also considered one of the essential characteristics manifested in her life as a whole and her worship. These inclinations exist not because asceticism is a goal in and of itself, nor on the basis that the flesh is evil in nature; but rather on a biblical and heavenly understanding: “For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). “Go your way, sell whatever you have and give to the poor … and follow Me” (Mark 10:21, Luke 18:22). “But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27).

This biblical understanding was found to be sweet by the Copts, whose hearts were inflamed with eternal love.

passages.text:
THE COPTIC ORTHODOX CHURCH & THE CHRISTIAN DOGMAS — 4. DOGMA AND ASCETICISM

Dogmas correlate to our ascetic attitude. As mentioned [12] before, the early Alexandrian theologians and clergymen were true ascetics, and as a result, asceticism still strongly affects our theology. This is not by denying our bodies, as some scholars charge. Still, by insisting on the soteriological aspect: The early Coptic ascetics were involved in enjoying the redeeming deeds of the Holy Trinity, i.e., in enjoying the sanctification of the soul, mind, body, and gifts, etc. through communion with the Father in His Son through His Holy Spirit.

Early Egyptian asceticism was biblical. It neither hated the body, senses, and capacities nor did it deny the human free- will or despise earthly life and all its properties. Coptic ascetic , in its essence, was not isolated from men but rather enjoyed unity with God. This attitude affected our theology and dogmas through concentration on the "deification," i.e., the return of man to the original image of God by restoring his soul, mind, and body, etc., in preparation for Paradise.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q5 “What are the basic principles of catechism in the Coptic Orthodox Church?”, p. 22
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › The Basic Principles of Catechism — 5. What are the basic principles of catechism in the Coptic Orthodox Church?

It is fitting for us as believers to benefit from the experience of our fathers through the stages of catechism over the centuries, that we may live with a spiritual, living, Biblical mindset in every aspect of our lives; whether in our study of the Holy Bible, our practice of the truly evangelical life, or in our daily conduct; even our eating and drinking, our worship in the spirit of truth, and our service for every person we meet, even if we do not know them personally, and in our conversations with believers and nonbelievers.

St. Clement of Alexandria describes the life of the Christian believer in his book The Instructor (Paedagogus). He explains that our faith in Christ must be translated into action. We live in Christ Jesus when we walk alongside the elderly whose movement is slow and when we walk alongside the young who are quick in their movements; in our smile and our refraining from inappropriate laughter; in our observance of table manners as those in the conscious presence of God; in our sleep …so the believer lives as an ambassador of Christ in all matters, whether they seem important or trivial. And he does all this without either the literalism that kills or tedious routine.

In all of this, there are two important considerations: our hearts should be inflamed with love for the Lord Christ while we await His swift coming on the clouds to take us into His heavenly bridal chamber; and we should also be constantly occupied with the salvation of the whole world, even of those who have fallen into what we may deem serious crimes or impure sins!

Notes: [23] I hope, if God wills, to present the approach of St. Clement of Alexandria—one of the pillars of the School of Alexandria—in The Life in Christ Jesus.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q603 “What are the features of the Coptic altar?”, pp. 464–465
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Mystery of the House of God — 603. What are the features of the Coptic altar?

The Coptic altar takes the shape of approximately a cube, which resembles Christ’s tomb.

It is located right in the middle of the sanctuary, to resemble the heavenly altar: “I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar” (Rev. 9:13).

It is often made of stone, marble, or brick, but exceptions do exist.

It must be hollow so that saints’ relics can be kept inside or beneath it.

On the eastern side of the altar, there exists a small opening showing an interior recess or cavity, which was used during persecution to hide the Holy Gifts when necessary.

The altar is never raised above the sanctuary but is fitted directly on its ground, as directed by the divine commandment (Ex. 20:26).

It does not have any form of engraving, not even crosses (Ex. 20:25).

Multiple altars in the same church were introduced to fulfill the needs of the ever-growing Christian congregation, since it is forbidden to pray more than one liturgy on the same altar in the course of a single day.

passages.text:
THE COPTIC ORTHODOX CHURCH & THE CHRISTIAN DOGMAS — 8. DOGMAS AND KNOWLEDGE

They were steadfast and strict concerning the faith they had received (2 Tim. 1:12, 14), and some historians described them with violence, but they were genuinely loving and kind men. St. Cyril wrote to Nestorius, telling him that he would never find a person who loved him like Cyril but never would this love be at the expense of his faith [17] . He hated heresy and error but loved the soul of the heretic and desired his salvation.

The Alexandrian Fathers used theological terms to explain the divine truths and their profound meanings to defend the Orthodox faith against heresies. Still, they were not enslaved to the terms themselves. St. Athanasius, who devoted his life to defending Christ's Godhead, stated that disputes merely about words must not be suffered to divide those who think alike [18] .

It was the duty of the early Church to offer the Christian faith in Greek terms for the Hellenist world. However, some theologians believe that the Church has to express its faith not in Greek terms but in simple words that modern man can accept. Leslie Dewart, a Canadian Roman Catholic philosopher, aims to achieve a "dehellenization" of the Christian faith in God. He feels it is time that the Christian faith took on a form in keeping with the experience of modern man. To do so, it must eliminate the philosophical categories of Greek philosophy, as that philosophy belongs to an ancient past. He states that we have to exclude three terms: Ousia (essence), Trias (Trinity), and Hypostasis (Person)."

a) Concerning the term "ousia" (essence), he says that God is beyond this term. We feel God as "presence" and not as "Supreme Being."

b) Concerning Trias, he says, that it could lead to "Tritheism."

c) He suggests abolishing the term "Hypostasis" in dealing with the Holy Trinity.

The Coptic Orthodox Church is well known as a conservative church, especially in dogma and doctrines. At the same time, it developed not by embracing new doctrines or new "articles of faith," but by explaining the same faith "once given to the saints" (Jude 3) in a contemporary language. In more details we can summarize our view of the dogmas with the following points:

An Indian theologian published his doctoral thesis in English in which he re-evaluates the Council of Chalcedon. It has also been translated into Arabic. He quotes excerpts from certain Orthodox Chalcedonian and Western scholars and churchmen who argue that certain expressions found in the Tome of Leo could be understood as leaning towards Nestorianism, if read in isolation.

I am not really concerned, here, with broadly defending the Coptic and Syrian Churches from the persecution they suffered in being placed under the authority of Melkite (i.e., appointed by the emperor) patriarchs, who were also given secular powers to persecute the faithful, leading to many being killed. Rather, it will suffice to present an extremely concise rectification of the accusations levelled against St. Dioscorus.

St. Dioscorus and Eutyches: Eutyches was an archimandrite and the abbot of a monastery in Constantinople with about three hundred monks under his guidance. He was an old ascetic, gifted with eloquence of speech; but he was not a true theologian. He played a significant role in the split that occurred in the Church in the fifth century. Eutyches enjoyed great fame throughout the see of Constantinople: within monastic circles, the imperial court, and among the people. This was due to his intelligence, eloquence, his ascetic life, and his close relationship with the emperor, especially through his relative Chrysaphius, the chief minister.

In reality, Eutyches represented neither Alexandrian theology nor Antiochian

theology. His extreme zeal against the Nestorianism that was rife in this region, and his defense of the Alexandrian formula led him to another heresy: he fell into the error of saying that there were two natures before the union; but only one nature after it, for the divine

nature absorbed the human nature, and the latter ceased to be.

records.answer:

The passages cover the development of the Coptic Orthodox Catechism through the ages, the role of ecumenical councils in defining orthodox faith, the rejection of certain heresies, the importance of Holy Tradition, and the theological contributions of Church Fathers such as St. Athanasius and St. Cyril of Alexandria [1][2][4][5][7][9][10][11][12][13][14][15][16]. However, none of these passages mention or explain the Catholic doctrine of papal infallibility.

Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?

I have written elsewhere about Pope Athanasius and Arianism, and the testimony of Western scholars regarding him.

b) The Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople in 381 A. D.

The second council focused on the heresy of Macedonius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who claimed that the Holy Spirit is created. The council also looked into the heresy of Apollinaris who, in defending the divinity of Christ, thought that the Word took flesh without a human soul. He thought that the human soul has a distinct human will, and thus Christ had two wills: the divine will and the human will, meaning that He was two persons. Pope Timothy of Alexandria, along with Nectarius, Patriarch of Constantinople; Gregory the Theologian, and Gregory of Nyssa took part in this council. The historian Sozomen mentioned that the number of bishops who participated was around 150 bishops, led by Timothy, the bishop of the See of Alexandria.

c) The Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus

The third council was held in the year 431 A. D. under the leadership of St. Cyril of Alexandria. Two hundred bishops participated in it to try Nestorius, who employed the term Christotokos (mother or giver of birth to Christ) to the Virgin Mary, thus differentiating the human Jesus born from Mary from the Son of God who dwelt in him. He thought that there were two distinct persons in Christ: the son of Mary and the Son of God. These two persons were not united essentially or hypostatically, but merely morally or in character. Thus, Christ is not to be called God but “Theophorus” or “God-bearer,” just as we would call the saints because of the work of divine grace in them. As a result, Mary is not the mother of God, but the mother of the human Jesus in whom the divinity dwelt. Nestorius and his followers criticized the Magi for their worship of the Child Jesus and held that His divinity was parted from Him at the moment of crucifixion.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q3 “How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?”, p. 7
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 3. How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?

I greatly desired to present a Coptic Orthodox Catechism to reveal our Christian understanding concisely and briefly; particularly because, due to ecclesiastical and political circumstances, our Church was isolated from Western churches in the fifth century A. D. and remained so to a large extent up until the twentieth century, when she was accused by many in the West of adhering to Eutychianism. The Coptic Church, therefore, did not have the opportunity to reveal her true teachings through the writings of her Fathers and her liturgies. Despite the Church’s participation in many international theological conferences in recent years, insisting upon her rejection of Eutychianism, some sources continue to attribute this heresy to our Church, of which the Church is completely innocent and strongly opposes through her liturgies and praises.

In a certain dialogue with the Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches, theologians were surprised to observe that the liturgies and praises that we enjoy to the present day lack even the slightest hint of Eutychianism, but rather, positively oppose it in a beautifully Christian manner; especially the daily Theotokias and those of the festal celebrations. Some of the theologians observed that they harmonize with the thought St. Cyril, or that perhaps he was their author.

A Greek theologian once asked me whether we use the word “Theotokos” to describe St. Mary and was astonished to learn that it is a term beloved in Coptic texts in every age.

Nestorius and his followers criticized the Magi for their worship of the Child Jesus and held that His divinity was parted from Him at the moment of crucifixion.

What impact did the three Councils have on the Catechism of the Christian Sees or

the Universal Church?

All the apostolic Churches — whether Orthodox Chalcedonians, non-Chalcedonians or the Roman Catholic Church — consider these three ecumenical councils as being responsible for clarifying the faith, especially with regard to the Holy Trinity; and for the defense against many of the heresies that appeared in this period. Although there were some small disputes over the language of some expressions, these councils carried on their discussions in a spirit of love and holy zeal for the faith.

As for the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451 A. D., some apostolic Churches hold that it did not introduce anything new, but only explained and clarified the first three ecumenical councils. Our unofficial and official dialogues with the apostolic Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches and the Catholic Church in the late twentieth century brought more openness. All of them came to realize that we are not Eutychians as they had thought; that is, we do not proclaim that His humanity was annihilated within His divinity.

Thus, we achieved positive results together with our Orthodox Chalcedonian brethren.

I recall, for example, that in the first official meeting between the two families, the Chalcedonians refused to call us “Orthodox,” insisting instead on referring to us as the “Ancient Eastern Churches.” After discussions filled with love, the following occurred:

First: After many years of dialogue with a Greek theologian, I asked him: “Do you remember the day when you refused to call us Orthodox?” He smiled and said: “We feel a sense of unity with you, perhaps even more than that which we feel among ourselves, between Orthodox Chalcedonians.”

Second: A well-known priest and dear friend took the initiative of supervising the doctoral thesis for some of Copts in England. He would answer every person who accused St. Dioscorus with heresy by saying: “I have the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon in the Greek language. They witness to the fact that this St. Dioscorus was not accused of heresy, but of insulting the Pope of Rome.”

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages?

Since the dawn of Christianity, the Copts were known for their zeal for the orthodox faith, and they played a positive role in resolving many theological issues, both in the East and the West. They did not interfere in the problems of other Churches, nor did they intrude upon them; but with a spirit of love and unity, and through genuinely fraternal relations, they were invited to resolve such problems, or responded through the exchange of messages.

When the emperors accepted the Christian faith and the waves of persecution calmed down, heretics found abundant opportunities to spread their dangerous thought; particularly Arius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Apollinaris, etc. It became necessary for the Alexandrian Fathers to play their positive role in the patient efforts to restore the heretics to the true faith; though, not at the expense of the Church’s biblical faith. Therefore, the Alexandrian Church participated in the three ecumenical councils.

a) The First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.

Here, the four sees of Jerusalem, Antioch, Rome, and Alexandria opposed the heresy of Arius, which denied the divinity of the Lord Christ. The council introduced the creed referred to by most scholars as the “Athanasian Creed,“ referring to Pope Athanasius the Apostolic of Alexandria. Most recent modern catechisms highlight this creed and summarize it for the general public and for the new generations, as well as for the scholars.

“From a very early stage, the Church of Alexandria appreciated the value of the theological contributions of St. Athanasius to the definition and formulation of the content of the faith, and the preservation of the apostolic tradition received by the Church from the disciples of the Lord Himself; and, in fact, his ‘unconquerable and apostolic knowledge,’ as St. Cyril of Alexandria described him. The high esteem of the twentieth Pope of Alexandria is evident from the fact that the Church describes him in her liturgical texts as ‘the apostolic’.”

I have written elsewhere about Pope Athanasius and Arianism, and the testimony of Western scholars regarding him.

b) The Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople in 381 A. D.
