passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST.

He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family’ and ‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement’ in the whole world, even though there have been some monastic movements prior to his.

The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched his life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never get bored." That came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life.

One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they started to undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

His Order of Seclusion:

In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with some beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of kings." However, when he was pressured, he answered the emperor’s message, for the sake of the Church peace. 5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the Church. That is why he eventually came down to help Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians came back to the Church.

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who founded the system of congregations; as one of his disciples and greatly rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any particular order. 8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it.

Of His Words:

 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ.  Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack of discernment, they stayed away from God.  There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are not like us.  Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over the beasts of the wilderness. The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba.

[The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 667–668
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

St. Pachomius (Father of the Koinonia): He was born in upper Egypt around the year 290 A. D. He became Christian in the city of Esna in Upper Egypt because of their generosity and their love for their enemies. He left the army and was baptized around the year 290 A. D. He became the disciple of St. Palamon the hermit, till an angel appeared to him and guided him to establish the system of the monastic communal life (coenobitic monasticism). He was a successful leader who loved the salvation of souls, so he established many monasteries in Upper Egypt following strict rules. He also established a convent for nuns under the leadership of his sister. His monastic rules were translated to Greek and Latin. St. Basil the Great used them, and they were used in the Gaul in the fifth century. They were also adopted by Benedict, the father of western monasticism, and by Caesarius of Arles.

St. Ammonas: He was contemporary of St. Anthony. He was born in 275 A. D., and when he was twenty-two years old, his uncle forced him to get married, so he lived with his wife as ascetics in Nitria. After eighteen years, his wife asked him to live in solitude away from her, so he went out to Mount Nitria and many gathered around him. So, he established the semi-eremitic monasticism, in which the monks are not required to have daily fellowship in worship or in meals, except for Saturdays and Sundays only. Usually, the monks of this order lived in cells or caves that were close to each other, around the church.

St. Macarius the Great: (around 300–390 A. D.) He is the founder of the semi-eremitic order of monasticism in the wilderness of Scetis. He visited St. Anthony at least twice. His father forced him to get married, but then God allowed his virgin wife to depart. He led an ascetic life in a small hut in a village for about ten years under the guidance of an ascetic. He longed for solitude, and so he moved to Scetis and a cherub accompanied him on the way. He loved worship and asceticism, so many came from the East and the West to the wilderness to become his disciples.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built. Abba Anthony’s idea was that if a monk wished to visit those living there, he could start walking after he finished eating at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone.

His Personality and the Role of Nitria;

Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away from the crowd and refrained from performing any miracles, claiming that he was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba Amon.

St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 258–259
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony

Many researchers talked about St. Hilarion (Ilarion), as being the disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who founded the monastic movement. Whereas, St. Jerome, who recorded his biography, said about him: “Many people glorified his asceticism; others were amazed by the miracles God performed on his hands; while still others admired the wisdom and virtues with which he was adorned, I (Jerome), on the other hand, do not marvel about any of these, as much as I do about how he despised the temporal glory, with which everyone surrounded him, and honored him everywhere whenever he was, and how the bishops, the priests, the monks, the rulers, the judges, the elites, and the commons approached him seeking his guidance, blessing, and prayers. He did his best to disappear from the scene. He fled from the East to the West, hiding in the most isolated locations where no one could endure to dwell.”

With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony:

St. Hilarion (291-371 AD) was born in a village called Tabatha, five miles south of Gaza, to wealthy pagan parents who sent him to Alexandria to learn the philosophical and practical knowledge. In Alexandria, he encountered a lot of scholars, mostly Christians, and the Holy Spirit led him to faith in the Lord Christ; and he was baptized when he was about fifteen years of age. As a Christian, he loved to pray and to worship in an ascetic manner.

By the year 306 AD, the sweet fragrance of Abba Anthony the Great filled the whole of Egypt and reached outside its borders. Then, once Hilarion heard about him, he put in his heart to visit him to get his blessing and listen to his teaching. When he finally met him, he viewed him as an angel of God and became one of his disciples for one year. Yet, because of the large crowds that came to see and seek the blessing of Abba Anthony, Hilarion sought his permission to leave Egypt and go back to Palestine, to live there in an atmosphere of seclusion, away from people.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of St. Anthony Mountain, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF ST. ANTHONY MOUNTAIN

On the 26th of Baba, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of seven martyrs who were martyred at the hands of the Barbarians, on the Mountain of St. Anthony, the Father of all monks.

[The Synaxarion: 26 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthonius, and Other Saints with That Name, pp. 195–196
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONIUS, and Other Saints with that Name (The martyrs) — ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr

Often confusion takes place between the martyrs who carried the name ‘Anthony,' among whom are:

ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr:

He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop assigned him to build a Church, the pagans were stirred up against him and killed him.

ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr:

St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to ‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his Christ, he ordered him chained and sent him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, pp. 161–162
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Miracles

His Miracles:

Some farmers once came to Abba Amon, carrying a little child mauled by a dog and suffering severe pain. The saint asked them: “Why should you come to me to do something beyond my worthiness, when, in your hands, you have the healing medicine for this child?! Now, give the stolen cow back to its widow owner, and the child will be healed." Having perceived that the saint revealed their hidden sin, they presented repentance and gave the cow back to its owner. The saint then prayed for the child, and the Lord healed him.

St. Athanasius told that story about St. Amon: He was once with his disciple ‘Tadros,’ and they needed to cross a river. Known for his great shyness, he sought from his disciple to go away from him, for each of them to take his clothes off and swim. Despite doing that, Abba Amon was too shy to take his clothes off, even in the absence of his disciple. In the middle of his confusion, he found himself all of a sudden on the other shore of the river. When his disciple saw him there with his dry clothes, he was persistence to know how he crossed over. The saint told him, seeking from him not to tell it to anyone before his repose.

His repose:

According to St. Athanasius, while Abba Anthony was sitting one day by his monastery, he saw somebody ascending to heaven, and a multitude of saints was welcoming him. Inquiring about him, he was told that he was Abba Amon. Thirty days later, some hermits came over from Mount Nitria, to inform St Anthony that their father has departed to heaven.

The Coptic Church celebrates his feast on the 20th of Bashons; and the Greek Church on the 4th of October.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — THE SPIRIT OF MARTYRDOM AND ASCETICISM

Besides his discipleship to Alexander, there were two other great influences in his life:

1- From his seventh year to the fifteenth he lived during a period of severe persecution (303 - 311 CE). He knew many among the Alexandrian martyrs and confessors from whom he learned the Orthodox faith and a loving intimacy with the Holy Scriptures. He did not accompany them to the arena of persecution but his heart was aflame with divine love, facing every struggle for the sake of Christ.

2- After he heard about St. Anthony the hermit, he hurried to the wilderness and lived with him for about three years, practicing the ascetic and righteous life and the deep fellowship with God. Providence arranged this close relationship with Anthony so that during his exiles and flight he never felt lonely. Instead he considered it a good opportunity for him to have a bit of solitude and seclusion, praying for his people and writing to them. He was obliged to become the historian of St. Anthony .

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Cyril, Metropolitan of Ethiopia, pp. 539–540
passages.text:
Saint: CYRIL, METROPOLITAN OF ETHIOPIA, ST. — Becoming a Monk

Becoming a Monk:

This saint was born in the town of ‘El-Kash´h’ in the district of ‘El-Baliana,’ of pious parents who gave him the name ‘Sidaros.’ In his childhood, his parents enrolled him in the preschool affiliated with the church. By nature, he loved seclusion, contemplation, prayers, and fasting. On reaching 19 years of age, he got the permission of his parents to set forth to the monastery of St. Anthony, to become a monk. In the monastery, he maintained his original name.

In his new monastic life, he started watching the nights, worship, and practice asceticism. He also joined the school, which was established there by the 112th pope ‘Cyril V’ (1874-1927). He spent seven years in the monastery, during which he learned the Christian virtues of love and humility.

His Ministry in Jerusalem and Upper Egypt:

As the monks of St. Anthony’s monastery were responsible for the ministry in the Holy Land, the head of the monastery ordained him as a Hegumen and sent him to Jerusalem. There, he strove in his ministry that his health started to fail, and the metropolitan of Jerusalem had to send him back to his monastery to recover.

Once he recovered, the head of the monastery decided to send him to the town of ‘Bahgoura’ in Upper Egypt. There, he was responsible for shepherding the congregation, in addition to taking care of farming land in the area which was possessed by the monastery, and to send its income back to his brothers the monks. The church of ‘Bahgoura’ was in the name of the Virgin St. Mary, and had a small room, in which he dwelt, dedicating himself to work entrusted to him. God granted him the spiritual transparency, the grace to heal the sick, and to drive out the evil spirits.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q874 “How did the monastic movement start in Egypt?”, pp. 665–666
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 874. How did the monastic movement start in Egypt?

From Egypt, all other monastic orders spread out to the whole world. In the fourth century, this movement served to restore the heart of the Church to the inner life after the state had accepted Christianity, and the doors of the emperor were opened to bishops and priests. These monastic orders established by the Copts did not emerge through a preorganized plan by the Church, but through the powerful love that inflamed the hearts of many of the early Christians.

In the apostolic age, many practiced a kind of monasticism, seeking to enjoy the perfection of the Gospel. The eschatological direction of the Church made the believers long for the coming of their Bridegroom, so some preferred to live a life of virginity, consecrating all their time for worship to prepare themselves for the heavenly wedding. In the second century, the Christian virgins in Smyrna and Corinth used to walk in liturgical processions behind the priests and in front of the widows. Moreover, many groups of virgins were found living in Alexandria and in many cities around the world. Articles about virginity represented an essential aspect of the writings of the Church Fathers in the first three centuries.

Virgins used to live together, while men preferred to leave the cities to live in simple huts in villages and were often called “consecrated.” Some people felt a thirst for the angelic life so they fled to the wilderness. We know of only a few of these, such St. Paul the Hermit who lived in the wilderness for almost ninety years (between 250–340 A. D.).

St. Anthony established the monastic movement and is considered the father of all monks in the entire world, even though many preceded him. This is because of his strong relationship with St. Athanasius, who wrote about him to the Roman world. It is also because he opened his cave after twenty years of solitude to disciple monastic leaders, converse with philosophers in the simplicity of his faith, and receive rulers. He had an active role in the Church and went to Alexandria to support the martyrs and stand against the Arians.

St. Pachomius, founder of cenobitic monasticism, felt that the order of solitude may not work for all those who want to become monks, so he started a monastic community within the walls of monasteries, and the hermits praised him for doing so.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Amon, the Bishop of Hermopolis, pp. 163–164
passages.text:
Saint: AMON, THE BISHOP OF HERMOPOLIS — In Nitria

In Nitria:

In the third year, in about the year 355 AD, Amon heard that his parents were searching for him everywhere and that his mother in an unfortunate condition because of him. So, he sought the permission of Father Tadros to go, accompanied by two monks, to see his mother before she dies. Father Tadros informed him that his mother became a Christian and that he could leave the monastery to see his parents, then from there, he would go to ‘Nitria.' In Nitria, he would be able to meet with some saintly men who pleased God, such as St. Amon, who was still alive; St. Alyrion and St. Amonius who reposed not long afterward; St. Bambu and St. Peroa the servant of God. Then, Fr. Tadros and St. Amon kissed each other before his departure, and Amon wept bitterly, then he set forth to his parents and from there to the wilderness of ‘Nitria.' In Nitria, he lived for 14 years, after which St. Athanasius ordained him a bishop on the city of Hermopolis Magna (El-Ashmonein); then was exiled by the intruding bishop ‘George of Cappadocia’ in the year 373 AD The saint, while he was a bishop, pretended to be ignorant that a woman spoke about him: “This old man is melancholia.” When the saint heard her saying that, he said to her: “I strove 50 years to acquire this melancholia; would I get rid of it now because of you?!” He instantly left her in the cell, forsook the bishopric, and went his way to live among the monks in the wilderness of Scetis. In his last days, the brethren brought the saint from his solitude on the mountain to live in the monastery among them in the year 430 AD, where he reposed after a little while. Most probably, he was 94 years old when he reposed. During the period of his last recluse after he forsook the bishopric, he spent his time as a mentor to the nearby monks and hermits. He became a model for every monk, not to desire bishopric as a work of authority.

[Armand Veilleux: Pachomian Koinonia; Vol. 2; pp. 71- 109]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 267–268
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

Then, he came back later after the death of the emperor in the year 361 AD, to be killed by the pagans mob (probably to steal his wealth).

In his self-imposed exile, Pope ‘Athanasius’ kept on moving from one monastery to another and from one location to another, with a heart enflamed with his love for God and his people.

During that time, he wrote and circulated an impressive array of hugely influential documents to keep shepherding his congregation. Among them was “the Biography of St. Anthony”, and “Apologia de Fuga”: a defense of his escape. He also has written the Encyclical Letters to the bishops of Egypt, Libya, ‘Lucifer’ Bishop of ‘Calaris’ (Cagliari, on the island of Sardinia, west of Italy), and to the Egyptian monks. He also wrote four essays against the Arians, five dogmatic messages to ‘Serapion’ Bishop of ‘Tammy,’ messages on the Holy Spirit, and a book on the Church Councils.

Throughout his years in exile, ‘Athanasius’ retained great support in Alexandria and whole Egypt, and his ecclesiastical and theological arguments won over many in both the East and West.

By the death of ‘Constantius II’ and the sitting of Emperor ‘Julian the Apostate’ (360-363 AD) on the throne, Pope ‘Athanasius’ appeared again in the year 362 AD, together with ‘Lucifer’ Bishop of ‘Cladius’ and ‘Eusebius’ Bishop of ‘Vershelly,’ who was exiled to Upper Egypt.

The pope held a Council in Alexandria in the year 362 AD, called ‘The Council of the Saints and the Confessors,’ since all those who attended have just come back from exile or have suffered tortures. But the peaceful situation did not last for long; for Emperor ‘Julian,’ feeling the danger of Pope ‘Athanasius’ on paganism, has sent to the governor of Alexandria, indicating that the decree of the return of the exiles was meant for them to go back to their countries, and not to their thrones. And, he ordered him to drive ‘Athanasius’ out of Egypt. Therefore, the pope had to hide in the tomb of his father for almost six months. And, as the emperor used more pressure on the governor, the pope had to leave Alexandria to Upper Egypt, sailing by boat, chased by the governor’s ship. When the soldiers inquired about ‘Athanasius,’ they were told: “He is not far from you.” Then, they hastened toward Upper Egypt, while ‘Athanasius’ returned to the city of ‘Memphis.’ After that, he spent a period of continuous movement from one monastery to another.

records.question: Who was St. Paul the First Hermit's wife?
records.answer: The passages do not mention St. Paul the First Hermit having a wife. They describe him as a hermit who lived alone in the wilderness for eighty years, sustained by God through a raven bringing him bread daily, and do not indicate any marriage or wife in his life [1][2][14].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 382–383
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — His Upbringing

Through Divine care, St. Abba Anthony the Great the Father of the Monastic family and its founder in the whole world, encountered this St. Paul who preceded him by long years in monastic life in the wilderness, where no one but God knew anything about him. God kept sustaining him by half a loaf of bread, carried to him by a raven every day all along many decades; in which God smelled the sweet fragrance of his prayers and praise, to call him: “My beloved Paul.”

His Upbringing:

St. Paul the 1st hermit was born in Alexandria around the year 228 AD. His father passed away leaving a great wealth for him and for his older brother Peter. However, Peter conspired to acquire the greater portion of the inheritance for himself, and when the disagreement escalated between the two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court. However, on his way to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened to be passing by. St. Paul asked himself: “Has that rich man taken anything from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he totally despised the temporal life. His heart was so inflamed with the Eternal inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking the Divine guidance.

Then, an angel appeared to St. Paul and guided him to the wilderness in the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea. There he lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven. The saint lived all that time on that bread with some dates from the palm trees or herbs from the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paula, the Elder, p. 387
passages.text:
Saint: PAULA, THE ELDER, ST.

St. Paula is considered the most famous Roman woman as far as her piety and dedication to the Lord are concerned. Besides, she had vast wealth, honor, and sharpness of mind. She was born on the 15th of May 347 AD to a very rich family among the Roman elites. Her man Toxotius passed away when she was only thirty-two years old and a mother to a son and four daughters: 1- The son was named Toxotius, after his father's name. 2- The oldest daughter was named Blesilla, after her maternal grandmother. She passed away three months after she completely changed her worldly lifestyle and lived in repentance. St. Jerome wrote a condolence letter to her mother, to assure her that she has gone to Paradise. 3- The second daughter was Paulina, the wife of Pammachius. After his young wife Paulina passed away, he distributed most of the possessions he inherited on the poor and he pursued an ascetic life, even though he was one of the elites. 4- The third daughter was Eustochium, who accompanied her mother all the way on a very tough ascetic road that angered her relatives. When her mother passed away in Bethlehem; she was on the brink of collapse. However, St. Jerome came to her support and exhorted her to complete the mission of her mother. 5- The fourth daughter was Rufina, who passed away in her youth in 386.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paula, the Elder, pp. 387–388
passages.text:
Saint: PAULA, THE ELDER, ST. — Her Widowhood

Her Widowhood:

St. Paula lived with her husband an ideal family life, to become a role model in Rome for the virtuous matrimony in the Lord. The man she dearly loved passed away, when she was only thirty-two years old. She was so overwhelmed with grief and was recovered by her friend St. Marcella, the widow who taught Rome by her repentance and despising of the world. God opened Paula's inner eyes to dedicate her life to Him in a firm monastic way of life. Her food became very simple, drank no wine, and slept not on a bed but on a mat on the floor. She abandoned arranging fun parties and all kinds of temporal pleasures and put all her capabilities in the service of the needy. She forsook all the worldly activities to focus her mind on the Lord and His Heavenly Kingdom.

St. Jerome said about Paula, at the beginning of his condolence letter to her daughter Eustochium:

If all my body members turned into tongues and if all my limbs uttered in a human voice, I would not be able to cover the virtues of that honorable Saint Paula. She was noble for her family status, but more so for her holiness. She was rich with the goods of this world but came to be distinguished with the poverty she chose for the sake of Christ. She preferred Bethlehem to Rome; forsook her splendid palace, covered with gold, to dwell in a cell made of mud. We should not grieve as though we have lost her, but we should rather thank God that we have not really lost her because she is still with us; “For all live to Him” (Luke 20:38). Those who return to God are still counted as part of His household. Yes, we may indeed think we have lost her, but the Heavenly dwellings have acquired her.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Thecla, St. Paul’s Disciple, pp. 232–233
passages.text:
Saint: THECLA, ST. PAUL’S DISCIPLE

This St. Thecla was a disciple of St.‘Paul the Apostle. She was considered as the first female martyr in Christian history, in the same way, St. Steven was considered as the first male martyr. She endured so many mortalities, even though her blood was not shed. Many Fathers viewed her as a small model of the Virgin Church adorned with every virtue, coming directly after the Virgin St. Mary. And, some of the Fathers used to commend any great female saint by calling her: The New Thecla.

This saint raised in Iconium in Asia Minor. She was known for her great beauty, high ethics, and great fortune beside her excellent education. Her father, who was one of the elites of the city, cared to educate her that she excelled in philosophy, poetry; and was eloquent, daring, yet full of decency.

Many young men wished to propose to her, but her parents chose for her a wealthy young nobleman by the name of Thamyris.

In the year 45 AD, St. Paul and St. Barnabas passed through the city of Iconium, in their first preaching trip (Acts 13:51). Thecla happened to be sitting on the window sill of her house when she saw St. Paul. Then, the Spirit of God drew her to be intrigued by his words about the Lord Jesus. She met St. Paul, listened to him, proclaimed her faith, and then got baptized.

During her continuous association with St. Paul, she felt a great longing for a life of virginity. Then, she cast off her vain adornments and stopped caring for jewelry, banquets, and worldly celebrations. This change in her life confused her mother, who tried hard to convince her to resume her early one and to get married and have children who would support her in her old age. But, the saint firmly proclaimed her desire for virginity for the Lord’s sake. Here, the mother started to threaten her and resorted to Thamyris to help convince her daughter to get married. The man flirted with her, counting he could draw her heart to the pleasures of the world. Yet she persisted on her longing for a life of virginity.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paul, the Simple, p. 385
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE SIMPLE, ST.

This saint was a marvelous example of a simple man, who by the grace of God, could strive to reach a high ascetic level, even though he started it at his 60th years of age. This St. Paul (Boulus) was a very simple and pious farmer who got married to a very beautiful girl. After living together for so many years, he started to take notice of so many rumors about his wife's evil behavior. However, whenever he inquired from her about the matter, she would pretend to be a pure woman. Eventually, by himself, he saw her in the evil act. On that day, he forsook the house to her and set forth to Abba Anthony the Great, hoping to become one of his disciples.

Getting to know that this simple farmer was sixty years old, Abba Anthony advised him to go back to his field and plow; on account of that it would be difficult for him to practice the monastic life at his age. Before his persistence, he sought from him to join a monastery in the valley to practice with the brethren what suit his old age; but the old man persisted on not leaving that mountain.

Here, Abba Anthony had no other choice but to put him under tough tests; and was amazed by his endurance, perseverance, and obedience. Among those tests that he left him four days without food or drink while watching him lest he would collapse. He sought from him to remain a whole week outside his cave, under the heat of noon and the severe cold nights, without leaving his place; and sought from him, after weaving eight meters of a cord, to loosen it and weave it anew. In all that he was obedient, worked with joy and extreme simplicity.

On seeing his persistence with the spirit of piety, Abba Anthony accepted him as a recluse and sought from him to build for himself a cell on the way between the base of the mountain and his own cell.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paula, the Elder, pp. 388–389
passages.text:
Saint: PAULA, THE ELDER, ST. — Her Friendship with St. Jerome

Her Friendship with St. Jerome:

Her name was tied up to St. Jerome and St. Jeromes' name was also tied up with hers through his fatherly friendship which was full of kindness as well as seriousness. He got to know her through St. Epiphanius, the bishop of Salamis and St. Paulinus, the bishop of Antioch, to whom she gave hospitality in her palace. Through them, she got acquainted with St. Jerome, who drew her to serve God when he was residing in Rome.

In doing that, St. Paula faced strong opposition from her family, especially because her daughter Eustochium has followed her steps and forsook all her relationships with the world to practice the ascetic life. This made the rest of her family uncomfortable, worrying about their future as elites. Yet, Paula stuck to her daughter and practiced that kind of holy life without the least of hesitation.

St. Paula passed through many trials that pressed upon her tender soul, that she was on the brink of collapse. However, with St. Jeromes' support, her trials turned her energies into the dedication and setting forth toward a better life. Among these trials was the sudden death of her oldest daughter Blesilla, the death of her other daughter Paulina, the wife of Pammachius while still young, and also Rufina; which left her only with Eustochom, out of her four daughters.

Paula's heart was day by day inflamed with the longing to the Heavenly life; while the atmosphere in Rome was suffocating for her because of the fame of her noble family and the criticism she got from her family elders, so she planned to leave Rome and go somewhere else to worship God in tranquility and peace away from her family and her old friends.

In the year 385 AD, she sailed along with her daughter Eustochium to Cyprus. There, they visited St. Epiphanius, the bishop of Salamis, and from there, they sailed to Antioch, where they met with St. Jerome. Then all of them set forth to the Holy places in Palestine, and from there, they went to Egypt to see some of its desert monks and hermits.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hermas, ‘the Shepherd's Author, pp. 245–246
passages.text:
Saint: HERMAS, ‘THE SHEPHERD'S AUTHOR

In the Muratorian Canon, it was mentioned that Hermas, the author of the book ‘The Shepherd,’ was the brother of the first bishop of Rome, Pius I (140- 155 AD). Origen (184-253 AD) believed that he was the same Hermas mentioned by St. Paul the Apostle (Rom. 16:14). In talking about himself, Hermas says that He was a slave, sold in Rome to a Roman lady called Rhoda. He began to love her as a sister. Then, seeing how beautiful she was, he desired to have her as his wife (Herm.Vis. 1:1). After she set him free, he became rich by working as a farmer and a merchant. He ended up marrying a talkative woman, and he became indifferent in caring for his family. His children plunged into evil (Herm.Vis. 1:3), and because of them, he became poor (Herm.Vis. 1:2, 2:3, 3:6). Sometimes, Hermas portrayed himself as being virtuous, chaste, simple, and free from all evil desires (Herm.Vis. 1:2). At other times, he portrayed himself as a liar and a hypocrite (Herm.Vis. 3). At the time of persecution, he and his wife held fast to their faith. However, their children denied their faith. Enthusiastic about repentance, Hermas authored his book “The Shepherd” to urge the sinners to repent. He pointed out that the purity of the Church was in danger, because of the spread of sin, and that the end was close at hand.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paphnutius, the Hermit, p. 362
passages.text:
Saint: PAPHNUTIUS, THE HERMIT, ST.

He was the head of a little congregation of monks at Heracleoplis (Ahnasia, in Upper Egypt).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 668–669
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

Many nuns were given the gift of true leadership and spiritual discernment, like St. Sarah of whom it was said that she lived for sixty years on the banks of a river, but never lifted her eyes to look at it. Many of her sayings were preserved in the sayings of the desert fathers and mothers.

St. Hilaria: In the fourth century, the daughter of Emperor Zeno fled to Scetis where she led a life of asceticism in the attire of a male monk. When her sister, Theopiste, was possessed by an evil spirit, the elders of the wilderness sent her to St. Hilaria to pray for her, and did not know that St. Hilaria was a woman. She prayed all night for her and embraced her. Theopiste was healed, and she told the emperor about the monk, “Hilarion,” who healed her and was embracing her, so her father was disturbed. He called for her to come to the palace, where she revealed to him that she was his daughter after he had promised not to prevent her from going back to her cave.

St. Syncletica: Some historians regard her to be the equal of St. Anthony, the star of the wilderness; for as St. Anthony was the father of all monks, St. Syncletica was a mother to that group of virgins which transformed the fertile valley of Egypt into a dwelling place for the grace of God. She was born to noble parents who settled in Alexandria to be close to the School of Alexandria. They had two sons and two daughters, so they wanted to educate them in all sciences, which were only offered in the School of Alexandria. This family was shocked at the death of Syncletica’s youngest brother in his childhood, while the older one departed on the night of his wedding. These two shocks caused Syncletica to ponder and contemplate the pleasures of the world and see them as nothing but a deceptive mirage. Syncletica persevered in her fasting, prayer, asceticism, and worship in her parents’ house till they departed to heaven. Then, she distributed her money on the poor and took her sister to their family’s tomb, where they lived for a few years. During this period, she redoubled her fasts, prayers, and ascetic practices. A substantial number of young women went to visit her. Some went simply to see her and take her blessing, while others came seeking solutions to their problems. It was natural for some of them to be influenced by her example and desire to stay with her and participate in the life of asceticism and contemplation.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Paula, the Elder, pp. 389–390
passages.text:
Saint: PAULA, THE ELDER, ST. — In Egypt

In Egypt:

St. Paula accompanied St. Jerome on his trip to Egypt and was most probably with him when he met with St. Didymus the Blind, the dean of the School of Alexandria. She studied at his school for one month; then set forth together with St. Jerome to the wilderness of Nitria. In Nitria, they stayed a long time. St. Jerome described the effect of that period on the life of that saintly widow, he said that she was excited and joyful to see these saints and longed to imitate their lives. The fathers received her with joy, for which she glorified God and felt unworthy of such an honor. She met with the two Macariuses, St. Serapion and others. She visited them in their cells, prostrated herself at their feet, feeling that the Lord Jesus Christ was in every one of them. She tolerated the harsh traveling between the cells and spent the nights in the open wilderness with joy and enthusiasm beyond the endurance of any woman. She forgot her fatigue and all her needs because of her spiritual joy.

In Bethlehem:

In the next year, she set forth to Jerusalem to live in Bethlehem. There, she built a guest-house to give hospitality to strangers, a monastery for monks and a convent for the nuns.

In the convent, she lived along with her daughter Eustochum a serious monastic life, and according to the convent's rules, all practiced the work of the hand, particularly sewing for the nuns or those outside.

Paula lived among the nuns as a mother who drew them with her love, tenderness and she was their role model. Even though she and her daughter partook of ministry and work, yet she was firm. If, for instance, she noticed a nun talk too much or showing anger; she would ask her to separate herself from the congregation, to pray outside, and to eat her meals alone for a certain period.

She cared for the poor, as well as for building churches. However, she made sure that the churches would not be luxurious in their structure or furniture, but modest; preferring to spend the money on the poor, being living members of the Lord Jesus Christ.

She helped St. Jerome in his studies and translations; having studied the Greek language from her father, the Latin language in Rome, and the Hebrew language on her own; to sing the psalms in their original languages. She also took part with her mentor St. Jerome in his sharp debate with John the bishop of Jerusalem concerning the Origenism.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Thecla, St. Paul’s Disciple, p. 234
passages.text:
Saint: THECLA, ST. PAUL’S DISCIPLE — On Mount Qalamon

On Mount Qalamon:

Saint Thecla set forth to St. Paul the Apostle in Mira Bilikia, and told him what God did with her, for which he glorified God and encouraged her to help him by preaching among the pagan women.

Moving Around:

Setting forth to Iconium, she found out that her would-be fiancée has died, but her mother was persisting on her stubbornness. There, she preached among the pagan women and then went to Syria to do the same, where a multitude of women proclaimed the Christian faith through her preaching. In Seleucia, she chose for herself a cave where she lived in tranquility for about 27 years. And, so many people came to listen to her words and to seek her prayers.

Her Departure:

It was said that many physicians were stirred up against her because their patients deserted them and went instead to the saint seeking her prayers for their healings. Those evil physicians provoked some wicked people to kill her. And, when they went to her place, they found her standing in prayer next to a rock. Without being disturbed by their presence, she raised her eyes to heaven, and behold! The rock split up, and she entered inside it, to set forth to her Heavenly Groom. In some manuscripts, it was mentioned that through that split rock, she found a way to set forth to Rom to repose and be buried beside her mentor Paul the Apostle.

[Butler’s Lives of Saints; Sept. 23]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Theodora, Ammas, pp. 239–240
passages.text:
Saint: THEODORA, AMMAS

This saint Theodora was one of the great female hermits who lived in seclusion in the wilderness. She was a contemporary of the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus of Alexandria (385-412), and occasionally she sought his council.

She was given the title Amma, which is equivalent to the title Abba for men. And, she had an active role in the monastic life; that her council was sought by some male monks. She was not Theodora, who was mentioned by St. Palladius, as the wife of a public tribune, and distributed all her possessions to live on alms. Then she joined convent Hesychas by the sea. But she was most probably St. Theodora who was mentioned in the Coptic Synaxarion (11 Baramouda), the only daughter of wealthy parents in Alexandria,who planned on giving her in marriage, and they bought for her plenty of precious attire and jewelry. However, she declined on account of that she decided to dedicate her life to worship, and she sold all what her parents purchased for her and distributed part of the proceeds on the poor, and with the rest, she built a church west of Alexandria. Then, she set forth to see the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD), who dedicated her as a nun in a convent near Alexandria. She lived a tough ascetic life, yet with the spirit of love, wisdom, and with open heart, to be worthy of the grace of seeing Divine visions and to enjoy a special spiritual status in the eyes of the Church clergy. She consummated her strife and reposed in peace when she was 100 years of age. She was a contemporary to five popes: Alexandros I, Athanasius, Peter II, Timothy I, and Theophilus.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mary and Ephcharistos, the Righteous, pp. 144–145
passages.text:
Saint: MARY AND EPHCHARISTOS, THE RIGHTEOUS — A Married Couple Living better than a Monk

Although so many monks among the great Fathers were characterized by the spirit of humility and enjoyed so many Divine gifts, they always wondered within themselves whether there were any others out there, who surpassed them spiritually to learn from them and follow their path. Among those Fathers were St. Anthony the Great, to whom the Lord revealed the existence of St. Paul the First Hermit, St. Zosima the Priest, whom the Lord guided to St. Mary the Egyptian, and St. Macarius the Great, to whom the Lord revealed the two married women in Alexandria, who lived by the spirit of love, sanctity, and asceticism.

A Married Couple Living better than a Monk:

Such a thought came upon one of the saintly elder monks, and a Divine voice informed him that there was a virtuous wife called Mary living with her husband Ephcharistos in a village in Egypt at a spiritual level higher than him. By the guidance of an angel, the elderly monk set forth to that village, to meet with that couple who did surpass him spiritually. Knocking at their door, the woman opened for him, while her husband was still away shepherding a flock of sheep. In the evening, Ephcharistos came home and joined in welcoming their guest. After they prepared dinner for him, the monk refused ultimately to eat until they would tell him about what was going on in their lives. Ephcharistos did not want to talk about their private life together. He just said: “I am a shepherd, and this is Mary, my wife.” The elder monk persisted on knowing more about them and revealed to the man that it was God who sent him to them. Here, the man started talking with the fear of the Lord. He said: “I shepherd the sheep we inherited from our parents, and whenever we make a little profit by the help of God, we divide it into three portions: one for the poor, one to accommodate the strangers and the third for our personal needs. Since we got married, my wife lives with me like a sister. Each of us sleeps separately. At night we wear sackcloth, and during daytime, we put on our regular attires. No one knows anything about our lives.” Here, Mary looked down and supplicated to the elder monk to keep their life secret until they repose.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Amatus, p. 145
passages.text:
Saint: AMATUS, ST.

In his account on the biography of St. Paula the First Hermit, St. Jerome mentioned ‘Amatus’ as a disciple of St. Anthony the Great.

According to St. Palladius, ‘Amatus’ worked together with St. Macarius of Upper Egypt to oversee the monastery, which was a ‘Cenobion’ for a congregation of anchorites, all of whom were disciples to St. Anthony. Also, it is believed that they were the two monks who buried St. Anthony after he reposed.
