passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

His Fellowship with our Lord Jesus;

Through his pure heart, he used to meet often with the Lord Jesus Christ on a friendship level. He used to see Him, to talk with Him, and to enjoy His Divine proclamations. It was said that, having been so persistent in his great ascetic life and prayers that the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, saying: “My chosen vessel ‘Bishoy,’ peace be with you; I saw your labor and strife, and behold, I shall always be with you!”

Another time, as our saint remained a long time fasting, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “You labored too much, My chosen vessel Bishoy!” The saint answered Him: “It was You O Lord who labored for me, but I have not labored at all!”

A third time, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Rejoice, My chosen vessel Bishoy. Do you see this mountain? I shall send you monks to fill that mountain to worship Me.” The saint asked Him: “Will You sustain them, Lord, in such a barren wilderness?” The Lord answered: “If they love one another and keep My commandments, I shall sustain them in everything!” The saint asked Him: “Will You save them from all the anguishes and afflictions mentioned in the Gospel?” The Lord answered: “Whoever fears, obeys Me and keep My commandments; I shall save him from all temptations!” He then blessed him and ascended.

Again the Lord appeared to him surrounded by angels. The Lord comforted him and blessed him. The saint worshipped Him and washed His feet with water in a basin, then the Lord ascended. St. ‘Bishoy’ drank from that water and left a portion for his disciple. The saint sought from him more than once to drink it, but the disciple was too slow. Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 359–360
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Strife

Then, when St. ‘Bishoy’ went to check on the basin, he found it empty. When the saint told his disciple what happened, he regretted it badly and was in bitterness for his disobedience.

As the monks knew that the saint would see the Lord now and then; they sought from him to intercede for them to enjoy seeing Him as well, so the Lord promised to appear to them on the mountain at a particular time. The brethren greatly rejoiced, and all of them set forth toward the mountain. The saint, because of his old age, was at the rear. There, he encountered an older man overcome with weakness and frailty, not able to walk, and none of the passingby monks cared to help him. Saint ‘Bishoy’ asked if he may carry him, and he did carry him and walked without feeling any labor. However, the older man started to get heavier and heavier; and the saint perceived that He was no one but the Lord Jesus Christ Himself. He then looked at Him and said: “The heaven is not wide enough to accommodate You, and Your majesty shakes the earth; how can a sinner like me carry You?” To this, the Lord Jesus Christ smiled at him and said: “Because you carried Me, My beloved ‘Bishoy,’ your body will never see decay!” Then, He disappeared. St. ‘Bishoy's’ body is still kept in his monastery without deterioration up to this very day. Once the brethren knew about what happened, they grieved deeply for passing by that Old Man and not gaining the blessing of carrying Him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 358–359
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Life in Seclusion

Life in Seclusion:

When Abba ‘Bemwah’ reposed in the Lord, his two disciples Abba ‘Bishoy’ and Abba ‘John (Yeĥness) the Short,’ spent the whole night praying to seek the guidance of God. An angel appeared to them and said that Abba ‘John the Short’ should remain alone in that location. In obedience, Abba ‘Bishoy’ left the place forsaking his friend, and dug for himself a cave near the southern rock, about two miles away from Abba ‘John the Short.’

His Strife:

As he loved prayer, he made a hole in a high spot on the cave wall, then he fixed a wedge in it and tied one end of a rope around it. Then, he used to tie the long hair of his head with the other end of that rope; so that whenever his head would get heavy and drop down due to sleepiness, the rope would pull it up, resulting in keeping him awake in prayers. As for fasting, he trained himself to fast the whole week and eat only on Saturdays. His prayers and fasting got to hand in hand with his intense love for the word of God. He memorized most of the Holy Bible by heart. The Book of ‘Jeremiah’ had a special place in his heart; that it was said that he used to see the prophet Jeremiah during his reading of his Book; that he was called ‘Bishoy the Jeremian.’

He considered hand-work as a significant part of building his spiritual life. He believed in the saying: “If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.” (2 Thess. 3:10). His friend Abba ‘John the Short’ said about him that when a rich man brought to him plenty of gold as a donation, he told him: “The dwellers of the wilderness have no need of gold and should not have any of it. Go instead to the villages of Egypt and distribute it to the poor. God bless you.” After the man went his way, and the saint returned to his cell, Satan came to him, saying: “You fatigued me so much, O Bishoy.” And, the saint answered him: “Since your fall, and all your fatigue is in vain.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 357–358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

Through the friendship of this saint with St. ‘Bigol,’ he was present when the young Abba ‘Shenouda the Archimandrite;’ St. ‘Bigol's’ nephew, first came out in the wilderness in his 7th year of age. He was clothed by his uncle the holy monastic Eskeem, in obedience to an angelic proclamation, and the presence of St. ‘Bishai.’ The three of them, despite the difference in age, worked with one spirit in a fantastic fellowship, realizing the saying of the wise ‘Solomon’: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Eccl. 4:12).

Each of them built for himself a cell on the mountain and another one near the church. It so happened that while they were setting forth to visit Abba ‘Jehnes’ (John) on Mount ‘Assiut,’ they heard a voice from heaven saying: “I have chosen you, O ‘Shenouda’ an Archimandrite.”

St. ‘Bishai’ reposed in the Lord on the 5th of Amshir, and was shrouded by St. ‘Shenouda.’ From his body, many signs and wonders appeared, which were all documented by Abba ‘Shenouda,’ who wrote his biography and described his ascetic life.

[Manuscript# 438/250: Asceticisms and Teachings of Abba Bishai (Peter), Library of the Patriarchate] [Nabil Niseem: SS. Bishai and Pasentaos in Mount ‘Tod.’ 1967]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 358
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — In Scetis (Shiheet)

Our great saint abba ‘Bishoy’ represents the simple life striving in the Lord, that was founded upon the love fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had a personal relationship with Jesus that broke the obstacles down to open up the heart by the Holy Spirit that the Heavenly Groom would transfigure within it and reign with power and dominion!

St. ‘Bishoy’ was born in ‘Shansa,’ a village in the governorate of ‘El- Menufyia,’ around the year 320 AD. He was one of six brothers, whose father reposed when they were relatively young, and their mother raised them up. One day the mother saw an angel who came to tell her: “The Lord says to you: ‘Give Me one of your children to serve Me all the days of his life.’” She answered: “Sir, they are all for the Lord. Let Him take whomever He chooses.” The angel put his hand on this saint, and said: “This is a good laborer for the Lord.” Being weakly built and frail in the body, his mother asked the angel to choose another one; but he answered her: “The Lord said ‘My strength is made perfect in weakness.’” (2 Cor. 12:9).

In Scetis (Shiheet):

Having reached twenty years of age in the year 340 AD, the young ‘Bishoy’ set forth to the wilderness of ‘Scetis,’ where he became a disciple of Abba ‘Bemwah’ (Bemen), the disciple of St. ‘Macarius’ (300-391 AD). There, he worshipped in seclusion for three years without going out of his cell. He grew in virtue and had his heart inflamed with love for God.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, p. 361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — His Love for the Salvation of All Souls

His Love for the Salvation of All Souls:

Saint ‘Bishoy’ had a disciple named ‘Isaac,’ who descended to the world and was seduced by a Jewish woman to forsake his faith, and he was converted to Judaism and lived with her. When he happened to encounter some monks, he asked them to tell St. ‘Bishoy’: “Your son, the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ has fallen and seeks from you to pray on his behalf to God to save him.” On hearing that, the woman said: “Even if ‘Bishoy’ come to me, I shall seduce him.” On returning to the monastery, the monks forgot what happened. Then, they were asked by the saint: “Has someone asked you to tell me something?” They answered in the negative. The saint asked them whether they have encountered the Jewish ‘Isaac,’ so they told him what happened and what ‘Isaac’ and the Jewish woman said. At that moment, they saw the saint retreat three steps backward and make the sign of the Cross on himself at each stage. Astonished, the monks said; “Even you, father, fear that woman?” St. ‘Bishoy’ humbly answered: “My children, the woman was the cause of the fall of ‘Adam,’ ‘Samson,’ ‘David’ and ‘Solomon.’ Who would be the poor ‘Bishoy’ to challenge her?! Nobody can overcome the tricks of Satan in women, except that one whom God is with.” He kept praying and fasting for the sake of his son ‘Isaac’ until God saved him, and he came back and repented.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1441 “How does St. John conclude the Book of Revelation, regarding the Day of the Lord?”, p. 557
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › Heaven and the Jerusalem Above — 1441. How does St. John conclude the Book of Revelation, regarding the Day of the Lord?

St. John concludes the Book of Revelation by describing the heavenly Jerusalem — or as St. Augustine calls it, “The heavenly Church” — the glories and blessings of the heavenly Church, and the desire of our Lord Jesus Christ to come quickly (Rev. 22:20–21) to take His bride the queen to His throne.

Many authors, poets, and philosophers such as Plato depict ideal cities (in their estimation) prescribing for them laws, arrangements, and principles dictated by their philosophy and way of thinking. However, very soon, mistaken or unrealistic principles infiltrate their models, and their ideal cities turn out in fact to be deficient and riddled with shortcomings.

St. John does not imitate their example but rather, ascending by the Spirit, his vision is of a true, ideal, and immortal Church, which is in essence “the tabernacle of God … with men” (Rev. 21:3). As this was difficult to depict or express in human language, he recorded for us what he actually saw, but in simple symbols that leave it to us to go deeper into them and savor the nature of this singular, heavenly city; so far as our spiritual stature allows us to comprehend through the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

Notes: [1360] Cf. St. Augustine of Hippo, City of God 20.17 (NPNF I/2:436).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1123 “Why was the Bible concluded with the book of Revelation, which frequently referred to the heavenly hosts?”, pp. 259–260
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 5: The Believer and the Heavenly Hosts › The Creation of the Spiritual World — 1123. Why was the Bible concluded with the book of Revelation, which frequently referred to the heavenly hosts?

Because the Lord of heaven wishes to make the heart of His church burn with the desire to depart to Him to enjoy the heavenly life.

God is present in His church (Cf. Rev. 2-3), heals her weakness, comforts her, and grants her the eternal heavenly joy together with the heavenly hosts.

It reveals how the heavenly hosts care for the church and support her that she may experience the sweetness of heaven.

The book of Revelation proclaims ‘Jerusalem’ the exalted heavenly city, being the “dwelling place of God with men”, and our eternal home.

Our knowledge of the heavenly hosts reveals to us certain aspects that apply to our current life of faith. In getting to know them, we learn more about their divine gifts and we desire to acquire these same features through God’s grace. Our study of the heavenly hosts in Scripture, the church’s Tradition, and the writings of the Church Fathers reveals to us hidden mysteries concerning the heavenly life, the holy church, and the spiritual life of the believer, especially servants.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 360–361
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian

An Encounter with St. Ephraim the Syrian:

By a Divine arrangement, Mar ‘Ephraim the Syrian’ came once to meet with Abba ‘Bishoy.’ As St. ‘Ephraim’ talked in the Syrian tongue, while St. ‘Bishoy’ talked in the Coptic tongue; the later sought from God to give them both the ability to understand each other without the need for an interpreter, and God granted them that, and they managed to spend a tremendous spiritual time together. St. ‘Ephraim’ learned from St. ‘Bishoy’ about the monastic experiences of the Egyptian fathers, particularly of St. ‘Macarius the Great.’

After a week, St. ‘Ephraim’ left. Then, a brother came to seek St. ‘Ephraim's’ blessing, but when St ‘Bishoy’ told him that he just left, the brother started to run to catch him. St. ‘Bishoy’ called him and said he would never be able to because St. ‘Ephraim’ was carried away by a cloud. It was also said that St. ‘Ephraim’ has left behind his stick, in front of the cave of St. ‘Bishoy.’

Emperor Constantine visited Him:

St. ‘John the Short’ once went to visit his friend St. ‘Bishoy,’ and while he was still outside his cell, he heard him talking to someone inside. Knocking on the door and entering, he found no one with the saint. Asking him with whom he was talking, he answered: “Emperor Constantine came to visit me and told me: ‘I wish I have abandoned my kingdom and became a monk; for I did not imagine how the monks enjoy such an honor and great glory. I see how those who depart were carried by the wings of eagles; and how they were received with great honor in heaven.’”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1415 “How can we prepare for the Day of Judgment?”, pp. 526–527
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › The Final Judgment — 1415. How can we prepare for the Day of Judgment?

When alms are as triumphant as planets, and the ranks of their givers are sublime, beautiful, and glorious.

When the abhorrent shortcomings of the sons of sin are exposed, and lying does not cover the one who clung to it.

When all forms are torn apart from all ranks, and stand there with necks uncovered, as it is written.

Then, let them who were glorified rejoice, and let no one grieve or be blamed.

In that victory, whoever conquers will be counted among the triumphants; whereas should he win here, he would not gain anything.”

Notes: [1276] Handwritten manuscript of the Memre of St. Ephrem the Syrian in the Dayr al-Surian [Monastery of the Syrians] collection — Memra No. 2000 dated 14 Amshir 1207 A. M. transcribed by the monk Samuel al- Suriany, Treatise 21: pp. 130–131. [1277] St. Basil of Caesarea, On the Judgment of God (FOTC 9:54). [1278] St Isaac The Syrian, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh. Trans., A. J. Wensinck. Amsterdam: Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen, 1923) 64.459–460: p. 308 amended. [1279] “To Monks in Monasteries and Communities” in Evagrius of Pontus: The Greek Ascetic Corpus, trans., Robert E. Sinkewicz., ed. Gillian Clark and Andrew Louth (Oxford University Press, 2003): p. 125. [1280] John Wortley, The Anonymous Sayings Of The Desert Fathers, trans., John Wortley, ed., John Wortley (Cambridge University Press, 2013) N.523: p. 357. [1281] St. Ephrem the Syrian, On The Second Coming of our Lord Jesus Christ 2. [1282] St. Augustine of Hippo, Lectures or Tractates on the Gospel According to St. John 54.5 (NPNF I/7:297) amended. [1283] St. Jacob of Sarug, Memre 68 On the End and the Fearful Judgment.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishoy, pp. 361–362
passages.text:
Saint: BISHOY, ST. ABBA — Forsaking Scetis

Forsaking Scetis:

In the year 407 AD, the first attack of the Berbers on the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ took place. At that time, the monks escaped from the desert. St. ‘John the Short’ asked St. ‘Bishoy’: “Do you fear death, O man of God?” He answered him: “No, but I fear a Berberian would kill me and goes to hell because of me!”

St. ‘John the Short’ went to mount ‘Kalzam,’ near the monastery of Abba ‘Anthony’ where he reposed. Whereas, St. ‘Bishoy’ went to ‘Ansena’ (the village of ‘Sheikh Abbadah’ near ‘Mallawy’), and he lived in the mountain. There, he formed a close relationship with ‘St. Abba ‘Paul of Tamouh,’ and sought from the Lord not to be separated from him when they would repose, and God granted them their wish.

St. ‘Bishoy’ remained in his expatriation until he reposed on the 8th of Abib in the year 417 AD, after reaching 97 years of age. He was buried in the castle of ‘Meniat el-Saqar’ near ‘Ansena.’ When St. ‘Paul of Tamouh’ reposed, St. ‘Athanasius’ of ‘Ansena’ gathered the two saints' bodies and buried them together in the monastery of abba ‘Bishoy’ in ‘Ansena’ (Monastery of El- Bersha). The bodies of these two saints were returned to the wilderness of ‘Scetis’ during the patriarchate of the 52nd pope Abba ‘Yusab I’ (831-849 AD).

They are now in the monastery of Abba ‘Bishoy’ in the Natron Valley.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1411 “What blessings shall the faithful who are righteous enjoy?”, p. 521
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › The Final Judgment — 1411. What blessings shall the faithful who are righteous enjoy?

The vision will differ from one person to another, according to the words of the Lord: “In My Father's house are many mansions” (John 14:2).

And St. Clement of Alexandria says, “Receive Christ, receive sight, receive your light, ‘In order that you may know well both God and man.’ ‘Sweet is the Word that gives us light, precious above gold and gems; it is to be desired above honey and the honey-comb’ (Ps. 19:10).”

Notes: [1253] St. John Cassian, The Conferences 11.15 (NPNF II/11:422). [1254] St. Isaac the Syrian, Hymns on the Church 49.16, quoted in PP 10:61. [1255] St. Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on Paradise 6.8 (PP 10:111). [1256] St. Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on Nativity 6.4 (NPNF II/13:238). [1257] St. Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on Paradise 3.2 (PP 10:91). [1258] St. Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus 1.3 (ANF 2:89–90). [1259] St. Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus 1.7 (ANF 2:91) amended. [1260] St. Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies 2.28.3 (ANF 1:399). [1261] See St. Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies 5.36.2 (ANF 1:567). [1262] Homer, Iliad v. 128. [1263] St. Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Heathen 11 (ANF 2:203) amended.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1379 “What is the millennial kingdom? And what is its true meaning?”, p. 497
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 7: Eschatology and the After Life › Millennialism (Chiliasm) — 1379. What is the millennial kingdom? And what is its true meaning?

Third: When the governor Pilate accused the Lord Christ of setting Himself up as a king, the Lord did not deny that He was a king, but said to him, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Is it plausible that the King of kings and the Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16) will change His mind and make Himself the king of an earthly kingdom?

Fourth: The Book of Revelation warns us against straying from its words: “For I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part from the Book of Life, from the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book. He who testifies to these things says: ‘Surely I am coming quickly.’ Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus! The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen” (Rev. 22:18–21).

Notes: [1225] Origen of Alexandria, De Principiis (On First Principles) 2.11.2 (ANF 4:297). [1226] Eusebius of Pamphili, Ecclesiastical History 7.24.1–4 (NPNF II/1:308; PG 20:693). [1227] St. Methodius of Olympus, The Banquet of the Ten Virgins 9.1–3 (ANF 6:344–346). [1228] St. Basil of Caesarea, Letters 186–368 263 (FOTC 28:241; PG 32:980). [1229] St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Letters 102 Also to Cledonius (NPNF II/7:443–445; PG 37:197). [1230] St. Epiphanius of Salamis, Against Heresies 77.36–39 (PG 42:697). [1231] St. Jerome, Commentary on Isaiah 9.33 (ACW 68:472). [1232] See St. Augustine of Hippo, City of God 20.7–9 (NPNF I/2:426–431).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dionysius Bar-Salibi, p. 596
passages.text:
Saint: DIONYSIUS BAR-SALIBI — His Writings

It is considered one of the most significant efforts ever done in that field, and he was among the few in Western Syria who contributed to the interpretation issue. In his interpretation, he depended upon the writings of St. ‘John Chrysostom,’ St. ‘Cyril,’ St. ‘Moses Bar-Kifa’ (son of rock), and St. John the Bishop of Dara. Parts of his interpretations were published, such as the Gospels, the Revelation, and a part of the Book of Ecclesiastes. Nowadays, the Book of Genesis is being ready for publication.

[The Precious Jewel in the History of the Church: by Bishop Isidore 3:5]

[Everett Ferguson: Encyclopedia of Early Christianity, 1998]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, pp. 356–357
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, ST. ABBA — His Monastic Life

The story of this saint reveals the fantastic plan of God for the salvation of every soul; how He uses every tool to draw them to Him, and how He sets them on the highest level if they receive His call and respond to it.

This saint, also (called ‘Peter’), was born in the village of ‘Epsona,’ a suburb of ‘Akhmim.’ In his youth, he walked in an evil path; but God did not leave him there but allowed for him to fall ill, and in a night vision, He revealed to him the place of the eternal sufferings which he was heading to. He bitterly wept, and raised his eyes to heaven and cried out: “My Lord and my God! If

you heal me of this illness; I shall repent, return to You and worship You

with all my heart.” ‘Bishai’ (Peter) was healed, and he did not forget his promise to the Lord, but he was inflamed in his heart with an intense longing to experience the monastic life. He forsook the sheep he was shepherding, and set forth to the monastery where he met with St. ‘Bigol,’ the uncle of St. ‘Shenouda’ (who was to become the Archimandrite in Mount Adriba).

His Monastic Life:

God used the illness to bring that young man out of the covetousness of the body, which would destroy the soul. Once he tasted the real spiritual life, his heart got filled with so much joy to set forth firmly and be willing to do so many labors enduring daily so many harsh sufferings with a joyful heart.

He lived with St. ‘Bigol’ in a fantastic friendship, partaking together in monasticism and worship without ever getting bored, watching the nights, and opposing the temptations of the devil.

God granted him an exalted capability beyond the limits of human endurance; he used to fast, in a way that defied imagination, for a whole month not tasting anything, and by a fantastic Divine allowance, he would stand the entire night praying. God, in His love, granted him to have the deeds of other people revealed before his eyes, which he used to support them on the life of true repentance. Because of God's grace working in him, many people came to him from all over Egypt to seek his blessings. They benefited greatly by his spiritual sermons, and he also wrote essays for the monks and those in the world.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Bishai, the Hermit, p. 356
passages.text:
Saint: BISHAI, THE HERMIT, ABBA

The biography of Abba ‘Bishai the Hermit,’ known as Abba ‘Bishai’ the dweller of the two graves at the entrance of ‘Tod’ (Mount Tod, east of the Nile river opposite to ‘Armant’), was linked to those of SS. ‘Pasantaos’ and ‘Sorus.’ The three of them were considered among the first monks who became disciples of St. ‘Pachom,’ the father of the ‘Koinonia’ (Coenobite).

He was a hermit who worshipped God from his early age and labored in his prayers day and night. He was also known for his love of the book of the prophet ‘Jeremiah;’ so that it was said that every time he read it, he would find the prophet ‘Jeremiah’ himself before him, kiss his head, then watch him ascending to heaven (which also happened to him when he read the other books of the prophets).

Giving his body no rest, he loved doing metanoias and long watching of the nights. After completing his strife, he reposed in the Lord on the 25th of Kiahk. His body was buried in his church, from which many signs and wonders appeared.

records.answer:
I could not find anything about St. Methodius, the brother of St. Cyril, or their mission to the Slavs in the loaded sources.

The sources do cover St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, who was a martyr in the early 4th century AD, but this is a different person. This St. Methodius was bishop in Lycia and Patara, opposed Origen's views, wrote several theological works, and was martyred around 311 AD in Greece [1][2][3][4][5].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 200
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Culture and Views

The Western Church celebrates st. Methodius (Eubilis) on the 20th of June and on the 18th of September. St. Methodius became the bishop of Olympus in Lycia in the southern part of Asia Minor, then became the bishop of Patara. He has martyred in the year 311 AD in Chalcis in Greece. He was forgotten or disregarded by the historian Eusebius of Caesarea, probably because he opposed Origen. This saint was not the same as Methodius, the bishop of Petaris in Syria or the bishop of Phoenicia, who was martyred in Syria.

His Culture and Views:

St. Methodius seemed to have read Plato's works and admired his dialogue style since he authored his essays using the same method. He opposed Origen's views about the prior existence of the souls, the resurrection of the bodies with the spirit, and that the body is a prison for the soul.

His Martyrdom:

According to St. Jerome, St. Methodius received the crown of martyrdom during the last days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284- 305 AD). However, others insisted that he was martyred at the time of Emperors Decius (249-251 AD) and Valerian (253-260 AD) in Chalcis in Greece. Yet, other scholars dismiss the idea of St. Methodius early martyrdom, on account of that he was briefly mentioned by Eusebius of Caesarea (265-339 AD), as being one of his contemporaries.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 201
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Writings

His Writings:

St. Methodius drew his fame from the many articles he wrote, among which were:

1. ‘On Virginity’ (Symposion e peri hagneias): It is a dialogue about commending the virginity. This dialogue ended with a long hymn sung by Thekla, and its verses were arranged in alphabetical order. It is considered as one of the earliest Christian hymns. He quoted from Psalm forty-five, saying: “The bride will sit at the right hand of Christ, adorned with gold.” This work is his only writing, which has been left complete. It revealed his admiration of Plato in following his dialogue style, from which he quoted not only some of its verses but also the idea of the work as a whole. Plato, in his work, commended love, while Methodius commended glories of virginity.

2. ‘On the Resurrection’ (Aglaophon e pen tes anastaseos): This article was lost, but many quotes from it remained in the work of Epiphanius of Salamis (315-403 AD) [Against the Heresies: 64], Photius of Constantinople (858-886 AD) [Codice 234] and John of Damascus (675-749 AD) [On Holy Images: Sermon 2]. In this work too, Methodius followed the Platonic dialogue style to refute Origen and his followers, who denied the resurrection of the material body, and believe that it was enough to say that what would resurrect is an adorned and glorified form of that body. In heaven, our bodies will be spiritual, and according to St. Paul the Apostle: "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corin. 15:44), and, "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; nor does corruption inherit incorruption" (1 Corin. 15:50). According to them, the man initially was in Paradise, namely in the 3rd heaven (2 Corin. 12), in a spiritual body, then having fallen, he was brought down to earth, where God provided him with a leather cover, namely, he got the material body as a punishment. Such a substantial body is the source of temptations and trials of the soul, and without it, the soul could not sin. Then, when we resurrect, we would be where there is no place for crime, we would be like angels, free from the body, which represents a burden on the soul. St. Methodius responded to that in his dialogue by saying that the body is a tool in the hand of the soul to use for doing good or doing evil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, pp. 201–202
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Writings

Then, when we resurrect, we would be where there is no place for crime, we would be like angels, free from the body, which represents a burden on the soul. St. Methodius responded to that in his dialogue by saying that the body is a tool in the hand of the soul to use for doing good or doing evil. When the Holy Bible says that we shall be like the angels of God, this did not mean that we shall be without bodies, but we shall be like the angels in their incorruptible and unchangeable nature.

He also said that by death, God did not plan to change us from what He intended for us when He created us. He is like a sculptor who would re-knead his hand-work when he finds it getting out of shape. He would re-knead it in such a way to conform to what he had for it in his mind originally. In the same manner by death, God would transform us to be free from the corruption of sin.

It was a bold dialogue in the house of a physician by the name Aglaophon in Patara. In that dialogue, Methodius confirmed the resurrection of the body, being a partner of the soul in her strife, to share in her glory, and he indicated that it was not another spiritual body, but he mentioned that this resurrected body would enjoy a heavenly renewal. He said about Christ: “He became a True Body and died a True Death, and not just in appearance, to show that He was the First of those who resurrected from death, to turn what is earthly to heavenly, and what is mortal to immortal.”

Methodius said that at the beginning, the man was immortal, body and soul, that death and the separation of the soul from the collection were the results of the envy of Satan, and that the goal of Christ's Redemption was to rejoin what was separated by Satan.

3. St. Jerome (347-420 AD) mentioned in his book: ‘Of Illustrious Men’ (sec 83), and in his two Letters 48 and 70: that Methodius argued very well in refuting Porphyry's fifteen letters which were written against the Christians.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 203
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — Of His Words

Of His Words:

• The church grows daily in stature and beauty through her cooperation and unity with the Logos, who descends to us to this very day and keep on descending in the commemoration of His passion. • No one should be lazy in welcoming the King; otherwise, he would be deprived of the beauty of the participation in the wedding. I wish no one among us would welcome Him with an ugly face, lest he would be condemned as an evildoer who refrained from receiving the King. Let us come to Him with gladness, receive Him with joy, and hold fast to our banquet with faithfulness. • I keep my soul pure for You, O Bridegroom. I would carry for You a lighted lamp and march to receive You.

[Dr. A. Rustom: The Church Fathers in the First Three Centuries] [H. Wace & W. Piercy: A Dictionary of Early Christian Biography, 1999]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Methodius, Bishop of Olympus, p. 202
passages.text:
Saint: METHODIUS, BISHOP OF OLYMPUS (The martyr) — His Writings

3. St. Jerome (347-420 AD) mentioned in his book: ‘Of Illustrious Men’ (sec 83), and in his two Letters 48 and 70: that Methodius argued very well in refuting Porphyry's fifteen letters which were written against the Christians.

4. St. Jerome also mentioned another work for Methodius. It is called ‘The Diviner,’ which was addressed against Origen, although it is now lost. It has the same title used by Ostatheos in his book; he wrote to refute Origen, who believed that the soul of Samuel the Prophet was under the control of the devil and that it was recalled by the diviner using sorcery. The response of Methodius was very different from that of Ostatheus, in which Ostatheus believed that the soul of Samuel was indeed called.

5. Socrates [The Ecclesiastical History 6:13] mentioned another work by Methodius, called ‘Xeno,’ which, according to some, was the same work referred to by Photius.

6. ‘On the Created Objects’: Some quotations from this work were kept by Photius, in which he refuted the Origen teachings, which called the eternity of the world. This teaching assumed that if God is eternal, then He was always the Almighty Creator, and at no time, He was not the Creator, and, since there is no Creator without creation, therefore, they concluded that there was creation since eternity. This Methodius work, too, came in the form of dialogue that responded to all those wrong assumptions.

7. ‘On the Freedom of Will’: A discussion to confirm that the will of man is free and responsible for his actions. It was most probably addressed against the followers of Valentinus and the Gnostics.

8. Lost works: Such as ‘On the Martyrs,’ ‘Interpretation of the Book of Genesis,’ and ‘Interpretation of the Song of Songs.’

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Dionisius, the Bishop, p. 594
passages.text:
Saint: DIONISIUS, THE BISHOP (The martyr)

This saint was a bishop on ‘Corinth’ and was martyred in the days of Emperors ‘Diocletian’ (284-305 AD) and ‘Maximian’ (286-305 AD) after being viciously tortured for the sake of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Finally, his head was cut off by the sword, and he received the eternal crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 23 Baba]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Philoromus, p. 452
passages.text:
Saint: PHILOROMUS (The martyr)

St. Philoromus was one of the prominent people of the city of Thmuis (Tell el-Timai) on the east side of the Nile delta in Egypt. He was a Christian military tribune, and he defended St. Philaeas, the bishop of his city when he rejected the appeals of his relatives and friends in trying to save him. Then, they both offered themselves to death and were martyred in the year 303 AD, during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). So they earned immortal palms from God. With them was crowned with martyrdom a countless multitude of the faithful of the same place, who followed the example of their pastor. The western church celebrates him on the 4th of Feb.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 390]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Mucius, pp. 259–260
passages.text:
Saint: MUCIUS (The martyr)

St. Mucius (Mocius) was a Christian priest who was martyred in the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). His biography indicates that he was a prominent sermon-giver who preached in Amphipolis in Macedonia.

It happened that during the feast of god Bacchus (Dionysus), this saint dared to cast on the ground whatever was on the idol's Altar with all their sacrifices. When the pagans wanted to kill him, the governor arrested him instead and brought him to trial. The judge condemned him to be burned alive. There in the fiery furnace, the saint was seen walking unharmed in flames, along with three strangers. Later on, the saint was sent to Heraclea, where he was tortured by the hinbazeen. Then, he was cast before hungry wild beasts, but they refrained from touching him. He was finally sent to Byzantium (Constantinople), where his head was cut off by the sword in the year 304 AD.

[Butler: May 13] [Hieromartyr Mocius, the Presbyter of Amphipolis in Macedonia: The Orthodox Church in America (On the Internet)]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Porphyrios, p. 479
passages.text:
Saint: PORPHYRIOS (The martyr)

The Synaxarion of the 3rd of Baramhat mentions another martyr with a similar name Porphyrios (Porphyry). Most probably, this saint was martyred in the days of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). He was a rich man of the city of Banias, who loved the poor and visited those imprisoned. On seeing the governor walking in front of his house, he proclaimed his Christian faith and ultimately received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Marcellus, the Bishop, pp. 55–56
passages.text:
Saint: MARCELLUS, THE BISHOP (The martyr) — Emperor Theodosius the Great Spreads Christianity

Emperor Theodosius the Great Spreads Christianity:

In the year 380 AD, the righteous Emperor Theodosius the Great (379-395 AD) planned on spreading Christianity all over the Roman Empire. The emperor sent a decree which urged everyone to confess the true Christian Faith taught by the popes of Rome and Alexandria. Eight years later, the emperor sent his deputy to Egypt, Syria, and Asia Minor, to make sure that the imperial order to destroy all the pagan temples was carried out in the whole Empire. This action naturally provoked the anger of the pagans.

When the imperial deputy arrived at Apamea in Syria, he sent soldiers to destroy the city's temple of the god Zeus. However, because the temple was huge and was very well built, the soldiers were unable to destroy it. The bishop of the region who was called Marcellus was observing what the deputy was trying to do, and he suggested to him to take his men to his next assignment and to leave the responsibility of destroying the temple of Zeus to him. On the next day, a contractor came to see bishop Marcellus and agreed with him to do the job if he would be paid double. The bishop approved, and the man and his workers started to dig underneath the main foundations of the temple, which caused the whole building to collapse. Bishop Marcellus repeated the same approach in destroying all the other temples.

Then, bishop Marcellus and his people reached a temple that the pagans decided to defend to their last man. So, while the bishop was trying to hide from the arrows aimed at him, some of the pagans charged against him and managed to throw him into a fire pit. In that way, he received the crown of martyrdom in the year 389 AD.

When his sons – as he was a married man – decided to avenge the death of their father, the pious governor stood in their way saying: “It is more befitting for you to rejoice that God found your father worthy to die for His sake.”

[Butler: August 14]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Olympas, the Apostle, p. 319
passages.text:
Saint: OLYMPAS, THE APOSTLE

St. Olympas (meaning "Heavenly" in Greek) was one of the seventy apostles who were sent by the Lord to preach the Word. He was a Roman Christian whom St. Paul the Apostle saluted (in Romans 16:15) around 65 AD. He was also called Paul, and he was the one who served the disciples, carried some of the epistles of St. Peter the Apostle to the Gentiles, entered with him into Rome, where he preached and taught many. When St. Peter was martyred, this apostle was the one who took his body off the cross, shrouded him, and took him to the house of one of the believers. Then, someone reported him to Emperor Nero (54-68 AD) of being one of the disciples of St. Peter. When Nero called him for questioning, he confessed before him that the Lord Jesus Christ is the true God. Nero brutally tortured him, then asked him how he would like to die, to which the saint replied: “I want to die for the sake of Christ, but it is up to you to kill me in whatever way you choose.” The emperor ordered to crucify him upside down the way his mentor died, and in this way, he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion of 6th Abib]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS (The martyr)

St. Hesychius (Esychius), an officer in the imperial court in Antioch, during the persecution stirred up by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD) against the Christians, was condemned to death by drowning in the river Orontes because he refused to sacrifice to the idols. This martyrdom took place most probably in the year 297 AD.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Hesychius (15) (Esychius), Vol. III, p. 10]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hesychius, the Monk, p. 252
passages.text:
Saint: HESYCHIUS, THE MONK, ST.

St. Hesychius was a saintly monk who lived in the 4th century AD. He was a faithful disciple of his mentor St. Hilarion, whom he accompanied in his travels from Palestine to Egypt. After St. Hilarion's reputation reached its peak in Gaza, he intended not to stay or to go back to Gaza, and he sailed secretly to the island of Sicily. For three years, Hesychius kept searching for the whereabouts of his mentor. Not finding him in the wilderness or the ports of Egypt, he searched for him in Greece. There, he heard about a saintly monk in Sicily who performed miracles. So, he set out to that island and cast himself on the ground, shedding tears on the feet of his mentor.

Wishing to enjoy a life of seclusion, the mentor and his disciple went to Dalmatia and from there to the island of Cyprus. Two years later, St. Hilarion sent Hesychius to Palestine to visit and follow up on the condition of the brethren there and to inspect their old monastery near Gaza. When he returned, he found his mentor disturbed by the frequency of the visitors, and planning to flee to another location. However, being too advanced in age, he managed to convince him to go deeper into the island to enjoy more seclusion. There, they lived until eventually St. Hilarion reposed, leaving his Holy Bible and some clothes to his disciple. After some time, Hesychius carried the relics of his mentor to Palestine, despite the objection of the inhabitants of the island. There, it was received by the multitudes of monks and people with hymns of praise. He was buried in the monastery he built-in Majuma. A few years later, Hesychius himself reposed.

[Baring-Gould: October 3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Amphilochius, the Bishop of Iconium, pp. 165–166
passages.text:
Saint: AMPHILOCHIUS, THE BISHOP OF ICONIUM, ST.

St. Amphilochius lived in the fourth century AD and was a close friend to St. Basil the Great, St. Gregory the Theologian, and St. Gregory of Nyssa.

He was born in Caesarea of Cappadocia between the years 340 and 350 AD He was raised to love the knowledge and culture, and he was characterized, beside his noble origin, with justice and wisdom. He succeeded his father in his work as a lawyer in Constantinople in the year 364 AD. Then, he became a judge and became known for his clean hands and integrity. His friend St. Gregory kept urging him to give more of his time to the study the Holy Bible, worship, and ministry, but he felt that he would rather minister to God through his loyalty and in doing his job as a judge with integrity.

He passed through a severe trial when he was unjustly accused of getting a bribe to acquit a guilty man. When St. Gregory, the Theologian hastened to write to the imperial palace in Constantinople to proclaim the innocence of his friend, his intervention was well received, and the saint came out of the trial with more honor. But the more significant benefit of that trial was his perception of the importance of the counsel of his old friend, who kept on urging him to dedicate himself to the ministry of God. He decided to forsake his job in the year 367 AD and to live as a hermit in his own house. He devoted his life to concentrate on the study of the Holy Bible, contemplation, spiritual worship, asceticism and taking care of his sick father in his old age.

Amphilochius took St. Basil the Great as his friend, spiritual mentor, and a guide of his life. There were so many messages exchanged between them, although Amphilochius used quite a bit of caution, to avoid being recommended for a pastoral position. God called him to be ordained as a bishop in the year 374 AD on the city of ‘Iconium’ in the region of ‘Lycaonia,' which was named ‘The second Pisidia.' It seemed that he consented to get ordained as a bishop through the pressure of St. Basil the Great, as it was obvious in the message from the later to him, saying: “God, who, in every generation, chooses the blessed man in whom He is well pleased, reveals the vessels of his choice, and uses them to minister to his saints. He is the One who catches you in the net of His grace, from which you cannot escape, despite your attempts to do so, not to escape from us, but from the call, God addressed through us… So, He brought you over in the middle of ‘Pisidia’ to captivate to the Lord those who were previously captivated by the devil, and to bring them out of the depths of darkness to light, according to His will."

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Domadius, the Syrian, pp. 631–632
passages.text:
Saint: DOMADIUS, THE SYRIAN (The martyr) — Receiving Faith

Receiving Faith:

This saint was raised in Persia, where he was taught astrology. He had a strong desire to be a Christian. So, it happened that in the market place, he met with a Persian monk called ‘Aughalis,’ from whom he learned the way to God. He was so jubilant that he kept teaching his household the way to faith. Then, he got baptized.

His Monastic Life:

Later on, he went to a monastery and became a monk. He lived a great ascetic life that brought on him the envy of some brethren. When he sensed what was happening, he left them and went to the monastery of St. ‘Sergius,’ where he became a disciple to one of their hermits for ten years. During all that time, he ate nothing cooked.

His Simplicity and Purity:

After that, he was ordained as a deacon. And, while he was ministering with the saintly hermit at the altar, he saw a lovely white dove that came on the altar. Thinking that it was an earthly dove and fearing for the vessel, he kept waving at it with his head and hands. After praying the Mass, when the priest asked him why he was so disturbed during the Liturgy, he told him what he had seen. The priest asked him to let him know if he would see it again. The next day, during Mass, the deacon saw it again, and alerted the priest: “There it is Father.” Looking and seeing nothing, the old priest cast himself before the Lord, raising tearful prayers, day and night, until he was found worthy of seeing that dove, which he came to know was a symbol of the Holy Spirit. He did not say anything to St. ‘Domadius’ to spare him from being overcome with pride. However, he told the story to the bishop, who ordained ‘Domadius’ as a priest.

When his fame spread and reached the Patriarch of that time, he planned to visit him. On hearing about it, the saint fled to the church of St. ‘Cosman,’ and dwelt next to it for some time, feeding only on the herbs of the ground.

His Martyrdom:

God performed so many miracles through this saint. When Emperor Julian the Apostate (360-363 AD) came out to fight the Persians, he passed by the cave of this saint. When he was told about his story, he ordered his men to stone him and his disciples to death; they left a great heap of stones on top of their cave.

Several years later, God allowed for his relics to be discovered; and a church was built in his name. God allowed for so many miracles to continue happening in that church.

[The Synaxarion: 25 Abib]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Euthymius, the Great Abbot, p. 89
passages.text:
Saint: EUTHYMIUS, THE GREAT ABBOT

Abbot Euthymius was born in Melitene in Armenia in the year 377 AD, where he was ordained as a priest and became an Abbot on a gathering of monks. On reaching 30 years old, he immigrated to Palestine, where he lived as a hermit in several places, mostly in caves. Finally, he settled down in a desolate town between Jerusalem and Jericho, where he was surrounded by many monks whom he guided, yet not at the expense of his way of seclusion.

Abbot Euthymius was one of the early great Father monks of Palestine and had a significant influence on the Nomads there. It happened that he healed a paralyzed son of one of their chiefs. And, he also had quite an impact on Empress Eudocia (401-460 AD), the widow of Emperor Theodosius II (402- 450 AD), who came to seek his counsel in particular issues. He finally reposed in Palestine on the 20th of January, 473 AD.

[The Penguin Dictionary of Saints, p. 123] [A Dictionary of Christian Biography: Euthymius (4), Vol II; p. 398-400]

records.question: What year did St. Barbara move to Egypt and where did she live there?
records.answer:
The sources do not mention St. Barbara moving to Egypt or living there. They state that she was born in the village of Gamis near the city of Leopolis in Nicomedia, and that according to some historians, she might have been martyred in Heliopolis, Egypt, but no specific year of moving or residence in Egypt is given [1][2][3].

Therefore, the year St. Barbara moved to Egypt and where she lived there are not described in the sources.
