passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1025 “How can we practice fasting so that we are led by love?”, p. 155
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1025. How can we practice fasting so that we are led by love?

The Church Fathers were saddened by those who fast by just replacing the types of food they eat, while still carrying within them the desire for food and practicing gluttony. Through fasting, we save the cost of expensive food so we can give this money to our needy brothers and sisters — the least of Christ’s brethren as He called them [see Matt. 25:40]. Through fasting, the believer’s heart and inner sight are opened to see the Lord of Glory in every person, especially in the needy and the suffering. For this reason, St. Augustine says that if one does not reserve some of his money during the fast to give to the poor, his fasting is without flavor. He also says, “Do you wish your prayer to fly toward God? … Make for it two wings: fasting and almsgiving.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1016 “What do the Church Fathers say about fasting?”, pp. 149–150
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1016. What do the Church Fathers say about fasting?

St. Basil the Great says, “[Fasting] is a good guardian of the soul, a safe companion for the body, the best weapon, a training regimen for contestants. It drives away temptations. It readies for piety. It is the companion of sobriety and the craftsman of selfcontrol. In war it teaches bravery, in peace stillness. It sanctifies the Nazirite [monk] and perfects the priest. For it is impossible to venture upon priestly activities without fasting, not only in the case of our present holy and true worship, but also in the prefigured worship set out in the law.”

“Fasting is likeness to the angels, companionship with the righteous, moderation in life. It made Moses the lawgiver. Samuel is the fruit of fasting. Hannah as she fasted vowed to God: O Lord God of Sabaoth, if you were to look upon your maidservant and give me a male child, then I will offer him in your presence as a gift. He shall drink no wine or strong drink until the day of his death (1 Sam. 1:11 LXX). The great Samson was reared on fasting, and as long as it was part of that man’s life, his enemies fell by the thousands (Judg. 15:16), the gates of the city were pulled down (Judg. 16:3), and lions did not withstand the strength of his hands (Judg. 14:6). But when drunkenness and fornication seized him, he was easily captured by his enemies. And after he was deprived of his eyes, he was set out as a plaything for little Philistine boys.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1027 “How can we practice fasting as worship in spirit?”, p. 156
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1027. How can we practice fasting as worship in spirit?

The Church Fathers linked fasting to worship in spirit and truth; namely, prayer, contemplation on the word of God, prostrations (metanoias), almsgiving, and the partaking of the holy mysteries.

St. Basil the Great says, “may the fast with which the Jews were threatened not come upon us: Behold the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon this land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord (Amos 8:11). It was for this reason that the Just Judge sent it, because he saw their mind was wasting away from a lack of the nourishment that comes from the doctrines of truth, yet their external man was growing enormously fat and obese. And so, in the coming days the Holy Spirit will give you a feast at both the morning and evening festivities. No one should willingly absent themselves form this spiritual banquet. Let all of us share in the sober cup. It has been prepared by Wisdom, who hands it to us equally, to the extent that each has the capacity to drink it. For she has prepared her cup and slaughtered her beasts (Prov. 9:2), that is, the food for the perfect, for those who have their faculties trained by practice to distinguish good from evil (Heb. 5:14). Filled with such an abundance, may we be found worthy too of the joy experienced in the bridegroom’s chamber, in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

The scholar Tertullian says, “They who are about to enter baptism ought to pray with repeated prayers, fasts, prostrations, and vigils all the night through, and with the confession of all bygone sins.”

St. Ambrose says, “Blessed is he that knows how to be full in Christ. Not corporal, but spiritual, is that satiety which knowledge brings about.”

St. Isaac the Syrian links fasting to prayer when he likens fasting to a live coal which, if no incense of prayer is sprinkled on it, will produce a choking smoke rather a sweet aroma of incense. Tertullian says that we should “feed prayers on fastings.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1015 “Why does the believer need to fast?”, p. 149
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1015. Why does the believer need to fast?

God — who created everything for the humans that He might make of them living kings queens — gave the humans one commandment: not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. He did not do so to deprive them of anything but wanted them to stretch out their hands and eat from the tree of life, and so to live, through obedience, in a blissful eternity, like the holy angels. Moreover, Adam and Eve could have resisted Satan and all his soldiers through obedience to the divine commandment, and thereby declare through their fasting that their love for God transcends everything. The Lord planted for them the Garden of Eden (Gen. 2:8) to make of their hearts an exalted paradise.

St. Basil the Great says, “Fasting began in Paradise when God said to Adam: ‘Do not eat from the tree of knowledge of the good and evil.’ Our first parents were driven out of Paradise for lack of fasting. Therefore, fasting is the way to enter the kingdom. Do not tremble or be afraid of fasting. Does your body not need medicine? Likewise, your soul also often needs medicine. Fasting is the medicine of the soul, to rid it of sin.”

Also, in the Old Testament deuterocanonical Book of Judith, the leaders and people trusted that the Lord would heed their prayers when they were steadfast in fasting and prayers in the sight of the Lord (Judith 4:8–15).

Notes: [412] See Elias Koyter al-Mukhlessy, St. Basil the Great (Arabic) (Publications of the Pauline Library in Beirut, 1989): p. 288.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1022 “Does God expect us to destroy the body when we fast?”, pp. 153–154
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1022. Does God expect us to destroy the body when we fast?

Fasting is the bowing down of the whole human being before the Holy Spirit that He may sanctify him. God does not desire the destruction of the body, but its sanctification. Thus, in addition to bodily fasting, the believer practices holy spiritual fasting, through which the soul is liberated from all impurities and becomes able to ascend freely towards heaven. St. John Cassian writes, “We ought therefore, whenever the outward man fasts, to restrain the inner man as well from food which is bad for him: that inner man, namely, which the blessed Apostle above all urges us to present pure before God, that it may be found worthy to receive Christ within.”

Notes: [428] St. John Cassian, Institutes 5.21 (NPNFII/11:241).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1027 “How can we practice fasting as worship in spirit?”, pp. 156–157
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1027. How can we practice fasting as worship in spirit?

St. Isaac the Syrian links fasting to prayer when he likens fasting to a live coal which, if no incense of prayer is sprinkled on it, will produce a choking smoke rather a sweet aroma of incense. Tertullian says that we should “feed prayers on fastings.”

St. Augustine links fasting with brotherly love saying, “In this question, however, of fasting or not fasting on the seventh day, nothing appears to me more safe and conducive to peace than the Apostle's rule: ‘Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat, and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats’ (Rom. 14:3) ‘for neither if we eat are we the better, nor if we do not eat are we the worse’ (1 Cor. 8:8). Our fellowship with those among whom we live, and along with whom we live in God, being preserved undisturbed by these things.”

Notes: [435] St. Basil of Caesarea, On Fasting and Feasts 2.8 (PP 50:81). [436] Tertullian, On Baptism 20 (ANF 3:678). [437] St. Ambrose of Milan, Duties of the Clergy 2.17.92 (NPNF II/10:57). [438] Tertullian, On Repentance 9 (ANF 3:664). [439] St. Augustine of Hippo, Letters 36.26 (NPNF I/1:268).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1031 “How is our Christ transfigured through the fasting of the Church?”, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1031. How is our Christ transfigured through the fasting of the Church?

The purpose of the fasts of the Church is to entreat the Savior to work in all humanity.

First. In weekly fasts (Wednesday and Friday): On Wednesday, the conspiracy to crucify Christ was hatched. Therefore, the believer fasts to thank God who turns the malice of the evil to the service of salvation. On Friday the believer sees, with St. Jacob of Sarug, Mount Golgotha turned into a wedding mount where Christ offers His bride, the Church, her dowry. Thus, the fasts of Wednesdays and Fridays lead us to the day of the Lord who rose from the dead, early on Sunday morning, so that our hearts rejoice and cry out that the Lord may grant us a resurrected life that prepares us for paradise.

Second. The annual fasts:

During the Nativity Fast [Christmas Fast], the believer does not cease praying for all humanity so that the Baby in the manger (Luke 2:7) may dwell in their hearts, minds, and emotions.

During Great Lent the believer rejoices as he shares in Christ’s fast, in order to celebrate the Christian passover. Every day he prays to the Lord to pass his mind, heart, and emotions over to the heavenly life.

During the Apostles’ Fast, the believer’s heart burns with longing to share with the Apostles in preaching of the gospel of Christ.

During Jonah’s Fast, we pray for non-believers that God may work in them as He did with the people of Nineveh.

During St. Mary’s Fast, we pray that Christ may dwell in our hearts just as the Word of God was incarnate in her womb.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1032 “What is the trajectory of the Church’s thought throughout the Lenten fast?”, pp. 161–162
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1032. What is the trajectory of the Church’s thought throughout the Lenten fast?

The Sunday Gospels of Lent reveal the Church’s understanding of the concept of fasting and sketch out the contemplations to which the Church invites us as we journey through the fast:

1. Sunday of Preparation: Nothing should occupy our minds or hearts while we prepare for fasting other than the encounter with God our heavenly Father. By fasting, we experience new depths of our relationship with God. On the Sunday before Lent, we ought to expel from ourselves every bondage to the desires for food and drink. The Church presents us with a positive, joyful perspective, which is the hidden encounter with our Heavenly Father. The Church reads to us the gospel passage that concerns the pillars of Christian worship, as Christ presented them in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 6:1–18), namely, almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. Here, we see that these ought to be offered as sacrifices of love, secretly offered to the heavenly Father behind closed doors, so that we can taste this mutual love. Our heavenly Father initiates love, and we respond to this love with love.

At the end of the Lenten fast, on Palm Sunday, the Church reads the gospel chapters about Christ’s entrance into Jerusalem. Having begun the fast by declaring our deep and secret attachment to God our Father, we conclude the fast by seeing Christ entering into our hearts to create from their depths His beloved Jerusalem and its divine kingdom. In fact, fasting is not so much about being deprived of food as it is about being satisfied with God and sharing in the banquet of angels.

2. Sunday of Treasures: With the beginning of Lent, the Church reads to us a passage concerning heavenly treasure (Matt. 6:19–33). To fast is to come into possession of a heavenly treasure, that is, Christ Himself our divine treasure (2 Cor. 4:7).

3. Sunday of Temptation: Our entering into new depths in our relationship with Christ provokes the devil, who wages spiritual wars and temptations against us. But we take shelter in Christ fasting in the wilderness, He to whom the angels came and ministered after His temptation (Matt. 4:11), and we share in the benefit of their ministry. Fasting is an invitation to receive this blessing.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1021 “How does fasting prepare us for spiritual warfare?”, pp. 152–153
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1021. How does fasting prepare us for spiritual warfare?

In the temptation on the mountain in the wilderness, Christ our Commander in war fasted (Matt. 4:1–2) that we may imitate Him, being His faithful soldiers. He is our perfect model and leader, who trains us to fast while fixing our gaze on our Commander who fasted and confounded Satan and his kingdom. The Fathers knew that the fasts of the Church are the seasons of the most intense demonic warfare. In their discriminating spiritual understanding, they took this to be a sign of the terror that those who truly fast instill in demons.

St. Augustine says, “When the tempter intensifies his warfare, we must fast so that the body may fulfil its Christian duty in striving against the desires of the world through repentance, urging the soul to conquer in humility.”

St. John Saba says, “Do not overfill your belly, lest fornication torture you. Do not greatly weaken your body, lest your enemy make you weary. Hold to a rule and, behold, henceforth you will go forward on the royal way and your journey will be without fear.”

St. Cyril says, “‘He afterwards hungered,’ because, on the other hand, it was necessary that He Who refused not our poverty should withdraw from nothing whatsoever that belongs to man’s condition, He consented for His flesh to require its natural supplies; and hence the words, ‘He hungered.’”

St. Isaac the Syrian says, “all strife against sin and its desires is to be preceded by the labour of fasting, especially if one is combating inward sin.” He again says, “And also our Saviour, when He manifested Himself to the world at the Jordan, began from that point. For when He had been baptised, the spirit led Him into the wilderness, and then He fasted forty days and forty nights. And all those who follow His steps, base the beginning of their struggle upon this action. That weapon was polished by God, who should despise it without being blameworthy? If the lawgiver has fasted, to which guardian of the law is it not necessary to do likewise?”

St. John of Thebes says, “Bodily fasting is abstinence from food, but spiritual fasting is hunger and thirst for righteousness.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1016 “What do the Church Fathers say about fasting?”, p. 150
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1016. What do the Church Fathers say about fasting?

After Elijah fasted, he shut up heaven for three years and six months (1 Kings 17:1). For when he saw that such great arrogance had been born of self-indulgence, he deemed it necessary to subject them to involuntary fasting with a famine, forcing an end to their sin, which had already increased beyond measure. It was fasting that, like a kind of cauterization or amputation, halted the rampant spread of vice.”

“Daniel, the man of desires (Dan. 10:11), neither ate bread nor drank water for three weeks (see Dan. 10:2–3). And he taught the lions to fast when he climbed down into their den (cf. Dan. 6:17–25). For just as lions cannot sink their teeth into anything constructed of stone or metal or any other solid material, so too fasting, by hardening the body of that man as tempering hardens iron, made it as steel to the lions. For they did not open their mouth against the saint. Fasting quenched the power of fire and kept away the mouths of the lions.”

Notes: [413] St. Basil of Caesarea, On Fasting and Feasts 1.6 (PP 50:61). [414] St. Basil of Caesarea, On Fasting and Feasts 2.6 (PP 50:78–79). [415] St. Basil of Caesarea, On Fasting and Feasts 1.7 (PP 50:63).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1029 “What is the purpose of fasting?”, p. 159
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1029. What is the purpose of fasting?

First. Acquisition of virtues: St. Jerome says, “Fasting is not itself an absolute virtue, but the foundation of virtues.”

Second. Motivation to give thanks: St. Evagrius believes that the person who fasts becomes aware of the grace of God at work within him: “Those who excessively feed their bodies to fulfil their desires (Rom. 13:14) … when they become no longer lustful, although they remain in the same body; and when they become active in their contemplation of the One God, the true Being, as much as possible; such people confess the Creator’s graciousness to them, for He granted them this body.”

Third. Appreciation of food as a blessing: St. Basil believes that while fasting is an opportunity to abstain from food, then end of fasting is an opportunity for rejoicing in food — not with excessive indulgence, but with a sense of the blessedness of food. “After all, just as thirst makes drinking pleasurable and hunger before a meal makes eating pleasurable, so too fasting enhances the enjoyment of food when it is partaken … Don’t you realize that … health is more appreciated after the experience of the contrary? So too is the table more charming after fasting.”

Fourth. Freedom from enslavement to one’s belly: Abba Theonas says, “We never read that anyone is condemned simply for taking food, but only when something was joined with it or followed afterwards, for which he deserved condemnation.” And St. John Climacus says, “Master your stomach before it masters you.”

Notes: [447] St. Basil of Caesarea, On Fasting and Feasts 1.8 (PP 50:64–65). [448] St. John Cassian, The Conferences 21.13 (NPNF II/11:365). [449] John Climacus: Ladder of Divine Ascent, trans., Colm Luibheid and Norman Russell (Paulist Press, 1982) 14.17: p. 142.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1024 “How can the believer offer his fast as a sacrifice of love?”, p. 155
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1024. How can the believer offer his fast as a sacrifice of love?

Through fasting, we declare the desire of our hearts to partake with our Christ in His sacrificial love. When the believer feels hungry or thirsty, he offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God who allowed him to partake in His cross or in His sacrificial love, and at the same time God inhales this sacrifice as a soothing aroma.

St. John Cassian says, “The duty of fasting becomes acceptable before God when it is perfected with the fruits of love.”

And St. Evagrius says, “When the soul desires to seek after a variety of foods then it is time to afflict it with bread and water that it may learn to be grateful for a mere morsel of bread.”

Notes: [433] St. Evagrius of Pontus, Evagrius Ponticus: The Praktikos. Chapters on Prayer, trans., John Eudes Bamberger (Cistercian Publications, 1972) 16: p. 21.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1023 “What does the prophet when he says, “Consecrate a fast … call a sacred assembly” (Joel 1:14; 2:15)?”, p. 154
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1023. What does the prophet when he says, “Consecrate a fast … call a sacred assembly” (Joel 1:14; 2:15)?

To consecrate a fast is to encounter the Holy God; and the calling of a sacred assembly is the whole believer’s engrossment in the vision of God and dialogue with Him, that he may partake in the divine nature (2 Pet. 1:4) and bear the marks of the Lord Jesus (Gal. 6:17). In our fasts, we pray to be united with our Christ by the work of His Holy Spirit, to become a holy icon of Him. We savor the divine commandment and pray for the divine promise: “You shall therefore consecrate yourselves, and you shall be holy; for I am holy” (Lev. 11:44). We resist evil, not out of fear of eternal punishment, but out of desire to become an icon of the Holy One.

St. Aphrahat says, “It is not fitting for a man to mix honey with wormwood (Prov. 5:3–4). Indeed, if a man fast from bread and water, he should not mix with his fast abuses and curses. For, there is only one door for your house, which is the temple of God. O man, it is not fitting for you that the door through which the king comes in it, that goes out from it excrement and filth. For, if a person abstains from all these hateful things and receives the body and blood of Christ, he should take care of his mouth through which the Son of the King comes in. You have no authority, O man, to bring forth foul language from your mouth.”

St. Basil also says, “True fasting is being a stranger to vice, controlling the tongue, abstaining from anger, distancing oneself from lust, evil speech, lying, perjury. The absence of these vices makes fasting true, and so shunning these vices makes fasting good.”

St. Evagrius says, “He who disciplines his body wisely becomes passionless, but when he feeds his body (with gluttony) suffers from the passions.”

Abba Dorotheos says, “One should also fast with the eyes, that is, not look at vain things, not give freedom to the eyes, not look shamelessly and without fear at anyone.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1030 “Why does the Church conclude most of her fasts with a relevant feast?”, pp. 159–160
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1030. Why does the Church conclude most of her fasts with a relevant feast?

The purpose of fasting is to enable us to enjoy the heavenly feast, or to experience heavenly joy. During our fasts, our minds are immersed in rejoicing in the Lord of Glory, Jesus, who was born to offer us His life as heavenly bread to satisfy our souls. We are occupied with His salvific work by which He granted us the resurrection of our souls, which were undone by death and corrupted by destructive sin.

In his fasts, the true believer does not know frowning but is always smiling as a reflection of his inner joy. The early Church Fathers often stressed the positive side of fasting, which is nothing but opening the way before the human soul to ascend to heaven by the working of grace, to see our Lord by faith and rejoice in Him.

Quite possibly, their attention was drawn to this principle by Christ’s advice to those who fast to anoint their heads and wash their faces (Matt. 6:17–18). There are perhaps two odd matters here. The anointing of the head, especially in the first century A. D., was not something practiced by men, youth, or children — so why is it necessary for them to do so if they fast? And the washing of the face is something we must do whether we fast or not, so what need is there for this advice to those who fast? Clearly, this is a symbolic invitation to live the life of joy. The anointing of the head refers to the ointment that is upon the head, the ointment of the Holy Spirit that comes down upon Christ, our Head [cf. Ps. 133:2]. Thus, the fragrance of Christ fills the world through us, and the world encounters the fruit of the Spirit through our love and joy. And the washing of the face refers to the removal of dust from the face that we may see the Lord without any hindrance, and thus we witness to Him with the smile on our inner faces.

St. Severus of Antioch says, “When Isaiah the Prophet raises them from this bottomless pit (i.e., their clinging to carnal matters), he raises them by drawing their minds upwards by declaring the greatness of fasting; and so he impels them towards spiritual joy and expels grief and sorrow from their spirits, and implores them saying, ‘Is it a fast that I have chosen, a day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head like a bulrush, and to spread out sackcloth and ashes?’ (Isa. 58:5). Therefore, when our Lord declares the splendor and joy of fasting, He also commands them clearly saying, ‘But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face’ (Matt. 6:17). He thus shows us that the flourishing and purity of the spirit are attained through the main members of the body.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1028 “What modern medicine’s view of fasting?”, pp. 157–158
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › Holy Fasting — 1028. What modern medicine’s view of fasting?

“For, quite the contrary, those who use the most frugal fare are the strongest and the healthiest, and the noblest; as domestics are healthier and stronger than their masters, and husbandmen than the proprietors; and not only more robust, but wiser, as philosophers are wiser than rich men.”

“Some men, in truth, live that they may eat, as the irrational creatures, ‘whose life is their belly, and nothing else.’ But the Instructor enjoins us to eat that we may live. For neither is food our business, nor is pleasure our aim; but both are on account of our life here, which the Word is training up to immortality. Wherefore also there is discrimination to be employed in reference to food. And it is to be simple, truly plain, suiting precisely simple and artless children—as ministering to life, not to luxury.”

“The food of those who are saved and those who perish is separate … For it were not seemly that we, after the fashion of the rich man’s son in the Gospel (Luke 15:11), should, as prodigals, abuse the Father’s gifts; but we should use them, without undue attachment to them, as having command over ourselves. For we are enjoined to reign and rule over meats, not to be slaves to them.”

And St. Basil says, “Fasting is truly the medicine of the soul and of the body also. Eating luxurious foods afflicts us with certain difficult illnesses of the body. But fasting is beneficial for health, granting the fasting person a good complexion, calm eyes, balanced gait, and composed movements. You will never see this person cackling, although he smiles; never screaming out, although he speaks calmly and with balance; and you will find that his words flow from a clean and pure heart.”

He also says, “What is required in fasting is not the abstinence of the mouth, but of the eyes, ears, hands, and entire body. We fast with pure hands that avoid theft, with legs that avoid forbidden places, with eyes that avoid looking upon anything that is provocative … I wonder what abstinence from meat means if we do not abstain from eating the flesh of our neighbors through gossiping and slander? And what does abstinence from food mean if we do not abstain from evil thoughts, adultery, malice, and hatred? … Fasting is the wing of prayer that raises it to heaven and breaks through to the throne of God … Fasting is the expansion of households, the mother of health, the pedagogue of youth, an adornment for seniors, a good companion on journeys … By fasting, I do not mean abstinence from necessary food, for this will lead to death. Rather, I mean abstinence from foods that cause the body to rebel.

Rather, I mean abstinence from foods that cause the body to rebel. The person who fasts truly is the one who abstains from all bodily passions, even those that are natural.”

Notes: [440] St. Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor (Paedagogus) 2.1 (ANF 2:237). [441] St. Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor (Paedagogus) 2.1 (ANF 2:242). records.question: St. Moses the Black
records.answer:
St. Moses the Black (also called the martyr) was born between 330 and 340 AD, probably from one of the Barbarian tribes known as the Saracens [1][2][9]. Before his repentance, he was extremely evil, committing every sin, and was a slave of a tribal chief who worshipped the sun. Because of his evil nature, his master cast him out. He became a gangster and head of a band of robbers [1].

Despite his evil life, he believed the sun was the true God and sought to be saved. He heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to meet the monks of Scetis. There he met St. Isidore, confessed his sins, and was taught the word of God. He repented deeply, shedding many tears, and was baptized by Abba Macarius the Great, who then sent him back under St. Isidore’s supervision [1].

Moses sought to become a monk. After testing his resolve, St. Isidore sent him to Abba Macarius, who instructed him and clothed him in monastic attire. Moses lived in the wilderness with great spiritual strife, fighting against demons and carnal desires, encouraged by his spiritual guides to stand firm [3][6].

Because of his virtues and strife, Moses was ordained a priest by Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD). The patriarch tested him by having priests drive him out of the sanctuary, but Moses accepted this humbly. After ordination, he lived a life of love, humility, and asceticism, performing miracles and showing great compassion [2].

Moses was known for his humility and forgiveness. For example, when invited to judge a monk’s sin, he carried a bag of sand with a hole, saying his own sins ran out behind him and he could not see them, so he would not judge others. This led the monks to forgive the sinful brother [2][4].

He was also known for hospitality, even breaking a fast to feed guests, prioritizing God’s commandment of hospitality over human rules [4].

Moses was martyred when Barbarians attacked the monastery. He had foreseen the attack and chose not to escape. Seven monks, including him, were killed. One who escaped saw seven crowns descending from heaven on the martyrs. Moses died on 24 Paona in 408 AD at the age of 75 or 85. He earned three crowns: for love and asceticism, for monasticism and priesthood, and for martyrdom. He was the first martyr in Scetis, and his body was kept with that of St. Isidore at Paramus monastery in Natrun Valley [4].

Among his teachings, Moses emphasized humility, repentance, love for neighbors, and avoiding judgment of others. He taught that one should focus on one’s own sins rather than those of others, and that hatred or grudges bring no peace. He encouraged prayer with tears and humility, and said that God helps those who sincerely seek Him [5][16].

In his monastic struggle, Moses endured severe attacks from demons and physical hardship, including being beaten by devils and carrying water pots at night to discipline his body. His spiritual father counseled him to moderate his asceticism and rely on God’s help rather than his own strength [6].

Summary of key points about St. Moses the Black:

| Aspect               | Details                                                                                     | Citation(s)  |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|
| Birth and Background | Born 330-340 AD, likely from Barbarian/Saracen tribes; former slave and gangster           | [1][2][9]    |
| Repentance           | Met St. Isidore, confessed sins, baptized by Abba Macarius, began monastic life             | [1][3]       |
| Monastic Life        | Lived in wilderness, fought demons and temptations, guided by St. Isidore and Abba Macarius | [3][6]       |
| Ordination           | Ordained priest by Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD) after a test of humility                | [2]          |
| Virtues              | Humility, love, asceticism, forgiveness, hospitality, miracles                              | [2][4][5][16]|
| Martyrdom            | Killed by Barbarians in 408 AD, first martyr of Scetis, earned three crowns                 | [4]          |
| Teachings            | Focus on own sins, avoid judging others, pray with tears, love neighbors, avoid hatred     | [5][16]      |
| Spiritual Struggle   | Severe temptations, physical hardships, counsel to rely on God’s help                       | [3][6]       |

The sources do not cover any comparison of St. Moses the Black with other churches or traditions.

retrieval.query: Who was St. Moses the Black?

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 249–250
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Upbringing

His Upbringing:

Not much is known about the past of St. Moses the Black before his repentance. He was most probably one of the Barbarian tribes. His life was so evil that it was said that there was no sin he did not commit. He was born between the years of 330 and 340 AD. It seems that he was a slave of a head of a tribe that worshipped the sun, but because of his extreme evil nature, his master got rid of him. He turned into a gangster who lived on robbing and killing people. He had a large, muscular stature, which helped him to become the head of an evil gang.

Having Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ:

Even though an extreme evil-doer, yet he kept raising up his eyes towards the sun, believing that it was the true God, seeking from it to proclaim itself to him. Then, he heard a voice telling him to go to the wilderness to encounter the monks of the Scetis, whose fame was widely spread all over the area at that time. He went there, carrying his sword, where he happened to meet with St. Isidore (The Priest of the Cells) coming out of his cell and heading to the church. Terrified by his appearance, the saint asked him: “What do you want from here, O brother?” Moses answered: “I heard that you are a good servant of God. Therefore, I escaped and came to you to let God save me the way he saved you.” He continued in persistence and with submission, saying: “I want to remain with you, despite my countless sins and my great evils.”

St. Isidore kept asking him about his past life and where he has been. Moses confessed to him all the sins he committed. On seeing how he opened his heart to him, St. Isidore started to teach him and preached him at length the word of God, he told him about the judgment to come and then left him to contemplate.

For hating evil and deciding to rid himself of it, Moses shed so many tears, and deep remorse swept his soul and disturbed his sleep, like a dreadful ghost. Then, he went to St. Isidore, prostrated himself before him, and in a loud voice, he confessed all his evil crimes again, with such contrition of heart that drew his compassion. He took him to Abba Macarius the Great, who put him under his care, taught him and guided him, gave him the grace of baptism, then put him back under the supervision of St. Isidore.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 252–253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Ordained as a Priest

Ordained as a Priest:

Because of his strife and virtues, they decided to ordain him as a priest. They arranged that the ordination would be performed at the patriarchate in Alexandria. However, the patriarch wanted to test Moses before ordaining him, so he ordered his priests that once they see him about to enter into the sanctuary, to drive him out saying: “Get out of here, O you with the blackface.” When they did that to him, the patriarch sent a deacon after him, and he heard him saying: “They did what you deserved Moses, for you are not a human, but dared to mix with men. Why then would you venture to sit among them?” St. Moses was ordained as a priest by the hand of the 23rd Pope St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), who heard at the time a voice saying: “Worthy, Worthy, Worthy,” and after putting the white robe on him, they said to him: “There you became all-white Moses.” He responded by saying with humility: “I wish this to be true on the inside as it is on the outside.”

His Virtues:

He lived denying himself that a governor, hearing about his virtues, longed to see him. When Moses knew about that, he ran away, but it happened that the saint passed by the governor in his way to the monastery, and he inquired from him about the location of father Moses' cell. St. Moses told him: “What do you want from such an old man, who is far from being upright.” The governor was disturbed and went to the monastery and told the monks about what happened. On understanding the monks how that monk looked like, they knew that it was no one but Fr. Moses, who denied himself.

Because of his love, humility, strife, and intense asceticism, he was granted by God to perform miracles and signs.

A monk fell into a specific iniquity, and a meeting was held to discuss an appropriate penance. Moses was invited to attend, but he refrained from going. When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 250–251
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Monastic Life

His Monastic Life:

After a while, Moses sought from Abba Isidore to make him a monk. However, Abba Isidore started to explain to him how tough the monastic life is with the constant fight against the demons and the other physical needs. He told him as a way of testing him: “It is better for you son, to go and live in the populated areas,” but after seeing his real intention and solid stand, St. Isidore sent him back to Abba Macarius the Great, the father of the wilderness.

Moses stood in the church and confessed publicly about all his sins and evil deeds. Abba Macarius said afterward that he saw during Moses confession a whiteboard with black writings, and with every sin Moses proclaimed, an angel wiped it out off that board until the board became allwhite. After Abba Macarius instructed him, he sent him back to the priest Isidore who clothed him in the monastic attire. He advised him: “Remain, my son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would leave it, all evil will come back to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure God will do mercy and grace on you and will crush the devil under your feet.”

His Strife:

St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macarius to find for him a secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept counseling him to stand fast until the devil would get tired of him. He gave him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it.” Father. Abba Isidore took him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, p. 253
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Virtues

When they insisted on having him, he came carrying a bag of sand with a hole in the back, which he explained by saying: “My sins run out behind me and I do not see them, but today I am coming to judge the errors of another.” On hearing this, the assembled monks forgave their sinful brother.

For some reason, it was proclaimed an obligation in the Scetis to fast for a week. During that week, some guests came to visit Fr. Moses. He prepared food for them to eat. On seeing smoke rising from his cell, the brethren said to one another: “Look, Moses has broken his fast and is preparing food for himself. We shall talk to him about it.” When they got to know the facts, they said to him: “Father Moses! You have disregarded the commandment of men, but kept that of God (i.e., giving hospitality to strangers).”

His Martyrdom:

Then, it happened that the Barbarians came to attack the monastery, an incident St. Moses knew by Spirit beforehand, and he sought from the brethren to escape. However, seven brethren stayed behind, and they asked him: “Are you not going to escape, father?” He answered: “For a long time, I waited for this day, for the words of the Lord Jesus Christ to be fulfilled: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). They said to him: “We shall stay with you and will not escape.” He told them: “There, they are already at the gate.” The Barbarians entered the monastery and killed them all. However, when one of the seven escaped to the stronghold out of fear, he saw seven crowns coming down from heaven on the seven martyred monks. Then, he hastened to come down and ran forward to receive his crown of martyrdom.

So, Abba Moses completed his strife on the 24th of Paona in the year 408 AD, when he was seventy-five years old (or eighty-five). He earned three crowns: the 1st for love and intense asceticism, the 2nd for monasticism and priesthood, and the 3rd for martyrdom. He was counted the first martyr in the Scetis, and he had so many great teachings. His body was kept along with that of his spiritual guide Abba Isidore in one tube at the Paramus monastery in Natrun Valley.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 254–255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?" (Psalm 118:6)” • Then, the brother asked: “If a man beat his servant for something wrong he did, what should the servant say?” The saint answered: “If he was a good servant, he would possibly say: ‘Have mercy on me, for I made a mistake.’ Thus, he would blame himself and draw the mercy of his master.” • In general, a man should never condemn his neighbor. When in the Old, the hand of God came heavy on the firstborn of the Egyptians, there was no house without a dead son in it. For us, it meant that we should concentrate on our sins and not worry about those of our neighbors, for it would be unreasonable for a man to leave his dead son, and go to mourn that of his neighbor.

To die about your neighbor means to worry about your sins and not to care for the sins of any man, good or bad. You should not do wrong to anyone, or think bad about anyone else in your heart or despise anyone for doing wrong. You should not obey anyone who harmed his neighbor or rejoice for him. You should never slander anyone, but always say that God knows everybody's heart. Do not go along with the man who talks bad about his neighbor, because it would make you fall in condemnation. Do not have hatred against anyone. Do not have a grudge in your heart against anyone, and do not hate the man who is hostile toward his neighbor. This would bring you peace.

[Sayings of the Strong Saint Abba Moses, Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria- Diocese of Los Angeles] [Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of OrthodoxWiki]

[Moses the Black: On the Internet Site of Wikipedia]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 251–252
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — His Strife

There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly angels, about whom the saint said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and returned to his cell.

Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks at night, take their water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to move, until some brethren happened to come to the well, and they carried him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he regained his ability to move.

Once four thieves tried to rob his cell, but he tied them together and carried them to the church. When the thieves realized that he was Moses, who used to be the head of a gang of thieves, they repented and wanted to become monks. St. Moses preached them with words that moved their hearts.

Because of his great strife, the devils were stirred more against him, that his mentor Abba Isidore counseled him to moderate in his ascetic practices to keep them from causing him more troubles. He sought from him to deliver himself to God, and He alone would be able to alleviate that fight on him. Abba Isidore told him that, to keep him from thinking that by his ascetic efforts, he could overcome the demons, but by humility and spiritual repentance, God would fight on our behalf.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, p. 258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands

If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take the monk to the nearest location of the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.

Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not having a steady residence, teaching, preaching, and converting multitudes to Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in the year 372 AD.

[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347]

[Baring-Gould: February 7]

Notes: [2] These tribes were known by the name ‘Saracens’… It is worth mentioning that the name ‘Saracens’ was given by the Greeks and the Romans to the nomadic tribes in the ‘Sino-Arabian’ desert…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Confessor, p. 257
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE CONFESSOR

This St. Moses (Moyses) was a Roman priest of Jewish roots. He was one of the main members of a congregation of confessors in the time of Cyprian, at the start of the heresy of Novatian. The rest of the confessors were: Fr. Maximus, the priest, the two deacons Nicostratus and Rufinus, the laymen Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, and Celerinus. According to Cyprian, they were the first group of confessors in the days of the persecution stirred up by Emperor Decius (249-251 AD). At the time of the persecution, they wrote down a message to exhort the confessors in Carthage to be committed to the system and wrote another message to Cyprian.

After spending about a year in prison (eleven months and few days), St. Moses reposed in January 251 AD, and was counted as a confessor, and even as a martyr. It was said that a little while before his departure, Moses refused to have any contact with Novatian or the five priests who were supporting him and followed his views. St. Moses was considering their faith and views as unorthodox.

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. III, p. 948]

[Baring-Gould: November 25]

Notes: [1] ‘Novatian’ was a Roman bishop and theologian of the 3rd century who took a strict position on readmission of apostates during the persecutions at the time…

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Recluse Bishop, pp. 257–258
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP, ST. — The Tribes of Saracens

The Tribes of Saracens:

The Arabian tribes populating the area of Rhinoclura in-between the eastern Egyptian border and the Asian shores, used to worship the stars. Then in the year 226 AD, these tribes embraced Christianity through the efforts of Origen (184-253 AD). Then, those tribes joined forces together and formed one State under the reign of a queen called Mavia. By their unity, they created a power block that brought fear to the Arian Emperor Valens (364- 378 AD) and forced him to seek a peace treaty with them.

Choosing Moses as a Bishop:

Those Christian tribes having united together, they felt the need for a bishop to shepherd them. It happened that in those days, there was a recluse monk named Moses in the eastern desert, he was so beloved by those tribesmen that they decided to choose him to be their bishop. Then, when Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those united tribes.

Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands:

On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20th Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then, St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, pp. 255–256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.

Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him in the form of a girl. She managed to convince him to spend the night at her place. Then, she claimed to him that she was the daughter of one of the kings and that she wanted him to marry her, quoting the honor of the marriage of the fathers: Ibrahim, Isaac, and Jacob. He accepted her request. Then, she claimed that she was a Jew, and he had to convert to her religion to be able to marry her. So, Moses was blinded, and he denied his Christ. Then, she (the deceptive devil) took him back to the wilderness, where a whole gang of devils ridiculed him and made so much fun of him. Finally, the hermit woke up and cast himself on the dust and kept crying and supplicating to the Compassionate God to forgive him. God sent him Abba Samuel, who told him that he would be departing after three days. Then, he took him to the church, where he gave him Communion in the Holy Sacraments after confessing all that the devil has done to him. St. Moses, the hermit, reposed in peace and was buried by Abba Samuel, who wrote his biography, and handed it to someone traveling to Alexandria for the benefit of the believers.

[The Hermit Fathers, Part 2, p. 25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, pp. 240–241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — The Bitterness of Anguish

St. Moises (Moses) was one of the prominent fathers and saints of the church in the 8th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.

St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Scetis, where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox faith. He used to spend most of his time in worship, that it was said that he did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

The Bitterness of Anguish:

During his bishopric, the Umayyad rulers of Egypt subjected the Copts to extremely severe persecutions, and great anguish dwelt upon the church. The bishops returned to their monasteries to concentrate on prayers and fasts, imploring God to lift that anguish. However, St. Moises remained among his people to encourage them and to keep them holding fast to their faith against the snatching wolves. St. Moises also got the grace to perform miracles and signs, healing sicknesses, as well as the grace of prophecy.

Due to these intolerable persecutions at the time, the number of Copts who converted to Islam reached 24,000 persons. When some archons came to seek from St. Moises to pray to the Lord to lift the anguish from His people, he told them: “My children, be assured that the governor who is persecuting you will perish within this month,” and this was what did happen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses the Hermit, p. 255
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES THE HERMIT — His Multiple Falls and Repentances

St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went deep in the wilderness and lived for thirty-five years in a spot having olive and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended the wild beasts.

His Multiple Falls and Repentances:

Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the devil.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 241
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — Imprisoned along with the Pope

Imprisoned along with the Pope:

The last of the Umayyad caliphs Marwan ibn Muĥammad (Marwan II: 744-750 AD), arrested the 46th Pope of Alexandria, St. Khael I (743-767 AD). Bishop Moises stayed in the company of the pope, and he longed to be martyred in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When the soldiers brought them to the tent of Marwan, they forced St. Moises on his knees, raised his feet, and beat him with bronze clubs on his sides and neck. His tormentors were seeking from him a bribe to set him free. The saint did not utter a single word, for he did not understand their Arabic language. When Marwan gave the order to cut the head of Pope Khael I, and the swordsman led him to the place of execution, St. Moises ran after him, despite the attempts of the swordsman to keep him away. An angry soldier intended to kill him if it was not for some officials who did not let him do it. Then, he was cast in prison along with Pope Khael I, and their feet were placed in chains, among many others. However, St. Moises prophesied that they would eventually come out safe from that prison, which was realized when Marwan was defeated by the Abbasids dynasty.

His Prophesy concerning the Umayyad Caliphate:

During the revolt of the Coptic Bashmurians (Coptic rebels) due to the intolerable Umayyad persecution, St. Moises disciple asked him a question concerning when that calamity would come to an end, the saint prophesied: “God will not forsake His church to the end, but He will save her, and this caliphate (of Umayyad) will vanish and be replaced by some other.” This prophecy was realized in 750 AD when the Umayyad dynasty was replaced by the Abbasids.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moises, Bishop of Osim, p. 242
passages.text:
Saint: MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. — His Departure

His Departure:

Abba Moises continued to accompany Pope Khael I, faithful to him and to the church all along during the bitter tribulations. Then, when he completed his strife and was in a right old age, he had a short illness and knew the time of his departure. So, he called his congregation, blessed them, commanded them, and asked them to pray for him. They all wept and asked him to remember them before Christ. He stretched out his hand, prayed, bid them farewell, and departed in peace.

The Church of Saint Mina in Marriott:

Bishop Moises was with pope Khael I when the Chalcedonians (Melkites Byzantine Christians) tried to take possession of the great church of St. Mina in Marriott to take away its marble pillars and adornments. They bribed the caliph Marwan II and asked him to issue an order to Ăbdel Malek ibn Mousa, the governor of Egypt, to give them the possession of St. Mina's church in Marriott. When the decree was delivered to Ăbdel Malek, he held a council under a judge by the name of Ăyssa to decide who had the possession of that church, and he asked the two parties to defend their rights before him. Here, Pope Khael I asked the most prominent of his bishops and archons, including St. Moises, to attend the governor's council. Still, as the Chalcedonians bribed the judge, he took the stand against the Orthodox Copts and refrained from listening to their defense. Some archons suggested paying a bribe to the judge to take their side, but St. Moises rejected such a counsel, saying that it would not befit for the pope or the bishops to pay bribes to anyone, and he prophesied that God would never forsake them. Then, when judge Ăyssa was about to write his verdict in favor of the Chalcedonians, he was fired from his position and was replaced by another judge called Abu el-Ĥuseiny, who happened to be just and honest. The new judge issued his verdict in favor of the Copts, and the Copts kept St. Mina church in their possession.

The church celebrates him on the 11th of Mesra.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 57]

[The Synaxariun: 11 Mesra] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Kha’il I, by Subhi Y. Labib, pp. 1410-2]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Libyan, p. 256
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE LIBYAN, ST.

This saint was from Libya. He was so humble and compassionate all the time that God granted him the grace to perform the miracles of healing the sick. He once said: “When I was young, I lived in a monastery. There, it happened that eight monks dug a well, and seventy others built a wall around it, in the hope that they would get water from it. They dug it down to the depth of about twenty yards, but no water was found. They were very much grieved and intended to fill it up with dirt. However, by noontime, when Abba Pieour came over suddenly to the location of the well and was informed about what they were doing, he rebuked them saying: ‘Why did you despair, O you of little faith?’ Then, he went down to the bottom of the well, and he prayed there. Afterward, he pushed an iron rod in the well bottom three times, saying: ‘O God of the saints, I pray, do not waste the effort of these men, but send them plenty of water.’ In a short while, the water erupted from the well and wetted everyone around.

After praying a thanksgiving prayer, Abba Pieour intended to go in his way. They tried to make him have a meal with them, but he said: ‘I have accomplished what I came here to do, I did not come here to eat.’”

This was a good lesson for the brethren about faith and the trust in God.

[The Paradise of the Saints, p. 69]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Moses, the Black, pp. 253–254
passages.text:
Saint: MOSES, THE BLACK (The martyr) — Of his Sayings

Of his Sayings:

• To a brother in the Scetis who sought from him a word of encouragement, he said: “Go and sit in your cell, it will teach you everything.” • The man who flees from the world is like ripe grapes, but he who dwells among the distractions of men is like sour grapes. • If we keep the commandments of our fathers, I promise you that the Barbarians would never come here, but if we do not, this place will soon become desolate. • According to Fr. Poemen, Fr. Moses was once asked: “How can a man become like dead to his neighbor?” The older saint said to him: “Unless a man keeps in his heart that he has been three days in the grave, he will not be strong enough to do that.” • It is better for a man to put himself to death rather than his neighbor, and he should not condemn him in anything. • It is good for a man to die to every work which is evil before he departs from the body, so as not to offend anyone. • Unless a man feels in his heart that he is a sinner, God will not listen to him. A brother asked him about the meaning of that, and the saint said: “Whoever focuses on his sins, would never see those of his neighbor.” • Unless your prayers conform to your behavior, your struggle would not be of any benefit. When the saint was asked to explain, he said: “We should apply what we pray about, for when man forsakes his own will, he reconciles with God and God will listen to his prayers.” • A brother asked him: “What would help the man in his every endeavor?” He answered him: “God is the One who helps, for it is so written: "God is our refuge and strength. A very present help in trouble" (Psalm 46:1).” • When the brother added: “What then is the benefit of fasting or spending sleepless nights, father?” The saint answered: “These practices make the soul meek and humble, for it is written: "Look on my affliction and my pain, and forgive all my sins" (Psalm 25:18). So, once the soul reaps the fruits of these practices, God would have compassion on her.” • Then, the brother asked: “What will man do with every temptation he encounters or every evil thought coming to him?” The saint answered: “He should pour tears in prayers before the goodness of God, for Him to help, and he would be getting comfort, if his prayer was from the heart, for it is written: "The Lord is on my side, I shall not fear. What can man do to me?"

records.question: Jesus Prayer
records.answer:
The Jesus Prayer is a short, simple prayer that expresses a deep cry to the Lord Jesus Christ, often phrased as: "My Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me" or "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" It is a prayer of praise and petition, invoking the mercy and help of Jesus, and is used as a spiritual practice in the Coptic Orthodox Church [1][5].

The Jesus Prayer aims at closeness to God through constant dialogue, enabling the believer to pray continually without ceasing. It can be repeated at any time—while working, eating, sleeping, or in any circumstance—to maintain a state of constant communication with God. The prayer is also called the "arrow prayer" because it pierces the heart of the devil and prevents distraction [2].

Practical steps to practice the Jesus Prayer include:
1. Concentrating thoughts gently and calmly on Jesus.
2. Reciting the prayer from the soul's depths with serenity and simplicity.
3. Being guided by the Holy Spirit so that calling on Jesus becomes a fruit of the Spirit.
4. Not despising other forms of prayer.
5. Forgetting oneself and decreasing the ego while the name of Jesus lives in the spirit.
6. Continuing participation in liturgical and church rites.
7. Praying when moved by the Holy Spirit.
8. Praising Jesus with heartfelt cries like "My Lord and God!" [3][7].

The Jesus Prayer has been practiced by many saints such as St. Anthony the Great, St. Macarius the Great, St. John Climacus, and St. Augustine. St. Anthony advised repeating the name of Jesus with the heart, mind, and tongue. St. Macarius called the name of Jesus a "pearl" sweeter than honey and urged believers to keep it in their hearts. St. Augustine emphasized praying for salvation through the name of Jesus [4][6][13].

The power of the name of Jesus is central to this prayer. Scripture and the Fathers affirm that calling on Jesus' name grants salvation, protection, and spiritual blessings. The name is described as a weapon against evil, a source of comfort, and a means to approach God the Father. The liturgical prayers of the Church also invoke the Jesus Prayer in various hymns and psalms, encouraging believers to praise and call upon Jesus continually [11][12].

A story of a Russian pilgrim illustrates the transformative effect of the Jesus Prayer: through persistent repetition, the prayer moved from the lips to the heart, filling him with love for Jesus and changing his outlook on life [14].

The ultimate goal of the Jesus Prayer is to praise Jesus, experience His presence, and receive from Him more than what is asked, including understanding divine mysteries and becoming worthy vessels bearing His name [3][15].

In summary, the Jesus Prayer is a simple, powerful, and continuous prayer invoking the mercy and presence of Jesus Christ, practiced with reverence and guided by the Holy Spirit, deeply rooted in Scripture, tradition, and the experience of the saints [1][2][3][5][6][7][11][12][14][15].

Notes: [790] See Michael O’Carroll, Verbum Caro: An Encyclopedia on Jesus, the Christ (The Liturgical Press, 1992) “Jesus Prayer, the”: p. 82; and Gordon S. Wakefield ed., The Westminster Dictionary of Christian Spirituality (Westminster Press, 1983) “Jesus, Prayer To”: pp. 223–224.
