passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q730 “What are the important obligations of the believer who repents?”, pp. 558–559
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 730. What are the important obligations of the believer who repents?

First: He or she thanks God for His blessings, His mercy, and His salvation, so that he may have the boldness to seek forgiveness.

Second: To admit that he is a sinner and unable to enjoy the holy life without God’s mercy and free grace.

Third: To be merciful to those who sin against him and to forgive them, so that the Savior may open for him the way of salvation.

Fourth: The believer’s focus on heaven, his anticipation of the eternal wedding and his love for others, elevates all his inner being as on the wings of the Holy Spirit so that the person may know the heavenly Bridegroom, who prepares for him eternal glory. He also acknowledges his weaknesses, and the grace of God that is capable of transforming the heart from corruption to incorruption and from an earthly heart to a new heaven, and from humans to angels.

Repentance to God and confession before Him in our private rooms and in the presence of a priest are the beginning of a change in one’s way of life, both at the inner level as well as the external behavior. It is a transformation in which we acknowledge the richness of

God’s love, and hence offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, in which we acknowledge our

weaknesses and wickedness, confident in His salvific work and His ability to raise use from corruption to an angelic life that is acceptable to the Father. This is how are continuously cleansed in the spirit of hope. “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:23).

St. John Chrysostom says, “Repentance is the evangelical path through which the soul passes to the kingdom,” and, “Therefore, beloved, when you commit sin, do not wait for another man to accuse you but, before you are accused and indicted, you yourself condemn what you have done. Then, if someone accuses you later on, it is no longer a matter of your doing the right thing in confessing, but of your correcting the accusation which he makes … Peter certainly sinned gravely in denying Christ. But he was quick to remind himself of his sin and, before anyone accused him, he told of his error and wept bitterly (Matt. 26:69–75; Mark 14:66–72). He so effectively washed away his sin of denial that he became the chief of the apostles and the whole world was entrusted to him.”

Notes: [1438] St. John Chrysostom, Discourses against Judaizing Christians 8.3.3–4 (FOTC 68:213–214).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q743 “Is it necessary to repent before God in our private rooms, and then again in the presence of the Father of Confession?”, p. 565
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 743. Is it necessary to repent before God in our private rooms, and then again in the presence of the Father of Confession?

The goal of confessing our sins is to encounter God, the Physician of our souls. Whoever does not feel his weakness or sins, will never feel the need for the heavenly Physician and will not therefore experience God’s love. Many times, we consider ourselves righteous, since we do not commit any dangerous sins that hurt others. A true believer, however, does not differentiate between big sins and trivial sins, since what truly concerns him is to be the icon of Christ, the Holy One’s ambassador, and an unblemished steward of heaven.

St. Basil the Great says, “it seems necessary that sins be confessed to those entrusted with the stewardship of the Mysteries of God (cf. 1 Cor. 4:1). For thus also those who repented of old are found to have confessed their sins before the saints. For it is written in the gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (cf. Matt. 3:6; Mark 1:5) and in the Acts of the Apostles, to the apostles, by whom they were also baptized (cf. Acts 2:37).”

He also says, “On the other hand, where sin is concerned, be your own accuser (Prov. 18:17), and do not wait for others to make the accusation. Thus, you will be like a just man who accuses himself in the first speech made in court, or like Job who was not deterred by the crowd of people in the city from declaring his personal guilt before all (Job 31:34).”

Notes: [1444] St. Basil of Caesarea, The Rule of St Basil in Latin and English: A Revised Critical Edition, trans., Anna M. Silvas (Collegeville, Minnesota: Liturgical Press, 2013) Q. 21: p. 129. [1445] St. Basil of Caesarea, Of Humility (FOTC 9:485).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q729 “What was Christ’s commandment to His disciples when He appeared to them after His resurrection?”, p. 558
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 729. What was Christ’s commandment to His disciples when He appeared to them after His resurrection?

He said to them, “‘As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.’ And when He had said this, He breathed on them, and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.’” (John 20:21– 23). He gave them this authority to show them that the world always needs repentance and confession so that the believers may never cease to confess the Lord’s blessings as well as the fact that they are sinners and hence offer repentance every time they pray the Lord’s prayer, “Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.” Therefore, Christ who is risen from the dead, calls them to be merciful with the people that the Lord may be merciful with them as well.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q761 “Is discipleship necessary?”, pp. 574–575
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 761. Is discipleship necessary?

Christianity exists wherever discipleship is, but is weakened and becomes dry, heavy, and fictional when discipleship is lost. That was why when the Lord ordered the disciples to preach, He said, “Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19–20). The Lord commanded them to prepare a new generation of disciples who will live as they lived, emphasizing the fact that discipleship is the primary method of teaching and the keeping of the commandments. Through discipleship, the disciples are filled with the Spirit of the Lord and Christianity is passed on from one generation to the next. For this reason, Christians were called “disciples,” and were first called Christians in Antioch (Acts 11:26). Perhaps, this was out of mockery from the pagans, by attributing to them the crucified Christ.

Since we are “Christians,” let us also acknowledge that we are “disciples.” I am not thus saying that we are all apostles or shepherds but that every Christian ought to be characterized by discipleship to our Lord Jesus at the hands of his or her mentor. The sacraments of baptism and repentance both fulfill that role through the sponsor and the Father in confession who are both responsible before God for the believer.

Confession, according to this concept, is the discipleship of a new generation that lives

by the spirit of their fathers the saints, for Christ the Lord. It is a union between the confessor, the Father in confession and Christ; not just for a certain time of the week, but continuously. A father gathers his children and delights in regularly meeting them, not just physically but also spiritually in his private prayers or on the altar. The son and daughter then love their father, pray for him, follow his example, and consult him in everything, to learn from his spiritual experiences in struggling against sin so that they may follow his example too, his faith, struggle, and watchfulness.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q762 “Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!”, pp. 575–576
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 762. Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!

(Acts 9:6) So He sends him to an older man, and thinks good to have him instructed by his teaching rather than His own, lest what might have been rightly done in the case of Paul might set a bad example of self-sufficiency, if each one were to persuade himself that he also ought in like manner to be trained by the government and teaching of God alone rather than by the instruction of the Elders. And this self-sufficiency the apostle himself teaches, not only by his letters but by his acts and deeds, ought to be shunned with all possible care, as he says that he went up to Jerusalem solely for this reason to communicate in a private and informal conference with his co-apostles and those who were before him that Gospel which he preached to the Gentiles, the grace of the Holy Spirit accompanying him with powerful signs and wonders: as he says And I communicated with them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles lest perhaps I had run or should run in vain. (Gal 2:2) Who then is so self-sufficient and blind as to dare to trust in his own judgment and discretion when the chosen vessel confesses that he had need of conference with his fellow apostles. Whence we clearly see that the Lord does not Himself show the way of perfection to anyone who having the opportunity of learning despises the teaching and training of the Elders, paying no heed to that saying which ought most carefully to be observed: Ask your father and he will show it to you: your Elders and they will tell you. (Deut. 32:7).”

Notes: [1469] St. John Cassian, The Conferences 2.14–15 (NPNF II/11:315–316).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q754 “What is our stance on those who conceal their sins?”, pp. 570–571
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 754. What is our stance on those who conceal their sins?

St. Basil the Great responds, “What shall we do about him who claims that his conscience does not condemn him for the sins he is committing. Thus, the question here is specific to him who speaks to someone about repentance, while the hearer conceals his sins. It is fitting for us to remind him without aggression with the words of the Lord: ‘For there is nothing covered that will not be revealed’ (Matt. 10:26); ‘For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’ (Matt. 12:34).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q697 “How do candidates for baptism confess their faith?”, pp. 530–531
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 697. How do candidates for baptism confess their faith?

Our hearts are also filled with longing for the second coming of Christ who ascended to the east and will return in the same way (Matt. 24:27, Acts 1:11), crying out with St. Methodius of Olympus: “Let us all hurry towards the east, let us be clothed in white garments and let us hold in our hands our lanterns.”

Note that this rite consists of two parts: facing the west to renounce Satan; and then facing the east to accept Christ. This was the clear and central principle found in all baptism liturgies in the early Church. Confessing the faith has a central theological importance in baptism.

First: Christian baptism was referred to as baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 8:16; 19:5) where the candidate for baptism, or his sponsor in the case of infants, confesses their faith in our Lord Jesus the Savior. Then, the person can approach the mystery of the cross and may partake in His burial and resurrection. Therefore, the confession of the crucified Christ who rose from the dead is the cornerstone of all the creeds used in baptism since the beginning of the Church, as the apostle says, “that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9). The apostle considers this the cornerstone of the faith he received: “For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4). Pagans knew this, which is why their concern was to oblige the faithful to renounce Christ.

Second: Since baptism is the gate by which one becomes a member of the Church, the confession of faith is the cornerstone on which the Church is built and is the reason for her existence.

Third: The confession of faith is an entry into a divine covenant or like a signed contract with God and is kept in a book in heaven. St. Theodore of Mopsuestia says of this: “We establish agreements and covenants with our Lord God by confessing the faith. By the mediation of the priest, we are prepared to enter His house, to see Him, to know Him and for Him to dwell within us that we may be counted among the citizens of that city and are counted trustworthy.” Again, he says, “By confessing the faith, you associate yourself with God by the bishop and you enter into a covenant in which you declare that you will be persistent in seeking the love of the divine nature.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q749 “How can the soul be completely convinced that God forgives its sins?”, p. 568
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 749. How can the soul be completely convinced that God forgives its sins?

St. Basil the Great answers, “She notices within herself this tendency that says: ‘I hate and abhor lying’ (Ps. 119:163). When God sent His only Son for the forgiveness of our sins, He forgave us as long as we believe in His role. David the Psalmist sings of mercy and justice (Ps. 101:1), testifying that God is merciful and just (Ps. 115:5), so it is very important for the words of the Apostles and Prophets that pertain to repentance to be entwined within us, and also their words about God’s righteous judgments and His perfect mercy in the forgiveness of sins.”

Notes: [1452] St. Basil of Caesarea, Regulae brevius tractatae 12.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q731 “Should someone who lives in sin constantly be in tears and fear? And with what hope must this person approach the Lord?”, pp. 559–560
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 731. Should someone who lives in sin constantly be in tears and fear? And with what hope must this person approach the Lord?

The path of repentance takes the believer away from sin. Our Christ draws him back, speaks to him and gives him life so that he may see His great divine glory by His grace.

St. Basil the Great says of the soul, “In the first place, it ought to hate its former reprehensible life, and shudder and be repelled at the very memory of it; for it is written: Iniquity I hated and abhorred, but your law I have loved (Ps. 118:163 LXX). Second, let it use the dread of eternal judgment and of everlasting punishment as a teacher, that it may gain a livelier fear, and let it acknowledge a season of tears through repentance, just as David taught in the sixth psalm (Ps. 6:6–8 LXX), that the purification of its sins can be achieved through an abundance of tears in the blood of Christ by the power of his mercy and the multitude of God’s compassions, who said: Although your sins be as crimson, I will make them white as snow; although they be as scarlet, I will make them white as wool (Isa. 1:18). After it has received the power and the capacity to please God, it says: You have changed my lamentation into joy for me, you have torn away my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, that I may sing psalms to you in my glory (Ps. 29:11–12 LXX). And so it draws near to the Lord singing psalms and saying: I will extol you, Lord, since you have upheld me and have not let my enemies rejoice over me (Ps. 29:2 LXX).”

Notes: [1439] St. Jacob of Sarug, On Repentance. [1440] St. Basil of Caesarea, The Rule of St Basil in Latin and English: A Revised Critical Edition, trans., Anna M. Silvas (Collegeville, Minnesota: Liturgical Press, 2013) Q. 117: p. 203.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q755 “What if a person says, “my conscience is clear”?”, p. 571
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 755. What if a person says, “my conscience is clear”?

St. Basil the Great answers, “A similar thing happens to physical sicknesses. There are many diseases that are not felt by those who have them, yet they trust the physician’s diagnosis more than their own feeling of sickness. So also, for spiritual sickness, namely, sin. If one is unaware of his sin but does not condemn himself, he ought to trust in those who can see his case clearer. This is explained by the holy Apostles who though they were very much attached to the Lord, when they heard the Lord telling them that, ‘one of you will betray Me’ (Matt. 26:21), they preferred to trust in His word and yielded to His declaration, saying: ‘Lord is it I?’ (Matt. 26:22). St. Peter teaches us, that even though he was zealous in his humility, he refused His Master, Lord and God’s ministry (in washing his feet) and so he heard the words: ‘If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me’ (John 13:8), and he was thus convinced of this truth and so said: ‘Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!’ (John 13:9).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q735 “What is the role of the tears of repentance in our lives?”, pp. 561–562
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 735. What is the role of the tears of repentance in our lives?

The first thing that sin does is to destroy one’s spiritual (inner) sight so that he loses his sight of God the Lover of humanity and the acknowledgment of the corruption he is in. Through love, the tears of repentance flow and the Lord opens the person’s sight as He did with the man born blind who washed in the pool of Siloam (John 9). Through tears, we see the divine beauty and cannot tolerate the uncleanness and corruption of sin.

St. Jacob of Sarug says, “Repentance requires me to offer her tears, for they are much loved by her. When the soul commits sin, sin destroys the soul’s love and distorts her vision, so that she does not weep for her corruption … If the soul fixed her eyes on God, regret comes quickly and opens the closed doors. She sees how abhorrent the sin she committed was and sees her weaknesses which she could not see when she committed it.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q698 “What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith?”, p. 532
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 698. What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith?

I renounce you. I renounce you.”

Then the priest breathes three times into the candidate’s face while saying, “Come out, O unclean spirit.” After that, the candidate looks towards the east and raises his hand to repeat after the priest: “I confess You, O Christ my God, and all Your saving laws, and all Your living service and all Your life giving works.”

Then the priest will teach him or her the faith as follows: “I believe in one God, God the Father the Pantocrator and His only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit the Giver of Life, and the resurrection of the flesh and the one, only, holy, catholic and apostolic Church. Amen.”

Then the candidate and/or sponsor are asked if they believe three times, to which they respond, “I believe” each time. All this occurs before they are baptized in the water.

Notes: [1358] Origen, Commentary on the Gospel of John (Books 13–32) 32.16 (FOTC 89:345).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q762 “Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!”, pp. 575–576
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 762. Why do I need discipleship to my Father in confession if I already knew the source of his teachings and instructions? I memorized the entire Bible and I even studied it much better than many priests!

In our intellectual and elitist age this kind of objection reveals how many Christians are spiritually lukewarm. Many of our Christian youth memorize many passages from scripture, but are content merely to study and memorize them without putting them into action; without living, tasting, and experiencing them. We live in an era where everyone competes to become a teacher and not a disciple, to convict others for their sins while hiding their own personal sins and ignoring scripture itself, which although it teaches that wisdom comes from the Holy Spirit, emphasizes the importance of discipleship to the Father in confession, to live with him in Christ.

Scripture testifies that when Saul of Tarsus met the Lord, he immediately asked him: “What do you want me to do?” The Lord’s response was to direct him to a spiritual father, Ananias (Acts 9:12). Samuel, great among the prophets, was more attentive to God’s voice than Eli the priest, yet Samuel learned and was trained at his hands (1 Sam. 3:10). Cornelius, to whom the Lord proclaimed the acceptance of his charities and prayers through an angel, was not guided by the angel but was commanded to call Peter the Apostle to guide him (Acts 10:5).

Abbot Moses says, “The Lord did not of Himself instruct by the method of a Divine colloquy the lad Samuel, when chosen for judgment, but suffered him to run once or twice to the old man, and willed that one whom He was calling to converse with Him should be taught even by one who had offended God, as he was an old man, and preferred that he whom He had deemed worthy to be called by Him should be trained by the Elder in order to test the humility of him who was called to a Divine office, and to set an example to the younger men by the manner of his subjection.

“And when Christ in His own Person called and addressed Paul, although He might have opened out to him at once the way of perfection, yet He chose rather to direct him to Ananias and commanded him to learn the way of truth from him, saying: Arise and go into the city and there it shall be told you what you ought to do. (Acts 9:6) So He sends him to an older man, and thinks good to have him instructed by his teaching rather than His own, lest what might have been rightly done in the case of Paul might set a bad example of self-sufficiency, if each one were to persuade himself that he also ought in like manner to be trained by the government and teaching of God alone rather than by the instruction of the Elders.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q736 “What boldness do the tears of repentance give someone before God?”, p. 562
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 736. What boldness do the tears of repentance give someone before God?

Joyful tears that are full of hope and confidence in the Savior, intercede for the soul before God so that her hidden voice may be heard, and her broken evil will may be transformed to a good will. If sin destroys holy thoughts and buries them in the dust, the tears of repentance intercede before Him who is the Resurrection that He may revive the soul and that it may be strengthened in the Lord, experiencing the words of the prophet: “Let the weak say, I am strong” (Joel 3:10). The soul renews her inner beauty and hears the voice of her Beloved saying, “You are all fair, my love, and there is no spot in you” (Song. 4:7).

St. Jacob of Sarug says, “O repentance … the sound of your agony comes to God … pursuers hurled me with arrows of sin. Like a spear, sin is lodged within me. It is good for you, O my soul, to weep for those, for there will be a good reward for your overflowing tears.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q527 “Does the Church have the authority to forgive sins?”, p. 416
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Church: House of Salvation — 527. Does the Church have the authority to forgive sins?

The early Church considered herself a “congregation of saints” and attributed the authority to forgive the sin to God alone. Origen says, “Moreover, just as the sun and the moon enlighten our bodies so also our minds are enlightened by Christ and the Church.”

Notes: [1062] A. Harnack, Lehrbuch der Dogmengeschichte (4 ed. rev.) (Tubingen: J. Mohr, 1909): p. 439ff; and Ernest Latko, Origen’s Concept of penance (Laval,1949): p. 69. [1063] Origen, Homilies on Genesis 1.7 (FOTC 71:55).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q744 “Why does God the Lover of humanity use different ways of chastisement?”, pp. 565–566
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Repentance & Confession — 744. Why does God the Lover of humanity use different ways of chastisement?

God reveals His love and providence not only when He forgives, but also when He disciplines. When He chastises like a Father, He elevates us from pampered infancy to maturity. Without discipline, we may not feel the seriousness of sin, nor struggle to live a life of holiness. Therefore, we would lose our victory and heavenly crown.

St. Basil the Great says, “We should learn, then, that it is because we have turned away from the Lord and disregarded His ways that God has inflicted these wounds upon us. He does not seek to destroy us, but rather endeavors to turn us back to the right way, just as good parents who care for their children are stern and rebuke them when they do wrong, not because they wish them harm, but rather desiring to lead them from childish negligence and the sin of youth to mature attentiveness.”

He also says, “How long will we not obey Christ who calls us to His heavenly kingdom? … This is the time of repentance and that is of receiving the reward. This is the time of toil and labor and that is of receiving the wages. This is the time of patience and that is of comfort.”

Notes: [1446] St. Basil of Caesarea, “In Time of Famine and Drought” 2, in On Social Justice (PP 38:75).

records.question: Anthony the Great
records.answer:
St. Anthony the Great, also known as the Father of the Monks and the Founder of the Monastic Movement, was born around 251 AD in the village of Komn Al-Aros (Qiman El-Arous), Egypt, to wealthy parents [2][6]. After his parents died, he was deeply moved by the Gospel reading in 269 AD: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), which he took as a personal call to dedicate his life to God [2][6]. He sold his possessions, gave the proceeds to the poor, and placed his sister in a convent [2][6].

Anthony began his ascetic life by dwelling beside the Nile, practicing strict prayer and asceticism. When he felt boredom, an angel appeared to him, teaching him the monastic practice of combining prayer with manual work, which became a foundation of monastic life [2]. He later moved to the inner wilderness around 285 AD, living in a cave on Mount Al-Kalzam near the Red Sea, where he faced spiritual battles with demons [2].

He lived a life of seclusion but did not isolate himself from the Church or the community. Around 305 AD, he briefly left his seclusion to guide beginners in monasticism, thus founding the monastic movement and the order of seclusion [1]. He also supported the Church by helping Pope Athanasius the Apostolic and supporting imprisoned confessors and martyrs [1][6]. He was known for his intense love of seclusion combined with a deep connection to the Church [1].

Anthony was illiterate but overcame Greek philosophers by the purity of his heart and drew some to the Christian faith [1][4]. He was known for his wisdom and spiritual sayings, such as the importance of loving one’s neighbor as a way to gain God, and the value of obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures [4].

He lived to the age of 105, maintaining good health until his repose in 356 AD [1][10]. His departure is commemorated on the 22nd of Toba in the Coptic calendar [4][6].

Anthony’s influence extended to many disciples and contemporaries, including St. Macarius the Great, St. Pachomius, St. Hilarion the Great, and others who continued the monastic tradition [1][5][8]. He is regarded as the father and model of Christian monasticism worldwide [2][6].

In summary, St. Anthony the Great is the pioneering figure of Christian monasticism, known for his ascetic life, spiritual wisdom, and role in founding the monastic movement that shaped the Church’s spiritual heritage [1][2][4][6].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 197–198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

His Order of Seclusion:

In about the year 305 AD, he had to break his seclusion to meet with some beginners who came to him longing to be trained under his supervision. He helped and guided them, then resumed his life of seclusion later on. Thus he was the founder of the movement of monasticism, his life revealed the concept of the Christian monasticism, particularly the order of seclusion: 4- St. Anthony came out to be a monk without any intention to become a member of the clergy. His movement was a civic one, not a clerical one; he did not want to interfere with the ecclesiastical structure. Even, when Emperor Constantine I sent to him seeking his blessing, he delayed his response to the message, and when asked by his disciples why he did so, he said, “I am preoccupied to respond to the message of God, the King of kings." However, when he was pressured, he answered the emperor’s message, for the sake of the Church peace. 5- His intense love of seclusion did not close his heart toward the holy congregation, but, in his seclusion, he believed in being a member of the Church. That is why he eventually came down to help Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (who was once one of his disciples). Moreover, on his entrance into Alexandria, the whole city was shaken, and its inhabitants came out exultant to welcome the man of God; that even some Arians came back to the Church.

6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who founded the system of congregations; as one of his disciples and greatly rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any particular order. 8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, pp. 196–197
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST.

He is considered worldwide as ‘The Father of the Monastic Family’ and ‘The Founder of the Monastic Movement’ in the whole world, even though there have been some monastic movements prior to his.

The saint was born in the village of ‘Komn Al-Aros’ – Beni-Sweif around the year 251 AD, to wealthy parents. When his father died, he stood before his corpse, contemplated in the mortality of the world, and his heart kindled toward eternity. In the year 269 AD, entering into the church, he heard the gospel saying: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21). Anthony considered it a personal message for him, and it touched his life. Moreover, when he returned home to his young sister ‘Dios,' he proclaimed to her his decision to sell his portion of the inheritance and give its proceeds to the poor, to dedicate his life to worship God. On her part, his sister also insisted on joining a convent in Alexandria.

The young man dwelt beside the River Nile and spent all his time praying in strict asceticism. Yet, when thoughts of boredom attacked him, he cried out to the Lord to guide him. An angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a man wearing a long robe, with leather cross-like Eskeem and a cover on his head. He sat weaving palm leaves for some time, got up to pray, then returned to work, and so on. The angel said to Anthony: “If you do so, you will never get bored." That came to be the attire of the monks, and the work of hand happened to be one of the basics of the monastic life.

One day, a woman and her maidservants came down to the river to wash their feet. Turning his head away, waiting for their departure, they started to undress to bathe. When the saint admonished her on such a behavior, she answered him: “If you are a monk, you should dwell in the inner wilderness, for this is not a place befitting for monks." On hearing these words, the saint said to himself, “This is the voice of the angel of the Lord rebuking me." He instantly forsook the location and set forth to the inner wilderness. That was around the year 285 AD. The saint dwelt in a cave on Mount ‘Al-Kalzam’ to practice the life of seclusion, North-West of the Red Sea. However, in that new location, the demons kept fighting against him, sometimes in the form of women and other times in the way of horrible wild beasts.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthonius, and Other Saints with That Name, pp. 195–196
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONIUS, and Other Saints with that Name (The martyrs) — ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr

Often confusion takes place between the martyrs who carried the name ‘Anthony,' among whom are:

ANTHONY, THE SYRIAN The martyr:

He was a 20 years old Syrian, a stone builder who was known for his great zeal against the idol worshipping. He lived as an anchorite for two years; then he returned to his hometown. There, he found the people worshipping the false gods. So, he went into their temple and broke all the idols down. He was expelled from the city, and he went to ‘Apamaea'. And, when its bishop assigned him to build a Church, the pagans were stirred up against him and killed him.

ANTONIUS AL-BEBAWY: The martyr:

St. ‘Anthony’ (Andona) was born in ‘Beba’ in Upper Egypt by pious and merciful parents. Hearing about the sufferings of the martyrs, he set forth to ‘Arianus,' the governor of ‘Ansena.’ and confessed the Lord Christ before him. The governor ordered his men to throw spears at him, but he was not harmed. Then, for the fear of that the audience would be encouraged to believe in his Christ, he ordered him chained and sent him to ‘Armanius,’ the governor of Alexandria. He sent with him ‘Abimachus’ and two other saints. ‘Armanius’ put the three in prison, crucified ‘Anthony’ upside down and tortured him, but God was glorified in him. Then, he was sent to the governor of ‘Al-Farma,' where he met with ‘St. Mina’ in the prison and both rejoiced by seeing each other. The governor of ‘Al-Farma’ ordered combing ‘Anthony’s body with sharp iron-teeth combs, and then he cut his head off by the sword. The saint received the crown of martyrdom.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Anthony, Father of the Monks, p. 198
passages.text:
Saint: ANTHONY, FATHER OF THE MONKS, ST. — His Order of Seclusion

9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the written text.

When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it.

Of His Words:

 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ.  Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack of discernment, they stayed away from God.  There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are not like us.  Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over the beasts of the wilderness. The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba.

[The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated by Hegumen Marcos Daoud]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 258–259
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony

Many researchers talked about St. Hilarion (Ilarion), as being the disciple of St. Anthony the Great, who founded the monastic movement. Whereas, St. Jerome, who recorded his biography, said about him: “Many people glorified his asceticism; others were amazed by the miracles God performed on his hands; while still others admired the wisdom and virtues with which he was adorned, I (Jerome), on the other hand, do not marvel about any of these, as much as I do about how he despised the temporal glory, with which everyone surrounded him, and honored him everywhere whenever he was, and how the bishops, the priests, the monks, the rulers, the judges, the elites, and the commons approached him seeking his guidance, blessing, and prayers. He did his best to disappear from the scene. He fled from the East to the West, hiding in the most isolated locations where no one could endure to dwell.”

With the Star of the Wilderness Abba Anthony:

St. Hilarion (291-371 AD) was born in a village called Tabatha, five miles south of Gaza, to wealthy pagan parents who sent him to Alexandria to learn the philosophical and practical knowledge. In Alexandria, he encountered a lot of scholars, mostly Christians, and the Holy Spirit led him to faith in the Lord Christ; and he was baptized when he was about fifteen years of age. As a Christian, he loved to pray and to worship in an ascetic manner.

By the year 306 AD, the sweet fragrance of Abba Anthony the Great filled the whole of Egypt and reached outside its borders. Then, once Hilarion heard about him, he put in his heart to visit him to get his blessing and listen to his teaching. When he finally met him, he viewed him as an angel of God and became one of his disciples for one year. Yet, because of the large crowds that came to see and seek the blessing of Abba Anthony, Hilarion sought his permission to leave Egypt and go back to Palestine, to live there in an atmosphere of seclusion, away from people.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q875 “Who were the most important monastic leaders?”, pp. 666–667
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement — 875. Who were the most important monastic leaders?

St. Paul of Thebes (the first hermit): St. Jerome documented his biography in 374 or 375 A. D. St. Paul grew up in northern upper Egypt and was well educated in Greek and Egyptian sciences. When he was sixteen years old, he received a big inheritance from his parents. During the persecution of Decius (around 250 A. D.), he went into the wilderness after his brother, Peter, took his share of the inheritance by force. When he was 113 years old, after leading an angelic life on earth, St. Anthony the Great met him. St. Paul addressed him by name, and they talked about the wonders of God and praised Him. At sunset, a raven flew down from a palm tree and brought a full loaf of bread to them, even though it was the raven’s habit to bring only half a loaf to St. Paul. On the third day, St. Paul asked St. Anthony to bring him St. Athanasius’ vestment, which he then gave to St. Anthony to bury him in it. When St. Anthony returned, he found that St. Paul had departed while bowing down in prayer. Then, two lions came and dug in the sand to bury St. Paul.

St. Anthony the Great: He was born around 251 A. D. in the city of Coma, Egypt (Qiman El-Arous). When he was eighteen years old, he heard the Gospel reading: “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me” (Matt. 19:21), and so he sold his possessions, placed his sister in a house of virgins, and dwelt in a small hut to learn from a saintly hermit there. After some time, he went into the western desert to struggle on his own in a tomb, that was carved in the mountain. At the age of thrity-five, he settled at the eastern bank of the Nile at Pispir (Dayr al-Maymūn), where he lived as a hermit, so many came to him and became his disciples. He went into the inner desert at Mount Colzim to live in peace and silence. Nonetheless, his love compelled him to visit Alexandria to support the martyrs in 316 A. D., and to support St. Athanasius against Arianism in 352 A. D. Many people came to be his disciples, and he departed in 352 A. D.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pelosianus, p. 396
passages.text:
Saint: PELOSIANUS, ST.

This saint was a friend of Abba Anthony the Great (251-356 AD). He took part in burying Abba Anthony along with his fellow monk Isaac. It seems that St. Jerome (342-420 AD), who told us about him, has met him somewhere.

[Jerome: Vita Hilarionis, 30; 31]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Amatus, p. 145
passages.text:
Saint: AMATUS, ST.

In his account on the biography of St. Paula the First Hermit, St. Jerome mentioned ‘Amatus’ as a disciple of St. Anthony the Great.

According to St. Palladius, ‘Amatus’ worked together with St. Macarius of Upper Egypt to oversee the monastery, which was a ‘Cenobion’ for a congregation of anchorites, all of whom were disciples to St. Anthony. Also, it is believed that they were the two monks who buried St. Anthony after he reposed.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — Abba Paul, the First Hermit, pp. 383–384
passages.text:
Saint: PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, ABBA — An Encounter with Abba Anthony

An Encounter with Abba Anthony:

One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to dwell in that wilderness. Then, an angel of the Lord appeared to Abba Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers, God has lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain.

On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St. Anthony set forth with Divine guidance, to the cave of St. Paul. When he got there, St. Paul called him by his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual but carrying a whole loaf of bread. St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.”

At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching. Abba Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment, and headed back to St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his soul to Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God.

On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling. For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.

When St. Antony wanted to bury St. Paul, he wondered how he could dig the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body of St. Paul, and shook their heads as if they were asking St. Anthony what to do. St. Antony knew that they were sent from God. He marked the place on the ground and they dug the grave with their claws; according to St. Antony's directions. St. Anthony then buried the holy body.

St. Anthony carried the garment of palm tree fibers and presented it to Pope Athanasius who greatly exulted to have it, and kept wearing it every year in the feasts of Christmas, Theophany, and Resurrection. Many signs were shown by that garment.

In the location where St. Paul the First Hermit used to live, a monastery was built where earthly angels dedicated all their lives to that of joyful praise for the Lord.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sisoes, the Great, pp. 168–169
passages.text:
Saint: SISOES, THE GREAT, ST. — Abba Anthony his Role Model

After the repose of Abba Anthony the Great, St. Sisoes (Shishoi/Shishai) was one of the most shining pillars of faith among the Fathers of the wilderness. Therefore, this saint is referred to as St. “Sisoes the Great.” Shishoi means: The Son of the High One. He was an Egyptian by birth, and when he reached 20 years of age, he forsook the world and sought refuge in the wilderness of Scetis in the year 340 AD, and became a disciple to St. Macarius. In the year 356 AD, longing for a life of more tranquility, he crossed the Nile to the Mountain of St. Anthony right after his departure, to have the blessings of the life and virtues of St. Anthony as light and helper in his new life. He set forth to a life of seclusion until the year 426 AD when he reached the age of 106 years, and because of old age, he returned to the wilderness of Scetis, and reposed after a little while when he reached 110 years of age. About him, Abba Poemen (Bemen) said: “He exalted beyond every limit, and surpassed all the achievements of the other saintly Fathers.”

Abba Anthony his Role Model:

St. Sisoes was acting as if Abba Anthony the Great was watching him and listening to his instructions to his disciples. He strove to imitate that great teacher in all his life: in his asceticism, in his spiritual practices, in his commitment to silence and his longing for prayers. Therefore, his fame spread, and so many people came to him requesting to be his disciples. At this point, he had to forsake his love for silence and seclusion, to fulfill a higher goal, namely loving care of his disciples. Abba Sisoes’s brother came to visit him in the cave of Abba Anthony, where he was staying. The saint amiably said to his brother: “In this cave, a lion used to live; now it is inhabited by a fox.”

St. Sisoes always was complaining that he did not reach the statue of St. Anthony. Once, a monk asked him: “Father! Have you not reached the level of St. Anthony?” He answered: “If I had only one of the virtues of that monk, I would have become a torch of Divine Love.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis, pp. 90–91
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, BISHOP OF THMUIS, ST. — With St. Anthony the Great

With St. Anthony the Great:

According to St. Jerome, St. Serapion was a personal friend of St. Anthony the Great, and his name was mentioned twice in the book “Life of Anthony” written by the Pope St. Athanasius the Apostolic. The first time, when the pope was talking to the brethren about the visions of Abba Anthony, who often used to suddenly interrupt his speech for a while before he resumes it again, and they would assume that the saint has seen a vision. St. Anthony used to tell St. Serapion about these visions. It was also said that St. Anthony while sitting on the mountain, he often saw what was going on in Egypt. The second time, when he knew that his departure was near, he requested that his clothes be distributed, giving one of sheepskin to Pope Athanasius and the one he has gotten new from bishop Serapion to be given back to him worn out, to keep.

Heading a Monastic Congregation:

According to the historian Sozomen, before St. Serapion was ordained as a bishop, he was the abbot of a monastic congregation in Upper Egypt, and that he was well known for his fantastic sanctity and eloquence. His close friend, Pope Athanasius, also mentioned in his letter to Dracontius, that he was the abbot of a significant number of monks.

His Support of Pope Athanasius:

St. Serapion supported the Pope in his strife against the Arianism. Being like his right hand, the pope used him as his deputy during his frequent absences from the throne. In the year 340 AD, the pope let him declare the date of the Passover; and it is believed that he let him write the Passover papal messages during the two years 341 and 342 AD.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Ammonius, the Anchorite, p. 151
passages.text:
Saint: AMMONIUS, THE ANCHORITE, ST

This saint was born in the year 294 AD near Marriott; and like his colleague ‘Anthony,' he was of a wealthy pious family. He lost his parents while still in his youth and became under the guardianship of his uncle. He desired to live as a virgin; his uncle betrothed for him a rich girl against his will. Not able to disobey his uncle’s wish, he kept talking to his betrothed girl with spiritual conviction and through his holy behavior, he managed to have a good impact on her and made her love purity and planted in her heart the desire to dedicate her soul to be a bride for the real Groom Jesus Christ. The couple agreed to go along with the wedding plan, yet persisted on living together like brother and sister. They remained for 17 years, strictly keeping their virginity. After that period, the wife departed to the eternal kingdom. In a night vision, the saint saw Abba Anthony calling him to put on the monastic ‘Eskeem.' Waking up, he went to St. Isidore who put on him the holy Eskeem. He stayed with him for some time; then, he set forth to Mount Tuna, where St. Anthony was dwelling. He lived a period with St. Anthony and became his disciple. He learned from him the holy monastic rules, then the saint built for him a cave in Mount Tuna and strove there in so many ways.

The devil envied him and came to him in the form of a nun knocking at his door. When he opened the door and sought her to pray, the devil turned into a flame of fire and went away. Then, the devil seduced a loose woman to try to make the saint fall in sin. So, she put on her best attire and came at sunset and knocked on the saint’s door, saying: “I am a stranger traveler, who lost my way. It is now close to night time. Do not leave me outside, lest a beast may devour me, and you shall be responsible for my blood." The saint opened the door for her and recognized the trick of the devil who sent her, so he began to preach her from the Bible, to warn her about the suffering in hell prepared for the sinners and told her about the happiness prepared for the righteous. God opened up her heart; she understood his sayings and threw herself at his feet, weeping and supplicating to him to help her save her soul. He made her discard her luxurious clothes, had her head shaved, clothed her in a woolen garment and called her ‘The Naïve.' He taught her the way of virtues, and she followed it very well. She surpassed some saints by her fasting and persistent prayers.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Serapion, the Great, p. 95
passages.text:
Saint: SERAPION, THE GREAT, ST.

A hermit in Mount Nitria, whose name is mentioned along with SS. Macarius, Pamponius, Heraclius and other saints. They became famous and drew many around them, in the days of Emperor Constantius II (337-361 AD), and kept the Upright faith, set by the Fathers of the Nicene Council.

St. Serapion the Great was a contemporary of St. Anthony the Great, and he was visited by St. Paula, the Elder in 386 AD, by Melania, the Elder in 387 AD, and by Palladius in 390 AD...

[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. IV, p. 614]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Sidrak St. Anthony and his Companions, p. 147
passages.text:
Saint: SIDRAK ST. ANTHONY AND HIS COMPANIONS (The martyrs)

A monk from the monastery of St. Anthony by the name of Sidrak, left his monastery with a colleague by the name of Fadl-Allah and accompanied them their close friend Daoud el-Banna. They all came down together from the mountain of St. Anthony to receive the crowns of martyrdom Those saints were martyred during the rule of the Circassian Mamluks (1382-1517) .

They were following the lead of St. Anthony, the Father of all Monks, who came down to Alexandria in the days of Emperor Maximian (286-305 AD) saying: “Let me go to where the fire of sufferings is. If the Divine care allowed for my martyrdom, I would be ready; and if not, I shall at the least stand by those persecuted among the children of St. Mark the Evangelist...”

[The Patriotism and History of the Coptic Church, p. 250]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Didymus, the Blind, pp. 583–584
passages.text:
Saint: DIDYMUS, THE BLIND, ST. — With St. Abba Anthony

With St. Abba Anthony:

St. ‘Didymus’ was a close friend of St. ‘Anthony the Great.’ Once while they were talking about the Holy Bible, St. ‘Anthony’ asked him, “Are you sad for having lost your eyesight?” St. ‘Anthony’ had to repeat the question three times. Finally, St. ‘Didymus’ told him that he was sad about it. St. ‘Anthony’ commented: “I am amazed about your sadness for losing what you share with the lowest of animals. The eyesight, the sense that these creatures have nothing else besides it. How come you do not have comfort that God granted you instead, a foresight, which He grants only to those He loves. He granted you, eyes like those of the angels, by which you see the Spirituals and perceive even God Himself, so His light would shine before you, taking away any darkness in your heart.” By those words of wisdom, St. ‘Didymus’ was greatly comforted for the rest of his life. Also, St. ‘Jerome’ had utilized this line of thought when he wrote a comforting message to a blind monk.

His Asceticism:

St. ‘Didymus’ impressed his contemporaries, not only by his knowledge but also by his asceticism. Most probably, he lived as an anchorite.

St. ‘Anthony’ visited him several times, and St. ‘Palladius’ visited him four times within ten years, and he wrote two stories about him: 95t. ‘Didymus’ once in his cell sought from me to pray, but I refused. Then, he told me the following story: “When St. ‘Anthony’ visited me for the third time, I asked him to pray. He instantly knelt on the ground to pray, and I did not have to repeat my request, giving me an example of obedience. So, if you are planning to follow his lead, as I understand since you are seeking the virtue and living in seclusion away from your relatives, then keep away from the spirit of obstruction.” 96e also told me the following story, “One day, while I was thinking about the life of that evil Emperor ‘Julian the Apostate’ (360-363 AD) and how he was persecuting the Christians, I was so distressed that I could not eat any food. And late at night, I saw white horses running and their riders were shouting aloud: ‘Tell ‘Didymus’ that ‘Julian’ died today at the 7th hour, so he should get up and eat, and he should send to ‘Athanasius’ the bishop (the 20th pope) to let him know as well.” He then added. “I wrote down the hour, the day and the month, and eventually, I found out that it was all true.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Abba Amon the Great, pp. 160–161
passages.text:
Saint: AMON THE GREAT, ABBA — His Monastic Life

After having lunch at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), Abba Anthony asked that they both would walk toward the South. They kept walking until sunset, when Abba Anthony stopped, prayed together and erected a cross to be a sign defining the place where the cells could be built. Abba Anthony’s idea was that if a monk wished to visit those living there, he could start walking after he finished eating at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone.

His Personality and the Role of Nitria;

Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away from the crowd and refrained from performing any miracles, claiming that he was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba Amon.

St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.

| St. Gadid                        | Pure celibate from Giza, martyred under Circassian Mamluks (1250-1517 AD), refused to follow grandfather's lead, declared Christ as only father. | [11]           |
| St. Gaiane, Rhipsime and their Companions | Rhipsime was a beautiful virgin in Rome's convent under Gaiane; faced persecution under Diocletian before his reign.                        | [12]           |
| St. Galatian and Episteme his Wife | Married couple from Ĥoms, Syria, lived celibate, tortured for faith, protected by God's power from humiliation.                             | [13]           |
| St. Gallicanus                   | Deputy of Emperor Constantine, converted to Christianity during military campaigns, lived in seclusion in Ostia after conversion.          | [14]           |
| St. Gatian, the Bishop           | One of six bishops from Rome to Gaul mid-3rd century, founder and first bishop of Tours, served about 50 years, died 301 AD.                | [15]           |
| St. Gawargy                     | Born to pious parents, left shepherding at 14 to pursue monastic life, resisted Satan's temptation on the way to St. Macarius wilderness.   | [16]           |
| St. Gelasius                    | Raised Christian, became deacon and priest, led monks in Scetis, example of longsuffering and perseverance, transcribed Holy Scriptures.    | [17]           |
| St. Gelasius of Caesarea        | Bishop of Caesarea, nephew of St. Cyril of Jerusalem, removed and restored due to Arian controversy, participated in 381 AD Council.       | [18]           |
| St. Gelasius of Cyzicus         | 5th-century ecclesiastical writer and church historian, authored important book on Nicene Council of 325 AD defending orthodox faith.       | [19]           |
| St. Gelasius, the Hermit        | Contemporary of Pope Peter II, cared for Alexandrian congregation during pope's hiding, called "The Warrior," later led monks in Scetis.     | [20]           |
| St. Genesius of Arles           | Christian catechumen and court clerk in Arles, refused to record anti-Christian decree, martyred for faith.                                  | [21]           |
| St. Genesius, the Clown         | Roman clown who mocked Christian baptism during Diocletian's arrival, converted and was martyred for faith.                                  | [22]           |
| St. Genevieve                   | Advocate of France, vowed virginity at age six, encouraged by St. Germanus of Auxerre, destined for salvation of France.                    | [23]           |
| St. Gennadius I of Constantinople | Bishop of Constantinople (458-471 AD), interpreter of the Bible, opposed teachings of St. Cyril and Timothy II of Alexandria, fought simony. | [24]           |
| St. Gentianus, Fuscianus, and Victoricus | Three martyrs; Gentianus converted through friends, all tortured and beheaded in 303 AD, relics kept in several cities.                     | [25]           |
| St. Genulf                      | Came from Rome in 3rd century with father to Gaul, preached Gospel, built church, lived in seclusion by river Nahon, died ~250 AD.           | [26]           |
| St. George of Alexandria       | Born to wealthy pagan parents, converted after visiting Lydda and hearing about martyr St. George, baptized and embraced Christian faith.   | [27]           |
| St. George, the Capaducian      | Martyr during Diocletian or possibly earlier under Persian king Dadianus, led revolt against Christian persecution in Cappadocia.           | [28]           |
| St. George, the Deacon          | Contemporary of Pope Simeon I (692-700 AD), served faithfully though not chosen pope, documented biographies of Alexandrian popes.           | [29]           |
| St. Gerasimus, Theodotus and Bishop Athanasius | Martyred after bishop Athanasius refused to prostrate to idols, tortured and beheaded under governor Arianos.                                | [30]           |

St. Gelasius of Cyzicus (entry heading: GELASIUS OF CYZICUS)
Gelasius of Cyzicus was an ecclesiastical writer in the 2nd half of the 5th century. As a church historian, he wrote the history of the church at his time, including the events of the Nicene Council of the year 325 AD. He based it on highly reliable sources. His book “Syntagma,” or “The collection of Acts of the Nicene Council,” 325 AD, is considered of great importance. records.question: why is coptic easter different than catholic
records.answer:
The difference between the Coptic Easter (Christian Pascha) and the Catholic Easter arises mainly from the method of calculating the date of Pascha.

1. The Coptic Church follows the Alexandrian Computus, devised by Pope Demetrius of Alexandria in the second century. This calculation combines the solar cycle with the lunar cycle, ensuring that Christian Pascha falls after the Jewish Passover, which is linked to the Jewish lunar calendar and harvest season in Palestine. The Alexandrian Computus sets Pascha to fall between the first week of April and the first week of May, based on a 19-year solar-lunar cycle with adjustments for the difference between lunar and solar years [1].

2. The Council of Nicaea approved this Alexandrian Computus, and the Church observed it worldwide until 1582 A.D. [1].

3. In the sixteenth century, the Roman Pope Gregory XIII introduced a reform (the Gregorian calendar) and requested that the Jewish Passover no longer be taken into account in the computation of Christian Pascha, but only the time of the spring equinox. The Catholic Church adopted this reform, which changed the calculation of Easter [1].

4. Protestants initially continued to use the Alexandrian Computus until 1775 A.D., but the Catholic Church's change led to a divergence in the date of Easter celebrations between the Coptic Church and the Catholic Church [1].

Therefore, the Coptic Easter differs from the Catholic Easter because the Coptic Church continues to calculate Pascha based on the Alexandrian Computus, which considers the Jewish Passover and uses the Julian calendar, while the Catholic Church uses the Gregorian calendar and calculates Easter based only on the spring equinox, disregarding the Jewish Passover [1].

No further details about the Catholic Church's Easter calculation or other differences are provided in the sources.
