passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Cairo, pp. 122–123
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF CAIRO

At the beginning of the reign of the Circassian Mamluks (Burji dynasty: 1382-1517 AD) over Egypt, in the year 1389 AD (791 AH), a large number of men and women who were forced earlier to convert to Islam, came into the city of Cairo (El-Fustat) in a vast procession and publicly proclaimed that they have forsaken ‘Islam’ and returned to the fold of the Lord Jesus Christ. They declared that they would never change their position again, even if their necks would be cut off. They kept saying, “We came here to atone for our weak faith and our earlier denial of Christ, and we are ready now to offer our lives on the altar of sacrifice to receive the blessing of martyrdom and the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The Muslim mob gathered around them and advised them to return to Islam, but the converted believers daringly refused. The Muslim mob tried to frighten them through the threat of death, but it was in vain. Then, the Muslim mob led many of them, men and women, to a public square before the “School of the ‘King el-Saleĥ,’” and there in front of everybody, they cut their necks one after the other. However, the faith of none of them was shaken. The mob took some women and tortured them, but they also held fast to their faith. So, the mob bared them of their clothes, dragged them to the valley beneath the Citadel, then cut their necks with such viciousness, that many moderate Muslims protested against those atrocities, and turned against the judge who issue such a verdict.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 234]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Basil, pp. 317–318
passages.text:
Saint: BASIL (The martyr)

There are historical accounts about a group of martyrs in Alexandria during the reign of Caesar ‘Septimius Severus’ (193-211 AD). They gained their martyrdom around the year 203 AD. Among those martyrs was ‘Leonides,’ the father of ‘Origen,’ ‘Artyrus,’ ‘Keriacus,’ and ‘Basil.’ We do not know much about those martyrs, except their names.

‘Septimius Severus’ [his name means: the 7th Cruel one], was known at the beginning of his reign for having an open mind and considerable leniency. He disregarded all the previous creeds concerning the persecution of Christians. However, his Syrian wife ‘Julia Domina,’ the daughter of one of the chief priests of the temple of the ‘Mount’ in the city of ‘Homs,’ had a severe role in changing her husband's behavior. She surrounded herself by a group of pagan religious men, and she managed eventually to stir her husband to persecute the church with extreme ferocity. It was as though the fire of persecution remained for a while hidden under the hay, and then suddenly and viciously flared up. In the days of ‘Septimius Severus,’ a multitude of believers received the crowns of martyrdom all over the Roman Empire, and in Egypt in particular. Many Christians were imprisoned, especially those who were dedicated to ministry, rich and poor. The jails turned into churches from which the voice of praise was always heard.

[Cheneau: Les Saintes d’Egypte, Tome 1, pp. 483-6]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of the Arian Heresy, p. 138
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF THE ARIAN HERESY — Among those Exiled were

Among those Exiled were:

• Bishops Amon and Adelphius, who were exiled to the Outer Oasis. • Bishops Muis, senosiris, Pilammon, Plenes, Marcos, and Athenodorus, who were exiled to Amon Oasis (Siwa Oasis), instead of being condemned to be burnt alive. • Bishop Dracuntius, who was exiled to the desert of Qalzam, near city of Suez. • Bishop Philon, who was exiled to Babylon. • Bishops Ammonius, Agathos, Agathodemon, Aplonius, Eulogius, Pavnotius, Apollon, Gaios, Flavius, Dioscorus, Heraclides, and Psain, along with the two priests Hierax and Dioscorus, who were exiled to Aswan. Then, they kept chasing them from one location to another. They forced many of them to toil in the mines and quarries. Also, they slaughtered some of them without any mercy. The bishops of Pentapolis were exiled to the Outer Oasis, while the bishops of Upper Egypt were exiled to Siwa Oasis.

This is not a complete list of the bishops and priests who were tortured or martyred, for the list wrote by Pope Athanasius was unfortunately lost. However, in another document, the names of 90 great priests were included, who were expelled from their churches. Pope Athanasius has advised that all of those who suffered should be honored by the Church on the same level as the blessed saints and martyrs.

[Encyclopedia of the History of the Copts; Part 11, Bk 4, p. 127]

[The Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 245]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Mount Sinai, pp. 128–129
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF MOUNT SINAI

During the 4th/5th century AD, 38 hermits on Mount Saini were martyred in a barbarian Arab (Saracens) raid on their area. Also, a significant number of more hermits in the desert of Raithu (by the Red Sea, about two days travel from the center of Sinai) were slaughtered in the same manner at the hands of those Arab raiders. Among the martyrs was a young 14 years old boy, who was starting a life of great strife in seclusion. When the Arab invaders found him, they threatened to kill him if he would not reveal the location of the older hermits. He told them that he did not fear death, and he was not ready to spoil his life by the sin of betraying his Fathers. Provoked to anger by his answer, they killed the young saint, and he received the crown of martyrdom. The above incidents were documented by St. Nilus of Sinai (died in 430 AD) who wrote the “Works about the Monastic Life” concerning the above slaughters in seven parts, and told about his own life in Sinai, the invasion of the Saracens’ the captivity of his son, etc.

[Baring-Gould, The Lives of the Saints, Vol. 1, 1897, pp. 202-9: January 14]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Patra, p. 377
passages.text:
Saint: PATRA (The martyr)

St. Patra (Matra) was martyred on the 10th day of the Coptic month Mesra, most probably in the year 250 AD, in the days of St. Dionysius the Great, the 14th pope of Alexandria (247-264 AD). When Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) issued a decree committing everyone to worship the idols and to deny the Lord Jesus Christ; St. Patra set forth to the idol temple, removed the golden hand of the idol, cut it into small pieces and distributed the pieces on the poor. Finding out what happened to his idol, the emperor in great anger arrested many people; but the saint daringly came to him on his own, proclaiming that he took the hand and gave its gold to the needy. The governor gave the order to burn him alive, but God sent His angel and saved him. Then, the governor ordered to cut off his hands and feet, and to nail him upside down on a tree. A blind man took some of the blood pouring from his body and put it on his eyes and he had his sight back. Ultimately the saint had his head cut off and received the crown of martyrdom.

[O'Leary: The Saints of Egypt, p. 103]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Akhmim, p. 118
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF AKHMIM

After the decree of the persecution of the Christians was issued by Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), Ariana, the governor of Ansenah made a tour through Upper Egypt to supervise by himself the execution of the imperial orders. Upon arriving at Akhmim on the day of the Holy feast of Nativity, Ariana found out that the Copts were assembled in the Church, with Abba Abadion the bishop of Ansenah, who was delivering to them a sermon of words of grace; because their own bishop Audacius reposed a short time before. Because the Copts were assembled in the Church and did not come to welcome him, Ariana was provoked to evil anger, and he gave the order to kill all those who were in the Church. The blood which was shed on that day ran from the Church to the streets of the city. Hearing about that massacre, those in the other towns and villages, hastened to come to Akhmim, proclaiming their faith. Before the governor Ariana, the fathers and mothers cried out with joy: “We are going to the Kingdom of Heaven,” and presented their children by their own hands to the sword and encouraged them by saying, “Have no fear; it is only moments, and you will be with Your Heavenly Groom.” It was hard to estimate the exact number of those martyrs who were killed in and outside the church on that day.

[Martyrdom in Christianity, p. 190]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Arsephius and Arkias, p. 248
passages.text:
Saint: ARSEPHIUS AND ARKIAS (The martyrs)

These two saints were martyred along with a significant number of believers in the city of ‘Assiut.' It happened when St. ‘Abaskhiroun’ was led to ‘Ansena’ to be tortured by its governor ‘Arianus,’ but because the governor has left to ‘Assiut’ to torture the Christians there, the saint was taken to ‘Assiut’ as well.

With ‘Arianus’ in ‘Assiut,’ there was ‘Maximas’ (most probable governor of Assiut), and the latter ordered that the two brothers ‘Arsephius’ and ‘Arkias’ be tied from behind, whipped then be led to the north of the city. There, they were tightly tied spread-eagle to anchors secured to the ground and left to suffer in agony, hoping that they would eventually submit and burn incense before the idols.

The two brothers endured the sufferings with joy and happiness and refused to burn incense before the idols. The governors were planning to carry them into a furnace of fire, but they found out that they already have died amid their sufferings, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.

[Church of the Virgin St. Mary, Moharrem Bek, Alexandria: The Biography of St. Abaskhiroun, the Soldier; 1977, pp. 23-25]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Atrib, p. 122
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF ATRIB

At the end of the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), Alexandros, the governor of Towa in the province of Atrib in the Nile Delta, attempted to convince the Copts to worship the idols. When all his trials ended up with failure, he killed 1,500 believers, and they all received the crowns of martyrdom.

[Encyclopedia of the History of the Copts, Part 11, Bk 4, p. 121]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John of Heraclea, pp. 429–430
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN OF HERACLEA (The martyr) — In Egypt

This saint was initially from Heraclea in Asia Minor. His father was a governor in the time of Diocletian (284-305 AD). He had a Christian upbringing, and when his father reposed, he was appointed to replace him when he was just twenty years of age. He eventually encountered Diocletian, refrained from worshiping the god Apollo, and rebuked the emperor. The latter cast him in prison, where the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him in a vision, encouraged him, and strengthened him.

In Egypt:

In an attempt to lure the saint to his side, the emperor Diocletian sent him to Egypt to collect the taxes for the treasury and to repair the ruined temples of the idols, a chance the saint used instead to break them down altogether.

His Martyrdom:

Later on, the saint was there with governor Keriakos while he was torturing the Christian confessors; and he saw angels placing heavenly crowns on their heads. St. John cried out confessing his Christian faith before the governor, who ordered to put him in chains and to send him to Arianus, the governor of Ansenah , along with the other confessors.

There, he was hanged on the Hinbazeen, scourged so violently that his blood was scattered all over the place; skinned; red-hot nails put on his face; tied to the tail of a wild horse and was dragged with his face down on earth. Finally, he had his hands, feet, and head cut off by the sword in Qusiah close to Assiut on the 4th day of Paona.

[The Martyrdom in Christianity; p. 131]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — Sts. Haeremon and Ischyrion, p. 423
passages.text:
Saint: HAEREMON AND ISCHYRION, SS. (The martyrs)

The 14th Pope of Alexandria St. ‘Dionysius’ (246-264 AD) in his letter to St. ‘Fabian’ of Antioch about the Egyptian Christians who endured torture during the persecution by Emperor ‘Decius’ (249-251 AD); he mentioned that so many of them fled to the Egyptian deserts, where they perished out of hunger, thirst, and wild beasts; while so many others were arrested and sold as slaves. He mainly referred to the name of St. ‘Chaeremon,’ an ancient Bishop of ‘Nilopolis,’ who fled with another person to the Arabian mountains, and they have not been heard from ever since. When the brethren went to search for them, not even their corpses were found.

St. ‘Dionysius’ also referred to St. ‘Ischyrion,’ a representative of a prince in one of the cities of Egypt, who was ordered by his master to sacrifice to the idols; and when he refused to do so, he was tortured, then he was killed on a stake and he received the crown of martyrdom in the year 250 AD.

[Butler: December 22]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. George of Alexandria, p. 169
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE OF ALEXANDRIA (The martyr) — His Martyrdom

His Martyrdom:

When the governor knew that it was his nephew George, the one who convinced his daughter to receive her new faith, he put him under arrest. Then, he tortured him fiercely and sent him to Arianus, the governor of Ansena, who tortured him more and finally had his head cut off, and he too gained the crown of martyrdom during the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). A deacon, by the name of Samuel, took his holy body, shrouded him with great respect, and took it Manuf in the province of Giza. On hearing about it, his uncle's wife took the body and buried it in Alexandria next to that of her martyred daughter. His relics now are in St. Mark's church in the city of Rashid.

th

[Synaxarion of the 7 of Hator] [OLeary: The Saints of Egypt, pp. 145-146]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of the Serapeum, pp. 139–140
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF THE SERAPEUM

When the 23rd Pope of Alexandria St. Theophilus (385-412 AD), got a decree from Emperor Theodosius I (379-395 AD) to turn the deserted pagan temple of Bacchus into a Christian church, this led the pagans to a great riot. During that time, they killed so many Christians on the streets. The pagan rebels made their headquarters in the temple of Serapis in Alexandria, from which they attacked the Christians. They caught many of them and gave them the choice, either to sacrifice to Serapis or to be killed without mercy. In that manner, they killed so many martyrs. Emperor Theodosius I proclaimed his admiration for the courage and brevity of those saintly Christian martyrs, and to honor them, he forgave those pagans who killed them. However, he issued a decree to destroy all the pagan temples on the land of Egypt. When the emperor’s decree was publicly broadcast, the pagans forsook the temple of Serapis. Then, after the idol was broken down, it was cast into the fire. The pagans imagined that as a result of the destruction of their temple and its idols, the heaven would fall, and a chaos would prevail on the whole land. However, on seeing that nothing changed, many of them proclaimed their faith in the Lord Christ.

Those Christian saints were martyred in the year 390 AD, and are celebrated by the Church of the West on the 17th of March. Two churches were built on the same place of the temple of Serapis in Alexandria, which was one of the most important landmarks in the old world.

[Butler: March 17]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John XIII, the 94th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 397–398
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN XIII, The 94th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Salib the Martyr

Salib the Martyr:

One of the famous names of the Coptic martyrs in the days of that revered pope was St. Salib, whose body is still there uncorrupted to this very day. Some of his relics were moved to the monastery of Mar Mina, the Wonder-Maker in Marriott. He received the crown of martyrdom after being crucified on a wooden cross. He paraded on a camel along the streets of Cairo, by an order from the four Muslim judges, yet he remained silent, with the grace of God showing on his face a shining light. Then, he was beheaded while saying, “I lived a Christian, and so I will die.”

The Anguish from the Mamluks:

The rule of the Mamluks in Egypt has lasted for a long time (1250-1517) and was extended to Syria, Cyprus, and Hijaz, and they managed to defeat the Crusaders and the Moguls. At the same time, on the hands of these Mamluk masters, the Egyptians endured every kind of discrimination, injustice, poverty, humiliation, and huge excessive “Jizyah” taxes they had to pay. Besides, the Copts were living in the middle of the Mamluks internal revolutions, riots and disturbances; and they had the most significant share of suffering from their tyranny, through which they crushed the Christian churches and monasteries.

Destruction of the Monasteries and Churches:

Of the most famous monasteries demolished in those days were:  The ‘Quseir (Short one)’ monastery, which used to have icons of the most beautiful portraits of the Virgin St. Mary.  The monasteries of Mar John and Abu-Mina in the cave of Shaqalqil on the top of the mountain looking over the River Nile, in the province of Manfalot.  The Boctor monastery in Abnoub's quarries, the monastery of Abu-Hermina the hermit, the monastery of the Seven Mountains in Akhmim, and the monastery of Abba Besada (Beshada), the Coptic scholar.  The Nohia monastery in Giza. Some historians considered it as the most beautiful monastery and in the best location.  The Isuos monastery, which had a well called Isuos. Its water used to rise in this saint's feast on the 15th of Bashons. This phenomenon gave the Egyptians the idea of constructing a water level monitor for the Nile flood, based on the fact that the level of water in that monastery well conformed to the Nile flood level.  The Yehness the Short monastery on the top of the mountain west of Assiut.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Ischyion, pp. 326–327
passages.text:
Saint: ISCHYION (The martyr)

In the days of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD), the Governor of Alexandria was so violent in persecuting the Christians. According to the historian Eusebius, this Governor started his persecution on his own a whole year before the emperor has issued his decree (in the year 249 AD).

The Christians in Alexandria were dragged to court to fall under so many kinds of tortures. It happened that one of those Christians who were on trial started to weaken when he saw those dreadful tools of torture, and he was about to collapse and deny his Christ. However, our Lord Jesus Christ did not forsake him, but all of a sudden, the man saw five soldiers, one of whom was called Ischyion, forcing their way into the court, declaring their conversion to Christianity. This incident drew the attention of everyone to find out what their intention was. They set forth to stand beside the accused Christians, proclaiming that they, too, were also disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The judge and all the audience were amazed to watch such a scene, mainly that those men carried cheerfulness on their countenances, as though they were coming, not to face torture, but to receive joy and crowns. Here, the believer who was on the brink of collapse, felt strength coming over him and got comfortable in his heart. After the judge was starting to exult in his eminent failure, everything changed when the man proclaimed his longing to endure any torture for the sake of his true faith.

When Ischyion began to testify to his Christ and to profess for Him in the court, the judge ordered someone called Arminius to torture that brave soldier by cutting off one member of his body after another. Then, they opened his belly up with a rod. In that way, St. Ischyion was martyred and was followed by his other friends.

[Cheneau: Les Saints d'Egypte; V. 2; p. 109]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martyrs of Dandara, p. 124
passages.text:
Saint: MARTYRS OF DANDARA

On the 16th of Bashons, the Coptic Church celebrates the memory of the martyrdom of 400 martyrs in the town of Dandara (on the west bank of the Nile, about 5 kilometers south of the city of Qena). They were executed after suffering many tortures because they were Christians. This happened near the end of the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD).

[The Synaxarion: 16 Bashons]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda, pp. 137–138
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA (The martyr)

He lived during the 2nd half of the 7th century when the Arab invasion to Egypt has just begun. This saint was raised in a truly Christian way. He observed a lifestyle within God's commandments and guidelines. He did not stop at fasting, prayers and attending masses, but he was also a generous giver to the poor, and always visiting the sick and imprisoned. Some evil people were annoyed by his piety, so they went to the Arab governor, claiming that the saint was mocking their religion. So, they brought him over for questioning. St. Shenouda declared that he believed in Christ, who commanded his followers to love everybody. He explained to the governor that he was just doing that, and he never made fun of any religion. The governor did not accept his reasoning and ordered him to deny his Christ and join Islam. The saint refused to proclaim his pride in being a Christian. The governor put him through so many tortures, which he accepted gladly.

Finally, they beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 13 Abib] [Iris El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church, vol. 2, p. 85]

records.answer:
Here is the list of the names of the Coptic months:

1. Thout (begins 11th September / 12th September in a leap year)  
2. Paopi (10th/11th October)  
3. Hathor (10th/11th November)  
4. Koiak (10th/11th December)  
5. Tobi (9th/10th January)  
6. Meshir (8th/9th February)  
7. Paremhotep (10th/11th March)  
8. Parmoute (9th April)  
9. Pashons (9th May)  
10. Paoni (8th June)  
11. Epip (8th July)  
12. Mesori (7th August)  
13. Al-Nasy or Pi-Kogi Enavot (Pikouji `n`abot) or the little month (6th September) [1][2]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1092 “What are the names of the Coptic months?”, pp. 242–243
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1092. What are the names of the Coptic months?

Certain papyri dating from the fifth century B. C. discovered on the island of Elephantine indicate that the Egyptians of the time celebrated great feasts in honor of the gods whose names were given to the months of the ancient Egyptian calendar. The Copts preserved the names of the ancient Egyptian months, despite the fact that they are the names of pagan gods or their feasts. The names of the months are:

1. Thout (begins 11th September / 12th September in a leap year): God of wisdom and knowledge, inventor of writing, protector of scribes, and designer of seasons and months. Thout presides over the “House of Life” and is the source of all the texts necessary to preserve and renew life.

2. Paopi (10th/11th October): The Feast of Opet. Amun-Ra was accustomed to travelling from the Temple of Karnak to the Temple of Luxor to celebrate this famous festival.

3. Hathor (10th/11th November): The goddess Hathor, the cow of the heavens, who gave birth to the sun and all beings: both divine and human; goddess of gold and of grains, especially wheat. Thus she was called, “Hathor the Golden.”

4. Koiak (10th/11th December): This name is derived from a certain ritual of incense used in funerary celebrations known as “union with the spirit (ka).” This was also the month for celebrating the feasts of Osiris.

5. Tobi (9th/10th January): Also called Botti.

6. Meshir (8th/9th February): “The Great” where “The Great Fire” is.

7. Paremhotep (10th/11th March). One of the harvest months for the ancient Egyptians.

8. Parmoute (9th April): Dedicated to Ernūtet, the goddess of harvest, who had the head of a cobra and sometimes nursed her son, Khepri, a god of grain.

9. Pashons (9th May): Derived from an ancient feast called Khonsu, a lunar deity, anciently referred to as the son of Amun and Mut.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1092 “What are the names of the Coptic months?”, p. 243
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1092. What are the names of the Coptic months?

9. Pashons (9th May): Derived from an ancient feast called Khonsu, a lunar deity, anciently referred to as the son of Amun and Mut.

10. Paoni (8th June): The Feast of the “Beautiful Valley” was celebrated during this month in the Valley of the Kings for ten days. It was considered the most important of the feasts of the ancient Egyptians, when sacrifices were offered, tombs were visited, and food was offered in honor of the deceased, all with the participation of relatives, dancers, and musicians.

11. Epip (8th July): Dedicated to the goddess of fertility, Ipy.

12. Mesori (7th August): The last month in which they celebrated the birth of the sun god, Ra.

13. Lastly, Al-Nasy or Pi-Kogi Enavot (Pikouji `n`abot) or the little month (6th September): Osiris is celebrated during the first days of this month.

Notes: [638] Derchain, Chronologie d’Egypte (Cairo, 1954).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1095 “What are the most important fixed feasts in the Coptic calendar?”, p. 245
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1095. What are the most important fixed feasts in the Coptic calendar?

The Coptic Church calendar is based on the Coptic months, but I will also provide the corresponding dates in the Gregorian calendar, although we should bear in mind that they may move by a day or two in leap years.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1088 “What is the relationship between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?”, p. 240
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1088. What is the relationship between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?

Ancient Egyptians developed their calendar at least as far back as 4240 B. C. The famous Greek historian Herodotus remarks that the Egyptians preceded the Greeks in correcting their calendar by adding an additional five days each year to the standard twelve months of thirty days each.

The Copts inherited an interest in the solar calendar from their ancestors, the Pharaohs, and until today, even illiterate Copts in Egypt still follow and pass on their oral traditions for the reckoning of times, by which they order the agricultural seasons, predict weather conditions, and worship using the liturgical calendar.

The Coptic year, which is of ancient Egyptian origin, is divided into twelve months, each of which contains thirty days, and to which are added five extra days at the end of the year called the “little month” or the Epagomenal days. Every four years, in a leap year, six days are added instead of five. The year is divided into three seasons with each season made up of four months. The first season is the season of the flooding of the Nile; the second is the season for sowing; and the third is the season for harvesting and gathering fruits. This seasonal structure continues to define the Coptic liturgical year in Egypt. It was also used outside of Egypt until the Holy Synod of the Coptic Church issued a decree to combine the prayers of the three seasons into a single unified litany of the air of the heaven, the fruits of the earth, and the waters of the rivers together, since in the diaspora, each land has its own agricultural conditions that are unlike those of Egypt.

Notes: [632] Herodotus. The Histories of Herodotus, trans., Henry Cary (D. Appleton and Company, 1904) 2.4: p. 86.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1079 “What is the monthly Church cycle?”, p. 226
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1079. What is the monthly Church cycle?

Every month is sanctified by our monthly commemoration of St. Mary the Mother of God, the Theotokos, on the 21st of each Coptic month. We look up to St. Mary as a living role model for the faithful and the First Citizen of the Church of the Lord Christ, learning from her to live as those who carry the Lord Christ wherever they go; He who establishes His kingdom in our depths.

On the 29th of every Coptic month, we commemorate the annunciation, nativity [or Christmas], and resurrection of Christ (except for the months of Tobe and Meshir). With these commemorations, the believer is dissolved into love through his union with the Savior every hour, every day, every week, and every month.

And we commemorate the chief of the army of the Lord, Archangel Michael, every 12th day of the Coptic month. Thus, the believer feels that he is a good soldier of our Lord Jesus (2 Tim. 2:3) and that he has joined the ranks of the heavenly powers.

This is the happiness of the believer and his continual joy on a daily, weekly, monthly, and annual basis.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1091 “What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?”, p. 242
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1091. What connection is there between the Coptic calendar and the ancient Egyptian calendar?

The Copts inherited the ancient Egyptian calendar from their ancestors, and with some slight modifications, used it to order their liturgical Church life and their daily affairs, especially agriculture. The Coptic liturgical day begins at sunset, like that of the Jews and the Greeks; and each week consists of seven days, the first of which is the Lord’s Day (Sunday).

In the fourth century, many Copts were martyred, and they therefore considered the reign of Diocletian as a golden age. They set the year in which Diocletian became emperor (November, 284 A. D.) as the first year of their calendar. They introduced the term, “The Year of the Martyrs” (Anno Martyrum), abbreviated as A. M. The scholar Tertullian said, “If the martyrs throughout the world were to be put in one side of the scales and the Coptic martyrs alone were to be put in the other, the latter would outweigh the former.”

Notes: [637] Iris Habib El-Masry, The Story of the Copts: Book 1, (Southern California, U.S.A: St. Anthony Coptic Orthodox Monastery, undated) 1.9.99: p. 100.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1107 “What are the most important occasions in the month of Mesore?”, pp. 247–248
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1107. What are the most important occasions in the month of Mesore?

a. St. Mary’s Fast (1st–15th Mesore / 7th–21st August).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1084 “What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?”, pp. 236–237
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1084. What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?

In addition to the monthly commemoration of the Virgin Mary on the 21st of every Coptic month, we celebrate the following feasts:

a. The annunciation of her birth (7th Mesore / 13th August). On this feast we celebrate the conception of St. Mary, the living ark of the covenant, the dwelling of the Most High, and the second heaven.

b. Her birthday (1st Pashons / 9th May). Copts usually commemorate the day a saint passed from this world; their martyrdom or departure to paradise — but they insist on honoring St. Mary on her the day of her birth as a joyful day.

c. Her entry into the temple (3rd Kiahk / 12th December). We learn from the tradition of the Church that St. Mary’s life was consecrated to God in fulfillment of her mother’s vow, for she had vowed to consecrate her firstborn — whether a son or a daughter — to serve the Lord all the days of his or her life.

d. Her departure (21st Tobe / 29th January).

e. The revealing of the assumption of her body (16th Mesore / 22nd August). This feast is preceded by the fifteen-day fast of St. Mary.

f. The consecration of the first church in her name at Philippi (21st Paone / 28th June). This feast also coincides with the commemoration of the Virgin’s miracle of melting iron in the city of Bartus.

g. The apparition of the Virgin Mary above her church in Zeitoun (24th Paremhotep / 2nd April). This apparition is considered unique among the whole history of Marian apparitions. It began on 2nd April 1968 and was repeated on most days for hours at a time and for many months. These apparitions appeared above the domes of the Church of St. Mary and were seen by several hundred thousand people, of all ages and positions, Christians and Muslims. Every night, the people would gather around the church, pray, and praise God, waiting to see the dazzling spectacle of St. Mary standing above one of the domes. She was seen kneeling before the cross, or at other times, carrying the baby Jesus. These apparitions were accompanied by the apparition of birds in the form of doves. Among the fruits of these apparitions were the repentance of many and the occurrence of countless miracles.

Notes: [624] Jerome Palmer, Our Lady Returns to Egypt (Culligan Publications, 1969): p. 1.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1090 “What connection is there between the Alexandrian Computus (Epact) and the”, pp. 241–242
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1090. What connection is there between the Alexandrian Computus (Epact) and the

Christian Pascha?

The difficulty in determining the date of Christian Pascha (Holy Week and Resurrection) for each year is due to the ancient condition it must fall after the Jewish Passover. Since the Jewish Passover is linked to the harvest for the Jews (Ex. 23:16), it always falls in the months of April or May; bearing in mind that the Jewish calendar is lunar. However, this calculation does not correspond to the seasons of Egypt because the time of harvest in Egypt differs from that in Palestine. Therefore, Pope Demetrius of Alexandria (second century) saw the need to devise a calculation that combines the solar cycle with the lunar cycle; according to which the Christian Pascha falls in the months of April or May, but not before the first week of April and not later than the first week of May.

This calculation consists of a cycle of nineteen solar-lunar years. Since the lunar year is eleven days shorter than the solar year, the number of days missing in nineteen lunar years from the corresponding number of solar years is two hundred and nine days. He distributed these days over nineteen years by adding a full month every two or three years. The Council of Nicaea approved this computation, and the Church observed it all over the world until the year 1582 A. D.

The Protestants broke away from the Roman Church in the sixteenth century. This was the same century in which the Roman Pope Gregory XIII requested that the Jewish Passover not be taken into account in the computation of the Christian Pascha, but that it is sufficient only to take into account the time of the spring equinox. Protestants continued to use the Alexandrian computus until 1775 A. D., that is for about two centuries.

Notes: [636] See Iris Habib El-Masry, The Story of the Copts: Book 1, (Southern California, U.S.A: St. Anthony Coptic Orthodox Monastery, undated) 4.A.24: p. 39.

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1100. What are the most important occasions in the month of Tobe?

a. Martyrdom of the innocent children of Bethlehem (3rd Tobe / 11th January), when we focus on the greatness of innocence of the heart and the chastity of soul and body.

b. Circumcision of Christ (6th Tobe / 14th January), when we honor the circumcision of the soul, senses, and emotions.

c. Paramoun of Theophany is the day before Theophany (can be two or three days some years).

d. Theophany (11th Tobe / 19th January), on which the Lakkan or Liturgy of the Water is prayed (also prayed on the Feast of the Apostles and Covenant Thursday):

i. We become acquainted with divine mysteries.

ii. He gave us what is His: through Christ we become children of the Father.

iii. We crush the heads of the dragon.

iv. We are blessed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.

e. Wedding at Cana of Galilee (13th Tobe / 21st January). The Master began His ministry by attending a wedding and concluded His ministry by offering His own blood to His bride as her dowry.

records.question: Compare baptism and chrismation
records.answer:
Here is a comparison of baptism and chrismation according to the Coptic Orthodox teachings from the provided passages:

| Aspect                         | Baptism                                                                                         | Chrismation                                                                                          |
|-------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Meaning and Role**           | Baptism is the new birth and the forgiveness of sins; it cleanses the believer and grants spiritual birth [1][4]. | Chrismation is the reception of the Holy Spirit to dwell within the believer; it is the anointing and sealing with the Spirit for growth and perfection [1][4][6]. |
| **Connection**                 | Baptism and chrismation are often performed together; baptism in a broad sense includes chrismation [1]. | Chrismation follows baptism and completes it by conferring an increase of grace and the fullness of the Holy Spirit [1][2]. |
| **Biblical and Patristic Basis** | Baptism involves immersion in water and the washing away of sins [1][7]. The apostles baptized and laid hands for the Holy Spirit to descend [2]. | Chrismation involves anointing with holy oil (Chrism or Myron) and the laying on of hands to invoke the Holy Spirit [2][3]. |
| **Effect on the Believer**     | Baptism grants spiritual birth, forgiveness of sins, and initiates the believer into the Church [1][4]. | Chrismation imparts the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, consecrates body and soul, enlightens the mind, and strengthens against evil [1][6][10][15]. |
| **Ritual Elements**            | Includes sanctification of water, threefold immersion, and washing [7]. | Includes anointing thirty-six times with Chrism on the body, laying on of hands, and breathing of the Spirit [2][11]. |
| **Symbolism of Anointing**    | Not directly anointed in baptism, but anointing follows immediately after [11]. | Anointing sanctifies thoughts, senses, deeds, and the whole person; it is a visible sign of the Holy Spirit's presence [2][8]. |
| **Sacramental Distinction**    | Baptism is the spiritual birth and cleansing from sin [1][4]. | Chrismation is the nourishment, sealing, and empowerment by the Holy Spirit [1][4][3]. |
| **Historical Practice**        | Apostles baptized and laid hands for the Spirit; early Church combined baptism and chrismation [2][3]. | Chrismation was administered by bishops with holy oil, often immediately after baptism [2][11]. |
| **Theological Emphasis**       | Baptism initiates new life in Christ and forgiveness [1][4]. | Chrismation confirms and strengthens the believer with the Holy Spirit for spiritual growth and warfare against evil [6][10][15]. |

This comparison is based entirely on the supplied passages and reflects the Coptic Orthodox understanding of these sacraments.

retrieval.query: What are the differences between baptism and chrismation?

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q715 “What is the role of the sacraments of baptism and chrismation?”, pp. 544–545
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 715. What is the role of the sacraments of baptism and chrismation?

In baptism, we enjoy the new birth and the forgiveness of sins; while in chrismation, we receive the Holy Spirit to dwell within us. Since the two sacraments are often performed at the same time, some Fathers talk about baptism in the broader sense which includes chrismation.

In the writings of Origen, he demonstrates both the specific and the broad meaning of baptism. He says, “In the Acts of the Apostles, the Holy Spirit was given by the imposition of the apostles’ hands in baptism.” This is the broad meaning of baptism, when combining both sacraments together. He continues later, “Lastly, for this reason was the grace and revelation of the Holy Spirit bestowed by the imposition of the apostles’ hands after baptism.” This is the specific meaning of baptism. The two phrases complete each other, illustrating the distinction between the two sacraments while being connected to each other.

Miltiades of Rome in the fourth century says, “The Holy Spirit, Who comes down on the waters of Baptism bearing salvation in His flight, bestows at the font, the fullness of innocence; but in Confirmation He confers an increase of grace. In Baptism we are born again unto life; after Baptism we are strengthened.”

Tertullian in the second century, says, “The hand is laid on us, invoking and inviting the Holy Spirit through benediction … Then, over our cleansed and blessed bodies willingly descends from the Father that Holiest Spirit.”

In the fourth century, Pacian of Barcelona distinguished between the two sacraments saying, “For by baptism sins are washed away; by chrism the Holy Spirit is poured out upon [the individual]. Yet both of these are obtained through the action and words of the bishop. And so it is that the whole man is born again and renewed in Christ.”

St. Augustine also distinguishes between baptism and chrismation, calling the former “spiritual birth” and the latter “nourishment of the Spirit.” In baptism, the believer is born by the Spirit and receives the forgiveness of sins. The first gift prepares the way for the other gifts of the Spirit. It is the gift of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit Himself by whom we are cleansed and are forgiven. He dwells in us to help us in every good deed, for our growth and our perfection.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q714 “How did the Apostles perform this sacrament?”, pp. 543–544
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 714. How did the Apostles perform this sacrament?

While the apostles were baptizing, they laid their hands on the baptized, praying for the indwelling of the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14–17; 19:1–6). Also, bishops laid their hands on the believers, immediately after their baptism, so that they received the gift of the Holy Spirit. As the number of those desiring to join the Church of Christ, as well as those born in Christian families, increased, priests began to anoint the newly baptized with the Chrism oil. The word “Chrism” is a Greek (and Coptic) word meaning “perfume” or “ointment.” This fragrant oil is a mixture of perfumes and spices, sanctified by God’s word and prayer, and prepared by bishops. The newly baptized is anointed thirty-six times by the sign of the cross on all their members. This anointing fills one’s entire being with the Holy Spirit and he becomes the Lord’s anointed. However, this anointing does not replace the laying on of hands. In the West, the Chrism or Myron, is known as the sacrament of confirmation. In the early Church, it was known as “the seal of the Spirit” and was administered together with Baptism.

What does this anointing over all the body members point to? Anointing the forehead points to the sanctification of thoughts, anointing the back points to the sanctification of the heart and desires, anointing the eyes, the ears, and the lips points to the sanctification of the senses, anointing the hands and feet points to the sanctification of the believer’s deeds and actions.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q717 “What is do the laying on of hands and chrismation mean?”, p. 545
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 717. What is do the laying on of hands and chrismation mean?

The laying on of hands is a sign of the transfer of power, not from one person to another, but from God, the source of all power and grace, to the one devoted to the divine work, just as Moses the prophet did by laying his hands on Joshua based on the Lord’s command (Num. 27:18). The apostles also did so for the Holy Spirit to descend upon those who had been baptized (Acts 8:17–18). This mystery is also called, the “seal of the Spirit,” the “sacrament of confirmation,” or “chrismation.” The laying of hands is used in ordinations (Acts 6:6; 2 Tim. 1:6; 1 Tim. 4:14); in absolutions (1 Tim. 5:22); and in the unction of the sick (Mark 16:18). St. Paul the Apostle considered “the doctrine of baptisms, of laying on of hands” to be one of the elementary principles of Christ (Heb. 6:1–2) or one of the basics of the Christian life.

Paul the Apostle uses four Greek terms in 2 Corinthians regarding the anointing of the Holy Spirit: establishment (or confirmation); chrism; seal; and guarantee of the Spirit. He says, “Now He who establishes us with you in Christ and has anointed us is God, who also has sealed us and given us the Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee” (2 Cor. 1:21–22).

Tertullian in the second century talks about chrismation as an established custom in his days, connected to baptism and the laying of hands. He says, “After this, when we have issued from the font, we are thoroughly anointed with a blessed unction … the unction runs carnally, (i.e. on the body,) but profits spiritually; in the same way as the act of baptism itself too is carnal, in that we are plunged in water, but the effect spiritual, in that we are freed from sins. In the next place the hand is laid on us, invoking and inviting the Holy Spirit through benediction.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q715 “What is the role of the sacraments of baptism and chrismation?”, pp. 544–545
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 715. What is the role of the sacraments of baptism and chrismation?

It is the gift of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit Himself by whom we are cleansed and are forgiven. He dwells in us to help us in every good deed, for our growth and our perfection.

Notes: [1384] Origen, De Principiis (On First Principles) 1.3.2 (ANF 4:252). [1385] Origen, De Principiis (On First Principles) 1.3.7 (ANF 4:254). [1386] Miltiades of Rome or Pope Melchiades: quoted in Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica 3.62.1. [1387] Tertullian, On Baptism 8 (ANF 3:672). [1388] Pacian of Barcelona, On Baptism 6 (FOTC 99:92). [1389] See St. Augustine of Hippo, The Works of St Augustine: A Translation for the 21st Century: Part III— Sermons; Volume III: Sermons 51–94, trans., Edmund Hill, ed., John E. Rotelle (New City Press, 1991) 71.19, 33: pp. 257–258, 266–267.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q700 “What prayers are recited while pouring the Myron oil (Chrism) into the water?”, p. 535
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 700. What prayers are recited while pouring the Myron oil (Chrism) into the water?

Therefore, he carries a new heart and a new spirit. In this water, God declares His choice of the church “Zion,” and accepts the believer to be a living member in it.

Indeed, it is a unique text that powerfully and simply brings us to all the secrets of baptism through the psalms. As for the custom of pouring the Chrism into the waters of baptism, as well as anointing the person being baptized with it, it is a very old custom. D. Stone says that this custom started in Egypt in the late fifth century and was found in the west in the sixth century. St. Dionysius the Areopagite says that the bishop “goes himself toward that mother of all divine adoption. With sacred invocations he consecrates the water, completing this by pouring the most holy ointment three times into it, each pouring being made in the form of a cross.”

Notes: [1367] Darwell Stone, Holy Baptism (Longmans, Green, 1899): p. 169. [1368] The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy 2.3.7 (396C), in Pseudo-Dionysius: The Complete Works, trans., C. Luibheid (Paulist Press): p. 203.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q713 “What is the role of the Holy Chrism in the life of the believer?”, p. 543
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 713. What is the role of the Holy Chrism in the life of the believer?

In the sacrament of baptism, the believer experiences the work of the Holy Spirit in the waters of baptism, receives the new birth, and acquires the nature of the new man according to the image of his Creator. The believer is born as a child under the faithful care of the Church and is in constant need of growth and maturity to be truly prepared for the eternal wedding. Then his soul becomes the bride who daily reflects the light of her Bridegroom, the King of kings. All this is what the word of God as well as the Church Fathers’ commentaries, would like us to experience through the chrismation.

St. Macarius the Great says, “And thus the commandments of the Lord being fulfilled by us through His Spirit, who alone knows the will of the Lord, and the Spirit having perfected us in Himself and Himself perfected in us, when we are once cleansed from every defilement and spot of sin, He will present our souls pure and faultless, like fair brides, to Christ, we resting in God in His kingdom, and God resting in us world without end.”

Our God wishes to make from His people a heavenly queen, bearing the icon of her Bridegroom, the King of kings. He grants us the daily experience of the work of the Holy Spirit within us, whom we have received in the holy sacrament of chrismation.

Notes: [1383] St. Macarius the Great, Fifty Spiritual Homilies of St. Macarius the Egyptian, trans., A. J. Mason (London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1921) Homily 19.9: p. 162.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q688 “What are the rites of the holy baptism?”, p. 523
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 688. What are the rites of the holy baptism?

Since the Early Church, baptism has always been rich with rites, profound in theological concepts, and powerful in prayers and effectiveness. Consequently, I wanted to gather some of these details from the Early Church, both in the east and west; as well as referring to the contemporary Coptic rite which bears the spirit of the Early Church and its spiritual and theological depth. Indeed, there are some minor differences in the rites from one Church to another. Therefore, I put together a general framework upon which all of them are built, while also highlighting the differences. I also present the theological and spiritual concepts behind every rite from a biblical and patristic perspective.

1. Preparation of the celebrant.

2. Examination of the candidates for baptism.

3. Learning the sign of the cross.

4. Recitations for exorcising evil spirits.

5. Removal of clothes.

6. Anointment of the candidate with oil.

7. Renunciation of the devil.

8. The mystery of the opening.

9. Confession of faith.

10. Sanctification of the water.

11. Pouring Chrism into the water.

12. Three-fold immersion.

13. Washing of the feet.

14. Anointment of the candidate with the Chrism.

15. Donning white garments.

16. Instruction of the sponsor.

17. Carrying candles.

18. Eating milk mixed with honey.

19. The prayer of untying the girdle.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q721 “Why is this holy sacrament called an anointing?”, p. 549
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 721. Why is this holy sacrament called an anointing?

And as Christ was in reality crucified, and buried, and raised, and you are in Baptism accounted worthy of being crucified, buried, and raised together with Him in a likeness, so is it with the unction also. As He was anointed with an ideal oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Spirit, called oil of gladness, because He is the author of spiritual gladness, so you were anointed with ointment, having been made partakers and fellows of Christ.

“But beware of supposing this to be plain ointment. For as the Bread of the Eucharist, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, is mere bread no longer , but the Body of Christ, so also this holy ointment is no more simple ointment, nor (so to say) common, after invocation, but it is Christ's gift of grace, and, by the advent of the Holy Spirit, is made fit to impart His Divine Nature … and while your body is anointed with the visible ointment, your soul is sanctified by the Holy and life-giving Spirit.

“And you were first anointed on the forehead, that you might be delivered from the shame, which the first man who transgressed bore about with him everywhere; and that with unveiled face ye might reflect as a mirror the glory of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18). Then on your ears; that you might receive the ears which are quick to hear the Divine Mysteries, of which Esaias said, The Lord gave me also an ear to hear (Isa. 50:4); and the Lord Jesus in the Gospel, He that has ears to hear let him hear (Matt 11:15). Then on the nostrils; that receiving the sacred ointment you may say, We are to God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved (2 Cor. 2:15). Afterwards on your breast; that ‘having put on the breast-plate of righteousness’ (Eph. 6:14), you may ‘stand against the wiles of the devil’ (Eph. 6:11). For as Christ after His Baptism, and the visitation of the Holy Spirit, went forth and vanquished the adversary, so likewise you, after Holy Baptism and the Mystical Chrism, having put on the whole armour of the Holy Spirit, are to stand against the power of the adversary, and vanquish it, saying, ‘I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me’ (Phil. 4:13).”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q724 “What is the difference between the anointing of the Old Testament and that of the New Testament?”, pp. 551–552
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 724. What is the difference between the anointing of the Old Testament and that of the New Testament?

The first mention of “anointing” in Scripture is when Jacob saw a ladder in a dream, which was set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and the Lord standing above it, and the angels of God were ascending and descending on it, and he said, “‘How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven!’ and then he took the stone that he had put at his head, and he poured oil on top of it.” (Gen. 28:12– 18). The anointing was used to proclaim the sanctification of the place and its consecration, for it to become “Bethel” or the “House of God.” Also, the Mosaic law instructed the anointing of kings, priests, places (the temple), and the vessels that were consecrated for the service of the Lord’s house.

Chrismation aims to make the person or object consecrated to God only. All this, throughout the generations, is a symbol pointing to the coming of the Messiah whom the Father has anointed with the oil of gladness (Ps. 45:7) to preach good tidings to the poor (Isa. 61:1). He is the center of the Father’s gladness and joy because while He is the Logos of God and the Only Begotten Son, He was incarnate to reconcile humanity with the Father. Thus, He is capable of transmitting this heavenly joy to the poor who were deprived of the joy of the exalted life. Christ was anointed with the oil of gladness so that we would be anointed in Him because we are members of His body, and therefore are anointed in Him.

St. Jacob of Sarug says, “All righteous people portrayed the chrismation and decorated it with their proclamations. Each one of them described its beauty during his time. Moses came, and he placed the table in the tabernacle of that time and sanctified it with the blood of sacrifices and with oil. By oil, Samuel gave the kingdom to the children of his people, and also Elisha ministered with the mystery of the kings’ anointing. As for Christ, He is the most exalted among all the Christian ranks and through Him, all the prophetic mysteries were served … The Shepherd designed the anointing.”

Notes: [1416] St. Jacob of Sarug, Memra on the Renewal of the Temple.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q726 “What is the role of Chrismation in the life of the baptized person?”, pp. 552–553
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 726. What is the role of Chrismation in the life of the baptized person?

First: The indwelling of the Holy Spirit as St. Paul says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

Second: The consecration of the body and soul. Tertullian says, “The flesh, indeed, is washed, in order that the soul may be cleansed (through baptism); the flesh is anointed, that the soul may be consecrated; the flesh is signed (with the cross), that the soul too may be fortified; the flesh is shadowed with the imposition of hands, that the soul also maybe illuminated by the Spirit; the flesh feeds on the body and blood of Christ, that the soul likewise may fatten on its God. They cannot then be separated (the flesh and soul) … when they are united in their service.”

St Cyril of Jerusalem says, “Which ointment [the Chrism] is symbolically applied to your forehead and your other senses; and while your body is anointed with the visible ointment, your soul is sanctified by the Holy and life-giving Spirit.”

St. Athanasius of Alexandria says, “Hence also, through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands, the Holy Spirit was given to those who were being born again … When has this been fulfilled, save when the Lord came and renewed all things by grace? Our spirit is renewed; but the Holy Spirit is not simply spirit, but God says it is his Spirit, whereby ours is renewed.”

St. Basil the Great says, “We were sealed by the Holy Spirit through God. And as we die in Christ to be born again, we are thus sealed by the Holy Spirit to receive His splendor, image and grace, which is undoubtedly our spiritual seal. Even though our bodies are visibly sealed, our hearts are spiritually sealed, for the Holy Spirit to engrave within us the heavenly icon.”

Third: The consecration of the soul as a heavenly bride. Psalm 45 is truly marvelous, where the Psalmist talks about the mystery of the unity between the Church and Christ the Lord, or their marriage. God the Father sees Himself performing this unique, unseen divine anointing, saying, “Therefore God, Your God, has anointed You with the oil of gladness” (Ps. 45:7). The Coptic Church took the rite of anointing the bride and the bridegroom with oil in the sacrament of holy matrimony from this specific psalm. The Church anoints them so they can understand that their marriage is an antitype of the heavenly wedding.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q703 “Is the newly baptized person anointed with the Holy Chrism?”, pp. 536–537
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 703. Is the newly baptized person anointed with the Holy Chrism?

St. Cyril of Jerusalem has a full lecture about the anointing with the Holy Myron (Chrism). This occurs immediately after baptism, being a sacrament on its own. St. Theophilus of Antioch says that are called Christians because we are anointed by God. St. Cyprian of Carthage says, “It is necessary also for him who is baptized to be anointed that, having received chrism, that is anointing, he can be anointed of God and have in himself the grace of Christ.”

The priest anoints all the body members, announcing the sanctification of this body and this soul, through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. Then he prays, “O Lord who alone are mighty, who performs every wonder and nothing is impossible for You, rather by Your will, Your power works in all things. Grant the Holy Spirit in the pouring out of the holy Myron. Let it be a life-giving seal and a confirmation to Your servants, through Your only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ Our Lord. Through whom the glory is due unto You …”

After the priest anoints the person thirty-six times from the top of the head to the smallest toe, the priest then lays his hands on him/her and says, “May you be blessed with the blessing of the heavenly and the blessing of the angels. May the Lord Jesus Christ bless you, and in His name …” — he then breathes in the face and says — “receive the Holy Spirit and be a purified vessel through Jesus Christ our Lord to whom is the glory with His good Father and the Holy Spirit.”

Here we notice three features of the Coptic rite: the use of the Holy Myron; the laying of the hands for blessing; and the breath of the Spirit in the person’s face.

Notes: [1372] St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Five Catechetical Lectures (On the Mysteries) 3 (NPNF II/7:149–150). [1373] St. Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus 1.12 (ANF 2:92). [1374] St. Cyprian of Carthage, The Epistles of Cyprian 70.2 (FOTC 51:260).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q723 “What is the difference between Christ’s anointing and the anointing of the Chrism (or Myron) of those who are newly baptized?”, pp. 550–551
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 723. What is the difference between Christ’s anointing and the anointing of the Chrism (or Myron) of those who are newly baptized?

The Spirit descended and remained upon the Word of God, who was incarnate, being united with Him and equal to Him. Hence, we the believers have received the right to receive the Holy Spirit as a free gift.

St. Ambrose says, “There was therefore a pouring out upon us of the Spirit, but upon the Lord Jesus, when He was in the form of man, the Spirit abode … Around us is the liberality of the Giver in abundant provision, in Him abides forever the fullness of the Spirit. He shed forth then what He deemed to be sufficient for us, and what was shed forth is not separated nor divided; but He has a unity of fullness wherewith He may enlighten the sight of our hearts according to what our strength is capable of. Lastly, we receive so much as the advancing of our mind acquires, for the fullness of the grace of the Spirit is indivisible, but is shared in by us according to the capacity of our own nature.”

He also says, “David has reason to cry, like a man renewed, ‘And I will go in to the altar of my God, to God, who gives joy to my youth’ (Ps. 43:4). Even as he had said earlier that he had grown old among his enemies, as we read in the sixth psalm, here he says that youth has been restored to him after the lengthy old age of man’s fall. For we are renewed through the regeneration experienced in baptism, we are renewed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, we shall be renewed also through the resurrection, even as he says in a later passage, ‘your youth is renewed like the eagle’s’ (Ps. 103:5). Learn the manner of our renewal: ‘You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed, you shall wash me and 1 shall be made whiter than snow’ (Ps. 51:9). And in Isaiah, ‘Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow’ (Isa. 1:18). One who changes from the darkness of sin into the light of virtue and into grace is properly renewed. Thus, one who earlier was stained with foul defilement may shine with a brightness that is whiter than snow.”

Notes: [1414] St. Ambrose of Milan, On the Holy Spirit 1.8.93 (NPNF II/10:105–106). [1415] St. Ambrose of Milan, The Prayer of Job and David 4.9.35 (FOTC 65:418–419).

Fourth: Enlightenment of the mind, and divine providence against the devil and the

powers of darkness. “But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, He will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you” (John. 14:26).

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “You are protected by your seal from the evil attacks of the wicked one, him who by your baptism has no authority over you. Keep This unspotted: for it shall teach you all things, if it abide in you, as you have just heard declared by the blessed John, discoursing much concerning this Unction. For this holy thing is a spiritual safeguard of the body, and salvation of the soul.” He also says, “Your name is now inscribed, and you are invited to enter the (spiritual) camp.” “Every one of you approaches, presents himself before God, in the presence of the innumerable host of angels, so that the Holy Spirit may place a mark on your souls. Thus, your souls are counted in the great army of the Lord.”

St Cyprian says, “I wished indeed to strive bravely, and, remembering my oath (sacramentum) I took up the arms of devotion and faith.” Tertullian says, “We were called to God’s army … when we responded to the words of this Sacrament.”

St. Basil the Great says, “How will the guardian angel defend you, how could he protect you from the enemy, if he is unable to see the seal? Did you not know that the destroyer passed over the houses sealed with blood, during the early days of Moses the savior, and he killed the firstborn of the unsealed? The unsealed treasure is easily stolen by thieves, the unmarked herd are safely stolen.”

St. Ambrose says, “The Holy Spirit has delivered us from that Gentile impurity … Excellent, then, is that grace which changes the rage of beasts into the simplicity of the Spirit.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q717 “What is do the laying on of hands and chrismation mean?”, pp. 545–546
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Chrismation — 717. What is do the laying on of hands and chrismation mean?

In the next place the hand is laid on us, invoking and inviting the Holy Spirit through benediction.”

St. Cyprian says, “For those who had believed in Samaria had believed in the true faith and had been baptized within by the deacon, Philip, whom the same Apostles had sent, in the Church, which is one and to which alone it is permitted to give the grace of baptism and to absolve sins (cf. Acts 8:14–17). And, therefore, it was not necessary for those who had received legitimate and ecclesiastical baptism to be baptized again, but only that which was lacking was supplied by Peter and John, after having prayed for them and imposed hands upon them that the Holy Spirit should be invoked and infused into them.”

St. Augustine also talks about the laying on of hands and chrismation in connection with the Holy Spirit as the gift of God, and not of the disciples personally, “For no one of His disciples gave the Holy Spirit, since they prayed that He might come upon those upon whom they laid their hands [Acts 19:6]: they did not give Him themselves.”

Notes: [1390] Tertullian, On Baptism 7–8 (ANF 3:672). [1391] St. Cyprian of Carthage, The Epistles of Cyprian 73.9 (FOTC 51:273). [1392] St. Augustine of Hippo, On the Holy Trinity 15.26 (NPNF I/3:224).

records.question: summarize what the catechism says about baptism
records.answer:
The Coptic Orthodox Catechism teaches that baptism is a sacrament instituted by the Church’s faith in the Orthodox Creed, involving triple immersion in water in the name of the Holy Trinity. It symbolizes burial with Christ, dying to sin, and rising to a new life of holiness by divine grace, necessary for entering the Kingdom of God [3]. Candidates must have true faith, sincere repentance, and be able to confess the Orthodox Creed [4].

The baptismal rite includes preparation of the celebrant, examination of candidates, learning the sign of the cross, exorcisms, removal of clothes, anointing with oil, renunciation of the devil, confession of faith, sanctification of the water, triple immersion, washing of feet, anointing with Chrism, donning white garments, instruction of sponsors, carrying candles, eating milk with honey, and the prayer of loosening the girdle [10].

Candidates confess their faith by responding to questions about belief in God the Father, the Son (Jesus Christ born of the Virgin Mary, who died, rose, ascended, and will judge), and the Holy Spirit, each followed by immersion [1][16]. The priest breathes on the candidate to expel unclean spirits and the candidate publicly renounces Satan and all his works before baptism [1][7][8][16].

The waters of baptism are consecrated with the sign of the cross and prayers invoking the Holy Spirit’s power to cast out demons and sanctify the candidate [6][7]. Baptism is linked to Old Testament prefigurations such as Noah’s dove, the crossing of the Red Sea, the bitter waters of Marah, Joshua crossing the Jordan, Elijah’s sacrifice, and Naaman’s healing, symbolizing purification, new life, and victory over evil [11][12].

After baptism, the newly baptized are anointed with Chrism to receive the Holy Spirit’s support in spiritual warfare [8]. They wear white garments symbolizing purity and new nature, girded to show their vital membership in the Church, and crowned as a sign of victory over Satan [14]. The prayer of loosening the girdle on the eighth day celebrates the baptized person’s steadfastness and growth in grace [14].

Catechumens are taught Scripture, important Church books, and simplified theological dogmas such as the Apostles’ Creed, preparing them for baptism and life in the Church [15]. Baptism is confessed once for the remission of sins and is not repeated if one returns to the faith after falling away [13].

In summary, baptism in the Coptic Orthodox Church is a profound sacrament of faith, repentance, spiritual cleansing, and new birth into the Church and the Kingdom of God, rich in biblical symbolism, liturgical rites, and theological meaning [1][3][4][10][13][16].

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q698 “What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith?”, pp. 531–532
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 698. What are the main articles of faith in the baptismal confession of faith?

The early Church focused on faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as well as the confession of the catholic (universal) Church and the remission of sins. The Canons of St. Hippolytus state that candidates for baptism should face the east and say, “I believe and kneel before You and before Your greatness, O Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Then, they are immersed in the water and stand facing the east. Another priest lays his hands on their heads and asks them: “Do you believe in God the Father the Pantocrator?” They would then respond saying, “I believe” and are immersed for the first time.

After the first immersion, they are asked: “Do you believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God who was born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, who died and rose from the dead on the third day, who ascended to the heavens and sat at the right hand of the Father and will come to judge the living and the dead?” And when they respond saying, “I believe,” they are immersed for the second time.

When they are asked, “Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?” They would respond saying: “I believe” and are immersed for the third and last time.

With every immersion, the priest says, “I baptize you in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” After that, they are anointed with the holy Chrism (or Myron oil) and they put on their clothes and enter the church. They kiss the hands of the bishop and greet him with the holy kiss and then the eucharist is offered.

Origen, in his commentary on St. John’s Gospel, says that if any of these basic points are missed in the confession of faith, the whole faith is lost.

In the current Coptic rite, the candidate for baptism (or his parents and/or sponsors) repeat the following words after the priest to renounce Satan, saying: “I renounce you Satan and all your unclean works and all your wicked angels and all your evil demons and all your power and all your abominable service and all your evil cunning and error and all your army and all your authority and all the rest of your impieties. I renounce you. I renounce you. I renounce you.”

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q697 “How do candidates for baptism confess their faith?”, p. 531
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Rites of Holy Baptism — 697. How do candidates for baptism confess their faith?

By the mediation of the priest, we are prepared to enter His house, to see Him, to know Him and for Him to dwell within us that we may be counted among the citizens of that city and are counted trustworthy.” Again, he says, “By confessing the faith, you associate yourself with God by the bishop and you enter into a covenant in which you declare that you will be persistent in seeking the love of the divine nature.”

In the current Coptic rite, the baptized or the sponsor publicly repeats the main aspects of the faith after the celebrant priest before baptism. In the early Church, the candidate would declare his or her faith from inside the waters of baptism. This was done in the form of questions that the priest or bishop would ask and to which the candidate would respond, as is mentioned in the Canons of St. Hippolytus.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q676 “What is the sacrament of baptism?”, pp. 509–510
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Baptism — 676. What is the sacrament of baptism?

First: This sacrament is declared by the faith of the Church in the Orthodox Creed.

Second: The one who being baptized is immersed in water three times in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Third: He accepts being buried with Christ to enjoy the resurrected life and dies to the life of lustful sin. He then lives a life that is appropriate of the children of God with respect to Christ’s holiness and righteousness by the power of the divine grace. Christ Himself declared that no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q680 “What is required of those who wish to be baptized?”, p. 515
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Sacrament of Baptism — 680. What is required of those who wish to be baptized?

For adults, they are asked to have true faith with sincere repentance and to be able to recite the Orthodox Creed. In the past, when people heard the word of God, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Men and brethren, what shall we do? Peter said to them, “Repent and let every one of you baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:37–38). The Gospel says, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16).

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q664 “What are the features of the baptistery?”, p. 500
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Church Nave — 664. What are the features of the baptistery?

The Dome: On ascending from the baptismal font, the baptized person sees the dome to remind him of heaven. It expresses the Church’s belief that baptism is the beginning of a heavenly life, whereby the newly-baptized partakes of the Kingdom of God.

The Stairs: In most of our ancient churches, there are two sets of stairs, one at the east and the other at the west. They form part of the font structure, which demonstrates some aspects of the baptismal rite. By one of the stairs, the candidate descends and goes into the water, while the celebrant of the mystery (the priest) stands on the other side of stairs, placing his hand on the candidate’s head and immersing him thrice in the water. St. Cyril of Jerusalem explains this rite, saying, “You descend three times into the water, and ascend again, here also is a hidden glance at the three day burial of Christ and his resurrection, since the redeeming water offers you death and life simultaneously.” And St. John Chrysostom gives a great analysis of this rite, saying, “The immersion of the head in the water resembles the burial of our old man, so that the new man may emerge. As it is feasible for us to dip then float, it is equally feasible for God to bury the old man and put on us the new man.”

The Baptistery Icon: In the majority of Coptic churches, a baptistery icon is fitted on the dome of the baptistery. It is usually the icon of Christ’s baptism in the Jordan by St. John the Baptist, which signifies an essential theological fact that was declared by the School of Alexandria. It assures us that our baptism is derived from and is an extension of Christ’s baptism; the former derives its effectiveness from the latter. As St. Clement of Alexandria says, the believer unites with Christ during His baptism in a unity that can never be dissolved.

Notes: [1276] See St. Clement of Alexandria, The Stromata, or Miscellanies 7.3 (ANF 2:526).

We cannot forget also the role of the sign of the cross in this matter. St. Augustine explains that the sign of the cross is made on the waters of baptism as well as on the oil of the Chrism and on the Eucharist.
