passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, p. 115
passages.text:
Saint: SEVERUS, PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH, ST. — The Saint and God’s Miracles

The Saint and God’s Miracles:

God performed so many miracles and signs on his hands. Many were documented in the manuscripts, which covered the saint's biography.Among those miracles, we may mention the following:

1- The Rain Fall because of his Prayer:

When a draught dwelt upon the land, followed by a mighty famine, St. Claudius, together with a group of believers, went to the cell of Abba Severus, and actively sought from him to pray to God to send rain to save the humans and animals. The saint cried hard and prayed together with the brethren, and Lo! The gates of heaven were opened, and rain heavily fell. On seeing that, they all glorified God, saying: “God set up for us a great prophet.” The eyewitness manuscripts writer added in amazement: “Truly, I kept quiet in my puzzlement; his face was shining like the sun's rays for his purity and for being filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

2- Healing of a Leper:

When Fr. Theodore was inflicted with leprosy in his hands and was banned from entering into the church. On hearing about the miracles God was performing in the hands of Abba Severus, he went to him. The saint first sought from him, not to partake in the heresy of the Nestorians, then sought from him to go and take a bath in the water of the nearby well, which he did, and he was healed. On seeing that, many of the Nestorians returned to the Upright faith.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Bessarion the Great, p. 351
passages.text:
Saint: BESSARION THE GREAT, ST. — God's Wonders through Him

God's Wonders through Him:

St. ‘Bessarion's’ disciple told those stories:

 “The saint was traveling along a road, and he came to the river ‘Chrysoroan,’ and there were no means available for crossing it. The saint then stretched out his hands and prayed and crossed over to the other side. When I saw that, I was amazed and gave the saint a metonia and asked him: ‘Father, while you walked on the river, how far up did your feet felt the water under you?’ To which he answered: ‘As far as my ankles, but all the rest of it was solid underneath my feet!’”  “On our way to visit one of the great wise men, it was going to be sunset before we would have reached our destination. The saint then prayed: ‘O Lord, keep the sun in its place until I reach Your servant,’ and God granted him his request.”  “I came once to talk to him in his cell, to see him standing while extending his hands towards heaven and praying. I waited for four days and four nights until he called me, saying: ‘Come my son.’ Then, we went out and kept walking, and in our way, I got thirsty and said to him: ‘Father, I am very thirsty.’ He separated for a little distance and prayed, then came back to me carrying water in his robe, out of air! I drank it, and we kept going on our way to ‘Lycopolis’ (Assiut) to Abba ‘John.’ After greeting one another, the saint prayed, sat, and told him about a night vision he saw. He said: ‘From the Lord, a decree came that all the temples of the idols will disappear,’ which happened at the time.”  “A man in Egypt had a paralyzed little boy. He carried him to Abba ‘Bessarion,’ then he left him crying at the door of his cell and went a little distance away. On hearing the voice of the little boy, the saint came out to see him, and he said to him: ‘Who are you? And how did you get here?’ The little boy answered: ‘My father brought me here and went his way, and here I am crying.’ The saint told him: ‘Get up and run after him.’ The paralyzed boy was instantly healed and ran after his father, who was so happy for that miracle, and they went their way.”  “Another time, a man with an evil spirit was brought to the church, where prayers were raised for him. However, the demon did not come out of him. The priests then said, ‘No one can drive him out except Abba ‘Bessarion;’ but if we asked him to do it, he will not even come to the church.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Hilarion the Great, pp. 260–261
passages.text:
Saint: HILARION THE GREAT, ST. — God's Miracles performed on His Hands

God's Miracles performed on His Hands:

In the city of Eleutheropolis (Beit Guvrin near Hebron), a barren noblewoman came to seek his prayers to ask God to give her a child. Running away from her, she kept chasing him while bitterly weeping. He finally had compassion on her, blessed her, and told her: “My daughter, be sure that God responded to your request.” The following year, she came to him carrying her child, and the news spread all over the area.

When the miraculous works of God kept happening again and again through this saint, multitudes of people came to seek his prayers. Many pagans proclaimed their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, and a lot of believers asked him to accept them among his disciples. Then, at the age of sixty-five, St. Hilarion felt by the spirit that Abba Anthony the Great reposed.

Fleeing from the Crowds:

When the life of St. Hilarion became so overcrowded, he started to get disturbed; and he said to himself: “Now, I have returned to the world, and got my reward in this life. All Palestine comes to me, and I have now fields and possessions under the veil of the needs of the brethren.” Accordingly, he decided to abandon the location. However, all the brethren tried to prevent him from leaving. So, he fasted for seven days without eating or drinking until they let him go. He took some of his disciples and set out along with them in the wilderness while fasting until sunset.

Arriving in Egypt, he set out to the Mountain of Abba Anthony and sought the place of his burial. Yet, his search was to no avail since Abba Anthony had already given a strict instruction to have his burial place concealed, for fear that some rich man might come and build a Church over his body.

Abba Hilarion returned to Aphroditiopolis (Atfiah), where he lived in silence and tranquility. But, smelling the sweet fragrance of the Lord Jesus Christ in him, great multitudes came again, seeking his prayers and blessing. Then, he decided to flee to someplace, where people did not know his language. He sailed together with a disciple and set out to the island of Sicily. Not being able to pay the expanses of his trip, he gave the captain his gospel he wrote by himself, but, seeing his poverty and the sanctity of his life, the captain gave it back to him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Petarpemtis, the Blessed, pp. 403–404
passages.text:
Saint: PETARPEMTIS, THE BLESSED — His Fatherhood and Miracles

His Fatherhood and Miracles:

At the end of the seven years, St. Petarpemtis returned from the wilderness bearing exalted spiritual virtues within himself, along with fantastic simplicity and strong asceticism. So, many others followed his example; mostly, they were young men.

According to St. Palladius (386-430 AD), this blessed man, whenever a Christian man would die, used to stay beside his body the whole night praying, then he would shroud him and bury him. On seeing him doing that, his disciple, longing to have the same portion, asked his mentor: “When I die, Father, will you do the same to me?” The father answered him: “I shall do this until you say Enough”. After a long time the disciple passed away, and his mentor stayed beside him the whole night; then he shrouded him by himself in the Divine fear and reverence; and while everyone was watching, he said: “Have I, my son, shrouded you well, or is there anything more you want me to do?” To the astonishment of all, they heard a voice coming out of the corpse (body), saying: “You shrouded me well, Father, and fulfilled your promise to me.” Those present got filled with fear and glorified God.

The saint kept on going back and forth between the wilderness and the dwelling place of his disciple, and it happened once he was going back to his disciples, and some of them were inflicted by fever; the sun was about to set, and he felt that he should not walk in the darkness; following what the Holy Bible said: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtakes you”

(John 12:35). However, because he was in a rush to see his sick brethren; he asked the Lord to hold the sun until he would reach them; which the Lord did, and when he saw how his disciples were astonished, he said to them: “Don't you remember the Lord's words; If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, “Move from here to there, and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you” (Matt. 17:25).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Joannes, the Short, p. 370
passages.text:
Saint: JOANNES, THE SHORT, ST. — His Love for the Salvation of Others

His Love for the Salvation of Others:

The repentance of the lady saint Paisa will remain a living testimony of the profound caring of St. John the Short - who was preoccupied with the contemplation in the Divinities - for the salvation of others.

His Compassion on Others:

While the saint was traveling in the Scetis along with some brethren, it happened that their guide lost his way in the darkness of the night. Abba John told the brethren: “I shall pretend that I am so tired that I cannot walk any more; and that I need to rest until the morning. For, if we alert our guide, he might become embarrassed and feel uncomfortable.” So they did, and in the morning they quickly found their way.

Healing the Sick:

St. Joannes the Short was granted from God the grace of healing the sick. Among the accounts which were written about him, the following stories:

Once, the saint encountered in a field a farmer inflicted with leprosy. The man sought his prayer to be healed. He prayed on some water, gave it to him to drink, anointed him in the name of the Holy Trinity, and the man was healed and glorified God. Another time, a woman came to him, she was possessed by an unclean spirit that tormented her quite often. The saint had compassion for her and prayed on her behalf. The unclean spirit came out of her, and she was healed.

He once encountered an older woman who asked him bread for herself and her blind son. The saint gave her all the bread that he had; prayed for the sake of her blind son; made the sign of the Cross on his eyes, and he instantly was able to see.

In the doxology of Abba Joannes the Short, it came: “You came to be a haven for salvation; you raised the dead, drove the demons out, and healed the sick. You became worthy, O father Abba Joannes, to sit together with the Apostles to judge your generation.”

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius of Alexandria, pp. 14–15
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS OF ALEXANDRIA, ST. — The Bunch of Grapes

The Bunch of Grapes:

It happened once that someone brought to St. Macarius a splendid bunch of grapes, which he has not tasted for so long. Yet he overcame his desire and gave the bunch to a sick brother, who, in turn, gave it to another, counting him more in need for it. The bunch of grape kept on being carried from one cell to another until finally it was brought back intact to St. Macarius, who rejoiced in the lovely relationships between the monks. (Some believe that this incident happened to St. Macarius the Great).

His Miracles:

The saint managed to heal a countless number of sick people and those who were possessed by evil spirits. He was granted that power that by merely making the sign of the Holy Cross on those people, they would get healed.

Once, a hyena came to his cell and attempted to drag him by his robe. He followed it to its cave, where it brought its three handicapped cubs to the saint. Amazed at the wisdom of that beast, he prayed, put his hand on the three cubs, healed them, and went his way to his cell. After a while, the hyena came back holding by its mouth a piece of leather hide, which the saint kept using as a floor-mat until the day he reposed.

When it happened that there was no rain in Alexandria for an extended period, he was called over by the pope. Once he reached the papal residence, the rain started pouring and kept on until they sought from the saint to stop it. He then prayed, and it did.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Pasantaos, the Bishop, pp. 372–373
passages.text:
Saint: PASANTAOS, THE BISHOP, ST. — His Miracles

His Miracles:

His biography tells us some of the miracles God performed on his hands: When the water in the vessels dried up while being on the mountain, and the brethren were on the brink of dying of thirst; the saint prayed, then sought from them to check the vessels. They found them full of water and they glorified God.

He once entered into a tunnel inside the mountain, where he found a dead body of a pagan man. The dead man talked to the saint about the hell he was experiencing before he went back to sleep.

Once two women afflicted by a disease came to see him seeking his prayers. On seeing them, he forsook his water pot, covered his head, and hastened to leave. Not being able to catch him, the two women just took some of the dust he stepped on with his feet, prayed and they were healed.

It was said that he could not find water in certain locations of the wilderness, so he prayed for three days, after which he found a well of fresh water. This well is still near the city of Naqqada, named after him, up to this very day.

Ordained as a Bishop on Qift:

St. Pasantaos was ordained as a bishop on the city of Qift by the 35th Pope of Alexandria St. Damianus (569-605 AD), around the year 598 AD. He was a contemporary of Abba Constantine, the bishop of Assiut; and the Persian invasion of Egypt.

He accepted the bishopric only by a Divine call; for while he was praying one evening, three angels of light appeared to him in the form of monks; they gave him peace and proclaimed to him that he would be ordained as a bishop on the city of Qift, and they sought from him not to reject the call, and then they disappeared. He prayed until the morning; when the priests came to seize him to be ordained as a bishop. He told them: “If I do not fear to disobey Him who commands me, I would never listen to you, even if you cut my head off.”

He was a good shepherd always watching on the flock of Christ and cared for the salvation of everyone. Also, he was a generous giver, he left nothing in his diocese except one dinar that he gained by the work of his hands; it was intended to be used only for the expense of shrouding him.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. Germanus, the Bishop, pp. 178–179
passages.text:
Saint: GERMANUS, THE BISHOP, ST. — His Miracles

The bishop took hold of the harness of his wild horse and calmed it down. Astonished at the courage of the older man, the commander promised to put his mission on hold, until the bishop would go to the emperor to get his permission to forgive those people.

Going to Italy to plead his case, the bishop spent the night in the house of a priest who was his friend. There he anointed his mute daughter with the holy oil, prayed for her, and she was healed.

In the way, he encountered an older man carrying a heavy burden and was trying to cross a canal. The saint took the load off him, carried it across the canal, then returned to carry the older man himself and crossed the canal again. The saint did all that although he was as old and frail because of his asceticism.

On his arrival to Rafina, he was received with great honor by its bishop Peter Chrislogos, as well as by Emperor Valentinian III (424-455 AD), and the queen mother Galla Placidia. There, he was granted by God to raise from death the son of the emperor's secretary, who fell into a fire and died. The emperor accepted the intercession of the bishop and forgave the people of Britain. It was also said that, on his way, passing by prison, the prisoners cried out, asking for his visit, but for fear that the bishop might request opening the gate of the prison, the guards closed the gates and fled away. The saint by his bare hands opened the gates, sat together with the prisoners, took them with him to the emperor, and the emperor forgave them too because of his intercession.

His Departure:

One day, the saint said to the bishops who came to visit him that his time of departure to heaven was close at hand. He requested from the queen mother who cared for his health to move his dead body home to his city. Eventually, the saint reposed in the Lord on the 31st of July in the year 448 AD, at seventy years of age.

[Butler, Lives of the Saints, August 3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abu Fana, pp. 79–80
passages.text:
Saint: ABU FANA, ST. — A Spiritual Center

A Spiritual Center:

Despite his great love for the life of solitude, he did not shut off his heart nor his cave in the face of his brethren. But his dwelling place turned into a center of spiritual radiation. The elder monks residing on the mountain used to come to seek his counsel, and he used to inflame their hearts with longing for the Christian perfection in the Lord.

His Prophesying About the Death of the King:

His disciple once saw him sad, and on asking him about the reason, the saint told him that on that day, the soul of emperor Theodosius the Great was sought, and the bonds of the State order were about to come apart. The disciple made a note of the prophecy date, and after some time, when he descended to the world, he came to know that the emperor has died on that exact day.

Examples of His Miracles:

1- A priest once came to him inflicted with a skin disease that exposed the bone of his forehead. And, despite the persistence of his disciple in seeking from the saint to come out and pray for the sick priest, he did not pay attention to him. Finally, he explained to his disciples that, because the priest has defiled the house of God by adultery and taking the church money to spend on his evil desires, he had no liberty to seek healing from God. Later on, he had compassion on him and asked his disciples to tell the priest that if he wanted to be healed, he should promise God to forsake the priesthood for the rest of his life and to repent regretting his horrible behavior. As the priest did promise, the saint came out to pray for him, until he was wholly healed of his sickness with true repentance.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Macarius, the Great, p. 21
passages.text:
Saint: MACARIUS, THE GREAT, ST. — His Gifts

His Gifts:

The ‘Apophthegmata Patrum’ (Sayings of the Fathers) referred to the saint's wrestling against the demons. According to St. Palladius, the saint was granted the gift of performing miracles. He raised someone from the dead to save a heretic who did not believe in the resurrection of the bodies.

St. Macarius and the Two Saintly Women:

When he once sought from God to show him someone equal to him in his behavior, a voice came to him from heaven, saying: “So far, you have not reached the level of two women in Alexandria.” He inquired until he reached their house. They welcomed him and washed his feet. Inquiring from them about their story, one of them said to him: “We were not related to each other in the flesh before we were married to two brothers. We sought from them to let us be nuns; and when they refused, we vowed to spend our lives fasting until the evenings, and to practice continuous prayers. Each of us got a boy; when one of those boys would cry, one of us would hasten to embrace him and nourish him, even if he is not her own. We go through our lives in unity of views, unity in our ways, and the unity of our hearts is our goal. Our husbands work in shepherding; we are poor, but we are satisfied with our daily bread, and what remains, we give to the poor.” On hearing this, the saint cried out, saying: “Indeed, God looks at the hearts; and grants His Holy Spirit to whoever seeks Him.” He bid them farewell and returned to the wilderness. Also, in Osim, there was a monk who led some people astray by claiming that there was no resurrection from the dead. When the bishop of Osim came to the saint and told him about that monk, the saint went to see him and managed to bring him back from his vanity.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Apollo and Amon, pp. 221–222
passages.text:
Saint: APOLLO AND AMON — Some of the Saint’s Wonders

It happened once, as the saint returned to his cave with a group of monks to hold the divine liturgy; afterward it was time to eat, so he said to them: “My children, if we are true believers and ministers of the Lord Christ, let each of us seek from God to give us something to eat.” Then he bowed on the ground and prayed with faith. As night came, they saw some strangers unknown to any of them stand before the door of the cave, carrying grapes, figs, pears, different kinds of nuts, honey, a box of butter, dates and a lot of warm bread; saying that a rich man sent these to them, and they hastened to depart. The monks kept eating from that provision until the feast of the Pentecost, believing that it was God who sent it to them. 12hortly after that last miracle, there was a famine in the region of Thebes. Many Christians with their women and children took refuge in the monastery. The blessed saint generously kept giving the guests food until there were only three baskets of bread left, just enough for one day, while the famine was still at its peak. At this point, the saint took the remaining food and cast it in the middle because of the brethren and the guests, and with a loud voice, he said, “Isn’t the Hand of God capable of adding more?! For the Holy Spirit is saying that ‘The bread in these baskets will not run out until we come to eat new bread.” And, it so actually happened that they kept eating off these baskets for as long as four months; and the same thing happened to the oil, wheat, etc. Satan was so furious that he appeared to the saint and told him: “What do you think you are?! Elijah, or one of the prophets or apostles to dare to do such a thing?” The blessed man answered him: “Why would I not do this? Were the blessed prophets and the holy apostles not human? Have the fathers not delivered to us such a tradition? Is God close to us only in certain times and far away at other times?! God, at all times, can do such things for us, and nothing is impossible for Him. If God is Good, why are you corrupt, you evil one?” 13- St. ‘Jerome’ repeated: “Now let me repeat what I saw by my eyes: The 500 brethren kept on eating from those baskets until they had enough, then they find those baskets become filled again, by the blessing of the saint.” 14- St. ‘Jerome’ told about another incident: He was in the company of two of his brethren going unannounced, to visit the saint’s monastery. And, while they were approaching the monastery, some monks received them with joy and praise, as was the custom of the monks.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Abu Fana, p. 80
passages.text:
Saint: ABU FANA, ST. — Examples of His Miracles

2- A man came to him with his son to get his blessing. But, it happened that the son fell from the mountain and died. The father carried him to the cave of the saint, placed him in front of the entrance, and without telling the saint about what happened, he asked him to bless him. The saint made the sign of the cross on the boy, and said to him, “Get up, go to your father, and hold his hand.” So the boy did. In great joy, the father cast himself on the ground before the saint, thanking him and glorifying God who performs miracles through His saints. 3- Getting to know the day of his repose, he asked the priest to come over to perform the Holy Eucharist. He had communion standing on his swollen feet, bid farewell from the brethren, blessed them, sought their blessing, prayed, and delivered his soul in the hands of the Lord on 25 Amshir.

His Monastery in Delga:

A monastery was built in his name close to ‘Beni Khaled, a village of ‘Delga’ about 20 kilometers south of the province of El-Ashmonein.

[Nabil Selim: Monasteries of the Fathers (9): St. Epiphanius (Abu Fana) on Mount Delga; an annex of his book on ‘The Monasteries of the Fathers (8) on SS Bishai and Basentaos of the Tod]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Badasuis, pp. 289–290
passages.text:
Saint: BADASUIS, ST. — His Strife

His Strife:

He loved the life of seclusion and tranquility under the guidance of his mentor abba ‘Paul,’ practicing a severely ascetic life in his attire, fasting, prayers, and continuous metanoias day and night.

God’s Wonders through Him:

A disabled man, since his birth, kept on visiting the monastery. Then, he heard about the holy pious life of St. ‘Badasuis.' So, he asked him to pray for him and make the sign of the Cross on him. When the saint did that, the disabled man was healed, and he jumped joyfully praising God. The same miracle happened with a blind man, and the fame of St. ‘Badasius’ spread so fast that a multitude of people came seeking his prayers and blessings in the Lord.

On seeing the work of God through him, the abbot of the monastery decided to let him wear the holy monastic ‘Eskeem’ (which is given to the monks of high spiritual stature). On hearing of that plan, St. ‘Badasuis’ secretly fled the area for two weeks. When he returned, he proclaimed his total rejection of such an honor, which he considered far beyond his actual stature. He told them that the miracles of healing attributed to him were all gifts from God for the sake of the faith of those concerned, and he had nothing to do with it. Persisting on his rejection, he was left alone.

Then, it happened that ‘Arsinoe,’ the wife of one of the church elders in the town of ‘Faw’ was inflicted with sickness in her face, with severe pain, mainly near her right eye. When the physicians could not help her, she was counseled by some to go to St. ‘Badasuis’ in the monastery of abba ‘Pachom.' So, the church elder went to the monastery and knocked on the door of the saint’s cell. He asked him to go with him out of the monastery, as though to seek his counsel concerning some serious issue away from everybody. Then, while he was talking to the saint, there came ‘Arsinoe’ and got hold of the saint’s hand, kissed it, and placed it on her face. God granted her healing on the spot.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Petarpemtis, the Blessed, p. 404
passages.text:
Saint: PETARPEMTIS, THE BLESSED — His Fatherhood and Miracles

Another time, when another one of his disciples reposed in the Lord, and he was surrounded by the brethren, the father came and kissed his (body) corpse and addressed him, saying: “Do you want, my son, to depart now to God, or you would rather remain in the body..?” Instantly the dead man replied: “It is better for me to forsake my body to be with Christ.” The blessed father then said to him: “Therefore, my son, lie in peace; and supplicate for my sake to God.” All those around were astonished and said: “This is truly a man of God.” He shrouded him and kept reading the psalms all night, then buried him.

Another time, standing before the deathbed of one of his disciples, who was known for his slothfulness and laziness, the brother kept weeping to beg the father to pray for him to be given another chance instead of the years he lost in slothfulness. Firmly, yet with love, the father rebuked him, and said: “I am ready to seek from God for your sake if you promise not to add to your sins new ones.” He fervently implored the Lord, then told the brother that God gave him three more years. The brother lived those three years in fantastic strife, and once those years came to an end, the father came to see his disciple before his departure. According to St. Palladius, this saint was not a regular man, but he came to be a chosen vessel by God whose actions amazed everybody!

In the simplicity of heart and fantastic faith, God performed countless miracles through St. Petarpemtis. According to his disciples, he walked on water. When they left him in a closed shut upper room, the angels carried him to the place he wished to reach, and he told his disciples that, in a night vision, God revealed to him the Heavenly Goodness prepared for the true monks, which no one could utter or describe. All that for the sake of his amazing faith together with the simplicity of his heart and his humility filled with love for God and men.

[St. Jerome: History of the Monks; ch. 16]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Martin, Bishop of Tours, pp. 113–114
passages.text:
Saint: MARTIN, BISHOP OF TOURS, ST. — Raising a Dead Man

Raising a Dead Man:

God performed at his hands many signs. One of those signs was while he was passing by, and saw a man stopping people carrying a casket in a funeral. That man kept the dead man’s family from burying him, claiming that he owed him 400 dinars. When the saint implored him to leave them alone, the man rudely refused. Then, the saint prayed to God to reveal the truth. At that point, the dead man instantly got up, rebuked the rude man, and exposed him as a liar. The liar died on the spot, whereas the dead man was raised by the prayer of the saint and went home where he lived many more years.

His Ministry among the Pagans:

As a fruit of his asceticism, miracles, and his spiritual zeal, the number of pagans in the area decreased, not only in the city of Tours but also in the entire land of Gaul. The saint got rid of so many of the idols’ temples.

Then, it happened once that, when he planned to cut down one of the idol’s sacred trees, their high priest approved on the condition that they would do the cutting themselves, under his supervision while he would stand where they chose for him. St. Martin did not hesitate to go along with their request. However, they tied him at the spot where the tree was supposed to fall, that he would be killed. They started cutting it, and when it was about to fall on him, the bishop made the sign of the cross on the tree, and it dropped the other way. Another time, while the saint was supervising the destruction of an idol’s temple, one of the pagans came charging with his sword attempting to kill him. St. Martin bravely uncovered his chest before the attacker, who was shocked and retreated, fell on his back, crying out, trembling, supplicating to the bishop to forgive him.

St. Martin cared every year to visit all the cities of his diocese, either on foot, riding on a donkey, or sailing on a boat.

He was known to strongly object to the killing of the heretics, seeking instead to expose their heresy and to excommunicate them with their bishops.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — Sts. George and Fronto, pp. 167–168
passages.text:
Saint: GEORGE AND FRONTO, SS.

The saint preached in Brantome, Angouleme and Saintes, then went to Bordeaux, where he was arrested by Count Sigebert, but when the saint healed him of paralysis, the count allowed him to build a church in the name of St. Stephen the first martyr, and he made another church in Blaye in the name of the Savior, and another one in Neuilly.

It was said that on the feast of the Pentecost when it was time for the Divine Liturgy, they realized that they were out of the wine. When St. Fronto prayed to God about it, a white dove came holding by her beak a bottle of wine and delivered it to the saint. This bottle is kept in the church of Neuilly as a holy treasure.

The history of this saint is full of a multitude of miracles performed by God on his hands. Those miracles were the cause of converting so many to the true faith and as a testimony to the Evangelic work. It was also said about these miracles that on his return to the city of Perigueux, a woman was planning to give a bath to her suckling and it was the custom in that city that the infant would be placed in a basin of water over a low fire until the water would become mildly warm. The mother would remove the fire from under the basin and bathe the baby. That woman put her infant in the water basin over the fire, and hearing the reception procession of St. Fronto, she forgot all about her baby and rushed to watch it. After about half an hour, she came back to find the water boiling in the basin and the suckling sitting up and cry, unconcerned with his scalding bath. It was also said that the saint, in a vision, saw the two saints Peter and Paul at the time of their martyrdom. There, he built a church in their names. The relics of St. Fronto are kept in the Cathedral of Perigueux.

[Baring-Gould: Lives of the Saints, October 25]

records.question: Give me a bullet list of what the Coptic Church teaches about the Immaculate Conception
records.answer:
I could not find anything about Immaculate Conception in the loaded sources.

The passages do cover related teachings about the Virgin Mary, including:

- The Coptic Orthodox Church calls Mary "Theotokos" (Mother of God), affirming that she gave birth to the Incarnate Word of God, not just a man [1][2][5][7][10][14][16].
- The union of divine and human natures in Christ began at conception in Mary's womb, with the Word of God united hypostatically to flesh from the very beginning [16][10].
- Mary is honored with several feasts commemorating her birth, conception, entry into the temple, departure, and apparitions, but no mention is made of the doctrine of Immaculate Conception [9].
- The Church emphasizes Mary's virginity and holiness, likening the Church itself to a virgin who begets children spiritually, as Mary gave birth to Christ while remaining a virgin [12].
- The incarnation involved the Holy Spirit overshadowing Mary, leading to the miraculous conception of Jesus, the Son of God [3][4][15].

These points reflect the Coptic Orthodox understanding of Mary and the incarnation but do not include the doctrine of Immaculate Conception.

passages.label: Mind of Christ Light: The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — MARIOLOGY (https://www.mindofchristlight.com/library-blog/blog-post-title-one-4p8fk-wslyt-7kd9z-rzzxd-xw8g5)
passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — MARIOLOGY

Cyril asserts the Theotokos ("Mother of God") for St. Mary as a sign of the orthodox faith that Jesus Christ who was born and crucified is truly the Incarnate Son of God. This term had been employed by the School of Alexandria for a long time. The English translation “Mother of God’’ brings into prominence that thought of the glory of her motherhood, the Greek term fixes attention rather on the Godhead of Him who was born. [552] To deny that she was Theotokos was really to deny that He who was born of her was Incarnate God. Cyril starts his 12 “Anathemas” thus: “ Whoever does not acknowledge Emmanuel to be truly God and hence the holy Virgin “ Theotokos ,” for she gave fleshly birth to the Word of God made flesh, shall be anathema. ”

He devoted to the defense of the Theotokos two whole treatises, the Quod Sancta Virgo Deipara Sitet non-Christi Para ('The Holy Virgin Mary, Mother of Christ') and the Quod beata Maria Sit Dei Para ('Blessed Be God for That') besides considerable portions of other works. For instance, the first book of the Adversus Nestorii blasphemias and the first part of the De recta fide ad reginas. [553]

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q3 “How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?”, p. 7
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism › (b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages — 3. How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages?

I greatly desired to present a Coptic Orthodox Catechism to reveal our Christian understanding concisely and briefly; particularly because, due to ecclesiastical and political circumstances, our Church was isolated from Western churches in the fifth century A. D. and remained so to a large extent up until the twentieth century, when she was accused by many in the West of adhering to Eutychianism. The Coptic Church, therefore, did not have the opportunity to reveal her true teachings through the writings of her Fathers and her liturgies. Despite the Church’s participation in many international theological conferences in recent years, insisting upon her rejection of Eutychianism, some sources continue to attribute this heresy to our Church, of which the Church is completely innocent and strongly opposes through her liturgies and praises.

In a certain dialogue with the Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches, theologians were surprised to observe that the liturgies and praises that we enjoy to the present day lack even the slightest hint of Eutychianism, but rather, positively oppose it in a beautifully Christian manner; especially the daily Theotokias and those of the festal celebrations. Some of the theologians observed that they harmonize with the thought St. Cyril, or that perhaps he was their author.

A Greek theologian once asked me whether we use the word “Theotokos” to describe St. Mary and was astonished to learn that it is a term beloved in Coptic texts in every age.

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › (c) Exposition of the Creed — 123. Why does the Creed include the phrase, “was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary”?

The history of the people of God is marked by a number of miraculous births, such as: God’s promise to Abraham and Sarah of the birth of Isaac (Gen. 17:16–19); Hannah and the birth of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam. 1:1–20); Manoah and his barren wife and the birth of their son Samson (Judg. 13:2–3); and Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth and the birth of John the Baptist (Luke 1:5–25). But a young, unknown virgin conceiving and bringing forth Jesus the Savior of the world surpassed all previous divine promises; for the Virgin bore in her body the promise of the salvation of the world. At the annunciation of the incarnation, the angel Gabriel said, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Highest will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

The existence of polytheism in the world cried out for the Son to come, as St. Cyril of Jerusalem explains: “Was it without reason that the Son came? or was it in order that the Father might be acknowledged? You have learned what moved the Only-begotten to come down from the throne at God’s right hand. The Father was despised, the Son must needs correct the error: for He Through Whom All Things Were Made must bring them all as offerings to the Lord of all. The wound must be healed: for what could be worse than this disease, that a stone should be worshipped instead of God?”

Notes: [318] St. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures 6.11 (NPNF II/7:36) amended.

For of two natures a union has been made. For this cause, we confess one Christ, one Son, and one Lord.

In accordance with this sense of the unconfused union, we confess the holy Virgin to be Theotokos, because God the Word became incarnate and was made man, and from the very conception united to Himself the temple taken from her. And as to the expressions concerning the Lord in the Gospels and Epistles, we are aware that theologians understand some as common, as relating to one Person, and others they distinguish, as relating to two natures, explaining those that befit the divine nature according to the Godhead of Christ, and those of a humble sort according to His Manhood.

I have written elsewhere about Pope Athanasius and Arianism, and the testimony of Western scholars regarding him.

b) The Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople in 381 A. D.

The second council focused on the heresy of Macedonius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who claimed that the Holy Spirit is created. The council also looked into the heresy of Apollinaris who, in defending the divinity of Christ, thought that the Word took flesh without a human soul. He thought that the human soul has a distinct human will, and thus Christ had two wills: the divine will and the human will, meaning that He was two persons. Pope Timothy of Alexandria, along with Nectarius, Patriarch of Constantinople; Gregory the Theologian, and Gregory of Nyssa took part in this council. The historian Sozomen mentioned that the number of bishops who participated was around 150 bishops, led by Timothy, the bishop of the See of Alexandria.

c) The Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus

The third council was held in the year 431 A. D. under the leadership of St. Cyril of Alexandria. Two hundred bishops participated in it to try Nestorius, who employed the term Christotokos (mother or giver of birth to Christ) to the Virgin Mary, thus differentiating the human Jesus born from Mary from the Son of God who dwelt in him. He thought that there were two distinct persons in Christ: the son of Mary and the Son of God. These two persons were not united essentially or hypostatically, but merely morally or in character. Thus, Christ is not to be called God but “Theophorus” or “God-bearer,” just as we would call the saints because of the work of divine grace in them. As a result, Mary is not the mother of God, but the mother of the human Jesus in whom the divinity dwelt. Nestorius and his followers criticized the Magi for their worship of the Child Jesus and held that His divinity was parted from Him at the moment of crucifixion.

It was on 10 April 428 CE that Nestorius, a monk of Antioch and disciple of Theodore was consecrated Patriarch of Constantinople. He us ed the term Christotokos ("mother of Christ") for St. Mary, and not Theotokos . [470] The battle lines were clearly drawn when one of his priests Anastasius, who he had brought from Antioch, preached before Cyril in December 428, saying: " Let no one call Mary “ Theotokos ,” for Mary was but a woman, and it is impossible that God should be born of a woman ." [471]

This teaching Nestorius publicly approved, and he himself preached a course of sermons in which he drew a plain distinction between the man Jesus, born of Mary, and the Son of God who dwelt in him. There were two distinct persons in Christ -- the Son of Mary and the Son of God -- who were united not hypostatically by only morally. Christ should be called not God but ‘‘God-bearer" ( Theoporon ), in much the same way as the saints can be called because of the divine grace given to them. Subsequently, Mary was not the mother of God, but of the man Jesus in whom the Godhead dwelt.

Nestorius and his followers criticized the Wise Men for kneeling to the Child Jesus, and preached that divinity was separated from humanity at the moment of Crucifixion. The matter came to Cyril, Pope of Alexandria who took occasion in his annual paschal letter (429 CE), without any personal reference to Nestorius, to state the doctrine of the Incarnation in the clearest and simplest terms. Namely that the real, true and perfect manhood in Christ was united to His divinity in one divine Person. Again, four months later, he wrote another letter to the monks of Egypt on the same subject, to put them on their guard. These letters came to the notice of Nestorius, stirring him to great wrath, and he engaged one Photius to answer them. He wrote to the court of Constantinople, trying to enlighten and win the support of the Emperor and the princesses who exercised so much influence on the mind and heart of Theodosius II.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 2 — Q1084 “What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?”, pp. 236–237
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 4: Church Worship as a Journey to Heaven › The Coptic Church Calendar and Joyful Daily Life in the Lord — 1084. What are the feasts of the Theotokos, the Mother of God?

In addition to the monthly commemoration of the Virgin Mary on the 21st of every Coptic month, we celebrate the following feasts:

a. The annunciation of her birth (7th Mesore / 13th August). On this feast we celebrate the conception of St. Mary, the living ark of the covenant, the dwelling of the Most High, and the second heaven.

b. Her birthday (1st Pashons / 9th May). Copts usually commemorate the day a saint passed from this world; their martyrdom or departure to paradise — but they insist on honoring St. Mary on her the day of her birth as a joyful day.

c. Her entry into the temple (3rd Kiahk / 12th December). We learn from the tradition of the Church that St. Mary’s life was consecrated to God in fulfillment of her mother’s vow, for she had vowed to consecrate her firstborn — whether a son or a daughter — to serve the Lord all the days of his or her life.

d. Her departure (21st Tobe / 29th January).

e. The revealing of the assumption of her body (16th Mesore / 22nd August). This feast is preceded by the fifteen-day fast of St. Mary.

f. The consecration of the first church in her name at Philippi (21st Paone / 28th June). This feast also coincides with the commemoration of the Virgin’s miracle of melting iron in the city of Bartus.

g. The apparition of the Virgin Mary above her church in Zeitoun (24th Paremhotep / 2nd April). This apparition is considered unique among the whole history of Marian apparitions. It began on 2nd April 1968 and was repeated on most days for hours at a time and for many months. These apparitions appeared above the domes of the Church of St. Mary and were seen by several hundred thousand people, of all ages and positions, Christians and Muslims. Every night, the people would gather around the church, pray, and praise God, waiting to see the dazzling spectacle of St. Mary standing above one of the domes. She was seen kneeling before the cross, or at other times, carrying the baby Jesus. These apparitions were accompanied by the apparition of birds in the form of doves. Among the fruits of these apparitions were the repentance of many and the occurrence of countless miracles.

Notes: [624] Jerome Palmer, Our Lady Returns to Egypt (Culligan Publications, 1969): p. 1.

These letters came to the notice of Nestorius, stirring him to great wrath, and he engaged one Photius to answer them. He wrote to the court of Constantinople, trying to enlighten and win the support of the Emperor and the princesses who exercised so much influence on the mind and heart of Theodosius II.

Cyril sent letters to Nestorius in which he explains the nature of Christ, as the Incarnate Son of God, one Person, and declared St. Mary’s right to be called “ Theotokos .” In his second letter to Nestorius (February 430 CE) he writes:

We do not mean that the nature of the Word was changed and became flesh, or that it was transformed into a complete human being consisting of soul and body. But rather, we affirm this, that the Word, hypostatically united to Himself flesh, animated with living soul, in a manner mysterious and inconceivable, and became man, and was called Son of Man. Yet not merely by way of divine favor or good will, nor again by the simple assumption to himself of a human person, and that while the natures which were joined together to form a real unity were diverse, one Christ and Son came from both of them -- not implying that the difference between the natures was abolished through their union, but that instead Godhead and manhood have given us the one Lord, Christ and Son by their mysterious and inexpressible unification. He was not at first born as an ordinary man of the holy Virgin, and then the Word simply descend ed upon him, but having been made one with the flesh from the very womb itself, He is said to have submitted to a birth according to the flesh, as appropriating and making his own the birth of his own flesh... Thus, we confess one Christ and Lord, not “worshiping” a man “along with” the Word but worshiping one and the same Christ because the body of the Lord is not alien from the Lord, with which body also he sits with the Father himself... But if we reject this hypostatic union either as impossible or unseemly, we fell into the error of making two sons... Thus, shall we find the holy Fathers to have held. So, did they make bold to call the holy Virgin “Theotokos.” Not as though the nature of the Word’ or His Godhead had its beginning from the holy Virgin, but inasmuch as His Holy Body, endued with a rational soul, was born of her, to which Body also the Word was hypostatically united, on this account He is said to have been born after the flesh. [472]

Afterward a local council was held in Alexandria and a syndical letter was sent to Nestorius, clarifying the same doctrines mentioned in Cyril’s letters, concluding with “The Twelve Articles or Anathemas.”

passages.text:
Catechism, Book 2: Christian Dogma › (b) Regarding the Coptic Orthodox Creed — 101. What did our Fathers of the Middle Ages transmit to us?

The libraries of Europe overflow with medieval manuscripts from Egypt, in both the Coptic and Arabic languages, that reveal the theological richness of the Coptic Church of the Middle Ages. This motivates me to present a sample of their writings about the Creed.

Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis, a priest from Manyat Bani Khusib (now called Minya), who died in 1357 A.D., has an exposition of the Creed in about fifty large manuscript pages attributed to him. He wrote this at the request of Anba Gabriel, the bishop of Qus, in reply to a Jewish person who criticized the Creed saying, “Where did you get this text? And why have you inscribed it among the books of the church?” Thus, the book contains a collection of texts from the Old Testament to substantiate each of the Creed’s clauses.

This work differs in its aims from other medieval Coptic expositions of the Creed: those of Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (around 940 A.D.); and a commentary at the beginning of the second chapter of Abu al-Barakat ibn Kabar’s work titled Mișbâḥ al-ẓulma wa-îḍâḥ alkhidma (The Lamp in the Shadows and the Illumination of Service, about 1310 A.D.). Abu al-Barakat quotes mostly from the New Testament. The Rev. Dr. Samir Khalil says that “the three Coptic commentaries complement each other in a felicitous manner.”

A summary of the text of Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis’ exposition:

1. We believe in one God: he cites the Torah (2 quotations), Isaiah (2 quotations), Jeremiah, and the Gospel (2 quotations; these are the only quotations from the New Testament).

2. The Father almighty, [Pantocrator] of all things visible and invisible: quotations from Zechariah (2), Nahum, and the books of Kings.

3. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten, born of the Father before all ages: quotations from Isaiah (2), David, Solomon (2), and Micah.

passages.label: Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church, Vol. 1 — Q536 “How can the Church be a virgin?”, p. 423
passages.text:
Catechism, Book 3: The Church: The Kingdom of God › The Eminence of the Church — 536. How can the Church be a virgin?

St. Augustine says, “Do you want to know how the church could be a virgin? Listen to Paul the apostle, listen to the zealous friend of the Bridegroom when he says: ‘But I fear, lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ’ (2 Cor. 11:3). As though the serpent, namely Satan, has defiled Eve’s purity and destroyed the virginity of her heart. So it is that we should not accept the devil’s deception and fall into evil desires and lose the virginity of our hearts.”

He again says, “If you would ask: ‘if the church is Virgin, how could she beget children?’ I will respond that she is a virgin but also begets children. She is likened to Mary who gave birth to Christ. Did Saint Mary not give birth to a child while remaining a virgin? So it is that the church begets children while remaining a virgin. She gives birth to Christ for whoever is baptized becomes His members.”

“The church is like Mary; her perfection was never defiled, and her fertility was never corrupted. What Mary was made worthy of in the flesh, the church received it spiritually. The only exception to that is that Mary gave birth to one son (Jesus Christ) but the church gave birth to many children for them to be gathered together in the one body in the one (Christ).”

Notes: [1089] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on the Liturgical Seasons 213.7 (FOTC 38:127). [1090] St. Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on the Liturgical Seasons 195:5 (FOTC 38:42).

On 22 June 431 CE, the Third Ecumenical Council was held in Ephesus at the behest of Emperor Theodosius the Lesser. It was attended by 200 Bishops and St. Cyril the Great, Pope of Alexandria, chaired the council. The council convened to try Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, for he divided Christ into two separate persons: The Son of God and the Son of Man. St. Cyril stressed the unity of the Godhead and manhood without mixing or mingling. He also emphasized the title Theotokos ("The Mother of God") for St. Mary in order to clarify that Who was born from her is truly God the Incarnate Word and not an ordinary man on whom the Godhead descended subsequently.

[521] Similarly the conception of Christ as the second Adam inaugurating a new, regenerated race of humankind demanded, he thought, [522] a much more intimate union of the Word with the flesh than Nestorius postulated [523] .

3 - The Hypostatic Union and the Nestorian Dualism

Cyril repeatedly confirms the Hypostatic Union as the opposite of the Nestorian Dualism. He did not hesitate to say that we are left in ignorance, and that at bottom the unity of Jesus Christ exceeds our comprehension and is unspeakable. [524] He teaches that the union began with the conception of Jesus. It is not a man who was born of Mary, but the Word of God according to the humanity. " For there was not born of the Holy Virgin, first an ordinary man, into whom the Word afterwards came down, but having united Himself (to the flesh) in the womb (of Mary) the Word was born according to the flesh, ascribing to Himself the birth of a flesh that is His own ." [525]

He confirmed that in the “union” humanity is not a ‘‘person,” not because He was an incomplete man, but because humanity does not exist apart. It does not exist by itself, nor does it belong to itself, for it belongs to the Word, who has made it His own. [526]

4 - The Hypostatic Union without Confusion

Cyril affirms that this hypostatic Union of the two natures had been realized without mixture or change or confusion ( synchysis ). He states:

Following in every point the confessions of the Holy Fathers, which they have drawn up under the guidance of the Holy Spirit speaking in them, and keeping close to their intentions taking the royal highway as it were, we affirm that the very Only-Begotten Word of God, begotten of the very substance of the Father... For our salvation came down, and of His condescension emptied Himself, and became Incarnate and was made Man having taken flesh of the Holy Virgin, and made it His own from the womb. He vouchsafed to be born as we, and came forth as a human being from a woman, without abandoning what He was, but remaining, even when He assumed flesh and blood, what He was, God in nature and in truth.

records.question: Who was St. George the Cappadocian?
records.answer:
St. George the Cappadocian was a martyr who most probably lived during the time of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD), although some Coptic manuscripts suggest he lived earlier, during the reign of a pagan king of Persia named Dadianus, who controlled Cappadocia [1]. He was born in Cappadocia in Asia Minor to pious, wealthy, and noble parents: his father Anastasius, the governor of Melitene in Cappadocia, and his mother Theobesta (Theognosta), daughter of the governor of Lydda in Palestine [1][2]. His father was martyred for his Christian faith when George was about fourteen years old [1][2].

After his father's martyrdom, his mother took George and his siblings to Palestine [2]. George was made a cavalryman by Prince Justus, who succeeded his father as governor and was a God-fearing man [2]. George excelled in his military career, becoming a leader of 5,000 warriors and earning the title "Prince George the Roman" from the emperor [2]. The governor intended to marry George to his daughter and appointed him as his deputy, but the wedding was postponed due to the young age of the girl [3].

When the emperor declared his intention to persecute Christians, George publicly opposed the decree, sold his inheritance to give to the poor, freed his slaves, and tore up the emperor's decree in public, preparing joyfully for martyrdom [3]. He was brought before the emperor, who tried to seduce and then torture him for seven years, but George remained steadfast, supported by divine miracles, including being raised from death three times and performing miracles such as making wooden chairs blossom and raising the dead [3][7].

The emperor's empress was converted to Christianity through George's prayers and was martyred for her faith [4]. Eventually, the emperor ordered George's execution by beheading on the 23rd of the Coptic month of Baramhat, fearing a public revolt due to the miracles performed through him [4].

The icon of St. George the Roman symbolizes the Church (represented by a young girl), Satan (the dragon), the Cross of Jesus (the spear), and the victory of faith over evil (the dragon's defeat) [4].

Throughout his trials, George resisted seduction and remained pure, converting even those sent to tempt him, who were then martyred for their new faith [9]. He is known as the Prince of Martyrs and is celebrated for his courage, faith, and miracles [1][2][3][4][7][9].
