passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, p. 133
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA

St. Shenouda is considered the most prominent personality representing the Coenobitic Monasticism in Egypt after St. Pachomius. Therefore, he was given the title of Archimandrite, meaning (the head of the anchorites), on account that he used to practice the life of seclusion now and then. He also encouraged some of his monks to retreat to the wilderness after they practice the life of fellowship for a few years, yet without completely losing their relationship with the monastery. While St. Pachom saw in the Fellowship the climax of the monastic exaltation, St. Shenouda saw it as a transition stage that would prepare the soul for the more elevated monastic life of seclusion.

St. Shenouda the Archimandrite was the Abbot of The White Monastery in Attrib near Sohag in the desert of Thebes in the 4th and 5th centuries for more than 56 years. According to his disciple, who succeeded him, he supervised about 2,200 monks and 1,800 nuns during that time.

In the year 431 AD, he accompanied the 24th pope of Alexandria St. Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to attend the third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus.

St. Shenouda never allowed a foreigner to join his monastic congregation, but all his monks were of Coptic descent. That is why many European scholars avoided mentioning his name when they spoke about the Fathers of the wilderness. For many centuries, they did not try to translate any of his works.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 136–137
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation)

This was expressed in their firm stand against the hateful Chalcedonian Council when they refused to bow their heads before Emperor Mercian (450-457 AD), when he thought that he would be able to force them to adopt his Chalcedonian belief; contrary to the Orthodox doctrine which they inherited from their Fathers.

A Spiritual and Social Reformer;

Abba Shenouda felt that worship was bound to the social life, and religion was both an applied love as well as a spiritual love. Therefore, St. Shenouda and the thousands of his monks did not try to isolate themselves from Egyptian society. As an example, when the Barbarians attacked Upper Egypt and looted all the possessions and took thousands of citizens as prisoners, St. Shenouda dared to face the invaders and convince them to take the spoils, but to let the captives go free. He then opened his monastery before the thousands of captives to dwell there for three months, during which the monks dedicated their time to serve them, including seven physicians among the monks, to nurse their wounds. During that period, 94 persons died and were buried in the monastery, 52 babies were born, and 8,500 bushels of wheat and vast amounts of lentil and beans were consumed. From this example, we can imagine the number of guests who were served in the monasteries within that extended period; and how the monks got to believe in the practical love, as more critical virtue than any monastic law or system.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, p. 137
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — His Care for the Nuns

His Care for the Nuns:

Abba Shenouda was a Father and Mentor, not only to thousands of monks but to 1,800 nuns as well. For them, he wrote multi-purpose letters to teach, guide, and hold them fast to the Upright Faith. But despite being a Father over such a vast number of monks and nuns, yet he kept on practicing his life of seclusion. So, he earned the title of Archimandrite. Every year, he used to spend some time in seclusion, during which no one dared to approach him.

He lived to reach 118 years of age, of which 66 years as the Abbot of several monasteries, some for monks and others for nuns. However, during those long years, until he reached that advanced age, God granted him health and strength to keep all his life working hard, from the time he received the leadership of the Red Monastery after the repose of his uncle Pistol. And through his persistent strife, he managed to establish the order of his monasteries; until he handed the flame shining to his disciple Wisa. He also managed to wake up in his fellow citizens their patriotic emotions toward their country.

[Fr. Tadros Yacob Malaty; The Coptic Church is a Church of Monasticism]

[The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute Saint, by K. H. Kuhn; pp. 2131-3]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 133–134
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — His Youth

His Youth:

Shenouda is the Upper Egyptian Coptic (Sahidic) version of the saint's name. He used only the Upper Egyptian dialect in his writings, sermons, and daily talks. The Lower Egyptian (Bohairic) version of his name is Shenoute, meaning (The servant of God or the one dedicated to God).

Shenouda was born to pious Christian parents, who raised their son on the ideal Christian principles. His father had a field where he and his farmers worked; he also had herds of sheep, which he trained his ten years old son Shenouda to shepherd. The little boy used to be all day long with the other shepherds, to whom he gave his food and kept fasting the rest of the day, and instead of going directly back to his parents, he used to stand beside a well and pray until late at night.

With his Uncle Pigol:

When his father became aware of his son's behavior, he took him to his maternal uncle, the well-known Abbot Abba Pigol, and sought from him to bless his young son. Abba Pigol took the boy's hand and laid it on his head, saying: “You bless me, my child, for you will be a Father for so many peoples.” On hearing this, Shenouda's father was immensely rejoiced and left his little son in the monastery in the care of his uncle. So, he learned all the Christian virtues. He kept striving for spiritual perfection through fasting, praying, perseverance, and humility. Watching him with great interest, his uncle rejoiced in his rapid and persistent growth in knowledge and virtue. And, his joy was concluded by a night vision in which an angel of the Lord told him: “Put the Holy Eskeem on the young man Shenouda.” In the very early morning, Pigol woke up, prayed the prayer of the Eskeem, and girded the young Shenouda with it.

Through the following years, Shenouda lived in the “Red Monastery,” where his uncle Pigol was the Abbot of the monks. Since he got the honor of the Eskeem, he doubled his efforts in studying the Divine books, not only for his benefit but also of the monks and the visitors who came to the monastery, whom he gathered around him and taught them the Upright Faith.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 135–136
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — His Monastic System

The families of the monks and all the people around the monasteries were allowed to visit the monasteries on Saturdays to attend the service of Vespers and to listen to a sermon given by Abba Shenouda. Then, on Sundays, they would partake of the Holy Liturgy and the Sacraments, along with the monks. After the service, the monks used to offer a meal of Agapi to all the guests. Abba Shenouda established two schools inside the White Monastery compound; he encouraged the monks to learn since he believed that teaching was the most potent weapon against the pagan customs. He, as well, cared to establish schools for the natives in the surrounding villages. Abba Shenouda lived in an era enflamed with fiery events. During his time, three Councils were held: The third Ecumenical Council in Ephesus (431 AD), which he attended in the company of Pope Cyril I; the second Ephesian Council (449 AD) and the Chalcedonian Council (451 AD), which caused the split in the Holy Church. In that era, the paganism ultimately came to an end, after Emperor Julian the Apostate (360-363 AD) attempted earlier in vain to bring it back to life. During that time, also, the Egyptian Patriotism was recognized; when all the Egyptians stood up as one entity against the Chalcedonian intruders and rejected them, even when they took the religious form.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, pp. 134–135
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — The Archimandrite

The Archimandrite:

One day, the elderly monks heard a voice, saying: “Shenouda became an Archimandrite.” (Meaning head of the anchorites). The enflamed zealously of Shenouda, his exalted holiness, and the many Divine proclamations granted to him by the heavenly Father; drew multitudes of people to live under his guidance to learn the Christian virtues. And when Abba Pigol departed to the Church of the firstborn, they chose Shenouda to replace him.

His Monastic System:

Even though Abba Shenouda followed the monastic system that was prevailing in Egypt, yet he set up a plan for his monks to adopt. In that plan, there were certain differences concerning the way to apply for joining the Fellowship, the administration style, the worship practices, the emphasis on studying, and hand-work in addition to the seclusion option. In this manner, Abba Shenouda combined some features from the monastic orders of Abba Anthony and that of Abba Pachom. The Fellowship (Coenobitic) Monasticism set by Abba Shenouda was stricter than that of Abba Pachom. Its main highlights could be summarized as follows: • The person seeking the monastic life had to spend a probation period in houses outside the walls of the monastery, and not inside as it was in the Pachomian system. Also, the applicant before becoming a monk has to write down and sign a pledge and read it before his brethren inside the church; then, the signed promise would be kept in the archives of the monastery. • Each monastery was managed by a Father-superior, who was assigned by and reported to the Archimandrite, being the Father of all the monasteries. Annually, four general assemblies were held and attended by the whole congregation of monks, including the anchorites. These assemblies were to discuss the conditions of all the monasteries. Concerning the worship practices, each congregation of monks would recite short prayers before starting their work. And the private prayers consisted of Psalms and Church praises, which were to be recited in each monk’s cell according to the guidance of his spiritual father. For the collective prayers, the monks have to assemble four times a day: in the morning, noon, sunset, and evening. Yet they have to come and go in complete silence. Thinkingly in the prayers, they were reciting. Besides those prayers, the Holy Liturgy of the Eucharist was held once a week. The families of the monks and all the people around the monasteries were allowed to visit the monasteries on Saturdays to attend the service of Vespers and to listen to a sermon given by Abba Shenouda. Then, on Sundays, they would partake of the Holy Liturgy and the Sacraments, along with the monks.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda, pp. 137–138
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA (The martyr)

He lived during the 2nd half of the 7th century when the Arab invasion to Egypt has just begun. This saint was raised in a truly Christian way. He observed a lifestyle within God's commandments and guidelines. He did not stop at fasting, prayers and attending masses, but he was also a generous giver to the poor, and always visiting the sick and imprisoned. Some evil people were annoyed by his piety, so they went to the Arab governor, claiming that the saint was mocking their religion. So, they brought him over for questioning. St. Shenouda declared that he believed in Christ, who commanded his followers to love everybody. He explained to the governor that he was just doing that, and he never made fun of any religion. The governor did not accept his reasoning and ordered him to deny his Christ and join Islam. The saint refused to proclaim his pride in being a Christian. The governor put him through so many tortures, which he accepted gladly.

Finally, they beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

[The Synaxarion: 13 Abib] [Iris El-Masry: The Story of the Coptic Church, vol. 2, p. 85]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 127–128
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Ordained as a Bishop of Education

Ordained as a Bishop of Education:

On the 30th of September 1962, Pope Cyril VI appointed him to the bishopric of Christian Education and as Dean of the Coptic Orthodox Theological Seminary. He renamed him Bishop Shenouda in honor of the most renowned scholar and writer in Coptic, St. Shenouda the Archimandrite (348- 466). Under the leadership of Bishop Shenouda, the number of students at the Coptic Orthodox Theological Seminary tripled. Bishop Shenouda used to have weekly lectures in Cairo for the general public, which was attended by a vast number of believers.

Ordained as a Pope:

Bishop Shenouda was enthroned as Pope Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria and patriarch of the See of St. Mark on the 14th of November 1971 by an “Altar Lot,” nearly nine months after the death of Pope Cyril VI of Alexandria. He was the third Alexandrian patriarch to take the name Shenouda; his namesakes were Pope Shenouda I (859–880) and Pope Shenouda II (1047– 1077). Less than one year after becoming pope of the Church of Alexandria, in October 1972, Pope Shenouda visited the ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople and the Pope of Rome, becoming the first Alexandrian pope to do so since the Christological schism of the Council of Chalcedon in 451. In May 1973, he penned a Christological statement that was agreed upon with the Roman Catholic Church and the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox Churches about the Nature of Christ, in a step towards settling the dispute of 451 and moving towards Christian Unity. On the 10th of May 1973, he celebrated the return by the Roman Catholic Church of part of the relics of the 20th pope of Alexandria St. Athanasius the Apostolic. In September 1974, he went on a pastoral trip to visit the Ethiopian Church during the reign of Emperor Haile Selassie (1930-1974) of Ethiopia.

In April and May 1974, he became the first Archbishop of Alexandria to visit North America when he visited the US and Canada. It was the first of many visits to that part of the world during his long papacy. He also visited Australia 6 times. The first visit was in 1989. The second was in 1991, the third in 1993, the fourth in 1995 and the fifth in 1996. His sixth and final trip took place in November 2002. He conducted an extended “Silver Jubilee” tour for about seven months in 1996, which took him to Europe, Canada, the USA, and Australia.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — Abba Shenouda, the Archmandrite, p. 136
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE ARCHMANDRITE, ABBA — Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation)

Ecclesiastical Political Leader (Against Byzantine Occupation):

Even though Abba Shenouda led a life of seclusion since his childhood, yet he was observing the world in which he lived. He attentively watched the events and the political disturbances taking place in the outside world. He perceived that the faithful disciple of Jesus Christ is the one who delivers His message to other men. On looking around, he noticed how his fellow citizens were burdened by the bitter servitude of worries and fears induced by paganism. He also realized that the Byzantine rulers were sucking the blood of the striving people and robbing the fruits of their labor. So, he dedicated himself to set them free; first from their fears, by confirming to them that the Divine care would protect them from any harm. He combined his teaching with action, by feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, treating the ill, and giving hospitality to the stranger. Above all that, he accompanied the oppressed to the court of justice to defend them; and when he failed to bring justice to them, he would bring their complaint up to the emperor. And, he would not have peace until the oppressed had judgment.

Once, in a public assembly, he stirred up the multitudes by saying: “The hearts of the rulers are filled with evil, deception, injustice, and greed. They have only one goal, to gather money at the expense of the poor. Who could count the troubles endured by our people from those rulers? I know some people who lack the necessary food for themselves and their cattle. I am sure they have the intention to turn the Egyptians to slaves and put the yoke on their shoulders.”

He used what God granted him of the gift of eloquence and writing to stir up the patriotic spirit in the people, addressing them only with the Coptic language in its Upper Egyptian dialect. By such pure Egyptian tongue, he managed to inflame their hearts with zeal, to wake up their spirit, and to make them perceive the honor of being Egyptians. That fire ignited in them by Abba Shenouda came to be the driving force, which enabled the Egyptians to stand firm before their occupation rulers. This was expressed in their firm stand against the hateful Chalcedonian Council when they refused to bow their heads before Emperor Mercian (450-457 AD), when he thought that he would be able to force them to adopt his Chalcedonian belief; contrary to the Orthodox doctrine which they inherited from their Fathers.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda III, the 117th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 125–126
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA III, The 117th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

On the 17th of March 2012, the long trip of pain which his holiness Pope Shenouda III has lived had ended and began the journey of the glories hidden from the human eyes. During those days when Egypt was living through his departure to Paradise, his funeral gathered all Egyptian categories; it included Muslims and Christians from all the denominations, leaders, and ordinary people. He had been a messenger of peace struggling in a difficult time and a man of peace, even in his departure from this world.

They all expressed their heart-felt deep grief, which shared by a lot of the presidents and institutions of the world uniquely and beautifully. His marvelous love for the leading figures in the Arab world; made some of them say: "He isn't the Pope for the Christians only, but he is the Pope for all the Arab countries." For his funeral, the people got crowded in such a compact fashion that three people died in the process, and six ambulances carried those who couldn't handle the unbelievable crowding. One of the broadcasters said: "I am not surprised to see some people here preferring to die in this crowded procession, just to have the blessings from his corpse!" The unique way that the people were expressing their grief of him after his departure was a natural fruit for the fertile seeds of love which he planted within them during his life.

Pope Shenouda III (1971-2012) was the 117th pope of Alexandria and the patriarch of the See of St. Mark. His episcopate lasted over 40 years from the 14th of November 1971 until his death on the 17th of March 2012. He was a conservative figure within the Church and was also highly respected within the Muslim community.

He became a monk in 1954 under the name Fr. Antonius el-Suriani. In 1958, he was ordained as a priest. In 1962, pope Cyril VI (1959-1971) summoned Fr. Antonius and consecrated him as a “General Bishop for Christian Education” under the name Abba Shenouda. In 1971, he was crowned as the 117th Pope of Alexandria under the title Shenouda III. In the end, pope Shenouda III died in March 2012 of lung and liver complications at his official residence.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda, the Monk, p. 138
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA, THE MONK, ST.

This saint was a hearing-impaired elder monk who lived during the Fatimid era (909-1171 AD), in a cell near the town of Nousa, the province of Aga in the Daqahlyia governorate. The biography of this saint was written in the great work The History of the Patriarchs, which was started by Severus ibn al- Muqaffaå (died 987 AD) and was completed by others to cover the period ending in 1167 AD. One of the authors of this book sent the saint a message asking for his prayers on his behalf and the behalf of his brother Fahd, for both were put in prison through an order made by Badr el-Gamaly (~1070 AD) the commander of the army of the caliph Al-Mustansir bi-Allah (1035-1094 AD). The saint answered him, saying: “Today, the Lord Jesus Christ will set you both free.” On the same day, they were released.

[The Patriotism of the Coptic Church and its History, p. 130]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda El-Bahnassawi, pp. 120–121
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA EL-BAHNASSAWI (The martyr)

St. Shenouda el-Bahnassawi was reported by some people to governor Maximus, who was appointed by Emperor Diocletian (284-305), that he was a Christian. The governor called him and inquired about his religion, and the saint confessed his faith in the Lord Christ. The governor ordered his men to cast him on the ground and to beat him with the rods to tear his flesh off and to scatter his blood around, then to throw him in a foul-smelling prison. God sent him the Archangel Michael, who healed his wounds, encouraged him, and gave him the good news that he would be receiving the crown of Glory.

In the morning, the soldiers found him standing in prayers. On reporting to the governor that they saw him sound with no wounds, he said that he was a sorcerer. Then, he ordered to hang him upside down and ignite fire underneath him. When it caused him no harm, he ordered pressing him in the Henbazin; and finally to cut his head off. His body was then cut to pieces and thrown away to the wild dogs. The dogs did not approach his remains all day. At night, the believers took his relics, covered them with precious spices, shrouded him, and buried him honorably.

[The Synaxarion: 14 Baramhat]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda I, the 55th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 123–124
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA I, The 55th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Shepherding

His Shepherding:

It happened once that during a papal pastoral visit to one of the monasteries of Upper Egypt, the Arabs attacked that monastery to rob and to kill. However, the pope bravely came out to them, carrying his cross. Once they saw him, they retreated before him and fled away. And with the repetition of attacks of those Arab barbers on so many monasteries, and because of the fear shown by the monks, the pope constructed a particular fortress building in every monastery.

After he returned to his throne, he sent a message of fellowship to his brother in the apostolic ministry: the Patriarch of Antioch, who not only replied by a similar note but, with it, he sent precious gifts.

His Care for the Upright Faith:

Being a pious scholar, this pope worked hard on confronting the heresies which spread among the believers.

In a village called Bukhnessa in the Marriott area, some people proclaimed that the Passions of Christ were not real, but they were imaginary. So, the pope went to them and guided them to the truth and brought them back to the true Faith. Also, during a visit to Upper Egypt, the pope found that the congregation of the town of Baliana has abandoned their two bishops and proclaimed the death of the Godhead. The pope debated with them and explained to them the upright faith, based on the Holy Bible and the Sayings of the Fathers, until they returned to the mother church and offered obedience towards their bishops.

That pope cared so much for the church's affairs and its various institutions. And, whatever remained in the patriarchates funds, he distributed among the poor. When he completed his unique struggle, he reposed in peace on the 14th of Baramhat 597 AM (869 AD), after he sat for about 21 years on St. Mark Seat.

[Fr. Menasseh Yohanna: History of the Coptic Church] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute I, by Subhi Y. Labib; pp. 2133-5]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda II, the 65th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 124–125
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA II, The 65th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Patriarchs Preoccupation with Wealth

The Patriarchs Preoccupation with Wealth:

During the ordination process, the clergy of Alexandria made it a condition on the papal candidate to promise that he would spend 500 dinars on their churches every year. Also, the archons made his pledge to refrain from receiving any bribes (simony) from those seeking clergy positions. Despite his promise to reject the Simonism in ordaining the clergy, yet he took a bribe to ordain a bishop for Assiut without even conferring with the people. That made the people of Assiut ban the new bishop from entering their city, and he had to go back in shame to his monastery. Not caring for the opposition of the archons, in particular Ibn Bakr, the pope issued a decree that all the possessions of the bishops should be inherited by the patriarchate after their death. The new system first applied to the bishop of Shenan, and then it continued to be applied until our present era; until pope Shenouda III (1971-2012), canceled it and decided to keep the diocese possessions of a reposed bishop for the one who would follow him. As a result of the erroneous behavior of that pope and his persistent seeking for wealth, the Church’s clergy wanted to deliver the affairs of the Church to a particular Council. However, the pope rejected their request. So, the whole congregation turned to prayers, asking God to protect His Church. The patriarch was inflicted by a problematic disease that caused him to shake violently, and all the physician’s attempt to cure it ended with failure; until he departed from this world in the year 1047 AD.

[Revealing the Secrets in the History of the Patriarchs, vol. 2, p. 11]

[Fr. Menasseh Yohanna: The History of the Coptic Church] [The Coptic Encyclopedia: Shenute II, by Subhi Y. Labib; p. 2135]

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Shenouda II, the 65th Pope of Alexandria, p. 124
passages.text:
Saint: SHENOUDA II, The 65th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Tolerance of the Caliph

After the repose of the 64th Pope Zecharias (1004-1032), the bishops and the archons recommended the monk Shenouda of the monastery of St. Macarius to sit on the papal seat. A night vision confirmed their choice to one of the bishops. He was ordained by the name of Pope Shenouda II (Sanutios: 1032-1046) in the year 1032; in the days of the Fatimid caliphate (909-1171).

The Tolerance of the Caliph:

At that time, it was the custom that the caliph would be paid by the Copts 6,000 dinars to get his approval on the appointment of their new patriarch. However, there was among the Copts a man of high status called Ibn Bakr. He managed to convince the caliph to issue an order to waive such a fee.

Out of the graces of God on the Copts during the time of this patriarch, the caliph Al-Zahir bi-Allah (1021-1036) followed the lead of his earlier ancestor the great caliph Al-Ăziz bi-Allah (975-996) in his tolerance with the non- Muslims, which resulted in a vast growth in the creative and artistic achievements in the country The caliph’s tolerance went so far to allow anybody converted to Islam to go back to his Christianity if that was his wish. He also allowed for building so many new churches.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 4 — St. Younan Nakhla El-Doweiry, the Archon, p. 362
passages.text:
Saint: YOUNAN NAKHLA EL-DOWEIRY, THE ARCHON

And adorned the building by an altar in the name of St. Anba Abram, which eventually turned into a church. • With his advanced age, his activity increased, and he set the foundation of a nursery and a house for the out-of-town female students, facing the building of the Society of el-MaĥAbbah on Jazerit Badran street. When the 116th Pope of Alexandria, St. Kyrillos VI (Cyril VI: 1959-1971) decided to establish a vast Cathedral in the name of St. Mark the Apostle on the land of Anba Roweis, the pope formed a committee to collect donations for such an enormous enterprise. He chose archon Younan Nakhla as one of its members. In the year 1972, the country president Anwar Sadat (1970-1981) bestowed on him the highest medal of Imtiaz (excellence) of the first grade. And, the governor of Cairo gave him a letter of appreciation on the day of Social Labor as an appreciation of his endless strife. After such shining conflict, he departed Paradise to enjoy the company of the Saints in the 1970s.

[The Faithful Synaxarion: 24 Toba]

records.question: Who was St. Athanasius the Apostolic?
records.answer:
St. Athanasius the Apostolic was the 20th Pope of Alexandria, born around the year 297 AD in Upper Egypt to a pious family. His father was a priest, and after moving to Alexandria, Athanasius became the personal disciple and later the personal secretary of Pope Alexandros I (312-328 AD). He was deeply devoted to theological studies and asceticism, having spent time as a disciple of St. Anthony the Great. Athanasius wrote important early works such as "Against the Pagans" and "The Incarnation of the Word" before 319 AD [1].

He was ordained a priest during the Nicene Council in 325 AD by Pope Alexandros I to enable him to address the council, where he strongly opposed the heresy of Arius and affirmed that Christ is "One with the Father in Essence" [2]. After Pope Alexandros' repose in 328 AD, Athanasius was ordained Pope of Alexandria at about 30 years old, despite opposition from Arians and Meletians. His early papacy was peaceful, during which he ordained the first bishop for Ethiopia, Abba Salama, around 330 AD [2].

St. Athanasius is renowned for his vigorous opposition to Arianism, which denied the divinity of Christ. For nearly 40 years, he faced relentless opposition, including multiple exiles, accusations, and conspiracies orchestrated by Arians and their supporters, such as Eusebius of Nicomedia and Emperor Constantius II. Despite these challenges, he remained steadfast, writing influential theological works and shepherding his flock from exile. He was exiled five times and spent over 17 years of his papacy in exile [3][4][7][14].

He returned from his fifth exile at age 70 and continued to lead the Church zealously until his death in May 373 AD at age 75. He held councils to defend Orthodox faith and left a lasting legacy by preserving the Christian Orthodox faith without deviation [4].

St. Athanasius was praised by contemporaries such as St. Gregory of Nazianzus, who called him "the true pillar of the Church" and an example for bishops, and St. Epiphanius, who called him the Father of Orthodoxy [14].

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 261–262
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

God prepared this chosen vessel to stand by the power of the Spirit and Truth before the forces of the heretic ‘Arius’ and his Arian followers. God used him to protect the faith of the Ecumenical Church, concerning the Godhead of the Lord Jesus Christ.

‘Athanasius’ was most probably born in Upper Egypt of a pious family around the year 297 AD. His father was a priest, from whom he absorbed the pious church life. The family then moved to Alexandria (perhaps after the repose of his father), to be seen by the 19th Pope ‘Alexandros’ (312-328 AD)

pretending to baptize a friend, while the pope was looking down from the terrace of the patriarchate on the beach. The pope sent for him and brought him inside to talk to him. The pope loved him very much and kept him as his personal disciple. Later on, ‘Athanasius’ became the pope’s personal secretary. God was preparing him to play a significant role in preserving the Church’s doctrines.

In the patriarchate, ‘Athanasius’ was not absorbed by the administrative tasks, but he focused his attention on studying the scientific, philosophical, cultural, and legal issues. He also cared for the Evangelical theological studies, which were based on the patristic teachings. What enflamed his heart was that some of his mentors were martyred for their holding fast to the faith in the Lord Christ. He might have witnessed some of these martyrdoms. Deep in his soul, ‘Athanasius’ felt that their strife supported the valuable teachings of those mentors until death.

As for the ascetic side, St. ‘Athanasius’ spent some time as a disciple of St. ‘Anthony the Great.' He learned from St. ‘Anthony’ how to despise the world, love worshipping, contemplating, and having no fear of death. His early ripening was manifested in his two articles: ‘Against the Pagans,’ and ‘The Incarnation of the Word.’ These, he wrote before the year 319 AD. In the first article, he called on the pagans to forsake paganism. And in the second, he gave the theological perspective about the Divine Incarnation scientifically.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 262–263
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — In the Nicene Council (325 AD)

In the Nicene Council (325 AD):

Pope ‘Alexandros I’ ordained ‘Athanasius’ as a priest during the Nicene Council, to give him the right to address the council. And, he proved to be the shining star who was able to overpower the Arians who denied the Godhead of the Lord Christ. And, he managed to stress that Christ “Is One with the Father in Essence.”

Pope of Alexandria:

After the repose of Pope ‘Alexandros’ in the year 328 AD, most of the clergy and the people wanted to ordain ‘Athanasius’ as a bishop of Alexandria. However, some people opposed to that ordination; such as the Arians and Meletians (followers of ‘Meletes,’ bishop of Assiut, who denied faith during the persecution, then came back to provoke the bishops on dissension, and to attempt taking the papal throne by force; while St. ‘Peter the Last Martyr’ was in prison). ‘Athanasius’ attempted to flee when he felt that they wanted to ordain him.

Eventually, St. ‘Athanasius’ was ordained as a Bishop and Pope of Alexandria, while he was still 30 years old. His first seven years on the papal throne were very peaceful, during which he ordained ‘Vermentius’ as a Bishop on ‘Eksom in Ethiopia’ by the name of ‘Abba Salama.’ This was the first step in establishing the Ethiopian Church around the year 330 AD; (although some scholars put it in the year 357 AD). During that period, he made a pastoral visit to Upper Egypt, during which he had a chance to meet with St. ‘Pachomius,’ who fled the scene until he was sure that he would not be ordained as a priest by the visiting pope.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, p. 263
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope:

The Arians and the Meletians were collaborating with ‘Eusebius’ bishop of ‘Nicomedia,’ plotting to destroy the Pope ‘Athanasius.’ For almost 40 years, the Pope ‘Athanasius’ did not enjoy any rest. This could be explained in the following points;  Provoked by ‘Eusebius’ Bishop of ‘Nicomedia,’ Emperor ‘Constantine the Great’ (306-337 AD) gave a direct order to ‘Athanasius’ to accept ‘Arius’ in his fellowship. The emperor claimed that ‘Arius’ has declared his repentance and wrote his Creed (although it was done in a twisted manner). Pope ‘Athanasius’ rejected the imperial order in the year 330 AD.  Three Meletian bishops went to ‘Nicomedia’ to accuse the Pope ‘Athanasius’ before the emperor. They accused him of destroying a chalice of the Eucharist, used by ‘Askhiras the priest’ and that the pope has killed bishop ‘Arsanius!' However, at the time, two priests who were in the emperor’s court exposed the Meletian bishops’ lies. The emperor called for the pope, who came and proved the deviousness of the bishops’ claims against him. The emperor condemned the Meletian bishops. And later on, ‘Askhiras the priest’ came in remorse to confess that they seduced him with a bribe to invent that lie; and for bishop ‘Arsanius,’ it turned out that he was hiding in ‘Tyre.'  In the year 335 AD, a Council was held in ‘Tyre.' That Council was headed by bishop ‘Eusebius of Caesarea,’ but it was controlled by bishop ‘Eusebius of Nicomedia.' In that Council, an evil woman was brought in and stood accusing Pope ‘Athanasius’ of raping her. Then, the pope’s disciple ‘Timothy’ the deacon confronted the woman, pretending to be pope ‘Athanasius.' And, she shamelessly insisted that he was the one who deprived her of her chastity and virginity. At this point, all the conspirators were put to shame! In that council, they also discussed the case of priest ‘Askhiras’ and bishop ‘Arsanius,’ bringing forth new Jewish witnesses claiming that they were a new catechumen.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, p. 268
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

Then, they hastened toward Upper Egypt, while ‘Athanasius’ returned to the city of ‘Memphis.’ After that, he spent a period of continuous movement from one monastery to another.

Emperor ‘Julian’ was killed and was replaced by ’Jovian’ (363-364 AD), who sent a cordial message to the pope, inviting him to return and ordered the return of all those who were exiled. The pope returned to Alexandria, where he held a Council, in which he documented in a letter “the Nicene Creed.” Then he set forth to meet the emperor who welcomed him, before he returned to Alexandria in February 364 AD, carrying with him the letters of the emperor.

Unfortunately, Emperor ‘Jovian’ died in February 364 AD, and he was replaced by ‘Valentinian I’ (364-375 AD) in the West, leaving the East to his Arian brother ‘Valens’ (364-378 AD).  ‘Valens’ sent a decree ordering the return of all those freed bishops who were previously exiled by his brother ‘Julian,’ back to their original exile spots. The pope had to leave Alexandria to a country house. But under the intense pressure of his people, he returned to his throne after about nine months (May 365-Feb.366 AD), among the great joy of his people of Alexandria.

Pope ‘Athanasius’ returned from his 5th exile, when he reached 70 years of age, to practice his shepherding on his people with a spirit kindled with zeal, in particular, to purify the land of every Arian thought.

In the year 369 AD, he held a Council in Alexandria attended by 90 bishops to care for the Orthodox Faith. And, he remained working hard until he reached 75 years before his death in May 373 AD.

By his endless struggle, St. ‘Athanasius’ managed to deliver to the following generations the torch of Christian Orthodox Faith without any trace of diversion.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius II, the 28th Pope of Alexandria, p. 260
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS II, THE 28th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA

He was a priest in Alexandria, known for piety and Orthodox faith. He was ordained as a patriarch (489-496 AD) after the repose of the 27th Pope St. ‘Peter III’ (477-489 AD). He was called ‘Athanasius Junior’ to designate him from ‘Athanasius the Great’ (The Apostolic).

He participated in the efforts of Caesar ‘Anstasius’ (491-518 AD) to bring back the peace to the East as a whole and Egypt in particular; after the church was torn apart because of what happened in the Council of Chalcedon. During that Council, St. ‘Dioscorus’ the 25th Pope of Alexandria (444-454 AD) was exiled because he proclaimed that the Lord Christ has One Nature and that He is One Hypostasis; and that the Unity between the Godhead and the Manhood is without mingling, without confusion and alteration.

Until recently, the Christian world wrongly assumed that our belief in ‘One Nature’ meant that the Manhood Nature was absorbed in the Godhead Nature, as proclaimed by the heretic ‘Eutyches and they used wrongly to describe us as ‘Eutychians.’

Pope Athanasius II lived a period of calm and peace until he reposed in the Lord on the 20th of Tout in the year 496 AD.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Alexandros I, the 19th Pope, pp. 131–132
passages.text:
Saint: ALEXANDROS I, THE 19th POPE — His Opposition to the Meletianism and the Arianism

The followers of Arius held two Councils: the first in ‘Bithynia’ in the year 322 AD, and the second in Palestine in the year 323 AD, which issued a decree that the judgment against Arius was not valid and sought his return to Alexandria and so he did go back to oppose the Truth.

The Pope had to declare the ex-communication of Arius and to expel him anew. Then, the young deacon Athanasius wrote a decree contesting the heresy of Arius, and it was signed by 36 priests and 44 deacons.

Eusebius of Nicomedia, by his connections and familiarity with Emperor Constantine, managed to lure the emperor towards favoring Arius, especially that the emperor’s sister ‘Constasia’ had a lot of respect for bishop Eusebius. The emperor then, sent ‘Ausius’ Bishop of ‘Cortoba’ from Spain (one of the confessors who endured torture in the days of Maximianus), to Alexandria to intervene at the Pope Alexandros to receive Arius and he sent a kind message with him describing Arius as a pious and devoted priest. When Cortoba’s bishop arrived in Alexandria, and he experienced by himself what the followers of Arius were doing; he joined the Pope and sought from the emperor to hold an Ecumenical Council to investigate the Arians.

That Council was held in Nicene in the year 325 AD Pope Alexandros brought with him to the Council St. Athanasius the Apostolic, who had a significant role in exposing the vanities of the Arians. So, the Council decided to excommunicate Arius and his followers, and they were all exiled to the Illyricum.

Pope Alexandros reposed around the year 328 AD, and is celebrated by the Western Church on the 26th of February; the Greek on the 29th of May and the Coptic Church on the 22nd of Baramouda.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 267–268
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

Then, he came back later after the death of the emperor in the year 361 AD, to be killed by the pagans mob (probably to steal his wealth).

In his self-imposed exile, Pope ‘Athanasius’ kept on moving from one monastery to another and from one location to another, with a heart enflamed with his love for God and his people.

During that time, he wrote and circulated an impressive array of hugely influential documents to keep shepherding his congregation. Among them was “the Biography of St. Anthony”, and “Apologia de Fuga”: a defense of his escape. He also has written the Encyclical Letters to the bishops of Egypt, Libya, ‘Lucifer’ Bishop of ‘Calaris’ (Cagliari, on the island of Sardinia, west of Italy), and to the Egyptian monks. He also wrote four essays against the Arians, five dogmatic messages to ‘Serapion’ Bishop of ‘Tammy,’ messages on the Holy Spirit, and a book on the Church Councils.

Throughout his years in exile, ‘Athanasius’ retained great support in Alexandria and whole Egypt, and his ecclesiastical and theological arguments won over many in both the East and West.

By the death of ‘Constantius II’ and the sitting of Emperor ‘Julian the Apostate’ (360-363 AD) on the throne, Pope ‘Athanasius’ appeared again in the year 362 AD, together with ‘Lucifer’ Bishop of ‘Cladius’ and ‘Eusebius’ Bishop of ‘Vershelly,’ who was exiled to Upper Egypt.

The pope held a Council in Alexandria in the year 362 AD, called ‘The Council of the Saints and the Confessors,’ since all those who attended have just come back from exile or have suffered tortures. But the peaceful situation did not last for long; for Emperor ‘Julian,’ feeling the danger of Pope ‘Athanasius’ on paganism, has sent to the governor of Alexandria, indicating that the decree of the return of the exiles was meant for them to go back to their countries, and not to their thrones. And, he ordered him to drive ‘Athanasius’ out of Egypt. Therefore, the pope had to hide in the tomb of his father for almost six months. And, as the emperor used more pressure on the governor, the pope had to leave Alexandria to Upper Egypt, sailing by boat, chased by the governor’s ship. When the soldiers inquired about ‘Athanasius,’ they were told: “He is not far from you.” Then, they hastened toward Upper Egypt, while ‘Athanasius’ returned to the city of ‘Memphis.’ After that, he spent a period of continuous movement from one monastery to another.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 264–265
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

So, he was able to provoke the emperor to recall the governor of Alexandria ‘Theodorus,’ who was a friend of the pope and send ‘Vilagios of Cappadocia’ to replace him (the latter was previously a governor on Alexandria (335-337 AD), and was a stern enemy of the pope).

The Arians caused a lot of destruction in Alexandria, to convince the emperor that in the presence of the pope, there would never be peace. They also accused the pope of confiscating the wheat belonging to the poor. Besides, they proclaimed that his reinstatement was not ecclesiastically legal because it came without a decision from a church Council. Then, abba ‘Anthony the Great’ came down from the wilderness to support his suffering pope.  Through the year 338 AD, ‘Eusebius of Nicomedia’ got preoccupied with moving from ‘Nicomedia’ to the bishopric of ‘Constantinople’; for the country’s capital has officially relocated there. Having done so, he concentrated his effort on opposing the pope. At the end of the year 338 AD, he managed to convince the Emperor ‘Constantius II’ (337-361 AD)

to hold a Council in Antioch, to issue a decree to depose the pope again. Having done so, the mob in Alexandria rushed, forcing their way into the church of ‘Theonas’ to kill the pope, who was able to flee away. However, the priests, the monks, and the rest of the believers, including women, were subjected to a bitter wave of persecution. Some of them were slain and others were imprisoned. Four days later, ‘Gregory of Cappadocia’ entered into the city of Alexandria as its new bishop, and he was in charge of suppressing the believers.

The monks did not stand idle, St. ‘Anthony the Great’ sent several messages to the intruding bishop and some of the officials to rebuke them on their behavior. St. ‘Pachomius,’ as well, sent two of his capable monks: ‘Zacaous’ and ‘Tadros’ to Alexandria to support the believers in the absence of their pope.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 263–264
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

At this point, all the conspirators were put to shame! In that council, they also discussed the case of priest ‘Askhiras’ and bishop ‘Arsanius,’ bringing forth new Jewish witnesses claiming that they were a new catechumen.

With the revelation of his innocence, the Council turned into confusion; and Pope ‘Athanasius’ abandoned it and set forth to ‘Constantinople.'

Feeling that danger was chasing them, ‘Eusebius of Nicomedia’ and his followers hastened to claim that the pope threatened to ban sending the wheat from Alexandria to Constantinople. Here the emperor, provoked to anger, exiled the pope to ‘Treve,’ in February 336 AD. The pope bravely said to the emperor: “May the Lord judges between you and me!”

After the Council of ‘Tyre,’ another Council was held by the Arians in ‘Jerusalem,’ after the consecration of the church of the ‘Holy Sepulcher.' The Arians issued a verdict for the return of ‘Arius’ to Alexandria, in the absence of the exiled pope. ‘Arius’ returned to Alexandria under heavy guards, however, the revolt of the people in Alexandria against him, forced the governor there to seek his return to ‘Constantinople.' The emperor called for him to get back.

‘Eusebius of Nicomedia’ exerted so much effort to force the return of ‘Arius’ to the Ecclesiastical fellowship. ‘Alexandros,’ the patriarch of ‘Constantinople’ was so bitter when he was forced to accept ‘Arius’ in his diocese that he prayed to God for help, and ‘Arius’ died in shame at a public restroom on his way to the church.

A year later, when Emperor ‘Constantine’ was on his deathbed, he recommended the return of pope ‘Athanasius’ to his throne. When St. ‘Athanasius’ went back to Alexandria, he was received by all the people who were waiting for his arrival on the shore as an angel coming down to them from heaven.  ‘Eusebius of Nicomedia’ did not cease to oppose the pope ‘Athanasius.' So, he was able to provoke the emperor to recall the governor of Alexandria ‘Theodorus,’ who was a friend of the pope and send ‘Vilagios of Cappadocia’ to replace him (the latter was previously a governor on Alexandria (335-337 AD), and was a stern enemy of the pope).

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Alexandros I, the 19th Pope, pp. 130–131
passages.text:
Saint: ALEXANDROS I, THE 19th POPE — His Ordination

His Ordination:

He was born in Alexandria and was ordained as a priest, then he was chosen as the 19th Pope of Alexandria (313-328 AD), according to a prophecy by the 17th pope St. ‘Peter; the Last of the Martyrs’ (300-310 AD). Although he has reached an advanced age, yet he served God with high energy.

About him, the historian Abba Severus said that, according to the 20th Pope St. ‘Athanasius the Apostolic,' Pope Alexandros never read in the Holy Bible while sitting down, but always standing; and because of his piety, the people called him ‘The Saint’; and because of his love of the poor and the needy, they called him ‘The Father of the Poor.'

His Opposition to the Meletianism and the Arianism:

The Meletians maintained a severe stance against the return to communion for those Christians who had renounced their faith during the persecutions of Diocletian. Earlier, Meletius took advantage of the exile of St. Peter, the 17th Pope of Alexandria, due to the persecution, and he invaded on the Pope’s authority by performing such actions as ordinations, consecrations, and excommunications. By this way, Meletius assembled for himself a supporting pack of 30 bishops, who declared their independence from the Pope and they even introduced some Jewish traditions into their worship. St. Peter objected to their actions and warned his people against Meletius.

After returning from his exile, Pope Peter held a Council in which he excommunicated Meletius from his rank, an action the Pope was not able to enforce. But later on, when the Nicene Ecumenical Council (325 AD) issued its judgment concerning the dispute of Meletius, he submitted to the decree of the Council and yielded to Pope Alexandros until he reposed in the year 330 AD.

In the beginning, the followers of ‘Meletius’ the bishop of ‘Lycopolis’ (Assiut) exerted great effort to hinder the ordination of St. Alexandros from becoming the Pope of Alexandria, while they supported their Arian candidates.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 266–267
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

A big fight started between the Emperor ‘Constantius II,’ who became the emperor of both the East and West and his brother’s killer ‘Magnentius’; that preoccupied the empire for three years. The Arians used the incident of killing the Emperor ‘Constans I,’ the friend of the Pope ‘Athanasius,’ and they accused the Pope ‘Athanasius’ of having a secret relationship with the murderer. So, it happened that after the Emperor ‘Constantius II’ got rid of ‘Magnentius,’ he focused on opposing the Pope, whom he had a deep hatred for. In his great anger, the emperor forced the bishops of the East and West to hold two Councils in ‘Arles,’ France and in ‘Milan,’ Italy. They were ordered to remove and exile the pope, along with some other bishops like ‘Paolinius’ Bishop of ‘Treve,’ ‘Lucifer’ Bishop of ‘Sardinia,’ ‘Eusebius’ bishop of ‘Vercelli,’ Italy, ‘Dionysius’ bishop of ‘Milan’ and ‘Hosius’ Bishop of ‘Cortoba’ (who was 100 years old). Pope ‘Liberius’ of Rome (352-366 AD), after resisting for some time, being in exile for two years, ultimately caved in and signed the Arians document.

The soldiers also attacked the church of ‘Theonas,’ while Pope ‘Athanasius’ was praying with the priests and the congregation. As chaos prevailed in the dark amid the glittering swords, the pope had the intention to stay with his people, but the priests and the monks committed him to withdraw and flee.

The pope remained in hiding for six years, while the emperor was vainly searching for him.

The emperor sent ‘George of Cappadocia’ as a bishop on the people of Alexandria. He took over the churches by force and confiscated their treasuries. However, he could not tolerate to stay longer in Alexandria and had to flee. Then, he came back later after the death of the emperor in the year 361 AD, to be killed by the pagans mob (probably to steal his wealth).

In his self-imposed exile, Pope ‘Athanasius’ kept on moving from one monastery to another and from one location to another, with a heart enflamed with his love for God and his people.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 265–266
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

The monks did not stand idle, St. ‘Anthony the Great’ sent several messages to the intruding bishop and some of the officials to rebuke them on their behavior. St. ‘Pachomius,’ as well, sent two of his capable monks: ‘Zacaous’ and ‘Tadros’ to Alexandria to support the believers in the absence of their pope.

Pope ‘Athanasius’ traveled to Rome to meet with his friend Pope ‘Julius I’ (337-352 AD), who wrote a letter to ‘Eusebius of Nicomedia’ and his group, as requested by the Council of Rome. In that visit to Rome, the Eastern form of monasticism was introduced to the Western Church, and the Latin dogma started to be saturated with the theological concepts of St. ‘Athanasius.' The followers of ‘Eusebius of Nicomedia’ considered the message stressing the innocence of Pope ‘Athanasius,’ which was sent by the Roman Pope ‘Julius I,’ as an insult to their integrity. So, they held a Council in Antioch and wrote him back mocking and threatening covertly.

In the year 342 AD, Pope ‘Athanasius’ met with ‘Constans I,’ the emperor of the West (337-350 AD) in Milan. Then, the ‘Eusebians’ went to his brother ‘Constantius II,’ the emperor of the East (337-361 AD), attempting to convince him that the pope’s meeting with his brother was deviously intended to arrange for holding a general council for the bishops from the East and the West. Pope ‘Athanasius’ declared that he did not request that, but the idea was already in Emperor ‘Constans I’ mind before they met.  The two emperors of the East and West decided to hold the bishop’s General Council in ‘Sardica (Sophia–Capital of Bulgaria), on the border between the two kingdoms, in the year 343 AD. The Arian bishops of the East came (as ‘Eusebius’ has already died) and refused to attend the Council because Pope ‘Athanasius’ and his group were in attendance. However, they assembled in the city of ‘Philippopolis’ opposite to ‘Sardica’ within the empire of the East, and wrote a letter and left it with ‘Justathios’ the priest of the church of ‘Sardica.’ In the letter, they indicated that they had to go back since the emperor called them after his return victorious over the Persians. Also, they excommunicated ‘Hosius.’ ‘Julius I,’ ‘Athanasius,’ and others. Accordingly, in return, the Fathers of the Council in ‘Sardica’ signed a declaration by which they excommunicated 11 Arian bishops.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 2 — St. John I, the 29th Pope of Alexandria, pp. 373–374
passages.text:
Saint: JOHN I, The 29th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — Ordained as a Patriarch

Ordained as a Patriarch:

After the departure of the 28th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius II (489- 496 AD), the entire congregation had their sight on a monk in the monastery of Abba Macarius by the name of John (Yoannis). This monk has spent so many years in spiritual strife that he filled the valley with his sweet fragrance. A delegation of bishops, priests and archons, set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis to meet him and to convey their desire to select him for the post. He first refused, but before the persistence of the delegates, he said to himself: “How would I know? The Holy Spirit might inspire the persistence of these men?! So, I should be careful lest I may be resisting God's will. I have to give my consent to this great responsibility, but with utmost humility and without any hesitation.”

Monk John proclaimed his thoughts to the delegates while confirming his unworthiness for such an honor. He declared to them that he was accepting it for the necessity imposed upon him. The representatives rejoiced and accompanied the hermit John to Alexandria, where he was ordained by the name of Pope John in the year 496 AD.

His Contemporaries:

Pope John I (496-505) was a contemporary of St. Severus of Antioch (465- 538), the star of his era in piety and knowledge. He also was a contemporary of Emperors Zeno (474-491) and Anastasius the Righteous (491-518). When Emperor Anastasius’noticed how Macedonius II, the Patriarch of Constantinople (495-511), has cut off his relationship with the church of Alexandria, taking the side of the Chalcedonian council and establishing a close relationship with the bishop of Rome; he tried in vain to convince him to correct his ways. Then, later on, the emperor held a council in Constantinople in the year 511, in which Macedonius II was expelled from his throne, exiled and was replaced by a virtuous man by the name of Timothy. Once ordained, patriarch Timothy I (511-518) held a council in which he confirmed the Orthodox faith and excommunicated Macedonius II.

passages.text:
The Coptic Orthodox Church as a Church of ERUDITION & THEOLOGY — POPE ATHANASIUS AND THE COUNCIL OF NICEA

St. Gregory of Nazianzus said, " When I praise Athanasius , virtue itself is my theme; for I name every virtue as often as I mention him; he possessed all virtues. He was the true pillar of the Church. His life and conduct was an example for Bishops, and his doctrine represents the Orthodox creed. "

St. Epiphanius called him the Father of Orthodoxy. [391]

Athanasius was ordained Patriarch (Pope) of Alexandria in 328 CE, presiding over the church for 46 years. However, over 17 years of his papacy were spent in exile due to his vigorous opposition to the spread of Arianism, which was supported by certain Emperors. He was exiled five times.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 1 — St. Athanasius the Apostolic, the 20th Pope of Alexandria, p. 266
passages.text:
Saint: ATHANASIUS the APOSTOLIC, THE 20th POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — The Arians’ Opposition to the Pope

‘Julius I,’ ‘Athanasius,’ and others. Accordingly, in return, the Fathers of the Council in ‘Sardica’ signed a declaration by which they excommunicated 11 Arian bishops.

The Arians took firm steps to keep ‘Athanasius’ and his men from entering into Alexandria, but the Lord dismantled their counsel by their own Arian hands. So, it happened that some Arians conspired and brought an evil woman into the chambers of two bishops, from among the delegates of Emperor ‘Constans I’ to his brother ‘Constantius II,’ the emperor of the East. When the woman entered into the chamber of one of the bishops, she found the reverend old man deep asleep. She screamed and ran away. Then she proclaimed the truth of what happened while the whole city was assembled. Because of her testimony, the conscience of the emperor of the East woke up to perceive the evil tricks of the Arians. He removed ‘Steven’ the Arian bishop of Antioch and issued an order to allow the return of all those bishops who were exiled because of the Arian's conspiracies. He even wrote three letters to Pope ‘Athanasius’ proclaiming his longing to see him, hoping for him to go back to his throne.

Before going to see the emperor, Pope ‘Athanasius’ went to meet with his close friend Pope ‘Julius I’ of Rome, who with his soul shaken with joy, wrote a message to the priests of Alexandria and their congregation to congratulate them on the return of their struggling Father.

The suffering pope met with the emperor, then returned to his country, to be received by his people with a fantastic joy in the year 346 AD, after an absence of 7 years. During these years, the congregation tasted the bitterness of being denied the care of their pope, together with falling under the persecution of the Arians and the Meletians. His return was the cause of great blessings, as he ordained many bishops for the vacant dioceses. The number of those dedicated to ministry, the virgins and the monks, significantly increased; and all set forth to make up for the lost years.  A civil war erupted in the Roman empire, during which the Western Emperor ‘Constans I’ was murdered after a coup by the usurper ‘Magnentius.' A big fight started between the Emperor ‘Constantius II,’ who became the emperor of both the East and West and his brother’s killer ‘Magnentius’; that preoccupied the empire for three years. The Arians used the incident of killing the Emperor ‘Constans I,’ the friend of the Pope ‘Athanasius,’ and they accused the Pope ‘Athanasius’ of having a secret relationship with the murderer.

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Vol. 3 — St. Peter II, the 21st Pope of Alexandria, pp. 408–409
passages.text:
Saint: PETER II, the 21st POPE OF ALEXANDRIA — His Ordination as the 21st Pope of Alexandria (373-380 AD)

His Ordination as the 21st Pope of Alexandria (373-380 AD):

This saint was raised in Alexandria, became a disciple of the 20th Pope of Alexandria St. Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373 AD). He took after him the life of the holy and the upright faith. The pope so loved him that he ordained him as a priest in Alexandria and when St. Basil the Great sought someone to help him oppose the Arian heresy that denied the divinity of the Lord Christ, St. Athanasius sent to him Fr. Peter with some others who carried out their mission with the spirit of true zealously. On coming back to Alexandria, the pope appointed him as his secretary, as though he was preparing him to follow him on the throne. When the pope fell severely ill and perceived that his departure was close at hand, he advised his people and the clergy to choose Peter as his successor. Pope Athanasius reposed in the Lord while the Arians were coveting to take his throne. The congregation hastened to fulfill the request of their reposed pope, and St. Peter was ordained as a pope in the year 373 AD. That was during the reign of the Arian Emperor Valens (364- 378 AD), who was filled with anger over the Copts for this act.

Valens Opposition against Him:

The Arians found out that their chance slipped from their hands by the ordination of Pope Peter II, but they were encouraged by the Arian emperor Valens, to whom they complained against the pope that he was not worthy of being a pope. Finding it a way to avenge the Copts, Valens wrote Palladius, the governor of Alexandria, commanding him to send the pope into exile and to set the Arian bishop Lucius in his place. That Lucius was an Egyptian who got the bishopric illegally outside of the country and coveted to be a patriarch on the St. Mark’s throne. On returning to Alexandria, he took refuge in his mother's house away from the wrath of the angry congregation against him. For fear of a revolt, the governor expelled him out of the country to save his life. But, eventually, by the command of Emperor Valens, Lucius returned to Egypt accompanied by a large regiment led by Maginus, the treasurer of the emperor. The regiment leader charged with his soldiers towards the church, but the believers kept them from reaching to their pope and the pope, under pressure from the congregation and for their safety, had to escape and to hide in a deserted house on the seashore. There, he wrote a Papal message to his people to hold them fast to the Upright Faith. In the meantime, the soldiers abused the sanctity of the church and killed some believers.

records.question: Who was St. Macarius the Great?
records.answer: St. Macarius the Great (~295-392 AD) was the founder of monasticism in the wilderness of the Scetis. He was influenced considerably by St. Anthony the Great, whom he visited twice. He was called ‘The Chosen Vessel’ by the historian Socrates and ‘The Aged Youth’ by Palladius due to his great discernment at the age of thirty. He was granted the gifts of healing the sick and foreseeing the future. He was born in Shubshir in the district of Menouf to pious parents. His father, Ibrahim, was initially childless but was told by a divine messenger that he would have a son whose fame would spread worldwide and who would have spiritual children. Macarius was obedient and graced by God since childhood. He was chosen as a church reader in his village and was married against his will, but after his wife died a virgin, he gave thanks to the Lord, distributed his inheritance to the poor, and was ordained a priest. He later moved to the wilderness of Scetis to live as a monk, where he endured trials including a false accusation and physical abuse. He lived in seclusion but cared deeply for others, showing love and compassion. He built a church for the many monks who gathered around him and was known for miracles, including raising someone from the dead. He died at the age of ninety-seven on the 27th of Baramhat, 392 AD. Among his teachings were admonitions about anger, forgiveness, perseverance, and the spiritual rewards of fasting and good deeds. He was known as a man of love who covered the sins of others and gained many pagans to the faith by his example [1][2][3][4][9][13].
